t: Human Origins: From Apes to Homo sapiens
d: Seven million years of human evolution in Africa, the many human species that once shared the Earth, and how our own species spread across every continent.
x: Humans are great apes. Our lineage split from the ancestors of chimpanzees roughly 6–7 million years ago in Africa. For most of the time since, several human species lived at once . Only in the last ~40,000 years has Homo sapiens been alone. Key dates ~7–6 million years ago: earliest possible hominins ( Sahelanthropus , Chad) 4.4 million years ago: Ardipithecus (Ethiopia), part tree-climber, part walker 3.2 million years ago: “Lucy” ( Australopithecus afarensis ) walks upright 3.3 million years ago: the oldest stone tools (Lomekwi, Kenya) ~1.9 million years ago: Homo erectus , with a human body plan, leaves Africa ~1.5 million years ago: Acheulean hand-axes at Attirampakkam , near Chennai (Pappu et al. 2011) ~300,000 years ago: earliest Homo sapiens fossils at Jebel Irhoud , Morocco (Hublin et al. 2017) ~70,000–50,000 years ago: modern humans spread out of Africa ~65,000 years ago: people reach Australia (Clarkson et al. 2017) A crowded family tree # The human species that shared the planet - ***Homo habilis*** ("handy man"), ~2.4–1.4 million years ago: larger brain, simple Oldowan tools. - ***Homo erectus***, ~1.9 million–110,000 years ago: long legs, controlled fire, crossed into Asia (Java Man, Peking Man). Probably the first to travel out of Africa. - ***Homo heidelbergensis***, ~700,000–300,000 years ago: likely ancestor of Neanderthals, Denisovans and us. - **Neanderthals** (*Homo neanderthalensis*), ~400,000–40,000 years ago: Europe and western Asia; stocky, cold-adapted, buried their dead, made jewellery and possibly cave art. - **Denisovans**: known mainly from DNA and a few fossils from Siberia, Tibet and Taiwan; a Denisovan gene variant (*EPAS1*) helps Tibetans live at high altitude. - ***Homo floresiensis*** ("hobbit"), Flores, Indonesia: about 1 m tall, lived until ~50,000 years ago. - ***Homo naledi***, South Africa: small-brained yet living ~300,000 years ago. What made us human # Walking upright freed the hands and saved energy over long distances. Tools and fire let early humans eat meat and cooked food, fuelling bigger brains (our brain uses about 20% of our energy). Long childhoods and cooperation : grandmothers, sharing food, teaching. Language and symbols : ochre engraved at Blombos Cave, South Africa (~75,000 years ago); shell beads; later cave art. Out of Africa, into India # Genetics shows all living non-Africans descend mainly from a group that left Africa around 70,000–50,000 years ago . They met and interbred with Neanderthals (non-Africans carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA) and Denisovans (up to ~4–6% in Papuans and Aboriginal Australians). Moving along the southern coast of Asia, they reached India, Southeast Asia and Australia. In India, stone tools at Jwalapuram (Andhra Pradesh) lie above and below ash from the Toba super-eruption of ~74,000 years ago, suggesting people survived it (Petraglia et al. 2007). The Andamanese peoples and the hunter-gatherer ancestry found in nearly all South Asians today (“Ancient Ancestral South Indian”) trace back to these early migrants (Narasimhan et al. 2019). Daily life of early humans # Small bands of 20–50 people moved with the seasons, hunting, fishing and gathering hundreds of plant foods. They lived in caves, rock shelters and huts of branches, hides or mammoth bones. Life expectancy at birth was low because many children died, but adults often lived into their fifties and sixties. Studies of modern hunter-gatherers suggest a working week of perhaps 20–40 hours on food, with much time spent on social life, storytelling and ritual. Next: Ice ages and humans · Species of past ages Sources: Smithsonian Human Origins · Hublin et al. 2017, Nature · Narasimhan et al. 2019, Science

t: From the Trees to Two Feet: How Our Ancestors Began to Walk
d: Why apes in Africa's changing forests started walking upright, the fossils that show each step, and what bipedalism made possible.
x: Every human story starts with a strange choice: walking on two legs. No other living primate does it all the time. Fossils show it came first , millions of years before big brains, tools or fire. A changing Africa # Between about 10 and 5 million years ago , Africa became cooler and drier as global climate shifted and the East African Rift uplifted. Continuous forests broke into a mosaic of woodland, gallery forest along rivers and grassland . Apes living at the forest edges had to cross open ground between patches of trees. The fossil steps # From Toumaï to Lucy - **~7 million years ago: *Sahelanthropus*** (Chad). Its skull opening suggests the head sat upright on the spine, a hint of bipedalism. - **~6 million years ago: *Orrorin*** (Kenya). Thigh bones built for carrying weight on two legs. - **4.4 million years ago: *Ardipithecus ramidus*, "Ardi"** (Ethiopia). Walked upright on the ground but still had a grasping big toe for climbing. Ardi lived in **woodland, not savanna**, overturning the old idea that we stood up because we moved onto open plains. - **3.66 million years ago: Laetoli footprints** (Tanzania). Three individuals walking with a human-like stride, preserved in volcanic ash. - **3.2 million years ago: "Lucy", *Australopithecus afarensis*** (Ethiopia). A pelvis and knee like ours, but long arms and curved fingers for climbing. Her species lasted nearly a million years. Why walk upright? Leading ideas # Energy efficiency: walking on two legs uses about a quarter of the energy chimpanzees spend knuckle-walking (Sockol et al. 2007). Carrying: free hands could carry food, infants and later tools. Seeing over grass and reducing heat : standing tall exposes less body to the midday sun and more to cooling breezes. Reaching fruit from the ground, like orangutans walking along branches. Most scientists think several of these worked together. The costs # Bipedalism came with trade-offs we still live with: back pain, knee problems, varicose veins and, above all, difficult childbirth , because a narrower walking pelvis meets a growing baby’s head. Human babies are born helpless partly because of this, which made cooperation and long childhoods essential. What it opened up # Free hands led to stone tools (3.3 million years ago), carrying meat and water , and long-distance walking and endurance running in Homo erectus . It set the stage for every later step: fire, language, migration across the world. Browse: Human species · Next: Fire and cooking Sources: Smithsonian: Walking upright · Wikipedia: Bipedalism · Wikipedia: Ardipithecus

t: The Human Family Tree: All the Human Species
d: The two dozen or so hominin species from Sahelanthropus to us, how they relate, which lived at the same time, and what DNA reveals about Neanderthals and Denisovans.
x: Human evolution is not a ladder but a bushy tree : many species branched off, overlapped and went extinct. For most of the last two million years several kinds of humans lived at the same time . Browse them all in the Human species catalog . The main branches # Group When Key species What changed Earliest hominins 7–4.4 million years ago Sahelanthropus , Orrorin , Ardipithecus Beginnings of upright walking Australopithecines 4.2–2 million years ago A. anamensis , A. afarensis (Lucy), A. africanus , A. sediba Habitual bipedalism, small brains Robust hominins 2.7–1 million years ago Paranthropus aethiopicus , boisei , robustus Huge jaws for tough plant food; a dead-end branch Early Homo 2.4–1.4 million years ago H. habilis , H. rudolfensis Stone tools, larger brains Homo erectus group 1.9 million – 110,000 years ago H. ergaster , H. erectus , Dmanisi people Human body, fire, left Africa Archaic humans 700,000 – 40,000 years ago H. heidelbergensis , Neanderthals, Denisovans, H. naledi , H. floresiensis , H. luzonensis Large brains (Neanderthals), island dwarfs Modern humans 300,000 years ago – today Homo sapiens Symbolic culture, global spread Who met whom # Our extended family - **Neanderthals** lived in Europe and western Asia from ~400,000 to ~40,000 years ago. They made spears and glue, controlled fire, buried their dead and decorated themselves. When *Homo sapiens* spread out of Africa, the two met; most people outside Africa carry about **1–2% Neanderthal DNA**. - **Denisovans** are known mainly from a finger bone and teeth from **Denisova Cave** (Siberia), a jaw from Tibet and, since 2025, the **Harbin skull** ("Dragon Man") identified as Denisovan from proteins and DNA. Papuans and Aboriginal Australians carry up to ~4–6% Denisovan DNA; Tibetans owe their high-altitude gene *EPAS1* to them. - **Homo floresiensis** (1 m tall) lived on Flores until ~50,000 years ago, and **Homo luzonensis** on Luzon. - In India, the **Narmada skull** from Hathnora (Madhya Pradesh) is an archaic human whose species is still debated. Why only one of us is left # Explanations include our larger social networks, more flexible technology and long-distance trade, faster population growth, climate swings that fragmented small archaic populations, and interbreeding that absorbed them. In a sense Neanderthals and Denisovans did not entirely vanish: they live on in our genes. Sources: Smithsonian Human Origins: Species · Green et al. 2010, Science · Wikipedia: Denisovan

t: How Fire Was Tamed and Cooking Changed Us
d: The evidence for early fire use, how people probably learned to control and make fire, and how cooking, warmth and the hearth reshaped human bodies and societies.
x: Nobody “discovered” fire; lightning and volcanoes have always made it. What our ancestors achieved, step by step over a million years, was using, carrying, controlling and finally making it. The steps # From wildfire to the hearth 1. **Opportunistic use (perhaps 2–1.5 million years ago):** early *Homo* may have scavenged animals cooked in bushfires and kept smouldering branches alive. Burned bones at **Swartkrans** (South Africa) and reddened earth at **Koobi Fora** (Kenya) are debated hints. 2. **Fire in a cave (~1 million years ago):** ash and burned bone deep inside **Wonderwerk Cave** (South Africa) show *Homo erectus* bringing fire indoors. 3. **Regular hearths (~400,000–300,000 years ago):** repeated hearths at **Qesem Cave** (Israel) and **Gesher Benot Ya'aqov** (~780,000 years ago) show fire becoming part of daily life. 4. **Making fire on demand:** Neanderthals probably struck flint against pyrite to make sparks (tools with strike marks ~50,000 years ago). Later people used **fire drills, bow drills and fire ploughs**, rubbing wood to make embers. Why fire mattered # Cooking: heat breaks down starch and protein and kills parasites. Primatologist Richard Wrangham argues that cooked food let our guts shrink and our brains grow; Homo erectus already had smaller teeth and a bigger brain than earlier hominins. Warmth: fire let humans survive Ice Age winters and colonise cold lands. Protection: predators avoid fire. Longer days: firelight extended evenings, perhaps giving time for storytelling, teaching and social bonding, the first “campfire culture”. Technology: fire hardened spear tips, made birch-tar glue (~200,000 years ago), heat-treated stone for sharper blades (~70,000 years ago), and much later fired pottery (~20,000 years ago) and smelted metals . Landscape management: people burned grassland to attract game and encourage useful plants, as Aboriginal Australians still do with “fire-stick farming”. Fire in culture and belief # Fire gods and rituals appear everywhere: Agni in the Rigveda, Prometheus in Greek myth, the sacred fires of Zoroastrian temples, Diwali’s lamps, Holika Dahan bonfires and the Olympic flame. Related: Inventions · Human species Sources: Berna et al. 2012, PNAS (Wonderwerk Cave) · Wikipedia: Control of fire by early humans

t: Hunter-Gatherer Life: How People Lived for 95% of History
d: Bands, camps, food, work, tools, art, beliefs and health among hunter-gatherers past and present, from Ice Age Europe to the Kalahari and the Andaman Islands.
x: For about 95% of the time Homo sapiens has existed , everyone lived by hunting, fishing and gathering. Some peoples, such as the San of the Kalahari, the Hadza of Tanzania, the Jarawa and Sentinelese of the Andamans and Arctic Inuit , kept these ways of life into recent times. Daily life # Bands, camps and moving with the seasons - **Group size:** bands of roughly **25–50 people**, linked by marriage and friendship into wider networks of hundreds. - **Mobility:** camps moved every few weeks or seasons, following ripening plants, migrating animals and water. Some rich coasts and river valleys allowed semi-settled villages. - **Homes:** caves and rock shelters (Bhimbetka in India), brush huts, hide tents, and mammoth-bone houses on the Ice Age Ukrainian plain. - **Division of work:** often men hunted large game and women gathered plants and small animals, but practices varied and many women hunted; children foraged too. - **Sharing:** meat was shared widely; stinginess was mocked. Many such societies were strikingly **egalitarian**, levelling bossiness with jokes and gossip. What they ate # Hundreds of plants, nuts, roots, honey, fish, shellfish, insects and game. At Ohalo II (Israel, 23,000 years ago) people collected wild barley and wheat. Diets were varied, but famine and seasonal hunger were real risks. Tools and knowledge # Hand-axes gave way to blades, microliths, spear-throwers (atlatls), bows and arrows (~70,000 years ago in Africa), harpoons, nets, fish-hooks, needles , baskets and boats. Hunter-gatherers held encyclopaedic knowledge of animal behaviour, plant medicines and poisons, star navigation and tracking. Art, music and belief # Cave paintings (Lascaux, Chauvet, Bhimbetka, Sulawesi), carved figurines, bone flutes (~40,000 years ago), body ornaments and burials with grave goods show rich symbolic lives. Many groups practised animism (seeing spirits in animals and places) and shamanic trance dances, as the San still do. Health # Life expectancy at birth was low (~30) because many children died, but adults who survived often reached 60 or 70. Hunter-gatherers had fewer crowd diseases and dental cavities than early farmers. The end of an era # Farming spread because it fed more people per square kilometre, not because it made life easier. Farmers out-reproduced foragers and pushed them into deserts, forests and the Arctic. Today, the remaining hunter-gatherers face land loss, and some, like the Sentinelese, choose isolation. Related: Peoples and tribes · The Agricultural Revolution Sources: Wikipedia: Hunter-gatherer · Wikipedia: Ohalo II

d: When humans began to speak, the families of the world's 7,000 languages, how languages split and change, and how writing grew out of counting.
x: No one knows exactly when language began, because speech leaves no fossils. Clues come from anatomy, genes, archaeology and the languages themselves. Browse language families and languages . When did speech begin? # Anatomy: Neanderthals had a hyoid bone like ours and ear structures tuned to speech frequencies, so they probably could talk to some degree. Genes: the FOXP2 gene, which affects fine control of speech, has the same human-specific version in Neanderthals. Symbols: engraved ochre (Blombos, ~75,000 years ago), beads and later art imply people who could share abstract ideas. Most researchers think fully modern language existed by at least 100,000–50,000 years ago , and possibly much earlier. Families of languages # About 7,000 languages are spoken today in roughly 140 families . The biggest: Family Speakers Homeland Examples Indo-European ~3.3 billion Pontic–Caspian steppe or Anatolia (debated) Hindi, Bengali, English, Spanish, Russian, Persian Sino-Tibetan ~1.4 billion Yellow River basin Mandarin, Tibetan, Burmese, Meitei Niger–Congo ~700 million West Africa Yoruba, Swahili, Zulu Afroasiatic ~500 million Northeast Africa / Levant Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic, Hausa Austronesian ~380 million Taiwan Malay, Tagalog, Malagasy, Māori Dravidian ~250 million South Asia Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam Austroasiatic ~120 million Southeast Asia Vietnamese, Khmer, Santali, Khasi India alone has languages from four major families (Indo-European, Dravidian, Austroasiatic, Sino-Tibetan) plus isolates such as Nihali and the Andamanese languages, and its 2011 census recorded 19,500+ mother tongues . How languages change # Splits, sound shifts and borrowing - **Divergence:** when groups separate, their speech drifts apart. Latin became Italian, Spanish, French and Romanian within about 1,000 years; Sanskrit's sister Prakrits gave rise to Hindi, Bengali and Marathi. - **Regular sound changes:** linguists discovered patterns like **Grimm's law** (Latin *pater*, English *father*). In 1786 **Sir William Jones** noticed that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin share roots (Sanskrit *pitṛ*, Greek *patēr*, Latin *pater*), founding comparative linguistics. - **Borrowing:** English took ~29% of its words from French and ~29% from Latin; Hindi–Urdu absorbed Persian and Arabic; Tamil and Sanskrit exchanged many words. - **Contact languages:** traders created pidgins and creoles; Swahili grew from Bantu and Arabic. - **Language death:** about **40% of languages are endangered**; the Great Andamanese languages now have only a few speakers. From counting to writing # Writing was invented independently at least three or four times: Mesopotamian cuneiform (~3200 BCE) grew from clay tokens used to count grain and sheep; Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared around the same time; Chinese oracle-bone script ~1250 BCE; and the Maya script in Mesoamerica. The Indus script (~2600 BCE) remains undeciphered. The alphabet was invented once, by Semitic-speaking workers in Sinai around 1800 BCE, and spread through the Phoenicians to Greek, Latin, Aramaic, Arabic, Hebrew and, probably, India’s Brahmi , the ancestor of almost every script from Devanagari to Thai. Related: Scripts · Ancient DNA papers Sources: Ethnologue · Wikipedia: Origin of language · Wikipedia: Indo-European languages

d: Why ice ages happen, what the world looked like at the Last Glacial Maximum, the giant animals people hunted, and how the end of the Ice Age made civilisation possible.
x: For the last 2.6 million years (the Quaternary period) Earth has swung between long cold glacials and shorter warm interglacials . We live in an interglacial, the Holocene , which began 11,700 years ago . All of human evolution happened in this restless climate. Why ice ages happen # Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković showed that slow changes in Earth’s orbit change how much summer sunlight reaches the far north: - Eccentricity (how oval the orbit is), ~100,000-year cycle; - Obliquity (tilt, 22.1°–24.5°), ~41,000-year cycle; - Precession (wobble), ~19,000–23,000-year cycle. When northern summers are cool, snow survives, ice sheets grow and reflect more sunlight, and CO₂ falls (from ~280 ppm in warm periods to ~180 ppm in glacial ones), deepening the cold. Ice cores from Antarctica record these cycles for 800,000 years. The world at the Last Glacial Maximum (~26,000–19,000 years ago) # A different planet Ice sheets up to 3–4 km thick covered Canada, the northern USA, Scandinavia and Britain Sea level was about 120 m lower : Britain joined Europe (Doggerland), Siberia joined Alaska (Beringia), Sri Lanka joined India, and Australia joined New Guinea (Sahul) Global average temperature was about 6 °C colder than pre-industrial Much of the tropics, including India, was drier ; the Thar expanded and the monsoon weakened The Himalayan glaciers extended far lower down the valleys The mammoth steppe and its giants # A vast cold grassland, the mammoth steppe , stretched from Spain to Canada. It supported woolly mammoths, woolly rhinos, cave lions, cave bears, giant deer (Irish elk), steppe bison and wild horses . In the Americas lived giant ground sloths, glyptodonts, sabre-toothed Smilodon and dire wolves; in Australia, Diprotodon and the giant lizard Megalania . In India’s Narmada valley, the giant elephant Palaeoloxodon namadicus roamed. Browse them in Species of past ages . Most of these megafauna went extinct between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago. The timing tracks the arrival of modern humans on each continent, combined with rapid climate shifts. The last woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago. How Ice Age people lived # People adapted brilliantly: sewn clothing using bone needles, mammoth-bone houses in Ukraine, spear-throwers and later bows, and dogs domesticated from wolves (by at least ~15,000 years ago). They painted the animals they hunted in caves such as Lascaux and Chauvet (France), Altamira (Spain) and in rock shelters such as Bhimbetka (India). The thaw # From about 19,000 years ago the ice melted, with a sudden cold relapse, the Younger Dryas (12,900–11,700 years ago). Seas rose by over 100 m, drowning coasts where many early sites now lie underwater. When the Holocene began, the climate became unusually warm and stable , and within a few thousand years people in several regions independently began to farm. See The Agricultural Revolution . Smaller ice ages in history # Late Antique Little Ice Age (536–660 CE): volcanic eruptions brought a decade of cold summers alongside Justinian’s plague (Büntgen et al. 2016). Little Ice Age (~1300–1850): frost fairs on the frozen Thames, Alpine glaciers advancing, famines in Europe. Sources: NOAA: Glacial–interglacial cycles · Wikipedia: Last Glacial Maximum · Büntgen et al. 2016

d: How farming began in at least eleven places, how it created villages, cities, inequality and disease, and how it reached India.
x: Around 11,500 years ago , soon after the Ice Age ended, people in the Fertile Crescent began cultivating wheat, barley and lentils and herding goats and sheep. Within a few thousand years farming had begun independently in China (rice, millet), New Guinea (taro, banana), Mesoamerica (maize, beans, squash), the Andes (potato, quinoa), Africa (sorghum, yams) and elsewhere. Before farming: Göbekli Tepe # At Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey, hunter-gatherers raised T-shaped stone pillars, carved with foxes, boars, vultures and scorpions, around 9500 BCE , centuries before pottery or farming in the area. Some archaeologists argue that the need to feed people at gatherings like these encouraged the cultivation of wild grain. Why people started farming # There is no single answer. Likely causes include a warmer, stable climate , population growth , the collapse of big-game hunting after megafauna extinctions, feasting and social competition , and plants gradually evolving under human harvesting. How it changed life # Gains and losses **Gains:** reliable food surplus, permanent houses, pottery, weaving, larger populations, specialist crafts, and eventually cities, writing and states. **Losses:** longer working hours; less varied diets; early farmers were often **shorter** and had more tooth decay and anaemia than hunter-gatherers. Living close to animals and in crowds brought **new diseases** (measles from cattle plague, influenza from birds, smallpox). Stored wealth made **inequality** and **war** worse. Village life in the Neolithic # At Çatalhöyük (Turkey, ~7100–5700 BCE) several thousand people lived in mud-brick houses packed together without streets, entering through holes in the roofs. They buried their dead beneath the floors and decorated walls with bulls’ horns and paintings. At Mehrgarh (Balochistan, ~7000 BCE), South Asia’s earliest known farmers grew barley and wheat, herded humped zebu cattle (domesticated locally), made beads of lapis lazuli and shell, and even drilled teeth, the earliest evidence of dentistry. India’s Neolithic # Farming villages spread across South Asia: Burzahom in Kashmir (pit houses, ~3000 BCE), the ashmounds of the southern Neolithic in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh (cattle pens burned in festivals), Chirand in Bihar, and early rice cultivation in the Ganga valley ( Lahuradewa ). Millets, pulses such as moong and urad, and later rice became staples, setting the stage for the Indus civilisation . Sources: Wikipedia: Neolithic Revolution · Diamond 2002, Nature · Wikipedia: Göbekli Tepe

d: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus, China, Mesoamerica and the Andes: six places where cities, states and writing arose independently, and what life was like in each.
x: A civilisation , in historians’ terms, usually means a society with cities, specialised jobs, social classes, monumental buildings, long-distance trade and (usually) writing . These arose independently in at least six “cradles”, most of them on great rivers whose floods renewed the soil. Cradle Earliest cities River Writing Mesopotamia (Sumer) ~3500 BCE (Uruk) Tigris, Euphrates Cuneiform, ~3200 BCE Egypt ~3100 BCE Nile Hieroglyphs, ~3200 BCE Indus (Harappan) ~2600 BCE (mature phase) Indus, Ghaggar-Hakra Indus script (undeciphered) China ~1600 BCE (Shang) Yellow River Oracle-bone script, ~1250 BCE Norte Chico (Peru) ~3000 BCE (Caral) Supe valley None (later quipu) Mesoamerica ~1200 BCE (Olmec) Gulf lowlands Maya script, ~300 BCE Mesopotamia: land between the rivers # Sumerian city-states such as Uruk (perhaps 40,000+ people by 3000 BCE) and Ur were ruled by priest-kings from temples on top of stepped ziggurats . Scribes invented cuneiform to record grain and beer rations. People ate barley bread and drank beer through straws, worshipped city gods, and told the Epic of Gilgamesh , with its flood story. Hammurabi’s code (~1754 BCE) set out 282 laws (“an eye for an eye”, but punishments depended on class). Egypt: gift of the Nile # Egypt was unified around 3100 BCE . Its year had three seasons set by the river: Akhet (flood), Peret (growing) and Shemu (harvest). Farmers paid taxes in grain and worked on royal projects such as the Great Pyramid (~2560 BCE), built by paid, organised labour crews, not enslaved people as once thought. Egyptians ate bread, onions, lentils, fish and beer; the rich ate beef, wine and honey. Belief in the afterlife led to mummification and the Book of the Dead . The Indus: cities without kings? # See the full article: The Indus Valley Civilisation . China: the Shang and the Mandate of Heaven # The Shang kings at Anyang asked their ancestors questions by heating oracle bones and reading the cracks, inscribing them with the earliest Chinese characters. The Zhou (from 1046 BCE) claimed the Mandate of Heaven : rulers who governed badly lost the right to rule. Millet was the staple in the north and rice in the south. The Americas # Caral in Peru built pyramids around the same time as Egypt’s, trading cotton and anchovies. In Mesoamerica the Olmec carved colossal stone heads; their successors, the Maya , invented a complete writing system, a calendar and a zero. Browse: all civilisations · archaeological sites Sources: Wikipedia: Cradle of civilization · Metropolitan Museum: Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

d: South Asia's first cities: planned streets, world-class drains, standard weights, an undeciphered script, trade with Mesopotamia, and a slow decline as the monsoon weakened.
x: The Indus Valley or Harappan Civilisation was the largest of the Bronze Age civilisations by area, spanning about 1 million km² of today’s Pakistan and northwest India. Its mature urban phase lasted from about 2600 to 1900 BCE . At a glance Discovered: 1920–21 , at Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni) and Mohenjo-daro (R. D. Banerji) Major cities: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Ganweriwala (Pakistan); Rakhigarhi, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Banawali (India) More than 1,000 sites known, over half in India, many along the dried-up Ghaggar–Hakra river Population: perhaps 1–5 million Script: about 400 signs on 4,000+ objects, mostly short seal inscriptions; still undeciphered Cities built to a plan # Streets ran in a rough grid . Houses of standard-ratio baked bricks (1:2:4) had private wells, bathing platforms and toilets that drained into covered street drains with inspection holes, sanitation not matched in many cities until the 19th century. Mohenjo-daro’s Great Bath may have been used for ritual bathing. Dholavira in Kutch had huge stone-cut reservoirs to store monsoon water, and a ten-sign “signboard”. Lothal in Gujarat has a large basin often interpreted as a dockyard. Daily life and food # Most people were farmers and herders . They grew wheat, barley, peas, lentils, chickpeas, sesame, mustard and cotton (among the earliest cotton anywhere), and, in Gujarat and the east, millets and some rice . They kept humped zebu cattle , buffalo, sheep and goats, and ate fish. Residue in pots from Haryana sites shows cooking of meat and dairy. Craftspeople made carnelian beads (some drilled with remarkable stone drills), shell bangles, bronze tools, terracotta toys on wheels and the famous “Dancing Girl” bronze. Trade reached Mesopotamia , where “Meluhha” (probably the Indus) supplied carnelian, timber and ivory. There is little sign of grand palaces, royal tombs or big armies, which has led some scholars to suggest an unusually egalitarian or merchant-led society, though this is debated. Who were the Harappans? # The genome of a woman from Rakhigarhi (Shinde et al. 2019) showed a mix of ancient South Asian hunter-gatherer ancestry and an Iranian-related ancestry that separated before farming, with no steppe ancestry . Most South Asians today descend partly from Indus-related people (Narasimhan et al. 2019). Decline # From about 1900 BCE the big cities emptied and people moved east and south into smaller villages. Explanations include: - a weakening monsoon around the 4.2-kiloyear event , shown in lake and cave records (Giosan et al. 2012; Sarkar et al. 2016); - rivers such as the Ghaggar–Hakra drying up or shifting ; - declining trade with Mesopotamia. Farmers adapted by switching to drought-tolerant millets and summer crops . It was not a sudden collapse but a transformation, and many Harappan traditions (weights, bangles, possibly some deities and yoga-like postures on seals) may have continued into later Indian culture. Browse: Indus sites · Indus script Sources: Giosan et al. 2012, PNAS · Shinde et al. 2019, Cell · Wikipedia: Indus Valley Civilisation

d: Around 1200 BCE the interconnected world of the eastern Mediterranean fell apart within decades. What happened, the suspects, and what grew from the ruins.
x: Around 1200–1150 BCE a whole system of kingdoms around the eastern Mediterranean collapsed. The Mycenaean palaces of Greece burned, the Hittite Empire vanished, the trading city of Ugarit was destroyed, and Egypt survived only after desperate battles. Writing disappeared from Greece for about 400 years (a “Dark Age”). The world before the fall # The Late Bronze Age was the first truly globalised era: Egypt, the Hittites, Babylon, Assyria and Mycenae exchanged letters (the Amarna letters ), royal gifts and princesses. Ships like the Uluburun wreck (~1300 BCE) carried copper from Cyprus, tin from Central Asia, glass, ivory and ebony. Bronze needed both copper and tin, so every kingdom depended on trade. The suspects # A "perfect storm" - **Drought:** pollen and lake records show a 150-year dry spell; letters from Ugarit beg for grain. - **Earthquakes:** a possible "earthquake storm" in the Aegean and Levant. - **The Sea Peoples:** raiders and migrants recorded by Ramesses III at Medinet Habu (~1177 BCE). - **Systems collapse:** when trade broke down, palace economies that depended on it failed one after another. - **Internal revolt** and new warfare (infantry with long swords against chariots). Historian Eric Cline argues that no single cause was enough, but together they toppled an interdependent system, a lesson often applied to our own globalised world. What came after # From the ruins came the Iron Age (iron ore is common, so metal no longer depended on long tin routes), the Phoenician alphabet , the kingdoms of Israel and Judah , the Neo-Assyrian Empire, and eventually Classical Greece. Sources: Wikipedia: Late Bronze Age collapse · Weiss & Bradley 2001, Science

t: The Axial Age: When Philosophy Was Born
d: Between about 800 and 200 BCE, thinkers in India, China, Persia, Israel and Greece asked new questions about ethics, the self and the universe. Their answers still shape billions of lives.
x: German philosopher Karl Jaspers named the period 800–200 BCE the Achsenzeit , or Axial Age , because so many of humanity’s lasting religious and philosophical traditions took shape in it, in separate places, at about the same time. Region Thinkers and traditions India The Upanishads (atman, brahman, karma, moksha); Gautama Buddha ; Mahavira and Jainism; materialist Charvaka ; grammarian Panini China Confucius (ethics and good government), Laozi (Taoism), Mozi (universal love), Mencius , legalists Persia Zoroaster ’s teachings on good and evil (dates debated) Israel The Hebrew prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah Greece Thales, Pythagoras, Heraclitus, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle Why then? # Suggested reasons include: iron tools and bigger harvests that fed cities and states; coinage and trade that created a wealthy, mobile, literate class; wars between states that made people question tradition; and new urban anxieties about suffering and meaning. In India, the second urbanisation of the Ganga plain, with its 16 mahajanapadas , provided the setting for the Buddha and Mahavira, who taught in Magadha and Kosala. Common threads # Many Axial teachers turned away from sacrifice and ritual toward inner transformation, ethics and compassion : ahimsa (non-violence) in Jainism and Buddhism, the Golden Rule in Confucius, the examined life for Socrates. Some historians (such as Ian Morris) link this to rising prosperity; others doubt whether the “age” was really unified. Browse: Religions and philosophies · People Sources: Wikipedia: Axial Age · Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius

d: How a small Italian city conquered the Mediterranean, Gaul and Britain; how ordinary Romans lived and ate; and why the Western Empire fell in 476 CE.
x: According to legend Rome was founded in 753 BCE by Romulus. It became a republic in 509 BCE, ruled by elected consuls and the Senate , and over five centuries conquered Italy and then the whole Mediterranean. Conquests # From city to empire - **Italy** (to 264 BCE), through alliances and colonies linked by roads like the **Via Appia**. - **Punic Wars** (264–146 BCE) against **Carthage**, including Hannibal's crossing of the Alps with elephants (218 BCE) and his crushing victory at **Cannae**. Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE. - **Greece and the East**: Macedonia, Greece (146 BCE), Asia Minor, Syria, Judea. - **Gaul**: **Julius Caesar** conquered it in 58–50 BCE, defeating **Vercingetorix** at Alesia; perhaps a million Gauls died and a million were enslaved, by ancient estimates. - **Egypt** (30 BCE) after Cleopatra's death. - **Britain** (from 43 CE under Claudius); **Boudica's** revolt (60–61 CE) burned London before being crushed; **Hadrian's Wall** (122 CE) marked the northern frontier. - **Dacia** (Romania) under Trajan; the empire peaked in **117 CE**, with perhaps 60–70 million people. After civil wars, Caesar’s heir Octavian became Augustus , the first emperor (27 BCE), beginning two centuries of relative peace, the Pax Romana . Life in Rome # Homes: the rich lived in domus houses with courtyards; most city dwellers rented cramped flats in multi-storey insulae that often burned or collapsed. Food: the poor ate wheat porridge ( puls ), bread, beans, vegetables and cheap wine; Rome gave free grain (later bread) to about 200,000 citizens. The rich held banquets with dormice, oysters and peacock, flavoured with garum (fermented fish sauce) and pepper imported from India’s Malabar coast . Work and slavery: perhaps 10–20% of the population of Italy was enslaved. Entertainment: chariot racing at the Circus Maximus (seating ~150,000), gladiators at the Colosseum , public baths . Pompeii and Herculaneum , buried by Vesuvius in 79 CE , preserve shops, bakeries, graffiti and food remains. Rome and India # Roman ships sailed with the monsoon winds from Egypt to Muziris (Kerala) and Arikamedu (Puducherry), trading gold coins, wine and glass for pepper, pearls, cotton, gems and ivory . Hoards of Roman coins are found across South India, and the writer Pliny complained that India drained Rome of 50 million sesterces a year. Why the West fell # The Western Empire ended in 476 CE when the Germanic general Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus. Causes, debated for centuries since Edward Gibbon, include civil wars and coups, economic and currency crises, the Antonine and Cyprian plagues , climate cooling, pressure from Huns and Germanic peoples, and the split into East and West. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 . Sources: Wikipedia: Roman Empire · Wikipedia: Indo-Roman trade relations · British Museum: Roman Empire

d: From meteorite iron to the blast furnace and wootz steel: why the Iron Age transformed farming, war, states and religion across Eurasia and Africa.
x: Copper and bronze were the first metals, but tin , needed for bronze, was rare and traded over thousands of kilometres. Iron ore is everywhere. Once people learned to smelt it, metal became cheap, and that changed who could farm, fight and rule. Learning to smelt iron # From sky metal to steel - **Meteorite iron** was hammered into beads in Egypt by ~3200 BCE (Tutankhamun's dagger, ~1350 BCE, is meteoritic). - **Smelting** needs about 1,200 °C and a reducing charcoal fire in a **bloomery** furnace, producing a spongy "bloom" hammered to drive out slag. The **Hittites** of Anatolia worked iron by the 2nd millennium BCE. - After the **Bronze Age collapse** (~1200 BCE) broke tin trade routes, iron spread rapidly across the Near East, Greece and Europe. - **India** developed iron independently or very early: iron objects in the Ganga valley and at sites like Malhar date to ~1800–1500 BCE. - **Africa** smelted iron by ~800–500 BCE (Nok culture, Meroë in Kush), and Bantu-speaking farmers carried it across the continent. - **China** invented **cast iron** with blast furnaces by the 5th century BCE, a thousand years ahead of Europe. - **South India and Sri Lanka** made **wootz crucible steel** from ~300 BCE, prized as Damascus steel. Delhi's **Iron Pillar** (~400 CE) has not rusted in 1,600 years. What iron changed # Farming: iron axes cleared dense forests and iron ploughshares broke heavy soils. In India, iron tools helped clear the middle Ganga plain , producing the surplus that fed the mahajanapadas and the “second urbanisation” of the 6th century BCE. War: cheap iron swords, spearheads and armour let kings equip large infantry armies of ordinary men, not just chariot elites. The Assyrians built the first great iron-armed empire. States and empires: larger surpluses and armies supported bigger states: Assyria, Persia, the Mauryas, Qin China, Rome. Ideas: the new wealth, cities and wars of the Iron Age coincided with the Axial Age philosophies of the Buddha, Mahavira, Confucius and the Greek thinkers. See The Axial Age . Africa: iron hoes powered the Bantu expansion, spreading farming and Bantu languages across central and southern Africa. From the Iron Age to the industrial age # Iron remained central: Chinese blast furnaces, Indian wootz, European water-powered bellows, then Abraham Darby’s coke smelting (1709) , Bessemer steel (1856) and the Tata steel plant at Jamshedpur (1907) . Today the world makes about 1.9 billion tonnes of steel a year. Sources: Wikipedia: Iron Age · Wikipedia: Iron Age in India · Wikipedia: Wootz steel

t: How Kings, Empires and Monarchies Rose and Fell
d: How chiefs became kings, why monarchy spread, the common patterns in the rise and fall of empires from Akkad to the British Empire, and how monarchy lost power.
x: From bands to states # Anthropologists describe a rough sequence (not a fixed ladder): bands of hunter-gatherers; tribes of farming villages; chiefdoms with hereditary leaders who redistributed food; and states with kings, taxes, armies, scribes and laws. Farming surpluses, the need to manage irrigation, war between neighbours and long-distance trade all pushed some chiefdoms into kingdoms. How monarchy came into play # Sources of royal power - **Divine kingship:** Egyptian pharaohs were gods; Chinese emperors held the **Mandate of Heaven**; Indian kings were consecrated in the Vedic *rajasuya* and later linked to Vishnu or Shiva; Khmer kings were *devaraja* (god-kings). - **Military power:** conquerors such as Sargon, Chandragupta, Genghis Khan and Babur founded dynasties by the sword. - **Law and order:** Hammurabi presented himself as giver of justice; Ashoka ruled by *dhamma*. - **Heredity and marriage:** dynasties held power through succession and alliances (the Habsburgs famously "married" their empire). - **Election or consent:** some kings were chosen, like Gopala of the Palas, or limited by assemblies such as the Vedic *sabha* and *samiti*, Viking *things* or the English Parliament. Patterns in the rise of empires # Empires usually rose with a military or technological edge (chariots, iron, cavalry, gunpowder, steamships), a strong founder and capable administrators (Chanakya, Li Si), control of trade routes (Silk Road, Indian Ocean, Atlantic) and a unifying ideology or religion . Patterns in their fall # The Arab historian Ibn Khaldun (1377) argued that dynasties lose their founding solidarity ( asabiyyah ) within about four generations. Common causes: 1. Succession crises (the Mughal wars of succession, Rome’s third-century crisis). 2. Overstretch and fiscal crisis (Spain’s debts, Rome’s debased coins). 3. Climate and disease : the 4.2-kiloyear drought (Akkad), the Late Antique Little Ice Age and plague (Byzantium), drought (Maya, Angkor), smallpox (Aztec, Inca). 4. Invaders and rivals (Huns, Mongols, Europeans). 5. Internal revolt (Yellow Turbans, Taiping, 1857). 6. New technology elsewhere (gunpowder ending nomad dominance; industrial Britain overtaking Mughal and Qing economies). Deadliest conflicts (estimated deaths, millions) World War II World War II 75 m Mongol conquests Mongol conquests 35 m Taiping Rebellion Taiping Rebellion 25 m World War I World War I 20 m Thirty Years' War Thirty Years' War 8 m Partition violence (1947) Partition violence (1947) 1 m Source: Mid-range estimates; Partition estimates range 0.2–2 million How monarchy lost power # From the Magna Carta (1215) and the English Civil War (1642–51) , through the American (1776) and French (1789) revolutions, to the collapse of the Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Qing monarchies around 1911–1922 , kings lost power to parliaments and republics. In India, the ~560 princely states merged into the Republic, and their privy purses were abolished in 1971 . Today about 43 countries still have a monarch, mostly as constitutional figureheads; Japan’s imperial line is the oldest continuous one. Browse: Dynasties · Civilisations Sources: Wikipedia: Ibn Khaldun · Wikipedia: Monarchy · Wikipedia: Societal collapse

t: India Through the Ages: A History from Bhimbetka to Today
d: A single scroll through Indian history: Stone Age India, the Indus cities, the Vedic age, the Mauryas, Guptas, Cholas, the Sultanate, Vijayanagara, Mughals and Marathas, colonial rule and the Republic.
x: India has one of the longest continuous records of human life on Earth. This overview links to the detailed catalog entries for every empire , person , event and site . ~1.5 Myr ago : Acheulean hand-axes at Attirampakkam, Tamil Nadu. ~74,000 yr ago : Toba ash falls across India; people at Jwalapuram survive. ~10,000+ yr ago : Rock paintings at Bhimbetka. ~7000 BCE : Mehrgarh, early farming. 2600–1900 BCE : Mature Indus civilisation. ~1500–500 BCE : Vedic period; the Rigveda, then the Upanishads. ~600 BCE : Sixteen mahajanapadas; second urbanisation. ~5th c. BCE : The Buddha and Mahavira teach in Magadha. 326 BCE : Alexander reaches the Beas. 322 BCE : Chandragupta founds the Maurya Empire. 261 BCE : Kalinga War; Ashoka turns to dhamma. ~300 BCE–300 CE : Sangam age in the Tamil south; Keeladi flourishes. 320–550 : Gupta golden age: Aryabhata, Kalidasa, Nalanda. 606–647 : Harsha; Xuanzang visits. 712 : Arabs conquer Sindh. 848–1279 : Chola Empire; Brihadeeswara temple (1010). 1192 : Second Battle of Tarain. 1206–1526 : Delhi Sultanate. 1336–1646 : Vijayanagara Empire. 1498 : Vasco da Gama lands at Calicut. 1526 : First Battle of Panipat; Mughal Empire founded. 1556–1605 : Akbar. 1600 : English East India Company chartered. 1674 : Shivaji crowned; Maratha state. 1757 : Battle of Plassey. 1770 : Great Bengal Famine. 1799 : Tipu Sultan killed; Ranjit Singh takes Lahore. 1857 : Indian Rebellion. 1858 : British Crown rule (the Raj). 1885 : Indian National Congress founded. 1919 : Jallianwala Bagh massacre. 1930 : Salt March. 1942 : Quit India. 1947 : Independence and Partition. 1950 : Constitution; India becomes a republic. 1991 : Economic liberalisation. 2023 : Chandrayaan-3 lands near the lunar south pole. How people lived in each age # Stone Age and Indus Hunter-gatherers lived in rock shelters such as Bhimbetka, eating game, fish, honey and wild plants. Indus city dwellers lived in brick houses with bathrooms; they ate wheat and barley flatbreads, pulses, dairy and meat, and wore cotton. Vedic and Mahajanapada age Cattle were the main measure of wealth; people ate barley cakes, milk, ghee, curd and, in early times, meat, while rice spread in the east. Villages (*grama*) grouped into clans and then kingdoms. Iron ploughs cleared the Ganga forests. Mauryan and Gupta India Megasthenes, a Greek ambassador, described Pataliputra's 9-mile wooden walls, guilds, markets and seven social groups. Most people farmed rice, wheat, barley, millets and pulses, with sugarcane and cotton as cash crops. Gupta-era towns were prosperous; Chinese pilgrim Faxian reported rest houses and free hospitals. Early medieval and the south Temple towns (Thanjavur, Kanchipuram, Madurai) became centres of land, crafts, music and dance. Chola inscriptions at **Uttaramerur** describe village assemblies elected by lottery (*kudavolai*). The south ate rice, millets, coconut, pepper and tamarind; the north wheat, barley and pulses. Sultanate and Mughal India Persian, Turkic and Indian cultures blended in music (khayal, qawwali), language (Urdu), architecture and cuisine (biryani, kebabs, naan, Mughlai gravies). Crops from the Americas, including **chilli, potato, tomato, maize, tobacco, cashew and pineapple**, arrived through the Portuguese and transformed Indian cooking. Around 1700, India produced roughly a quarter of world output (Maddison), and Bengal's muslin and Gujarat's cottons clothed the world. Colonial India Railways and telegraphs were built mainly to move raw materials and troops. Handloom weaving collapsed under British mill cloth; **famines** killed tens of millions; per-capita income stagnated. Social reformers (Ram Mohan Roy, Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule, Vidyasagar, Ambedkar) challenged sati, caste and illiteracy. See [The East India Company and the Raj](/wiki/india/east-india-company-and-the-raj.html). India's share of world GDP (%, Maddison estimates) 0 10 20 30 40 1 1000 1500 1600 1700 1820 1870 1913 1950 1973 2000 2024 1: 32 1000: 28 1500: 24 1600: 22 1700: 24 1820: 16 1870: 12 1913: 7.5 1950: 4.2 1973: 3.1 2000: 4.2 2024: 8 Source: Angus Maddison, The World Economy (2003); recent years PPP estimates, rounded Sources: NCERT: Themes in Indian History · Wikipedia: History of India · Maddison Project Database

t: The East India Company and the British Raj
d: How a London trading company became the ruler of India, how it governed and taxed, the famines and the 1857 uprising, and what Crown rule meant from 1858 to 1947.
x: On 31 December 1600 , Queen Elizabeth I granted a royal charter to “the Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading into the East Indies”. Within 160 years this private company had its own army and was collecting the taxes of Bengal, one of the richest regions on Earth. From traders to rulers # Key steps - **1608–1615:** the Company trades at **Surat**; Sir Thomas Roe wins trading rights from Mughal emperor Jahangir. - **1639–1690:** forts and factories at **Madras** (Fort St George), **Bombay** (from Portugal, 1668) and **Calcutta** (1690). - **1746–1763:** **Carnatic Wars** against the French in the south. - **1757:** **Battle of Plassey**. Robert Clive defeats Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah, mainly thanks to Mir Jafar's betrayal. - **1764–65:** after **Buxar**, the Treaty of Allahabad gives the Company the ***diwani***, the right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. - **1767–1799:** **Anglo-Mysore Wars**; **Tipu Sultan** dies at Srirangapatna (1799). - **1775–1818:** **Anglo-Maratha Wars** end Maratha power. - **1845–1849:** **Anglo-Sikh Wars**; Punjab annexed and the Koh-i-Noor taken. - **1848–1856:** Lord Dalhousie's **Doctrine of Lapse** annexes Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur; Awadh is annexed in 1856. By 1803 the Company’s armies numbered about 260,000 , around twice the size of the British Army. Revenue, trade and famine # The Company used Bengal’s revenues to buy Indian goods for export, so Britain gained Indian textiles without paying for them, part of what Dadabhai Naoroji later called the “drain of wealth” . The Permanent Settlement (1793) fixed land tax through zamindars; the ryotwari system in Madras and Bombay taxed farmers directly. In the Bengal famine of 1770 , about a third of Bengal’s people died, while revenue collection continued. Indian textile exports collapsed as British machine-made cloth flooded India after 1813. The Company also grew opium in Bihar and Malwa and forced it on China, leading to the Opium Wars . 1857: the great uprising # In May 1857 sepoys at Meerut mutinied, angered by cartridges said to be greased with cow and pig fat, by annexations and by deep economic grievances. They marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor. Leaders included Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Nana Sahib , Tantia Tope , Begum Hazrat Mahal of Lucknow and Kunwar Singh . The British crushed the rising with great brutality. In 1858 the Company was abolished and India passed to the Crown . The Raj (1858–1947) # Government: a Viceroy ruled British India directly, while ~560 princely states were ruled indirectly. Infrastructure: about 67,000 km of railway by 1947, canals in Punjab, telegraphs, ports; designed mainly for exports and military control. Famines: the famines of 1876–78 , 1896–97 and 1899–1900 killed perhaps 12–29 million people in total as grain kept moving to markets and Britain. The 1943 Bengal famine killed about 2–3 million. Economy: India’s share of world GDP fell from roughly 16% in 1820 to about 4% by 1950 (Maddison); life expectancy in the 1920s was around 25 years. Society: the census fixed caste categories; English education created a new middle class that would lead the national movement. Major famines in British India (deaths, millions, mid estimates) 10 m Bengal 1770 11 m Chalisa 1783 8 m 1876–78 5 m 1896–97 4 m 1899–1900 2.5 m Bengal 1943 Source: Mid-range historical estimates (Wikipedia, Davis 2001) Debate # Some historians emphasise lasting legacies such as railways, a unified administration, English and parliamentary institutions; others stress extraction, deindustrialisation and famine. Most agree the Indian economy barely grew per head during two centuries of British rule. Continue: The freedom struggle and Partition Sources: Wikipedia: East India Company · Wikipedia: Indian Rebellion of 1857 · Wikipedia: Famines in India

t: The Freedom Struggle, Independence and Partition
d: From the Congress of 1885 to Gandhi's mass movements, revolutionaries, Bose's INA, the end of the Raj, and the human cost of Partition.
x: Early nationalism (1885–1915) # The Indian National Congress met first in Bombay in 1885. Its “moderates” (Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale) petitioned for reforms and documented the drain of wealth . The “extremists” , Bal Gangadhar Tilak (“Swaraj is my birthright”), Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal, demanded self-rule. The 1905 Partition of Bengal sparked the Swadeshi movement , a boycott of British goods. The Muslim League was founded in 1906. The Gandhian era (1915–1947) # Mass movements - **Champaran (1917)** for indigo farmers and **Kheda (1918)**: Gandhi's first Indian satyagrahas. - **Jallianwala Bagh (13 April 1919):** troops under General Dyer fired on a peaceful crowd in Amritsar, killing hundreds. - **Non-Cooperation (1920–22):** boycotts of courts, schools and cloth; called off after violence at Chauri Chaura. - **Salt March (1930):** Gandhi walked 390 km to **Dandi** to make salt, launching **civil disobedience**; tens of thousands were jailed. - **Quit India (August 1942):** "Do or die"; leaders were arrested and the movement went underground. Other currents ran alongside: revolutionaries such as Bhagat Singh , Chandrashekhar Azad and Ram Prasad Bismil ; Subhas Chandra Bose’s Indian National Army , whose 1945–46 trials stirred the country and helped trigger the 1946 naval mutiny ; tribal rebellions ( Birsa Munda’s Ulgulan , the Santhal Hul ); peasant and labour movements; and B. R. Ambedkar’s struggle against caste. Independence and Partition # Exhausted by the Second World War, Britain agreed to leave. On 15 August 1947 , India became independent and Pakistan was created from the Muslim-majority regions of the northwest and Bengal. The border, drawn in five weeks by Cyril Radcliffe , who had never visited India, was published two days after independence. About 15 million people crossed the new borders, and between 200,000 and 2 million were killed in riots and massacres, with mass abductions and assaults on women. Punjab and Bengal were split. The princely states were integrated by Sardar Patel and V. P. Menon ; the disputes over Kashmir and Hyderabad led to conflict. On 26 January 1950 India adopted its Constitution , drafted under Ambedkar , guaranteeing universal adult franchise from the first general election (1951–52). Sources: Wikipedia: Indian independence movement · Wikipedia: Partition of India · 1947 Partition Archive

d: From the cradle of humankind to Egypt, Kush, Aksum, the empires of Ghana, Mali and Songhai, Great Zimbabwe, the slave trade, colonialism and independence.
x: Africa is where humanity began and where every other human story branches from. Its history is often told only through outsiders; this page follows Africans themselves. See all African events and civilisations . ~7–2 Myr ago : Hominins evolve in East and South Africa; first stone tools (3.3 Myr). ~300,000 yr ago : Homo sapiens at Jebel Irhoud. ~75,000 yr ago : Symbolic art at Blombos Cave. ~11,000–5,000 yr ago : Green Sahara with lakes, herders and rock art. ~3100 BCE : Egypt unified. ~1070 BCE : Kingdom of Kush; 25th dynasty rules Egypt (~744–656 BCE). ~1000 BCE onward : Bantu expansion spreads farming and iron. ~500 BCE : Nok culture terracottas and iron in Nigeria. ~100–940 CE : Aksum; Ethiopia adopts Christianity (~330s). 7th c. : Islam spreads across North Africa. ~300–1200 : Ghana Empire. 1235–1670 : Mali Empire; Mansa Musa's pilgrimage (1324). ~1100–1450 : Great Zimbabwe. ~1430–1591 : Songhai Empire. 1526–1867 : Atlantic slave trade (~12.5 million people). 1884–85 : Berlin Conference partitions Africa. 1896 : Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa. 1957–1975 : Wave of independence. 1994 : End of apartheid; Rwandan genocide. Life across the ages # Herders, farmers, kingdoms and cities - **Pastoralists** in the green Sahara herded cattle ~8,000 years ago; as it dried, many moved to the Nile, helping create Egyptian civilisation. - **Farming** developed independently: sorghum, pearl millet, African rice, yams, teff, coffee and enset. - **Kingdoms** grew on trade: gold and salt across the Sahara, ivory and gold from the Swahili coast to Arabia and India. - **Cities**: Meroë's iron furnaces, Aksum's stelae, Timbuktu's manuscript libraries, Kilwa's coral mosques, Great Zimbabwe's stone walls, Benin City's earthworks. - **Oral history**: griots preserved royal genealogies and epics such as the *Sundiata*. Colonial rupture # The slave trade drained West and Central Africa of young people for three centuries. After 1880 European powers seized almost the whole continent; only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed independent. Colonial borders, forced labour (the Congo Free State killed millions) and extraction shaped modern states. Since independence, Africa has the world’s youngest and fastest-growing population. Sources: UNESCO General History of Africa · Wikipedia: History of Africa

d: The Fertile Crescent, Sumer, Babylon, Persia, the birth of Judaism, Christianity and Islam, the caliphates, Crusades, Mongols, Ottomans and the modern Middle East.
x: The lands from Egypt to Iran saw the first farms, cities, writing, empires and three world religions. ~12,500 BCE : Natufian villages. ~9500 BCE : Göbekli Tepe; farming begins. ~3500 BCE : Uruk, the first city; cuneiform (~3200 BCE). 2334 BCE : Sargon's Akkadian Empire. ~1754 BCE : Hammurabi's code. ~1200 BCE : Bronze Age collapse. 911–609 BCE : Neo-Assyrian Empire. 550–330 BCE : Achaemenid Persia. ~30 CE : Jesus in Judea. 224–651 : Sasanian Persia. 622 : Hijra; Islam grows. 750–1258 : Abbasid Caliphate; House of Wisdom. 1096–1291 : Crusades. 1258 : Mongols sack Baghdad. 1453 : Ottomans take Constantinople. 1501 : Safavid Iran. 1916–1923 : Ottoman collapse; new states. 1948 : Israel founded; Palestinian Nakba. 1979 : Iranian Revolution. 2010–12 : Arab Spring. Heritage and knowledge # Mesopotamians gave us writing, the wheel, base-60 time, astronomy and law codes; Persians the Royal Road and qanats; Phoenicians the alphabet; Islamic scholars algebra, optics, hospitals and the preservation of Greek and Indian learning. See The Islamic Golden Age . Daily life # Farmers in the river valleys grew barley, wheat and dates and paid taxes in grain; nomadic herders of sheep, goats and camels moved between desert and sown land. Cities had bazaars, bathhouses and caravanserais on trade routes linking India, China, Africa and Europe. Sources: Wikipedia: History of the Middle East · Metropolitan Museum Timeline

d: Neanderthals and Ice Age artists, the first farmers and steppe migrants, Greece and Rome, the Middle Ages, Renaissance, empires, revolutions and the world wars.
x: ~1.2 Myr ago : Homo antecessor in Spain. ~400,000–40,000 yr ago : Neanderthals. ~45,000 yr ago : Modern humans arrive; Chauvet (~36,000), Lascaux (~17,000). ~7000–4000 BCE : Farmers from Anatolia spread farming. ~3000 BCE : Yamnaya herders arrive from the steppe; Stonehenge built. ~1900–1450 BCE : Minoan Crete. 508 BCE : Athenian democracy. 27 BCE – 476 CE : Roman Empire in the West. 793–1066 : Viking Age. 800 : Charlemagne crowned. 1347–1351 : Black Death. ~1400–1600 : Renaissance; printing press (~1440). 1517 : Reformation. 1760 onward : Industrial Revolution. 1789 : French Revolution. 1914–1945 : World wars. 1957/1993 : European integration. 1989–1991 : Fall of the Berlin Wall; end of the USSR. Who Europeans are # Ancient DNA shows most Europeans descend from three groups: Ice Age hunter-gatherers , Neolithic farmers from Anatolia (from ~7000 BCE) and Yamnaya steppe herders (from ~3000 BCE), who probably brought Indo-European languages (Haak et al. 2015). Society through time # Classical city-states and Rome built roads, law and aqueducts; medieval feudal society tied peasants to lords and manors; plague raised wages and weakened serfdom; overseas empires and the Atlantic slave trade fed new wealth; industrialisation crowded workers into cities; mass democracy, welfare states and the European Union followed the catastrophes of the 20th century. Sources: Haak et al. 2015, Nature · Wikipedia: History of Europe

d: China, Korea, Japan and Mongolia from Peking Man and the first rice and millet farmers to the dynasties, the Mongol empire, the Opium Wars and the modern era.
x: ~780,000 yr ago : 'Peking Man' (Homo erectus) at Zhoukoudian. ~18,000 BCE : Oldest pottery (Xianrendong). ~7000 BCE : Rice (Yangtze) and millet (Yellow River) farming. ~14,000–300 BCE : Jōmon culture in Japan. ~1600–1046 BCE : Shang dynasty; oracle bones. ~551 BCE : Confucius born. 221 BCE : Qin unifies China. 206 BCE – 220 CE : Han dynasty; paper; Silk Road. ~300 BCE onward : Yayoi rice farmers in Japan. 618–907 : Tang golden age. 960–1279 : Song: gunpowder, compass, printing. 1206 : Genghis Khan. 1368–1644 : Ming; Zheng He's voyages. 1443 : Hangul created in Korea. 1603–1868 : Tokugawa Japan. 1839–1860 : Opium Wars. 1868 : Meiji Restoration. 1911 : End of imperial China. 1949 : People's Republic of China. 1950–53 : Korean War. Technology and knowledge # China gave the world silk, paper, porcelain, the compass, gunpowder, printing, cast iron, the crossbow and the seismoscope ; Korea metal movable type (Jikji, 1377) and the scientific Hangul alphabet; Japan refined woodblock printing, swordsmithing and later rapid industrialisation. How people lived # Most East Asians were farmers growing rice in the south and millet and wheat in the north, organised around families, ancestors and Confucian duties. Scholar-officials chosen by exams ran the Chinese state from the Sui–Tang era to 1905. Sources: Wikipedia: History of China · Wikipedia: History of Japan

t: Southeast Asia and Oceania Through Time
d: Island-hopping early humans, the 'hobbits' of Flores, Austronesian voyagers, Indianised kingdoms, Angkor and Srivijaya, Polynesian navigators and colonial empires.
x: ~1.5 Myr ago : Homo erectus in Java. ~65,000 yr ago : Humans reach Australia. ~51,200 yr ago : Cave art in Sulawesi. ~100,000–50,000 yr ago : Homo floresiensis on Flores. ~7000 BCE : Farming at Kuk Swamp, New Guinea. ~3000 BCE onward : Austronesians sail from Taiwan. ~1000 BCE : Lapita settlers reach Fiji, Tonga, Samoa. ~1st c. CE : Funan and Indianised kingdoms. ~650–1377 : Srivijaya. 802–1431 : Khmer Empire; Angkor Wat (~1150). ~1000–1300 : Polynesians settle Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand. 1293–1527 : Majapahit. 1511 : Portuguese take Malacca. 1788 : British colonisation of Australia. 1945–1957 : Independence for Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia. Indian influence # From about the 1st century CE, traders and priests carried Sanskrit, Hindu and Buddhist ideas and Brahmi-derived scripts across the Bay of Bengal. Kingdoms such as Funan, Champa, Srivijaya, the Khmer and Majapahit adopted Indian epics, temple architecture and royal titles. The Ramayana is still performed in Thailand (Ramakien), Cambodia and Bali. Later, Islam spread through trade from Gujarat and Arabia. Masters of the ocean # Austronesian and Polynesian navigators settled from Madagascar to Easter Island using outrigger and double-hulled canoes, reading stars, swells, clouds and birds, the greatest maritime expansion before the age of European sail. Sources: Wikipedia: History of Southeast Asia · Wikipedia: Austronesian peoples

d: The peopling of the Americas, the first farmers, Caral, the Olmec, Maya, Teotihuacan, Aztec and Inca, the conquest and the Columbian Exchange, independence and the modern Americas.
x: ~23,000–21,000 yr ago : People at White Sands, New Mexico. ~14,500 yr ago : Monte Verde, Chile. ~13,000 yr ago : Clovis hunters; megafauna extinctions follow. ~9,000 yr ago : Maize domesticated in Mexico; squash and potato in the Andes. ~3000 BCE : Caral, Peru. ~1200 BCE : Olmec. ~250–900 CE : Classic Maya cities. ~100 BCE–550 CE : Teotihuacan. ~1050–1350 : Cahokia. ~1000 : Norse at L'Anse aux Meadows. 1428 : Aztec Triple Alliance. 1438 : Inca expansion under Pachacuti. 1492 : Columbus. 1521 / 1532 : Fall of the Aztec and Inca empires. 1776 : US independence. 1804 : Haiti's independence. 1810–1826 : Latin American independence. 1861–65 : US Civil War ends slavery. Achievements before 1492 # Mesoamericans domesticated maize, beans, squash, chillies, tomatoes, cacao and avocados ; Andeans potatoes, quinoa, llamas and alpacas . The Maya developed a full writing system, zero and calendars ; Aztec chinampas fed Tenochtitlan (~200,000 people); the Inca built 40,000 km of roads , terraces and storehouses and kept records on quipu knots, all without iron tools, wheels for transport or large draught animals. The conquest # Epidemics of smallpox, measles and flu killed perhaps up to 90% of the Indigenous population, with conquest and forced labour. The Columbian Exchange reshaped diets worldwide. See The Age of Exploration . Sources: Wikipedia: Settlement of the Americas · Wikipedia: Pre-Columbian era

t: Central Asia and the Steppe Through Time
d: Horse domestication, chariots, Scythians, the Silk Road cities, the Huns, Turks and Mongols, Timur, and the Soviet era.
x: The great grassland from Hungary to Mongolia, and the oasis cities south of it, linked East and West for 5,000 years. ~3300 BCE : Yamnaya herders with wagons. ~2200 BCE : Modern horses domesticated. ~2000 BCE : Spoke-wheeled chariots (Sintashta). ~2300–1700 BCE : Oxus civilisation (BMAC). ~900–200 BCE : Scythians. 138 BCE : Zhang Qian opens the Silk Road. ~30–375 CE : Kushan Empire. ~370–469 : Huns in Europe. 552 : First Turkic Khaganate. 751 : Battle of Talas. 1206 : Genghis Khan. 1370–1405 : Timur. 1420s : Ulugh Beg's observatory, Samarkand. 1860s–1880s : Russian conquest. 1960s– : Aral Sea collapse. 1991 : Independent Central Asian republics. How the steppe shaped history # Horse riding and chariots transformed warfare across Eurasia; steppe migrations probably spread Indo-European languages to Europe and South Asia; nomad empires (Xiongnu, Huns, Turks, Mongols) repeatedly shaped China, Persia, India and Europe. Silk Road cities such as Samarkand, Bukhara, Merv and Kashgar were melting pots of Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Nestorian Christianity, Manichaeism and Islam. Sources: Wikipedia: History of Central Asia · Wikipedia: Eurasian nomads

t: The Silk Road and the Indian Ocean Trade
d: The overland and maritime routes that for two thousand years carried silk, spices, cotton, horses, paper, religions and plague between China, India, Persia, Africa and Europe.
x: The name Silk Road ( Seidenstraße ) was coined by German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877. It was never one road but a web of caravan routes, linked to an even larger network of sea lanes across the Indian Ocean , active from about the 2nd century BCE (Han dynasty) to the 15th century . What travelled # From Goods China Silk, porcelain, tea, paper, later gunpowder and the compass India Cotton cloth, pepper and spices, indigo, gems, ivory, steel, sugar, and the numerals we use today Central Asia Horses (the “heavenly horses” of Ferghana), jade Persia and Arabia Carpets, glass, frankincense, dates Rome / Byzantium Gold and silver, glass, wine, coral Africa Gold, ivory, enslaved people Ideas and faiths on the move # Buddhism travelled from India to Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan; pilgrims like Faxian (5th c.) and Xuanzang (7th c.) walked to India and studied at Nalanda . Islam , Nestorian Christianity and Manichaeism spread east; Indian mathematics and astronomy reached Baghdad and then Europe. Cities such as Samarkand, Bukhara, Kashgar, Merv and Dunhuang (with its Buddhist cave library) grew rich. The monsoon seaway # Sailors learned to ride the monsoon winds : southwest in summer toward India, northeast in winter back to Arabia and Africa. Ports such as Muziris, Calicut, Cambay, Masulipatnam , Aden, Hormuz, Malacca and Quanzhou linked a world of Arab, Gujarati, Tamil, Malay, Chinese and Swahili merchants. The Ming admiral Zheng He led giant treasure fleets to Calicut and East Africa (1405–1433). Dark cargo # Trade routes also spread disease. The Black Death travelled along Mongol caravan routes to Crimea and then by ship to Italy in 1347. See Plagues and pandemics . Sources: UNESCO: Silk Roads Programme · Wikipedia: Silk Road

d: From the 8th to the 13th century, scholars in Baghdad, Cordoba, Cairo and Bukhara translated, preserved and advanced Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge.
x: After the Abbasid caliphs founded Baghdad in 762, the city became one of the largest in the world. Paper, learned from Chinese papermakers after the Battle of Talas (751), made books cheap. The House of Wisdom # The Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad sponsored translations of Greek (Aristotle, Euclid, Ptolemy, Galen), Persian and Sanskrit works into Arabic. The Indian astronomical text Brahmasphutasiddhanta was translated as the Sindhind , bringing Indian numerals and zero to the Arab world; from there they reached Europe as “Arabic numerals”. Great minds # Scholars and discoveries - **Al-Khwarizmi** (~780–850): *Al-Jabr* gave us **algebra**; his name gave us **algorithm**. - **Al-Kindi**: philosophy and cryptanalysis (frequency analysis). - **Al-Razi (Rhazes)**: distinguished smallpox from measles. - **Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen)**: *Book of Optics*, an early experimental scientist. - **Al-Biruni**: measured Earth's radius; wrote the *Kitab al-Hind*, a detailed study of Indian science and society. - **Ibn Sina (Avicenna)**: *Canon of Medicine*, used in European universities for 600 years. - **Ibn Rushd (Averroes)**, in Cordoba: commentaries on Aristotle that shaped European thought. - **Al-Zahrawi**: the father of surgery in al-Andalus. - **Fatima al-Fihri** founded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez (859), often called the oldest continuously operating university. Daily life # Cities had hospitals ( bimaristans ), public baths, paper mills and great markets. New crops spread across the Islamic world, sometimes called the Arab Agricultural Revolution : rice, sugarcane, citrus, cotton, aubergine, spinach . Coffee drinking began in Sufi circles of Yemen in the 15th century. The end # The Mongol sack of Baghdad (1258) destroyed the House of Wisdom; the Tigris was said to run black with ink. Learning continued in Cairo, Persia, Central Asia (Ulugh Beg’s observatory, 1420s), the Ottoman Empire and Mughal India. Sources: Wikipedia: Islamic Golden Age · Wikipedia: House of Wisdom

d: How Genghis Khan's steppe horsemen built the largest contiguous land empire in history, the destruction and the exchange it brought, and how India escaped conquest.
x: In 1206 a council of steppe tribes proclaimed Temüjin as Genghis Khan , “universal ruler”. Within 70 years his descendants ruled from Korea to Hungary , about 24 million km² , the largest contiguous land empire ever. How they did it # Horse archers: each warrior had several horses and could ride for days; composite bows outranged most enemies. Organisation by tens (arban, jaghun, mingghan, tumen) that broke up tribal loyalties. Promotion by merit , religious tolerance, and the use of captured engineers for siege warfare. Terror: cities that resisted, such as Merv, Nishapur and Baghdad (1258) , were massacred. The cost and the exchange # Estimates of deaths from the Mongol conquests reach tens of millions ; Iran’s irrigation systems and population took centuries to recover. Yet the Pax Mongolica made trade across Eurasia safer: Marco Polo travelled to Kublai Khan’s court; the yam relay post system carried messages; and paper money, gunpowder, printing, foods and medical knowledge spread. So did the Black Death . The Mongols and India # The Delhi Sultanate repeatedly repelled Mongol invasions under Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316), sparing India the devastation of Persia. A descendant of both Genghis Khan and Timur, Babur , later founded the Mughal dynasty (from Mughal , Persian for “Mongol”). Daily life on the steppe # Mongols lived in felt gers (yurts), moved with herds of horses, sheep, goats, yaks and camels, and ate meat and dairy: dried curds, butter and airag (fermented mare’s milk). Women managed camps and herds and often held real power, such as Genghis’s wife Börte and Kublai’s mother Sorghaghtani Beki . Sources: Wikipedia: Mongol Empire · Wikipedia: Mongol invasions of India

d: From the Plague of Athens to COVID-19, how epidemics killed millions, toppled empires, transformed societies and drove medical science.
x: Infectious disease has killed more people than all wars combined. Most great epidemics came from animals (zoonoses) and spread along the routes of trade, war and empire. Deadliest pandemics (estimated deaths, millions) Black Death (1346–53) Black Death (1346–53) 75 m Spanish flu (1918–20) Spanish flu (1918–20) 50 m Plague of Justinian (541–) Plague of Justinian (541–) 30 m HIV/AIDS (1981–) HIV/AIDS (1981–) 40 m Third plague pandemic Third plague pandemic 15 m COVID-19 (reported) COVID-19 (reported) 7 m Antonine Plague Antonine Plague 7 m Source: Mid-range estimates (Wikipedia, WHO); highly uncertain for early pandemics The three plague pandemics # The bacterium Yersinia pestis , carried by fleas on rats and other rodents, caused three great pandemics. Ancient DNA from victims confirmed it (Bos et al. 2011). From Justinian to Bombay 1. **Plague of Justinian (541–~750 CE):** struck Constantinople in 541, killing perhaps a fifth of the city, and returned in waves for two centuries, weakening the Byzantine and Persian empires before the Arab conquests. 2. **Black Death (1346–1353):** spread from Central Asia along Mongol trade routes, reaching Crimea, then Sicily in 1347. It killed perhaps **30–60% of Europe's population**. Labour shortages raised wages and helped end serfdom in western Europe; Jews were massacred as scapegoats; art and religion became obsessed with death. Recurrent outbreaks continued for 400 years (London's Great Plague, 1665). 3. **Third pandemic (1894–1950s):** spread from Yunnan to Hong Kong and then **Bombay (1896)**, killing about **12 million in India**. Harsh British plague measures (house searches, segregation camps) provoked protest; the assassination of plague commissioner W. C. Rand in Pune (1897) by the Chapekar brothers became a nationalist landmark. **Alexandre Yersin** identified the bacterium in 1894; **Waldemar Haffkine** developed a plague vaccine in Bombay (1897). Other killers # Smallpox : killed perhaps 300 million people in the 20th century alone; it devastated the Americas after 1520. Indian and Chinese variolation came before Jenner’s vaccine (1796) ; the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980 , after India’s last case in 1975. Cholera : the first pandemic began in Bengal in 1817 ; John Snow traced London’s 1854 outbreak to a water pump, founding epidemiology. Malaria : still kills about 600,000 a year; quinine from cinchona bark was used in colonial India (tonic water with gin). 1918 influenza : about 50 million deaths worldwide, with India losing perhaps 12–17 million, the most of any country. HIV/AIDS (from 1981): about 40 million deaths. COVID-19 (2020–2023): about 7 million reported deaths, with excess-death estimates several times higher. What pandemics changed # Quarantine (from Venice’s 40-day quaranta giorni ), public health boards, sewage and clean water, vaccination, germ theory, and today’s genomic surveillance all grew out of epidemics. Sources: Bos et al. 2011, Nature · WHO: Smallpox · Wikipedia: List of epidemics

t: The Age of Exploration and the Columbian Exchange
d: How Portuguese and Spanish ships connected the world after 1492–98, the crops, animals and diseases that crossed the oceans, and how chillies and potatoes reached Indian kitchens.
x: In the 15th century the Ottomans controlled the land routes to Asia, so Europeans looked for sea routes to India’s spices. Portugal pushed down Africa’s coast; Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope (1488); Christopher Columbus , sailing west for Spain, reached the Caribbean (1492); Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in May 1498 ; Magellan and Elcano completed the first circumnavigation (1519–22). The Columbian Exchange # Historian Alfred Crosby named the transfer of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Old and New Worlds the Columbian Exchange . Americas → Old World Old World → Americas Maize, potato, sweet potato, cassava, tomato, chilli pepper , peanut, cashew, pineapple, papaya, guava, cacao, vanilla, tobacco, rubber, turkey Wheat, rice, sugarcane, coffee, bananas, citrus, horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, chickens, smallpox, measles, malaria Within a century, chillies had conquered Indian, Thai, Sichuan and Korean cooking; potatoes fuelled population booms in Europe (and Ireland’s catastrophic dependence on them); maize and sweet potato fed China’s growing population. The human cost # Smallpox , measles and flu killed perhaps up to 90% of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas within a century or so. The Aztec (1521) and Inca (1532) empires fell to small Spanish forces helped by disease and Indigenous allies. To work plantations and mines, Europeans shipped about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic between 1526 and 1867. Silver from Potosí (Bolivia) flowed through Manila into China, creating the first global economy. In India # The Portuguese took Goa (1510), controlled sea trade by force with the cartaz pass system, and introduced chillies, cashew, papaya and pineapple. The Dutch, English, Danes and French followed, setting the stage for the East India Company . Sources: Wikipedia: Columbian exchange · Wikipedia: Age of Discovery

d: How coal, steam and machines transformed Britain and then the world after 1760, what factory life was like, and why it deindustrialised India.
x: Between about 1760 and 1840 Britain shifted from hand production to machines powered by water, then steam and coal . It was the biggest change in human life since farming. Key inventions # Textiles: the flying shuttle (1733), spinning jenny (1764), water frame (1769), spinning mule (1779), power loom (1785). Power: Newcomen’s steam engine (1712), improved by James Watt (1769–76). Iron and coal: coke smelting; canals and then railways (Stephenson’s Rocket, 1829). Communication: telegraph (1830s–40s). Why Britain? # Historians point to cheap coal , expensive labour (which made machines worth buying), colonial markets and raw cotton , banks and patents, and a culture of practical science. A key driver was the effort to copy Indian cotton cloth (calico, chintz, muslin), which British consumers loved; British laws even banned Indian printed calicoes (1700, 1721) to protect domestic producers. Life in the factories # People moved from villages to crowded towns such as Manchester . Children as young as five worked 12–16 hour days in mills and mines until Factory Acts slowly limited hours. Cholera and typhoid spread in slums. Over the long run, though, wages and life expectancy rose and child mortality fell. India deindustrialised # India had been the world’s largest textile producer. After 1813 British machine-made cloth entered India with low tariffs while Indian cloth faced high duties in Britain. Weavers of Dhaka and Bengal were ruined; Dhaka’s population fell sharply. India’s share of world manufacturing output fell from about 25% (1750) to about 2% (1900) (Bairoch’s estimates). The first Indian cotton mills opened in Bombay in the 1850s, and the Tata steel plant at Jamshedpur in 1907. The long legacy # Industrialisation began the rise in atmospheric CO₂ (from ~280 ppm to over 420 ppm today), and with it modern climate change. Sources: Wikipedia: Industrial Revolution · Wikipedia: Deindustrialisation of India

d: The causes, course and cost of the First and Second World Wars, the Holocaust and the atomic bombs, and the role of over 3.8 million Indian soldiers.
