x: World War I (1914–1918) # Causes: rival alliances (Germany and Austria-Hungary vs France, Russia and Britain), an arms race, nationalism and imperial competition. The spark was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 . On the Western Front , trench warfare with machine guns, artillery and poison gas killed millions for a few kilometres of ground (Verdun, the Somme). About 20 million people died. The war destroyed four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, Ottoman) and produced the Russian Revolution (1917) and the League of Nations . India’s role: about 1.3 million Indian soldiers served in France, Mesopotamia, Gallipoli, Egypt and East Africa; around 74,000 died. Indian Victoria Cross recipients included Khudadad Khan . India Gate in Delhi commemorates them. Promises of self-government were broken, fuelling the 1919 protests. Between the wars # The Great Depression (from 1929), resentment of the Versailles Treaty and fear of communism helped fascists take power in Italy (Mussolini, 1922) and Nazis in Germany (Hitler, 1933). Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) and China (1937). World War II (1939–1945) # Main phases - **1939–41:** Germany conquers Poland, France and much of Europe; the Battle of Britain. - **1941:** Germany invades the Soviet Union; Japan attacks **Pearl Harbor**, bringing the USA into the war. - **1942–43:** turning points at **Midway**, **El Alamein** and **Stalingrad**. - **1944:** D-Day landings in Normandy; Soviet advance in the east; **Kohima and Imphal** stop Japan's invasion of India. - **1945:** Germany surrenders (8 May); atomic bombs on **Hiroshima** (6 Aug) and **Nagasaki** (9 Aug); Japan surrenders (15 Aug, signed 2 Sept). About 70–85 million people died, most of them civilians, including about 27 million Soviet citizens and perhaps 15–20 million Chinese. In the Holocaust the Nazis systematically murdered six million Jews , along with Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners and others. India’s role: the British Indian Army grew to 2.5 million , the largest volunteer army in history, fighting in North Africa, Italy and Burma. The Bengal famine of 1943 killed 2–3 million people. Subhas Chandra Bose’s Indian National Army fought alongside Japan. d: How empires ended after 1945, the Cold War and Non-Alignment, the Green Revolution, the digital age, and the challenges of the 21st century.
x: In 1945 European empires still ruled much of Africa and Asia. Within 30 years almost all colonies were independent, with India and Pakistan (1947) leading the way, followed by Burma and Sri Lanka (1948), Indonesia (1949), Ghana (1957), most of Africa around 1960 , Algeria after a brutal war (1962), and the Portuguese colonies in 1974–75 (India took Goa in 1961 ). The Cold War (1947–1991) # The USA and USSR competed for influence through alliances (NATO, Warsaw Pact), proxy wars (Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan), a nuclear arms race and the space race (Sputnik 1957, Apollo 11 in 1969). India’s Jawaharlal Nehru , Egypt’s Nasser, Yugoslavia’s Tito, Indonesia’s Sukarno and Ghana’s Nkrumah founded the Non-Aligned Movement (Belgrade, 1961). The Cold War ended with the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the dissolution of the USSR (1991) . A transformed world # Population grew from 2.5 billion (1950) to over 8 billion today. Food: the Green Revolution averted famine in Asia. Health: life expectancy worldwide rose from about 46 years (1950) to about 73. Technology: computers, the internet (1969/1989), mobile phones and now AI. India: from the 1951 elections to 1991 liberalisation, the IT boom, Chandrayaan-3 (2023) and becoming the world’s most populous country (2023). d: What a day was like for an ordinary person in the Ice Age, a Neolithic village, Harappa, Rome, a medieval village, Mughal Agra and an industrial city: homes, work, clothes, children, health and fun.
x: History often tells of kings and battles. This page is about everybody else. Each era page in the Eras catalog also describes “How people lived”. Era Home Work Clothes Life expectancy at birth Ice Age hunter-gatherer (~20,000 years ago) Caves, hide tents, mammoth-bone huts Hunting, gathering, toolmaking Sewn furs and hides ~30 (many children died; adults could reach 60+) Neolithic farmer (~7000 BCE) Mud-brick or wattle houses Farming, herding, pottery, weaving Wool, flax ~25–30 Harappan city dweller (~2300 BCE) Brick house with a bathroom Farming, crafts, trade Cotton ~30 Roman citizen (~100 CE) Rented flat (insula) or villa Trades, farming, army Wool tunic, toga ~25–30 Medieval European peasant (~1300) One-room cottage shared with animals Field work for the lord Wool, linen ~30 Mughal Agra (~1600) Mud or brick house; havelis for the rich Crafts, trade, farming, court service Cotton, silk for elites ~25–30 Industrial Manchester (~1840) Back-to-back slum housing 12–16 hour factory shifts Cheap cotton ~25–30 in slums Today (2025) Apartments, houses Services, industry, farming Synthetics, cotton ~73 (world), ~72 (India) Low life expectancy mostly reflects very high child mortality : in most pre-modern societies about a quarter of babies died in their first year and nearly half of children before age 15 (Our World in Data). Childhood # Children worked from an early age: herding, carrying water, spinning. Toys appear in every era: Harappan clay carts and whistles, Egyptian dolls, Roman marbles. Schooling was rare: Indian gurukuls and pathshalas , Buddhist monasteries and maktabs / madrasas taught some boys; girls’ education was rarer until the 19th–20th centuries (Savitribai Phule opened a girls’ school in Pune in 1848). Fun and festivals # People played board games (the Royal Game of Ur; India’s chaturanga , ancestor of chess; pachisi , which became Ludo; snakes and ladders, from moksha patam ), told stories, sang and danced, wrestled and raced. Festivals marked harvests and seasons. Health # Without germ theory, infections were the big killers: diarrhoeal diseases, malaria, tuberculosis, smallpox and plague. Yet ancient medicine had real successes: Sushruta’s surgery, Egyptian bone-setting, Chinese and Indian variolation against smallpox. Related: Food through history · Peoples and tribes Sources: Our World in Data: Child and infant mortality · Wikipedia: Life expectancy

d: What people ate from the Ice Age to today: hunter-gatherer diets, the first bread and beer, Roman garum, Indian spices, the Columbian Exchange, famine, and the modern food system.
x: Hunter-gatherers # Ice Age people ate a wide range of foods: mammoth, reindeer, horse, fish, shellfish, birds, eggs, nuts, roots, berries and wild grains. Starch grains on 30,000-year-old grinding stones show they made a kind of flour. Cooking with fire, possibly for a million years, made food easier to digest. The first farmers’ food # Early farmers ate porridge and flatbread made from wheat, barley, millet or rice; pulses ; and dairy once animals were milked (traces of milk fats appear in pots ~9,000 years old). Beer appears in the Near East by ~5,000 years ago and possibly much earlier; wine in Georgia by ~6000 BCE. Ancient cuisines # From Egypt to the Indus to Rome - **Egypt:** bread and beer were wages; onions, garlic, lentils, figs, dates, fish; feasts of goose and beef for the rich. - **Indus:** wheat and barley breads, millets, lentils, peas, sesame oil, dairy, beef and mutton; scientists have found turmeric and ginger residues in Harappan pots at Farmana. - **Vedic India:** barley cakes, milk, curd, ghee, honey; later rice dishes such as *payasa* (kheer). - **China:** millet and rice, soybeans, pork; soy sauce and tofu later; tea from the Han era onward. - **Rome:** wheat porridge, bread, olive oil, wine, *garum* fish sauce; pepper from Kerala. - **Maya and Aztec:** maize tortillas and tamales (with nixtamalisation, soaking maize in lime), beans, squash, chillies, turkey and **chocolate drinks**. - **Inca:** potatoes (freeze-dried as *chuño*), quinoa, maize, llama meat, guinea pig. India’s food story # Indian cuisine grew in layers: native millets, rice, pulses, dairy and spices ( black pepper, cardamom, turmeric, ginger, long pepper ); Persian and Central Asian influences under the Sultanate and Mughals ( biryani, pulao, kebabs, naan, kormas, sherbets ); Portuguese-brought American crops ( chilli, potato, tomato, maize, cashew, papaya, pineapple , groundnut); and British-era tea drinking, which became mass culture only in the 20th century. Traditional texts such as the Manasollasa (12th century, Chalukya king Someshvara III) describe recipes for dosa-like dishes, rice preparations and sweets. Famine and plenty # For most of history, harvest failure meant famine : the Great Famine of Europe (1315–17), Bengal 1770, Ireland 1845–52, India 1876–78, China 1959–61. Today the world produces enough calories for everyone; about 700 million people still go hungry because of poverty and conflict, while more than a billion are obese. Sources: Wikipedia: History of Indian cuisine · Wikipedia: Columbian exchange

d: Ongoing research streams in archaeology and history, with the latest status and sources.
x: Status date: 15 November 2026 . # Stream Status Next milestone 1 Herculaneum scrolls PHerc. 1667 read end to end without being opened (25 June 2026) ~600 scrolls remain unopened 2 Keeladi (Tamil Nadu) 11th phase since 18 Mar 2026: continuous brick structures, drains, 1,300+ artefacts, iron furnace Ancient-DNA papers expected by Dec 2026 3 Indus script Still undeciphered Computational analyses 4 Ancient DNA of South Asia Rakhigarhi (2019); Keeladi, Adichanallur and Sivagalai markers (2026) More genomes 1 · Herculaneum scrolls **Status:** On **25 June 2026** in Naples, the **Vesuvius Challenge** announced that scroll **PHerc. 1667** had been virtually unwrapped and read **from beginning to end**, the first Herculaneum papyrus read in full without being opened. Another scroll was identified as Philodemus, *On Gods*, Book 8. The work used X-ray scans (including ESRF's BM18 beamline) and machine learning, building on Brent Seales's virtual-unwrapping research at the University of Kentucky. The challenge has awarded about **$1.8 million** in prizes since 2023. **Next:** More than **600** Herculaneum scrolls remain unopened. Sources: [Vesuvius Challenge: "We read an entire scroll"](https://scrollprize.org/firstscroll) · [ESRF](https://www.esrf.fr/home/news/general/content-news/general/the-day-the-herculaneum-scrolls-began-speaking-again.html) · [Reuters via Express Tribune](https://tribune.com.pk/story/2615079/researchers-use-ai-to-unlock-the-complete-text-of-burnt-herculaneum-scroll-for-the-first-time) · [Pompeii and Vesuvius](/wiki/events/eruption-of-vesuvius.html) 2 · Keeladi (Tamil Nadu) **Status:** The Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology began the **11th excavation phase** on **18 March 2026**. Excavators exposed continuous brick structures in all nine quadrants, a terracotta pipeline and closed drain, and more than **1,300 artefacts**, including beads, spindle whorls, iron knives and swords, ivory dice and gold ornaments. An **iron-working furnace** was reported in July 2026. Madurai Kamaraj University's ancient-DNA lab has extracted about **75,000 genetic markers** from the Konthagai burial site; results so far show affinity with present-day South Indians and Sri Lankan Tamils, with papers expected by December 2026. Sources: [South First](https://thesouthfirst.com/tamilnadu/keeladi-excavation-unearths-rare-furnace-reinforcing-evidence-of-early-tamil-iron-production/) · [Deccan Herald](https://www.deccanherald.com/amp/story/india/tamil-nadu/75000-markers-decoded-genetic-roots-of-ancient-tamils-unveiled-4099243) · [Sangam-era Tamilakam](/wiki/civilizations/sangam-era-tamilakam.html) 3 · Indus script **Status:** About 400 signs on 4,000+ objects; no bilingual text has been found and inscriptions average only about five signs, so the script remains undeciphered. Sources: [Indus script](/wiki/beliefs/indus-script.html) · [Indus Valley Civilisation](/wiki/ancient/indus-valley-civilisation.html) 4 · Ancient DNA of South Asia **Status:** The Rakhigarhi genome (Shinde et al. 2019) and the 2019 South and Central Asia study (Narasimhan et al.) reshaped understanding of Indian ancestry; Tamil Nadu labs are now analysing Sangam-era burials. Sources: [Research papers](/wiki/papers/index.html)

d: Known from a crushed skull nicknamed Toumaï ('hope of life'), found in 2001 in the Djurab desert of Chad, Sahelanthropus tchadensis lived about 7 million years ago, near the time humans and chimpanzees split. Its brain was chimp-sized (about 360 cm³), but its small canine teeth and a forward-placed foramen magnum (the hole where the spine meets the skull) suggest it may have walked upright. A thigh bone found nearby has fuelled debate. Its location, 2,500 km west of the Rift Valley, showed early hominins were widespread in Africa.

d: Orrorin tugenensis ('original man' in the Tugen language) is known from about 20 fossils found in Kenya's Tugen Hills in 2000, dated to about 6 million years ago. Its thigh bones have a long neck and features suggesting it walked on two legs, while its curved finger bones show it still climbed trees. Its teeth have thick enamel, more human-like than chimp-like. It lived in a mix of forest and open woodland.

Its canine teeth were somewhat ape-like, rubbing against lower teeth to sharpen themselves. It may be the ancestor of Ardipithecus ramidus.

d: Ardi, a partial female skeleton from Aramis in Ethiopia, about 4.4 million years old, was described in 2009 after 15 years of painstaking work. She stood about 1.2 m and weighed about 50 kg, with a pelvis adapted for upright walking but a grasping, opposable big toe for climbing. Fossil plants and animals around her show she lived in woodland, overturning the idea that bipedalism began on open savanna. Males had small canines, perhaps suggesting less aggressive competition.

d: Living about 4.2–3.8 million years ago in Kenya and Ethiopia, A. anamensis is the earliest known Australopithecus. A nearly complete 3.8-million-year-old skull from Woranso-Mille, Ethiopia (2019) revealed its face. Its leg bones show clear bipedalism. It is probably the ancestor of A. afarensis, though the two may have overlapped.

d: Lucy, discovered in 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia, by Donald Johanson and Tom Gray, is a 40% complete skeleton about 3.2 million years old, named after the Beatles song played in camp. Her species lived from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago, stood 1–1.5 m, and had a brain of about 400–500 cm³. The Laetoli footprints and the 'First Family' fossils show they walked upright and lived in groups; long arms and curved fingers show they still climbed. Cut-marked bones at Dikika suggest they may have used stone to butcher meat.

d: Kenyanthropus platyops ('flat-faced man of Kenya') is known from a 3.5-million-year-old skull found in 2001 at Lomekwi, west of Lake Turkana. Its flat face and small molars distinguish it from Lucy's species, showing early hominin diversity. Some researchers think it made the 3.3-million-year-old Lomekwi stone tools found nearby.

d: The first australopithecine identified, by Raymond Dart in 1925 from the Taung Child skull in South Africa, which revealed that humanity's roots lay in Africa. Living about 3.3–2.1 million years ago, it is also known from Sterkfontein's 'Mrs Ples' and 'Little Foot', a nearly complete skeleton about 3.67 million years old. Brains were about 450 cm³. Damage to the Taung skull's eye sockets shows an eagle killed the child.

d: Discovered in 2008 by nine-year-old Matthew Berger at Malapa, South Africa, A. sediba lived about 2 million years ago. Its skeletons show a mosaic: a small brain (420 cm³) and climbing arms, but a human-like hand with a long thumb and a modern-like pelvis. Some researchers suggested it could be close to the ancestor of Homo.

d: Discovered by Mary Leakey at Olduvai Gorge in 1959, 'Nutcracker Man' lived about 2.3–1.2 million years ago in East Africa. Its huge molars and massive jaw muscles were long thought to crack nuts, but chemical studies of its teeth show it ate mostly grasses and sedges. It coexisted with early Homo for about a million years before dying out.

Its brain (about 550–700 cm³) was larger than australopithecines', and it is associated with Oldowan stone tools. Its long arms suggest it still climbed. Some scientists think its fossils include more than one species.

He was a youth about 8–12 years old and 1.6 m tall, with long legs and modern body proportions suited to walking and running long distances in heat. Some scientists treat H. ergaster as African Homo erectus. They made Acheulean hand-axes.

d: Homo erectus ('upright man') appeared about 1.9 million years ago in Africa and spread to Georgia, Java ('Java Man', found by Eugène Dubois in 1891), China ('Peking Man' at Zhoukoudian) and India. It had human-like body proportions, a brain of about 600–1,100 cm³, made Acheulean hand-axes and likely controlled fire. It survived in Java until about 110,000 years ago — over 1.5 million years, the longest of any human species.

The Narmada skull from India may be related.

d: Found in 2013 deep in South Africa's Rising Star cave by Lee Berger's team (who recruited slim 'underground astronauts'), H. naledi lived about 335,000–236,000 years ago — surprisingly recent for its small brain (about 560 cm³). Its feet and hands were human-like, but shoulders were adapted to climbing. Researchers controversially argue it buried its dead and engraved cave walls.

d: Homo neanderthalensis lived across Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. Stocky and cold-adapted, they had brains as large as ours (about 1,500 cm³), made Mousterian tools, controlled fire, buried their dead, made jewellery from eagle talons and may have painted in Spanish caves. They interbred with Homo sapiens; most non-Africans carry 1–2% Neanderthal DNA. Svante Pääbo sequenced their genome (Nobel 2022).

d: Known mostly from DNA extracted from a finger bone found in 2008 in Denisova Cave in Siberia, Denisovans were sister to Neanderthals and lived across Asia. A jaw from Tibet (Xiahe) and a molar from Laos confirm their range. Melanesians and Aboriginal Australians carry up to 4–6% Denisovan DNA, and Tibetans inherited a Denisovan gene (EPAS1) that helps at high altitude.

d: A large skull found in Harbin, China, hidden in a well in 1933 and revealed in 2021, about 146,000 years old, was named Homo longi. Its brain was large (about 1,420 cm³). In 2025 proteins from the skull identified it as a Denisovan, giving that group its first face.

d: Found in Liang Bua cave on Flores, Indonesia, in 2003, H. floresiensis stood about 1.1 m with a brain of about 400 cm³, yet made stone tools. It lived from about 100,000 to 50,000 years ago, and ancestors on Flores date back 700,000 years. Its small size may result from island dwarfism. It hunted pygmy elephants (Stegodon).

d: Teeth and bones from Callao Cave in Luzon, Philippines, described in 2019 and about 50,000–67,000 years old, belong to H. luzonensis. Small teeth and curved toe bones show yet another island-dwelling human species. How its ancestors crossed the sea is unknown.

d: The oldest Homo sapiens fossils, from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco (about 315,000 years ago), Omo Kibish, Ethiopia (about 233,000 years ago) and Florisbad, South Africa, show modern faces with braincases that became rounder over time. Early sapiens made Middle Stone Age tools, used ochre, collected shellfish and made beads. Genetic studies suggest our species emerged from several connected African populations.

d: Some Homo sapiens reached Arabia and the Levant earlier, but the main dispersal from Africa happened about 70,000–50,000 years ago. Within 20,000 years they reached South Asia, Southeast Asia and Australia; by 45,000 years ago Europe; and by about 20,000–15,000 years ago the Americas. They interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans, and became the only surviving human species.

t: Pangaea and the age of dinosaurs
d: From about 335 to 175 million years ago most land formed one supercontinent, Pangaea, surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean. The Mesozoic Era (252–66 million years ago) — Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous — began after the Great Dying, the worst mass extinction, and saw dinosaurs dominate land, pterosaurs the air and marine reptiles the seas. Mammals appeared about 200 million years ago but stayed small and mostly nocturnal; birds evolved from feathered dinosaurs, and flowering plants spread in the Cretaceous. India drifted north as an island, and the Deccan Traps erupted near the end.

How people lived # No humans existed; the ancestors of mammals were shrew-sized creatures living in the shadows of dinosaurs, feeding on insects and seeds at night. What people ate # — Species of the time # Dinosaurs, early mammals, cycads, conifers

d: After the Chicxulub impact 66 million years ago, mammals diversified into the niches left by dinosaurs: early whales evolved in the Tethys Sea near India and Pakistan (Pakicetus), horses, elephants and primates appeared, and grasslands spread as the climate cooled. India collided with Asia, raising the Himalaya and creating the monsoon. Apes evolved in Africa and Eurasia around 25–20 million years ago, and the human line split from chimpanzees about 7 million years ago.

What people ate # — Species of the time # Early whales, horses, primates, grasslands

d: Between about 4.2 and 2 million years ago, Australopithecus species such as anamensis, afarensis (Lucy) and africanus lived in eastern and southern Africa. They walked upright with an arched foot but still had long arms for climbing and ape-sized brains of 400–500 cm³. The Laetoli footprints and Lucy's skeleton (found 1974 at Hadar) are their most famous evidence; some may have used sharp stones to butcher meat. Robust Paranthropus with huge chewing teeth lived alongside early Homo.

How people lived # Small groups foraged in woodland and grassland mosaics for fruit, roots, nuts, termites and occasional meat, sleeping in trees for safety from big cats and hyenas. What people ate # Fruit, seeds, roots, termites Species of the time # Australopithecus afarensis (‘Lucy’), Paranthropus, giant hyenas

d: The Lower Paleolithic, from the first stone tools 3.3 million years ago to about 300,000 years ago, is the longest chapter of human history. Oldowan choppers gave way to Acheulean hand-axes around 1.76 million years ago, made by Homo erectus, who spread out of Africa to Georgia, Java, China and India (Attirampakkam, about 1.5 million years ago). Control of fire appears by about 1 million years ago (Wonderwerk Cave), and wooden spears at Schöningen show big-game hunting by 300,000 years ago.

What people ate # Scavenged and hunted meat, marrow, plants Species of the time # Homo habilis, Homo erectus, mammoths, sabre-toothed cats

d: From about 300,000 to 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals in Europe and western Asia and early Homo sapiens in Africa made tools with the Levallois technique, striking prepared cores to get flakes of a planned shape. Homo sapiens appeared by 315,000 years ago (Jebel Irhoud); Denisovans lived in Asia. People buried their dead, used ochre and shell beads, made glue from birch tar, and spread Out of Africa around 70,000–50,000 years ago, interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans.

How people lived # Groups lived in caves and open camps, hunting deer, bison and horses with hafted spears, gathering plants and shellfish, and caring for injured or elderly members, as Neanderthal skeletons with healed injuries show. What people ate # Hunted large game, shellfish, plants Species of the time # Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo floresiensis, cave bears, woolly rhino

d: Between about 50,000 and 12,000 years ago, Homo sapiens spread across the globe, reaching Australia, Siberia and the Americas. Blade tools, bone needles, spear-throwers, bows and harpoons appeared, along with explosive creativity: cave art at Sulawesi, Chauvet and Lascaux, the Venus figurines, bone flutes and personal ornaments. Neanderthals disappeared around 40,000 years ago, and dogs were domesticated. In India, Bhimbetka's rock shelters contain some of the oldest art.

Neanderthals disappeared around 40,000 years ago, and dogs were domesticated. In India, Bhimbetka’s rock shelters contain some of the oldest art. How people lived # Hunter-gatherers lived in larger, networked bands, sewing fitted clothing, building mammoth-bone huts in Ukraine, trading shells and stone over hundreds of kilometres, and holding feasts and rituals. What people ate # Mammoth, reindeer, horse, fish, wild plants Species of the time # Woolly mammoth, cave lion, Irish elk, giant ground sloth, Megalania

d: Around 26,000–19,000 years ago ice sheets reached their maximum. Sea level was about 120 m lower, opening land bridges like Beringia; much of northern Europe was polar desert and people retreated to southern refugia. Deserts expanded, and in India the Thar was larger and drier. Mammoths, woolly rhinos and reindeer roamed the steppe-tundra.

What people ate # Hunted reindeer, mammoth Species of the time # Mammoths, woolly rhinos, cave bears

d: The Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age), from about 12,000 to the arrival of farming (varying by region), followed the Ice Age. Forests spread over Europe, and people adapted with microliths — tiny flint blades set into arrows and harpoons — fishing and canoes. In India, sites like Bagor, Langhnaj and Sarai Nahar Rai show microlithic hunters and early burials, and Bhimbetka's paintings depict hunting and dancing.

How people lived # Communities gathered seasonally by rivers, lakes and coasts, eating fish, shellfish, deer, nuts and wild grains; some became semi-settled, like the Natufians of the Levant. What people ate # Fish, deer, nuts, wild grain Species of the time # Aurochs, red deer, wild boar

d: Beginning about 10,000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent and independently in China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica, the Andes, Africa and India, people domesticated plants and animals. Wheat, barley, lentils, sheep and goats came first in West Asia; rice and millet in China; maize in Mexico. In South Asia, Mehrgarh (from about 7000 BCE) grew barley and wheat and kept cattle. Farming fed more people, leading to villages, pottery, property and later inequality, though early farmers were often shorter and less healthy than foragers.

Farming fed more people, leading to villages, pottery, property and later inequality, though early farmers were often shorter and less healthy than foragers. How people lived # Families lived in mud-brick or wattle houses, grew grain, kept animals, ground flour on stones, made pottery and polished stone axes, and buried ancestors under house floors. What people ate # Wheat, barley, rice, millet, maize, lentils; goats, sheep, cattle, pigs Species of the time # Domestic animals; aurochs (wild cattle) still roam

d: From about 5000 to 3000 BCE (later in some regions), people used copper alongside stone. Copper smelting appeared in Serbia, Iran and Anatolia; Ötzi the Iceman (about 3300 BCE) carried a copper axe. In India, Chalcolithic cultures such as Ahar-Banas, Malwa and Jorwe flourished, and early Harappan villages grew. The wheel, plough and wool sheep spread, and the first towns appeared in Mesopotamia.

How people lived # Villagers farmed with ox-drawn ploughs, made painted pottery, traded copper and shell, and began to live in larger towns with craft specialists and chiefs. What people ate # Grains, dairy, wine Species of the time # Domestic horses (Botai, ~3500 BCE)

d: Bronze — copper alloyed with tin — became widespread from about 3300 BCE in the Near East, Indus Valley and Aegean, and later in China and Europe. Cities, writing, kings, temples, armies and long-distance trade developed: Sumer, Egypt's pyramids, the Indus cities, Shang China and Minoan Crete. Tin had to be traded over long distances, linking civilisations. Horses and chariots spread around 2000 BCE.

Farmers paid taxes in grain, and many worked on state building projects. What people ate # Bread, beer, dates, fish Species of the time # Domestic horses, camels, chickens spread

d: Around 2200 BCE a mega-drought lasting about two centuries affected regions from Egypt to India and China, coinciding with the end of the Akkadian Empire and Egypt's Old Kingdom and stress on the Indus cities. The International Commission on Stratigraphy uses it to mark the start of the Meghalayan Age, named after Mawmluh cave in Meghalaya, whose stalagmites record it.

d: Around 1200–1150 BCE, the interconnected world of the eastern Mediterranean fell apart: the Hittite Empire collapsed, Mycenaean palaces burned, Ugarit was destroyed, and Egypt was weakened by the Sea Peoples. Drought, earthquakes, famine, migrations, rebellions and the breakdown of trade networks probably combined in a 'systems collapse'. Writing disappeared in Greece for centuries.

What people ate # Famine Species of the time # —

d: Iron working, harder to master than bronze but using common ore, spread after about 1200 BCE across the Near East and Europe, and independently or earlier in India (iron at sites in the Ganga valley and south India by 1800–1500 BCE) and in Africa (Nok, Meroë). Cheap iron tools and weapons let farmers clear forests and armies equip more soldiers. In India the Iron Age saw the later Vedic period and the rise of the mahajanapadas; in Europe, Celts and the Greek city-states.

d: The Vedic period (about 1500–500 BCE) is named after the Vedas, composed in Sanskrit by Indo-Aryan-speaking people in the northwest and later the Ganga plain. Early clans herded cattle and fought over pastures; later kingdoms (janapadas) formed, the varna system developed, and the Upanishads explored philosophy. Iron, rice farming and cities emerged by its end.

What people ate # Barley, milk, ghee, later rice Species of the time # Cattle central to wealth

d: Between about 800 and 200 BCE, new philosophies and religions emerged almost simultaneously: the Upanishads, Buddha and Mahavira in India; Confucius and Laozi in China; Zoroaster in Persia; Hebrew prophets; and Greek philosophers from Thales to Aristotle. Karl Jaspers named it the Axial Age. These traditions questioned ritual and emphasised ethics, personal transformation and reason.

What people ate # — Species of the time # —

d: Classical antiquity in the Mediterranean ran from about the 8th century BCE to the 5th century CE — Greece's city-states and philosophers, Alexander's Hellenistic world, and the Roman Republic and Empire. It produced democracy, theatre, history, geometry, Roman law, roads and concrete, and the spread of Christianity. It ended with the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

What people ate # Bread, olive oil, wine, garum fish sauce Species of the time # Lions and elephants captured for arenas

d: From 322 BCE the Mauryas united most of India; after 185 BCE the Shungas, Satavahanas, Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushans ruled different regions. Trade with Rome boomed, Gandhara and Mathura art flourished, Buddhism spread, and the Sangam poets wrote in Tamil.
x: Overview # From 322 BCE the Mauryas united most of India; after 185 BCE the Shungas, Satavahanas, Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushans ruled different regions. How people lived # Cities like Pataliputra, Taxila and Ujjain hosted guilds of merchants and artisans; farmers grew rice, wheat and cotton; and monasteries became centres of learning. What people ate # Rice, wheat, pulses, spices Species of the time # War elephants

d: From about 200 BCE to 200 CE, the Han dynasty in China and the Roman Empire were the world's two great empires, each with about 60 million people. The Silk Road linked them through Parthia and the Kushans. Both built roads, standardised coins and administered vast territories, and both fell into crisis in the 3rd century.

How people lived # Peasants paid taxes in grain and labour; soldiers guarded frontiers; and silk, spices and glass moved across Eurasia. What people ate # Millet, rice, wheat Species of the time # —

d: From about 320 to 550 CE, the Gupta Empire under Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and Chandragupta II ruled north India from Pataliputra and Ujjain. It was a classical age of Sanskrit literature (Kalidasa's Shakuntala and Meghaduta), mathematics and astronomy (Aryabhata's place-value system and rotating Earth), the codification of Puranas and law books, early stone temples such as Deogarh, and the paintings of Ajanta under the allied Vakatakas. Nalanda was founded around 427. Huna invasions and the rise of feudatories ended Gupta power by the mid-6th century.

Guilds of merchants and artisans were powerful, gold coins circulated, and kings increasingly granted land to Brahmins and temples. What people ate # Rice, wheat, sugar Species of the time # —

d: Three major volcanic eruptions in 536, 540 and 547 CE cooled the Northern Hemisphere by up to 2 °C for over a century (until about 660), according to tree rings. Crop failures, the Plague of Justinian from 541 and migrations of steppe peoples like the Avars coincided. The Byzantine and Sasanian empires were weakened just before the Arab conquests, and the Chinese Sui and Tang dynasties rose from the turmoil.

d: From about 500 to 1000 CE, the Western Roman Empire gave way to Germanic kingdoms — Franks, Visigoths, Anglo-Saxons — while the Byzantine Empire continued in the east. Islam rose and spread from Spain to Sindh; Tang China flourished; in India, the Chalukyas, Pallavas, Rashtrakutas, Palas and Pratiharas competed, and temple architecture blossomed. The Vikings raided Europe from 793, and Charlemagne briefly revived a western empire.

The Vikings raided Europe from 793, and Charlemagne briefly revived a western empire. How people lived # In Europe most people were peasants tied to lords’ estates under feudalism, while monasteries preserved learning; in India, village assemblies and temples organised local life. What people ate # Bread, porridge, ale Species of the time # —

d: From roughly the 8th to the 13th century, scholars in Baghdad's House of Wisdom, Cairo, Córdoba, Bukhara and Samarkand translated and expanded Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge. Al-Khwarizmi founded algebra and spread Indian numerals; Ibn al-Haytham pioneered optics and experimental method; Ibn Sina wrote the Canon of Medicine; al-Biruni studied India; astronomers built observatories. Paper, learned from China, made books cheap. The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 is often seen as its end.

Vikings settled Iceland and Greenland and reached North America; Europe's population roughly doubled; vineyards grew in England. Elsewhere it brought droughts, contributing to the decline of the Ancestral Puebloans and possibly Angkor's water stress later.

Conquests killed millions, but the Pax Mongolica revived the Silk Road, allowing Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta to travel, and spreading gunpowder, printing and paper money west. d: The Black Death, caused by Yersinia pestis, reached Crimea in 1346 and swept through the Middle East, North Africa and Europe by 1353, killing about a third to half of Europe's people and many elsewhere. Labour shortages raised wages and weakened serfdom; peasants rebelled (England 1381); Jews were persecuted; art became preoccupied with death. Plague recurred for centuries.

Greek scholars fleeing Constantinople, the printing press and wealthy patrons like the Medici fuelled art (Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael), literature (Petrarch, Shakespeare), and science (Copernicus, Vesalius). Independence movements ended most empires after 1945.

d: The first civilisation with cities and writing.
x: Overview # The first civilisation with cities and writing. Government and society # Each Sumerian city-state (Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish, Nippur, Eridu) was independent. Early power lay with the temple, whose priests managed land, herds and storehouses; by about 2800 BCE war leaders (lugal, ‘big man’) became hereditary kings who built palaces beside the temples. Assemblies of elders and citizens may have advised rulers in early times. Society ranged from the royal family and priests through scribes, merchants and craftsmen to farmers, labourers on temple estates and enslaved war captives. Reforms by Urukagina of Lagash (~2350 BCE) tried to curb officials’ abuses, one of the first recorded attempts at social justice. How people lived # Most Sumerians were farmers and herders working temple and palace lands, paid in barley rations. Cities held craftsmen, merchants, scribes and priests; children of the elite trained for years in scribal schools (edubba). Homes were mud-brick houses around a courtyard. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Each city had a patron god (Inanna at Uruk, Nanna at Ur) living in the temple. Festivals such as the New Year Akitu, epic poetry, lyres from the Royal Tombs of Ur and cylinder seals show a rich culture. Food # Barley was the staple: baked as flat bread and, above all, brewed into thick beer drunk through straws, with temple workers paid daily rations of bread and beer. Dates, onions, garlic, lentils, chickpeas, fish from canals and marshes, and mutton for the wealthy filled out the diet; the Yale culinary tablets (~1750 BCE, Babylonian) preserve the oldest written recipes, mostly stews. Construction and architecture # Sumerians built almost entirely in mud brick, since stone and timber were scarce. Temples stood on raised platforms that grew into stepped ziggurats, such as the Ziggurat of Ur (~2100 BCE), with a shrine on top where the city god lived. Cities had thick walls (Uruk’s were about 9 km long), narrow lanes, courtyard houses, canals, harbours and palaces. They used the arch, the vault and the dome long before the Romans, and decorated walls with cone mosaics. Technology and knowledge # Sumer produced many of civilisation’s foundational inventions: cuneiform writing (from ~3200 BCE, first for accounts), the potter’s wheel and the wheeled cart, the seed plough, large-scale irrigation canals and dykes, bronze casting, a sexagesimal (base-60) number system that survives in our 60-minute hour and 360° circle, standard weights and measures, and early astronomy tracking lunar months. Scribal schools taught mathematics, including multiplication tables and area calculations for fields. How it rose # Farming villages of the Ubaid period (~6500–3800 BCE) in the marshy south of Mesopotamia grew larger as irrigation produced surpluses. Temples organised labour and redistributed food, and trade in timber, metals and stone, absent in the alluvial plain, required administration. During the Uruk

d: Collapsed around the 4.2-kiloyear drought.
x: Overview # Collapsed around the 4.2-kiloyear drought. Government and society # Sargon created the first territorial empire, ruling diverse city-states through loyal Akkadian governors and a standing army of perhaps 5,400 men who ‘ate bread daily before him’. His grandson Naram-Sin went further, declaring himself a living god and ‘king of the four quarters’ of the world. Akkadian, a Semitic language, became the language of government beside Sumerian. How people lived # Farmers and soldiers supplied a standing army; Akkadian became the language of administration alongside Sumerian. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Sargon’s daughter Enheduanna, high priestess of Ur, is the first named author in history. Food # Like Sumer, Akkad lived on irrigated barley and emmer, turned into bread and beer, with dates, sesame oil, onions and fish. State workshops issued standard rations, and sheep and goats supplied wool, milk and meat for feasts. Construction and architecture # Akkadian kings built palaces and temples in their capital Akkad, which archaeologists have never found. Their art is known from victory monuments such as the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin, showing the king climbing a mountain above his defeated enemies, and from a bronze head possibly of Sargon. Technology and knowledge # The empire standardised weights and measures and the calendar across Mesopotamia, built roads and a courier system, and developed a bureaucracy that recorded taxes and trade on clay tablets. Akkadian cuneiform became the script used across the Near East for 2,000 years. How it rose # Sargon, according to legend a foundling raised by a gardener who became cupbearer to the king of Kish, seized power around 2334 BCE, defeated Lugalzagesi of Uruk and conquered all of Sumer, then campaigned from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean and Anatolia. He controlled trade routes for metals, timber and stone. How it declined or fell # Revolts broke out under almost every ruler. Around 2200–2150 BCE a severe drought, the 4.2-kiloyear event, ruined harvests in northern Mesopotamia; settlements like Tell Leilan were abandoned. Gutian highlanders from the Zagros overran the weakened state, and Akkad collapsed into a period of chaos remembered in the poem ‘The Curse of Akkad’. Legacy # The Akkadian Empire became the model of universal kingship for later Mesopotamian, Persian and even Roman rulers. Akkadian remained the international diplomatic language of the Bronze Age, used in letters between Egypt, the Hittites and Babylon.

d: Babylonian astronomers tracked planets and eclipses for centuries.
x: Overview # Babylonian astronomers tracked planets and eclipses for centuries. Government and society # Babylon’s kings ruled with governors, judges and scribes. Hammurabi (r. ~1792–1750 BCE) united Mesopotamia and published 282 laws on a stele, covering trade, property, family, wages and crime, with punishments that depended on social class (nobles, commoners and slaves). The Neo-Babylonian kings (626–539 BCE), notably Nebuchadnezzar II, ruled a large empire through provincial governors and deportations. How people lived # Babylon was a cosmopolitan city of perhaps 200,000 under Nebuchadnezzar, with merchants, astronomer-priests and canal farmers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Akitu festival, the Enuma Elish creation epic and records of planetary motion kept for centuries. Food # Babylonians ate barley bread, beer, dates, lentils, onions, leeks and garlic, cooked with sesame oil; the Yale tablets record some 25 stews of lamb, pigeon and vegetables seasoned with mint and coriander. Fish and dates were cheap staples, and the Code of Hammurabi even regulated beer sellers. Construction and architecture # Babylon became one of the largest cities in the world, with double walls, the blue glazed-brick Ishtar Gate decorated with dragons and bulls, the Processional Way, the great ziggurat Etemenanki (probably the origin of the Tower of Babel story) and Esagila, temple of Marduk. The Hanging Gardens, one of the Seven Wonders, may have been in Babylon or, as some historians argue, in Nineveh. Technology and knowledge # Babylonian scholars developed advanced mathematics, including place-value notation in base 60, solutions to quadratic equations and approximations of √2 accurate to six decimal places (tablet YBC 7289). Astronomers kept nightly diaries for over 600 years and could predict lunar eclipses and planetary positions, knowledge later used by Greek and Indian astronomers. They also produced the zodiac. How it rose # Babylon was a minor town until the Amorite king Hammurabi conquered rival cities such as Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari in the 18th century BCE. Its central position on the Euphrates and control of trade made it the cultural capital of Mesopotamia for over a thousand years. How it declined or fell # The first Babylonian dynasty ended when the Hittite king Mursili I sacked the city in 1595 BCE; Kassites then ruled for four centuries. After Assyrian domination, the Neo-Babylonian Empire rose under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar, but in 539 BCE Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon, reportedly without a battle, after the unpopular king Nabonidus alienated the priesthood of Marduk. Legacy # Hammurabi’s law code, Babylonian astronomy, mathematics, the 7-day week linked to planets and the zodiac influenced Greece, India and the Islamic world. Babylon became a symbol of grandeur and decadence in the Bible.

d: Ashurbanipal's library preserved thousands of clay tablets.
x: Overview # Ashurbanipal’s library preserved thousands of clay tablets. Government and society # Assyrian kings were the god Ashur’s earthly representatives and led annual military campaigns. The empire was divided into provinces governed by royal appointees, with vassal kings paying tribute. Assyrians used mass deportation, moving perhaps 4.5 million people over three centuries, to break local resistance and supply labour. A network of royal roads and relay posts carried messages, letting kings track distant provinces. How people lived # A militarised society where conscripted farmers fought seasonal campaigns and conquered peoples were resettled across the empire. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Lion-hunt reliefs, winged bull guardians (lamassu) and the Library of Ashurbanipal. Food # Assyrians farmed barley and wheat in rain-watered northern Mesopotamia and kept sheep and cattle. Ashurnasirpal II’s banquet stele boasts of feeding 69,574 guests with oxen, sheep, deer, fowl, fish, bread, beer and 10,000 skins of wine. Construction and architecture # Kings built grand capitals: Assur, Nimrud (Kalhu), Dur-Sharrukin (Khorsabad) and Nineveh. Palaces were guarded by colossal winged human-headed bulls (lamassu) and lined with carved stone reliefs of battles, sieges, hunts and tribute. Sennacherib built an aqueduct at Jerwan and gardens at Nineveh watered by canals. Technology and knowledge # Assyria was the first empire to equip mass armies with iron weapons. Its engineers built siege towers, battering rams and ramps, and organised cavalry and logistics on a new scale. Ashurbanipal’s library at Nineveh collected about 30,000 clay tablets on medicine, omens, literature and science, preserving the Epic of Gilgamesh. How it rose # Assur was a trading city whose merchants ran a famous network into Anatolia (the Kültepe tablets, ~1900 BCE). After centuries of ups and downs, the Neo-Assyrian Empire expanded from 911 BCE under kings such as Ashurnasirpal II, Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II and Sennacherib, eventually ruling from Egypt to western Iran. How it declined or fell # After Ashurbanipal’s death (~631 BCE), civil war between his sons weakened the empire. Babylonians under Nabopolassar and the Medes under Cyaxares rebelled and sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE; the last Assyrian army was defeated at Harran (609) and Carchemish (605). A drought may also have contributed. Legacy # Assyria created the model of the provincial empire later used by Babylon and Persia. Its reliefs are treasures of the British Museum and the Louvre, and its library preserved much of Mesopotamian literature.

d: Lasted three millennia, ending with Cleopatra and Rome.
x: Overview # Lasted three millennia, ending with Cleopatra and Rome. Government and society # The pharaoh was a living god, son of Ra, responsible for maat, the cosmic order. Beneath him the vizier ran the government, with officials for treasury, granaries and public works, and nomarchs governing the 42 provinces (nomes). Priests controlled enormous temple estates. Scribes, trained for years, kept records of taxes, harvests and labour. Women could own property, run businesses and sue in court, more rights than in most ancient societies. How people lived # Farmers’ lives followed the Nile’s three seasons; during the flood they worked on royal projects for pay. Scribes, priests and artisans lived in towns; workers’ villages like Deir el-Medina left letters, receipts and even records of strikes. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Gods such as Ra, Osiris, Isis and Hathor; festivals like Opet; mummification and the Book of the Dead; painted tombs, music, board games (senet) and cosmetics. Food # Bread and beer made from emmer and barley were so basic that wages were paid in them; onions, garlic, lentils, chickpeas, lettuce and Nile fish were everyday foods. The rich ate beef, roast fowl, figs, pomegranates, honey cakes and wine; tomb paintings show bakeries and breweries in detail. Construction and architecture # Egyptians built in stone for eternity: the Step Pyramid of Djoser (~2670 BCE, designed by Imhotep), the Great Pyramid of Giza (~2560 BCE, 146 m tall), the Sphinx, the temples of Karnak and Luxor with their forests of columns, Hatshepsut’s terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari, the rock-cut tombs of the Valley of the Kings and Ramesses II’s Abu Simbel. Ordinary homes were mud brick. Technology and knowledge # Egypt developed hieroglyphic writing and papyrus paper, the 365-day calendar based on the Nile and the star Sirius, advanced surveying and geometry for re-marking fields after floods, medicine described in the Edwin Smith and Ebers papyri (including surgery and hundreds of remedies), mummification, glass and faience, sails and large ships, the shaduf for lifting water, and remarkable stone-cutting and transport techniques. How it rose # Farmers and herders settled the Nile valley as the Sahara dried after about 5000 BCE. Chiefdoms in Upper and Lower Egypt competed until King Narmer (or Menes) united them around 3100 BCE. The Nile’s predictable flood gave reliable harvests; the desert protected Egypt from invasion; and the river was a highway for trade and administration. How it declined or fell # Egypt’s 3,000-year history passed through the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, separated by ‘intermediate periods’ of division often linked to droughts and weak kings. After the New Kingdom collapsed around 1070 BCE, Egypt was ruled by Libyans, Nubians (Kushites), Assyrians and Persians. Alexander the Great conquered it in 332 BCE, founding the Greek Ptolemaic dynasty, which ended when Cleopatra VII died

d: Fell in the Bronze Age collapse.
x: Overview # Fell in the Bronze Age collapse. Government and society # The Hittite great king ruled from Hattusa with a council of nobles (the panku), managed vassal kings by written treaties sworn before gods, and had a law code with fines rather than mutilation for many crimes. How people lived # Farmers, chariot warriors and scribes in a kingdom bound by treaties with vassals. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The ‘thousand gods’ of Hatti, laws milder than Babylon’s, and royal archives at Hattusa. Food # Hittites ate barley and emmer bread in dozens of named shapes, porridge, lentils, figs, grapes, honey and cheese. Beer and wine were offered to gods, and royal storage pits at Hattusa could hold grain for thousands of people for a year. Construction and architecture # Hattusa had 6 km of walls with the Lion Gate, the Yazılıkaya rock sanctuary with carved gods, and huge granaries. Technology and knowledge # Early iron working, light three-man chariots, and archives of thousands of cuneiform tablets in several languages. How it rose # Hattusili I unified central Anatolia around 1650 BCE; Mursili I sacked Babylon in 1595 BCE; Suppiluliuma I made the Hittites a superpower rivalling Egypt. How it declined or fell # Around 1180 BCE drought, famine, attacks by the Kaska and Sea Peoples and internal strife led to the abandonment of Hattusa during the Bronze Age collapse. Legacy # The Treaty of Kadesh (~1259 BCE) with Ramesses II is the oldest known peace treaty; Hittite is the oldest written Indo-European language.

d: Their alphabet is the ancestor of Greek, Latin and Arabic scripts.
x: Overview # Their alphabet is the ancestor of Greek, Latin and Arabic scripts. Government and society # Independent city-states such as Tyre, Sidon and Byblos were ruled by kings with powerful merchant councils. How people lived # Sailors, merchants, dyers and shipbuilders lived in crowded island and harbour cities. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Gods Baal and Astarte; ivory carving, glassware and the alphabet carried across the Mediterranean. Food # Phoenicians ate barley and wheat bread, olives and olive oil, fish, figs and dates, and traded wine across the Mediterranean in amphorae. Their colonists spread vine and olive cultivation to North Africa and Spain. Construction and architecture # Harbour cities with breakwaters and dry docks; Carthage’s circular military harbour (cothon). Technology and knowledge # The 22-letter consonantal alphabet (~1050 BCE), Tyrian purple dye made from murex snails, glass production, and navigation by the Pole Star that took them past Gibraltar and possibly around Africa (Herodotus). How it rose # After the Bronze Age collapse weakened Egypt and the Hittites, the Phoenician cities filled the trade vacuum from about 1200 BCE and founded colonies across the Mediterranean. How it declined or fell # They fell under Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian domination; Alexander destroyed Tyre in 332 BCE after a seven-month siege. Legacy # Their alphabet is the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Arabic and possibly Brahmi scripts.

d: Its scriptures shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
x: Overview # Its scriptures shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Government and society # Early Israelites were tribes led by judges; according to the Bible, Saul, David and Solomon ruled a united monarchy (~1050–930 BCE), which split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Prophets criticised kings for injustice. How people lived # Most people farmed hill terraces growing grain, olives and grapes; life centred on clans and village elders. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Sabbath, Passover and Temple worship; the Hebrew Bible’s law, prophecy and poetry. Food # The Seven Species of the Bible — wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates (honey) — were the basis of the diet. Most people ate bread, lentil stews, cheese and yoghurt from goats and sheep; meat was for festivals and sacrifices, and dietary laws (kashrut) defined permitted animals. Construction and architecture # Jerusalem’s First Temple (traditionally Solomon’s), Hezekiah’s water tunnel (~700 BCE) and fortified cities like Megiddo and Lachish. Technology and knowledge # Terrace farming of hill country, water cisterns, and early Hebrew alphabetic writing. How it rose # Hill-country villages emerged around 1200 BCE; the kingdoms formed around the 10th–9th centuries BCE. How it declined or fell # Assyria destroyed Israel in 722 BCE and deported its people; Babylon destroyed Judah and the Temple in 587 BCE and exiled its elite to Babylon. Legacy # The Hebrew Bible, ethical monotheism, the Sabbath and prophetic ideas of justice shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

d: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt.
x: Overview # Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt. Government and society # Kushite kings were chosen from the royal family with priestly approval; queen mothers and ruling queens (kandakes), such as Amanirenas who fought Rome, held great power. How people lived # Farmers along the Nile, herders and ironworkers; powerful queen mothers (kandakes) shaped politics. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The lion god Apedemak, Nubian pyramids and Meroitic script. Food # Kushites grew sorghum, millet and barley along the Nile and kept large herds of cattle, which were symbols of wealth. They also ate fish, dates and dom palm fruit and drank sorghum beer. Construction and architecture # Over 200 steep pyramids at Meroë and Nuri, temples at Jebel Barkal and Naqa. Technology and knowledge # Meroë was a major iron-smelting centre with slag heaps still visible; Meroitic script (still only partly understood). How it rose # Kush grew south of Egypt and, under Piye, conquered Egypt around 744 BCE, ruling as the 25th dynasty. How it declined or fell # Assyrians drove them out of Egypt (~656 BCE); Kush continued at Meroë until Aksum conquered it around 350 CE. Legacy # One of Africa’s great early states; Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt.

d: Destroyed by Rome in the Third Punic War.
x: Overview # Destroyed by Rome in the Third Punic War. Government and society # A republic led by two annually elected suffetes, a council of elders and a popular assembly; Aristotle praised its constitution. How people lived # A merchant and maritime people with large farming estates in Tunisia. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Gods Baal Hammon and Tanit; famous agriculture treatise by Mago. Food # Carthaginians farmed wheat, barley, olives, grapes and pomegranates (the ‘Punic apple’) on rich estates, guided by Mago’s farming manual. They ate puls-like porridge, fish and garum, and Romans copied their recipe for placenta cake. Construction and architecture # A circular naval harbour sheltering ~220 warships and tall housing on Byrsa hill. Technology and knowledge # Shipbuilding with prefabricated, numbered parts, and agriculture described by Mago. How it rose # Founded by Phoenicians from Tyre around 814 BCE, it built a trading empire across North Africa, Spain, Sardinia and Sicily. How it declined or fell # It lost the three Punic Wars to Rome; in 146 BCE Rome destroyed the city. Legacy # Hannibal’s campaign remains a classic of military strategy.

d: At its height ruled ~44% of the world's population (estimates vary).
x: Overview # At its height ruled ~44% of the world’s population (estimates vary). Government and society # The ‘King of Kings’ ruled about 20 satrapies through satraps watched by royal inspectors (‘the king’s eyes and ears’). Darius I standardised taxes, coinage and laws, while respecting local religions and customs. How people lived # Farmers paid tribute; craftsmen from across the empire built Persepolis for wages recorded on tablets. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Zoroastrian fire temples, the Nowruz new year, and audience reliefs of 23 nations bringing gifts. Food # Persians ate wheat bread, rice in some regions, mutton, fruit such as pomegranates, apricots and pistachios, and drank wine. Greek writers marvelled at the royal table, which fed up to 15,000 people a day, and at desserts served throughout the meal. Construction and architecture # Persepolis with its Apadana audience hall of 72 columns and reliefs of tribute bearers; Pasargadae and Cyrus’s tomb. Technology and knowledge # The 2,700 km Royal Road with relay stations, qanat underground canals, the gold daric coin, and a canal linking the Nile and the Red Sea. How it rose # Cyrus the Great overthrew the Medes (550 BCE), conquered Lydia and Babylon (539 BCE), and his successors took Egypt and northwest India. How it declined or fell # Costly wars with Greece, palace intrigue and revolts weakened it; Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela (331 BCE). Legacy # A model of tolerant, multi-ethnic empire; the Cyrus Cylinder; Persian administrative practices adopted by later empires.

d: One of the four great powers of its time (according to Mani).
x: Overview # One of the four great powers of its time (according to Mani). Government and society # Aksumite ‘kings of kings’ ruled vassal states in Ethiopia, Eritrea and at times South Arabia. How people lived # Farmers grew teff and barley; merchants traded ivory and gold to Rome and India. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Early Christianity, giant stelae and the Ge’ez script still used in Ethiopian liturgy. Food # Teff, the tiny grain used for injera flatbread, and barley were staples, with cattle, sheep and honey. Aksum also traded for spices and wine with India and Rome. Construction and architecture # Monolithic stelae up to 33 m tall; one was taken by Italy in 1937 and returned in 2005. Technology and knowledge # Own gold, silver and bronze coins; terraced farming; Ge’ez script with vowels. How it rose # Control of Red Sea trade between Rome, India and Africa made Aksum rich from the 1st century CE. How it declined or fell # Islamic control of Red Sea trade, soil exhaustion and climate change led to decline by the 10th century. Legacy # Ethiopian Christianity (from King Ezana, ~330s) and Ge’ez.

d: 'Land of gold' for Arab geographers.
x: Overview # ‘Land of gold’ for Arab geographers. Government and society # The king (ghana) ruled from Koumbi Saleh and taxed gold and salt trade; succession passed through the king’s sister’s son. How people lived # Soninke farmers and traders controlled gold coming from the south and salt from the Sahara. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Royal courts with elaborate ceremonies described by Arab geographers. Food # People grew millet, sorghum and rice in the Sahel and herded cattle, sheep and goats. Salt, traded from Saharan mines, was so valuable it was exchanged weight for weight with gold in some accounts. Construction and architecture # A twin-town capital with a Muslim merchant quarter of stone houses and the royal town. Technology and knowledge # Organised trans-Saharan caravan trade with camels. How it rose # Soninke kings controlled trade between Saharan salt and gold fields of Bambuk from around 300 CE. How it declined or fell # Almoravid pressure, drought and shifting trade routes led to decline by 1200. Legacy # West Africa’s first great empire; the modern nation of Ghana took its name.

d: Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage spread gold through Cairo.
x: Overview # Mansa Musa’s 1324 pilgrimage spread gold through Cairo. Government and society # The mansa ruled with a council and provincial governors; the Kurukan Fuga charter (1236) traditionally organised clans and rights. How people lived # Farmers, herders, fishers and traders lived under clan-based social orders; griots preserved history in song. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Sundiata epic, Timbuktu’s Sankore university and manuscripts, mud mosques renewed each year. Food # Mali’s farmers grew millet, sorghum and African rice along the Niger, and used shea butter as cooking oil. Ibn Battuta (1352) described millet porridge, fish and baobab sauce. Construction and architecture # Mud-brick mosques such as Djinguereber in Timbuktu, designed by the architect Es-Saheli for Mansa Musa. Technology and knowledge # Manuscript libraries with works on astronomy, medicine and law. How it rose # Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru at Kirina (1235). How it declined or fell # Succession disputes, Tuareg raids and the rise of Songhai. Legacy # Timbuktu’s scholarship; the Sundiata epic.

d: Fell to Moroccan musketeers.
x: Overview # Fell to Moroccan musketeers. Government and society # Askia Muhammad organised provinces, a professional army and Islamic courts. How people lived # River fishermen, farmers and merchants along the Niger. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Islamic scholarship in Timbuktu and Gao. Food # Songhai farmers grew rice, millet and sorghum in the Niger bend floodplain; Sorko fishermen supplied fish. Cattle-herding Fulani supplied milk and butter. Construction and architecture # The Tomb of Askia in Gao (UNESCO). Technology and knowledge # A river fleet on the Niger. How it rose # Sonni Ali (r. 1464–1492) captured Timbuktu and Djenné. How it declined or fell # Moroccan musketeers defeated Songhai at Tondibi in 1591. Legacy # Largest empire in West African history.

d: Gave its name to modern Zimbabwe.
x: Overview # Gave its name to modern Zimbabwe. Government and society # Kings ruled from the Hill Complex; a population of perhaps 10,000–18,000 lived around the stone enclosures. How people lived # Cattle herders and farmers; an elite lived inside the stone enclosures. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Soapstone bird carvings now on Zimbabwe’s flag. Food # Cattle were the main wealth and source of meat and milk, with sorghum, finger millet and beans grown on hillsides. Construction and architecture # Walls up to 11 m high built of granite blocks without mortar, including the Great Enclosure and its conical tower. Technology and knowledge # Gold mining and trade with the Swahili coast. How it rose # Cattle wealth and gold trade from the 11th century. How it declined or fell # Overgrazing, depleted resources and shifting trade routes led to abandonment around 1450. Legacy # Colonial authorities long denied Africans built it; it became a symbol of Zimbabwe’s independence.

d: A blend of Bantu, Arab and Persian cultures.
x: Overview # A blend of Bantu, Arab and Persian cultures. Government and society # Each town had its own sultan and merchant elite. How people lived # Merchants, sailors and craftsmen in coral-stone towns. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Swahili poetry, Islamic architecture and Indian Ocean dress and food. Food # Swahili towns ate rice, millet, coconut, bananas, fish and spices traded across the Indian Ocean. Construction and architecture # Coral-stone mosques and palaces such as Husuni Kubwa at Kilwa. Technology and knowledge # Dhows sailing with the monsoon to Arabia, India and China. How it rose # Bantu coastal communities trading with Arab and Persian merchants from the 8th century. How it declined or fell # Portuguese attacks and the shift of trade after 1500. Legacy # The Swahili language, now spoken by about 200 million.

d: The British looted the bronzes in 1897; some are now being returned.
x: Overview # The British looted the bronzes in 1897; some are now being returned. Government and society # The Oba ruled with chiefs and guilds of artisans. How people lived # Guild craftsmen, farmers and court officials lived in a planned walled city. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Bronze plaques recording court history; the Igue festival. Food # Yams were the central crop, eaten with palm-oil soups, plantains and bushmeat; kola nuts were shared in hospitality. Construction and architecture # Earthworks around Benin City estimated as among the largest built by people before the mechanical era. Technology and knowledge # Brass and bronze casting. How it rose # Emerged in the forests of southern Nigeria around the 12th century; expanded under Oba Ewuare (~1440). How it declined or fell # A British punitive expedition burned the city in 1897. Legacy # The Benin Bronzes, now being returned.

d: Lasted over six centuries.
x: Overview # Lasted over six centuries. Government and society # The sultan ruled with a grand vizier and the Imperial Council; the devshirme system recruited Christian boys to become janissaries and officials; non-Muslim communities (millets) governed their own religious affairs. How people lived # Farmers under the timar system, urban guilds, merchants and a multi-faith population organised in millets. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Coffee houses, Iznik tiles, Sinan’s mosques, calligraphy, music and the Turkish bath. Food # Ottoman palace kitchens at Topkapı fed up to 10,000 people a day; dishes included pilaf, kebabs, börek, dolma, yoghurt and baklava. Coffee houses spread from Istanbul in the 16th century. Construction and architecture # Mimar Sinan’s Süleymaniye and Selimiye mosques, Topkapı Palace and the Blue Mosque. Technology and knowledge # Large gunpowder artillery (the cannons that breached Constantinople), cartography (Piri Reis’s map) and an efficient postal system. How it rose # Osman I’s frontier principality in Anatolia expanded into the Balkans; Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453; Selim I took Egypt and Arabia; Suleiman reached Vienna (1529). How it declined or fell # Military defeats from 1683, nationalism in the Balkans, economic dependence on Europe and defeat in World War I led to its dissolution and the Turkish Republic (1923). Legacy # A multi-faith empire lasting six centuries; modern Middle Eastern and Balkan borders took shape from its collapse.

d: 'Isfahan is half the world.'
x: Overview # ‘Isfahan is half the world.’ Government and society # Shahs ruled with Qizilbash tribal elites; Shah Abbas I built a slave-soldier army to curb them. How people lived # Silk farmers, carpet weavers and merchants; Isfahan held perhaps half a million people. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Miniature painting, carpets, Shia festivals such as Muharram. Food # Rice dishes (polow and chelow) with saffron, herbs and fruit, kebabs, flatbreads and sherbets; tea and coffee spread later. Construction and architecture # Isfahan’s Naqsh-e Jahan square, the Shah Mosque and the Si-o-se-pol bridge. Technology and knowledge # Silk and carpet industries organised for export. How it rose # Shah Ismail I founded the dynasty in 1501, making Shia Islam the state religion. How it declined or fell # Weak rulers and the Afghan sack of Isfahan in 1722. Legacy # Iran’s Shia identity and Persian art.

d: Its cities had some of the best urban drainage of the ancient world.
x: Overview # Its cities had some of the best urban drainage of the ancient world. Government and society # We do not know how the Indus cities were ruled because the script is undeciphered. There are no obvious royal palaces, royal tombs or monuments to rulers, and few weapons. The striking uniformity of brick sizes, weights, seals and city plans over a vast area suggests strong coordination, perhaps by merchant councils, priestly groups or competing elites rather than a single king. Some scholars think it may have been one of history’s more egalitarian early civilisations, though this is debated. How people lived # Most people farmed or herded; city dwellers worked as potters, bead-makers, metalworkers and traders. Brick houses had wells and bathrooms; children played with clay carts and whistles. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Seals with animals and the ‘unicorn’, terracotta figurines, the Dancing Girl bronze, and possible fire altars at Kalibangan. Food # Indus farmers grew wheat, barley, millets, peas, lentils, sesame and cotton, and ate dates and mangoes; residues in pots show stews of meat and dairy. Cattle, buffalo, goat and fish were common, and grinding stones, ovens and large granaries suggest organised food storage. Construction and architecture # Cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan were laid out in grids, often with a raised ‘citadel’ and a lower town. Houses of standard-ratio baked bricks (4:2:1) had courtyards, private wells, bathing platforms and latrines connected to covered street drains with manholes. Mohenjo-daro had the Great Bath (12 × 7 m, waterproofed with bitumen), granary-like structures and around 700 wells. Dholavira carved huge rock reservoirs to store rain, and Lothal had a basin interpreted as a dock. Technology and knowledge # Harappans used a standardised system of cubic chert weights (in a binary-then-decimal series), precise measuring scales, the earliest known cotton cultivation and textiles, drilled carnelian beads with stone drills so fine they remain hard to replicate, bronze tools, wheel-thrown pottery, stoneware bangles, ploughed fields (Kalibangan), and seals carved with animals and script for trade. Dentistry at Mehrgarh, the ancestral site, goes back to ~7000 BCE. How it rose # The civilisation grew from farming villages that began at Mehrgarh around 7000 BCE. Over thousands of years villages across the Indus and Ghaggar–Hakra plains grew wheat, barley and cotton and kept humped cattle. Early Harappan towns (~3300–2600 BCE) developed craft traditions and long-distance trade; around 2600 BCE a rapid transformation produced planned cities, writing and standard weights. How it declined or fell # From around 1900 BCE the big cities were gradually abandoned and people moved to smaller villages in the east (Haryana, the Ganga–Yamuna doab) and south (Gujarat). The evidence points to a weakening monsoon linked to the 4.2-kiloyear climate event,

d: Foundation of Hindu traditions.
x: Overview # Foundation of Hindu traditions. Government and society # Clans (jana) were led by a chief (rajan) whose power was checked by assemblies: the sabha (elders) and samiti (the wider tribe). Priests (purohitas) held great influence through ritual. Over time, clans merged into territorial kingdoms (janapadas) and society hardened into the four varnas. How people lived # Clans of herders and farmers measured wealth in cattle; later, settled villages grew barley and rice. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Hymns of the Rigveda, fire sacrifices (yajna), gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna, and the oral tradition that preserved the Vedas. Food # The Rigvedic diet was based on barley (yava), milk, curd, ghee and honey, with meat at sacrifices; later rice (vrihi) grew in the Ganga valley. Soma, a ritual drink, was praised in hymns. Construction and architecture # Early Vedic people built in wood, thatch and mud, so little survives; archaeologists link the period with Painted Grey Ware sites in the Ganga–Yamuna doab. Fire altars (vedi) were built of bricks to precise geometric plans described in the Shulba Sutras. Technology and knowledge # The Shulba Sutras (~800–200 BCE) contain geometry for altar construction, including statements of the Pythagorean theorem and approximations of √2. Horse-drawn chariots, iron ploughs in the later period, and an extraordinary oral technology of memorisation preserved the Vedas word-for-word for 3,000 years. How it rose # Indo-Aryan-speaking pastoralists, whose ancestry ancient DNA links partly to the steppe, settled in the Punjab (Sapta Sindhu) around 1500 BCE, mixing with local populations descended from Indus-era people. Over centuries they moved east into the Ganga plain, clearing forests with fire and later iron. How it declined or fell # The Vedic period did not ‘fall’ but transformed: by about 600 BCE the clans had become 16 mahajanapadas with cities, coins and kings, and new movements such as Buddhism and Jainism challenged Vedic ritualism. Legacy # The Vedas and Upanishads remain foundational for Hinduism; Sanskrit, ritual traditions, and the concepts of dharma, karma and moksha took shape.

d: Became the core of the Mauryan Empire.
x: Overview # Became the core of the Mauryan Empire. Government and society # Magadha’s kings, from the Haryanka Bimbisara onward, built a strong monarchy with officials, a standing army and land taxes collected directly. How people lived # Rice farmers, ironworkers and traders in a fertile, rising kingdom. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Home ground of the Buddha’s and Mahavira’s teaching; early stupas and viharas. Food # Magadha’s wealth rested on wet rice cultivation in the Ganga plain, along with pulses, sugarcane and fish. Construction and architecture # Rajagriha (Rajgir) was ringed by 40 km of cyclopean stone walls; Pataliputra, founded by Ajatashatru’s successors at the Ganga–Son confluence, became the greatest city of India. Technology and knowledge # Rich iron mines in the Chota Nagpur region, war elephants from the eastern forests, and new siege weapons described in Buddhist texts gave Magadha a military edge. How it rose # Fertile rice land, iron, river trade and capable kings let Magadha conquer Anga, Kosala, Kashi and the Vajji confederacy in the 6th–5th centuries BCE. How it declined or fell # It did not fall but became the core of successive empires: the Nandas, Mauryas and Guptas. Legacy # The Buddha and Mahavira taught in Magadha; it was the seed of India’s first empire.

d: Ashoka turned to Buddhism after Kalinga (261 BCE).
x: Overview # Ashoka turned to Buddhism after Kalinga (261 BCE). Government and society # The Mauryas built one of the most centralised states of the ancient world. The emperor ruled from Pataliputra with a council of ministers (mantriparishad), with provinces under royal princes at Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri. The Arthashastra, attributed to Chanakya (Kautilya), describes departments for revenue, mines, trade, weights, forests, elephants and a network of spies. Megasthenes, the Seleucid ambassador, reported city boards managing trade, foreigners, births and deaths, and an army of perhaps 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants (likely exaggerated). Ashoka added dhamma-mahamattas, officials to promote ethics, welfare and religious harmony. How people lived # Farmers paid around a quarter of their harvest in tax; cities had guilds, markets and wooden mansions. Megasthenes described seven social groups and well-run cities. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ashoka’s dhamma, Buddhist missions to Sri Lanka and beyond, polished stone pillars and the Sanchi stupa. Food # People ate rice, wheat, barley, pulses, sugarcane, dairy and fruit; Megasthenes noted rice eaten from golden bowls. The Arthashastra set rules on storehouses, fair prices and famine relief. Construction and architecture # Pataliputra was protected by a timber palisade about 14 km long with 570 towers, and had a pillared palace hall at Kumrahar. Ashoka erected polished sandstone pillars topped with animal capitals, such as the Lion Capital of Sarnath (India’s national emblem), built thousands of stupas including the core of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, and cut the earliest rock-cut caves at Barabar for the Ajivika sect. Technology and knowledge # The Mauryas built a royal highway (Uttarapatha) from Taxila to Pataliputra and on toward Bengal, with trees, wells and rest houses that Ashoka describes in his edicts. They operated state mines, mints for punch-marked silver coins, irrigation such as the Sudarshana lake in Gujarat, shipbuilding and a polished stone-working technique (the ‘Mauryan polish’) that still gleams. Ashoka’s edicts were the first large body of written Indian texts, in Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts. How it rose # Chandragupta Maurya, advised by the Brahmin strategist Chanakya, overthrew the unpopular Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 322 BCE, after Alexander’s withdrawal from Punjab left a power vacuum in the northwest. In about 303 BCE he defeated or made peace with Seleucus I, gaining Afghanistan and Baluchistan in exchange for 500 war elephants. His son Bindusara expanded into the Deccan, and Ashoka conquered Kalinga (261 BCE), bringing almost the whole subcontinent except the far south under one rule. How it declined or fell # After Ashoka’s death in 232 BCE the empire split between successors, provinces broke away, and revenue fell. Some historians blame the costs of a vast bureaucracy and army; others cite Ash

d: Issued coins with kings' portraits.
x: Overview # Issued coins with kings’ portraits. Government and society # Kings ruled the Deccan through feudatories (maharathis) and queens sometimes acted as regents; inscriptions name kings with their mothers’ names (e.g. Gautamiputra Satakarni). How people lived # Deccan farmers and merchants trading with Rome; Buddhist monasteries supported by traders. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Amaravati sculpture and Karla caves. Food # Rice in coastal areas, millets in the Deccan, pulses and dairy; pepper and textiles were exported to Rome. Construction and architecture # The chaitya hall at Karla, the caves at Nashik and Bhaja, and the richly carved stupa at Amaravati. Technology and knowledge # Coins with ships show maritime trade; they issued lead and potin coins and controlled ports for Roman trade. How it rose # After the Mauryas declined, Simuka founded the dynasty around the 1st century BCE in the western Deccan. How it declined or fell # Wars with the Western Kshatrapas and internal division split the realm into smaller kingdoms by the early 3rd century. Legacy # Linked north and south India; patrons of Prakrit literature such as the Gatha Saptashati and of Buddhist art.

d: Sangam poems describe love and war across five landscapes.
x: Overview # Sangam poems describe love and war across five landscapes. Government and society # Three crowned dynasties, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, ruled with numerous chieftains (velir); bards and poets were honoured at court and assemblies (manram) settled disputes. How people lived # People lived by five landscapes (tinai): hills, forests, farmland, coast and desert, each with its own work and gods. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Sangam love and war poetry (akam and puram), hero stones, Murugan worship.
