Food # Tamils ate rice, millet, fish, meat and fruit; Sangam poems describe five landscapes each with its own food. Black pepper was exported to Rome. Construction and architecture # Brick towns with drainage and wells at Keeladi, port cities such as Kaveripattinam and Muziris, and memorial hero-stones (natukal). Technology and knowledge # Iron smelting (iron furnaces and steel), a Tamil-Brahmi script found even on everyday pottery at Keeladi suggesting widespread literacy, and long-distance shipping to Rome and Southeast Asia. How it rose # Iron Age farming and port trade with the Romans and Greeks enriched the Tamil coast from about the 3rd century BCE. How it declined or fell # The obscure Kalabhra period (~3rd–6th century) displaced the three dynasties until the Pallavas and Pandyas revived. Legacy # Over 2,000 Sangam poems, the Tirukkural and the foundation of Tamil literary culture.

d: Spread Mahayana Buddhism to Central Asia.
x: Overview # Spread Mahayana Buddhism to Central Asia. Government and society # Kushan emperors such as Kanishka called themselves ‘son of heaven’ (devaputra) and ‘king of kings’, ruling through satraps from Bactria to the Ganga. How people lived # A mix of nomad elites, farmers and Silk Road merchants. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Gandhara and Mathura art made the first Buddha images in human form. Food # Wheat, barley, grapes, melons and wine in Bactria; rice and dairy in India. Construction and architecture # Buddhist stupas and monasteries of Gandhara and Mathura, and the giant Kanishka stupa at Peshawar. Technology and knowledge # They issued abundant gold coins and controlled the Silk Road’s southern branches, linking Rome, Persia, India and China. How it rose # The Yuezhi nomads, pushed from China’s frontier, conquered Bactria; Kujula Kadphises united them in the 1st century CE. How it declined or fell # Defeats by the Sasanians in the 3rd century and the rise of the Guptas in India reduced them to minor rulers. Legacy # Gandhara art made the first human images of the Buddha; Mahayana Buddhism spread along their trade routes to China.

d: Weakened by Huna invasions.
x: Overview # Weakened by Huna invasions. Government and society # The Guptas ruled the Ganga heartland directly but most of their empire through feudatories and tributary kings who acknowledged their supremacy. Kings took grand titles such as Maharajadhiraja. Land grants to Brahmins and temples, recorded on copper plates, began a process of decentralisation. Faxian, a Chinese monk who visited around 400 CE, described light taxes, few death penalties and rest houses and free hospitals in the towns. How people lived # Prosperous farmers and guilds; Faxian described peaceful towns and free hospitals. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Kalidasa’s drama, Ajanta murals, temple building, Sanskrit learning and the Puranas. Food # Rice, wheat, pulses, milk products, sugar (crystallised sugar was an Indian invention) and spices; Faxian noted that many people avoided meat, onions and alcohol. Construction and architecture # Gupta builders made some of the earliest free-standing stone Hindu temples, such as the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh and the temple at Bhitargaon in brick, the Udayagiri caves with the great boar (Varaha) relief, Buddhist sculpture at Sarnath, and the paintings of Ajanta (under the contemporary Vakatakas). The Delhi Iron Pillar, over 7 m tall and nearly rust-free after 1,600 years, was made in this era. Technology and knowledge # Indian mathematics and astronomy reached a peak: Aryabhata (476–550) proposed that the Earth rotates on its axis, explained eclipses, calculated π as 3.1416 and used place value; the decimal system with zero was being developed (formalised by Brahmagupta in 628). Medicine (Sushruta and Charaka traditions), metallurgy, textile dyeing and Sanskrit grammar flourished. Nalanda university was founded under Kumaragupta I. How it rose # The Guptas began as a minor family in Magadha. Chandragupta I (r. ~320–335) married Kumaradevi, a princess of the powerful Licchavi clan, which raised his status. His son Samudragupta (r. ~335–375), celebrated in the Allahabad pillar inscription, conquered or subdued kings across northern India and received tribute from the south. Chandragupta II (r. ~375–415) defeated the Western Kshatrapas, gaining Gujarat’s sea trade. How it declined or fell # From around 460 CE the Alchon Huns (Hunas) invaded from Central Asia. Skandagupta repelled them at first, but later attacks under Toramana and Mihirakula devastated the northwest and drained the treasury. At the same time feudatories such as the Maukharis and Maitrakas became independent, trade with the Roman world declined, and the dynasty faded by around 550. Legacy # Called India’s ‘Classical’ or ‘Golden Age’: Kalidasa’s plays and poems, the Puranas compiled, temple architecture, decimal mathematics with zero that later spread to the Arab world and Europe, and art styles that influenced Southeast and East Asia.

d: Spread Indian scripts to Southeast Asia.
x: Overview # Spread Indian scripts to Southeast Asia. Government and society # Pallava kings ruled from Kanchipuram with ministers and village assemblies, using Sanskrit and Tamil. How people lived # Farmers in the Kaveri and Palar basins; port trade from Mamallapuram. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Rock-cut temples and the bhakti poetry of the Alvars and Nayanars. Food # Rice, millets, coconuts, pepper and fish. Construction and architecture # The rock-cut monuments of Mamallapuram, including the Shore Temple, the Pancha Rathas and the giant relief ‘Arjuna’s Penance’, and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram. Technology and knowledge # Developed the Pallava–Grantha script, ancestor of many Southeast Asian scripts. How it rose # Rose in the 3rd–4th centuries around Kanchipuram after the Satavahanas. How it declined or fell # Defeated by the Cholas around 897. Legacy # The foundation of Dravidian temple architecture.

d: Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha.
x: Overview # Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha. Government and society # The Badami Chalukyas ruled the Deccan through feudatories; Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha on the Narmada around 618. How people lived # Farmers and traders of the Deccan plateau. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Temple experiments mixing northern and southern styles at Pattadakal. Food # Millets (jowar, ragi), rice and pulses. Construction and architecture # Cave temples at Badami, the experimental temples of Aihole, and the UNESCO group at Pattadakal blending northern and southern styles. Technology and knowledge # Advanced stone carving and temple engineering. How it rose # Pulakeshin I founded Badami as capital in 543. How it declined or fell # The Rashtrakutas overthrew them in 753; a later branch ruled from Kalyani. Legacy # The Vesara temple style and Kannada inscriptions.

d: Arab travellers ranked its king among the world's four greatest.
x: Overview # Arab travellers ranked its king among the world’s four greatest. Government and society # A powerful Deccan monarchy; Arab traveller Sulaiman listed its king among the four great rulers of the world. How people lived # An agrarian empire of the Deccan with powerful feudatories. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Kannada literature and the Ellora Kailasa temple. Food # Jowar and other millets, rice, pulses and dairy. Construction and architecture # The Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved from a single rock by removing about 200,000 tonnes of stone. Technology and knowledge # Masterful rock-cut engineering. How it rose # Dantidurga overthrew the Chalukyas in 753. How it declined or fell # Western Chalukyas defeated them in 982. Legacy # Kannada literature (Kavirajamarga) and Ellora.

d: Rajendra I raided Srivijaya in 1025.
x: Overview # Rajendra I raided Srivijaya in 1025. Government and society # The Chola king ruled through a hierarchy of provinces (mandalams), districts (valanadus) and village groups (nadus), but villages enjoyed remarkable self-government. Inscriptions at Uttaramerur (~919–921 CE) describe village assemblies (sabhas) choosing committee members by lottery (kudavolai, ‘pot ticket’) from qualified candidates, with rules disqualifying the corrupt and their relatives. Temples were economic hubs, employing hundreds of people and lending money. How people lived # Rice farmers under elected village assemblies; temple towns employed dancers, musicians and craftsmen. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Bronze Nataraja, temple festivals, Tamil devotional poetry and Bharatanatyam roots. Food # Rice from the Kaveri delta, coconut, tamarind, pepper and fish; temple kitchens served thousands. Construction and architecture # The Cholas built some of India’s greatest temples: the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur (1010), whose granite tower rises about 66 m and is crowned by an 80-tonne capstone; the temple of Gangaikonda Cholapuram; and Airavatesvara at Darasuram, all UNESCO World Heritage sites. They also built tanks, irrigation channels and maintained the ancient Kallanai dam on the Kaveri. Technology and knowledge # Chola artisans perfected lost-wax bronze casting, producing the iconic Nataraja (Shiva as cosmic dancer). Engineers moved and raised enormous granite blocks, built irrigation systems in the Kaveri delta, and the navy mastered the monsoon winds to sail to Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Southeast Asia. Land surveys under Rajaraja I recorded tax for every village. How it rose # The early Cholas appear in Sangam literature, but the Imperial Cholas began when Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars around 848. Rajaraja I (985–1014) conquered the Cheras, Pandyas, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives; his son Rajendra I (1014–1044) marched to the Ganga, founding Gangaikonda Cholapuram (‘city of the Chola who conquered the Ganga’), and sent a naval expedition against the Srivijaya empire in 1025. How it declined or fell # Long wars with the Western Chalukyas drained resources. In the 12th–13th centuries, provincial chiefs grew powerful, the Pandyas revived in the south and the Hoysalas in the west. The last Chola king, Rajendra III, was defeated by the Pandya Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan around 1279. Legacy # Dravidian temple architecture, Chola bronzes, the spread of Tamil culture and Hindu-Buddhist influence to Southeast Asia, and an early example of local democratic administration.

d: Last great Buddhist empire in India.
x: Overview # Last great Buddhist empire in India. Government and society # Founded by Gopala, elected by local chiefs to end anarchy (matsyanyaya, ‘law of the fishes’); later kings were Buddhist patrons with feudatory chiefs. How people lived # Rice farmers and traders of Bengal and Bihar. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Buddhist universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila and Pala sculpture. Food # Rice, fish, pulses and sweets made from milk. Construction and architecture # The Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur (Bangladesh), one of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalaya. Technology and knowledge # Pala bronze and stone sculpture and palm-leaf manuscript painting. How it rose # Gopala’s election around 750; Dharmapala and Devapala expanded the realm across north India. How it declined or fell # Weakened by Pratihara and Rashtrakuta wars, they were overthrown by the Senas in the 12th century. Legacy # Nalanda and Vikramashila universities; Pala art shaped Tibetan Buddhism.

d: Razia Sultan was its only woman ruler.
x: Overview # Razia Sultan was its only woman ruler. Government and society # Sultans ruled with Turkic, Afghan and later Indian nobles who received iqtas (revenue assignments) in return for military service. Alauddin Khalji controlled market prices, measured land and built a large standing army to repel Mongols; Muhammad bin Tughlaq experimented boldly with token copper currency and moving the capital to Daulatabad, with disastrous results. How people lived # Peasant villages paid revenue to iqta holders; cities grew with Persian-speaking elites and Indian artisans. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Sufi shrines, qawwali (Amir Khusrau), Indo-Islamic architecture and the birth of Hindustani. Food # Wheat bread, rice, meat dishes such as samosa (sanbusa) and pilaf, and sweets; Persian cuisine mixed with Indian. Construction and architecture # The Sultanate introduced the true arch and dome to India: the Qutub Minar (72.5 m), the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Alai Darwaza, the fortress cities of Tughlaqabad and Siri, and the tombs of the Lodis in Delhi. Technology and knowledge # Paper, the Persian wheel for irrigation, the spinning wheel, gunpowder (late), and new building techniques arrived or spread; Persian became the language of administration. How it rose # Muhammad of Ghor defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain (1192); after his death his slave general Qutb ud-Din Aibak ruled from Delhi (1206). Five dynasties followed: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi. How it declined or fell # Overexpansion, rebellions in Bengal and the Deccan, the founding of the Bahmani and Vijayanagara states, Timur’s devastating sack of Delhi (1398), and finally Babur’s victory over Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat (1526). Legacy # Indo-Islamic architecture, the Hindustani language, Sufi orders, and repelling the Mongols from India.

d: Defeated at Talikota (1565).
x: Overview # Defeated at Talikota (1565). Government and society # Kings ruled through nayakas, military chiefs given territory (amaram) in return for troops, a system later continued by the Nayaka kingdoms of Madurai and Thanjavur. Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529) was a great general, administrator and poet. How people lived # Farmers, temple communities and merchants; Hampi’s bazaars sold rubies and horses. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Mahanavami festival, Carnatic music and Telugu and Kannada poetry. Food # Rice, ragi, pulses and spices; Domingo Paes described markets full of food. Construction and architecture # The capital Hampi had massive walls, the Virupaksha and Vittala temples (with musical pillars and the stone chariot), the Lotus Mahal, elephant stables, stepped tanks and aqueducts across a landscape of giant granite boulders. Technology and knowledge # Advanced water engineering with tanks, canals and aqueducts; large armies using cavalry and later firearms; a busy trade in diamonds, spices and horses. How it rose # Brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family founded the empire in 1336 to resist the Delhi Sultanate’s raids into the south. How it declined or fell # An alliance of the Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565; Hampi was sacked for months. The dynasty continued weakly until 1646. Legacy # Carnatic music (Purandara Dasa), Telugu and Kannada literature and the UNESCO ruins of Hampi.

d: Lasted nearly 600 years.
x: Overview # Lasted nearly 600 years. Government and society # The Ahom king (swargadeo) ruled with great ministers (gohains) and the paik system, in which every adult male owed labour or military service in rotation. How people lived # Wet-rice farmers organised by the paik labour system. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Buranji chronicles and Bihu festivities. Food # Rice, fish, bamboo shoots and rice beer. Construction and architecture # Rang Ghar, Asia’s oldest surviving amphitheatre pavilion, the Talatal Ghar palace and the maidam burial mounds of Charaideo (UNESCO, 2024). Technology and knowledge # Gunpowder and cannon, river naval warfare, and embankments along the Brahmaputra. How it rose # The Tai prince Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills in 1228 and united local peoples. How it declined or fell # Civil war, Burmese invasions (1817–1826) and British annexation after the Treaty of Yandabo (1826). Legacy # Repelled the Mughals at Saraighat (1671); Assamese identity and the Buranji chronicles.

d: Ended after the 1857 uprising.
x: Overview # Ended after the 1857 uprising. Government and society # The emperor held absolute power, supported by the mansabdari system: nobles (mansabdars) held numbered ranks determining their salary and the cavalry they must supply, and were paid through revenue assignments (jagirs) that were regularly transferred to prevent local power bases. Akbar’s finance minister Raja Todar Mal measured land and fixed tax as a share of average produce (the zabt system). Akbar also abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, took Rajput nobles into high office and promoted sulh-i-kul, ‘peace with all’. How people lived # Most people were peasants paying a third or more of their harvest; cities held weavers, merchants and nobles’ households. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Miniature painting, Persian and Urdu poetry, Hindustani music, gardens, and cuisine such as biryani. Food # Mughal kitchens blended Persian, Central Asian and Indian cooking: biryani, pulao, kebabs, kormas, naan and kulfi. Babur missed Kabul’s melons; ordinary people ate khichdi, roti and dal. Construction and architecture # Mughal architecture blended Persian, Timurid and Indian traditions: Humayun’s Tomb (1570) with its charbagh garden; Akbar’s red sandstone city of Fatehpur Sikri and Agra Fort; Jahangir’s gardens in Kashmir; and under Shah Jahan, the white-marble Taj Mahal (1632–1653), the Red Fort and Jama Masjid of Delhi. Pietra dura inlay, domes, arches, minarets and symmetrical gardens defined the style. Technology and knowledge # The Mughals used gunpowder artillery and matchlock muskets (Babur won at Panipat with Ottoman-style tactics), built a road network with sarais, minted high-quality silver rupees (a standard introduced by Sher Shah Suri), and supported astronomy and the production of world-leading textiles. The Mughal economy produced roughly a quarter of world output around 1700 by Angus Maddison’s estimates. How it rose # Babur, a Timurid prince from Fergana descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded India and defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527). His son Humayun lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri (1540) and regained it in 1555. Akbar (r. 1556–1605) won the Second Battle of Panipat and built a stable empire through conquest, alliances and reforms. How it declined or fell # Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707) expanded the empire to its largest extent but spent 25 years at war in the Deccan against the Marathas, emptying the treasury, while reimposing the jizya alienated many subjects. After his death, wars of succession, rebellious governors (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad), Maratha expansion, Sikh and Jat revolts, Nadir Shah’s devastating sack of Delhi (1739) and Afghan invasions shattered central power. The East India Company reduced the emperors to pensioners, and the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was exiled after 1857. Legacy # Indo-Persian architecture, Mughlai c

d: Became the dominant Indian power in the 18th century.
x: Overview # Became the dominant Indian power in the 18th century. Government and society # Shivaji created a council of eight ministers (Ashta Pradhan), paid soldiers in cash rather than land grants, and collected chauth (a quarter of revenue) and sardeshmukhi from neighbouring territories. Under the Peshwas (prime ministers) from 1713, power shifted to Pune, and great chiefs (Holkar, Scindia, Gaekwad, Bhonsle) formed a confederacy. How people lived # Deccan peasants, soldiers and hill-fort garrisons. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Bhakti saints like Tukaram and festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi. Food # Bhakri of jowar or bajra, dal, onion and chillies — a portable diet for fast cavalry. Construction and architecture # Hundreds of hill and sea forts such as Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad and Sindhudurg; the Peshwas’ Shaniwar Wada in Pune; and temples and ghats across India restored by Ahilyabai Holkar. Technology and knowledge # Guerrilla tactics (ganimi kava) suited to mountains; a navy under Kanhoji Angre that challenged the British and Portuguese; and later European-trained artillery under Mahadji Scindia. How it rose # Shivaji (1630–1680) built a state in the Western Ghats by seizing Bijapur forts, defeated Afzal Khan (1659), escaped from Aurangzeb’s custody at Agra (1666) and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. After Aurangzeb’s death the Marathas expanded across India under Peshwa Bajirao I. How it declined or fell # Defeat by Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) cost a generation of leaders. Internal rivalries let the British win three Anglo-Maratha Wars; the confederacy ended in 1818. Legacy # A powerful symbol of regional pride and resistance; the Maratha navy, Marathi culture and much of central India’s princely history.

d: Annexed by the East India Company in 1849.
x: Overview # Annexed by the East India Company in 1849. Government and society # Maharaja Ranjit Singh ruled a secular state in which Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims served in high office; his Khalsa army was modernised by European officers. How people lived # Punjabi farmers and soldiers in a multi-faith state. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Gurdwara langar, Baisakhi and the gilding of the Golden Temple. Food # Wheat roti, dairy, and the langar community kitchen that fed everyone equally. Construction and architecture # He gilded the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple), and built Lahore’s palaces and the gurdwara at the Guru’s birthplace. Technology and knowledge # A modern artillery corps and infantry trained on European lines. How it rose # Ranjit Singh unified the Sikh misls and captured Lahore in 1799, then Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar. How it declined or fell # After his death in 1839, court intrigue and assassinations weakened the state; the British won the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–46, 1848–49) and annexed Punjab. Legacy # The memory of Sikh sovereignty and the Golden Temple’s golden dome; the Koh-i-Noor was taken to Britain.

d: Tipu's Mysorean rockets influenced British rocketry.
x: Overview # Tipu’s Mysorean rockets influenced British rocketry. Government and society # Ruled by the Wodeyar family from 1399; Hyder Ali, a commander, took power in 1761, and his son Tipu Sultan modernised revenue, trade and the army. How people lived # Farmers and silk weavers; artisans for the court. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Mysore Dasara and Mysore painting. Food # Ragi balls (ragi mudde), rice and sambar. Construction and architecture # Srirangapatna fort, Tipu’s Daria Daulat Bagh summer palace and later the Mysore Palace. Technology and knowledge # Iron-cased Mysorean rockets used against the British, which inspired the British Congreve rocket; silk farming introduced by Tipu. How it rose # Hyder Ali seized power from the Wodeyars and expanded Mysore across the south. How it declined or fell # Four Anglo-Mysore Wars; Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, and the British restored the Wodeyars as subordinate rulers. Legacy # Rocketry and Mysore Dasara.

d: A private company ruled India with its own army of ~260,000.
x: Overview # A private company ruled India with its own army of ~260,000. Government and society # A joint-stock company governed by directors in London, supervised from 1773 by Parliament, ruled through a Governor-General in Calcutta and presidencies in Madras and Bombay, with a private army of Indian sepoys. How people lived # Peasants paid high land revenue; weavers lost markets to British cloth. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Company paintings and early printing presses in Calcutta. Food # Indians ate traditional grains and pulses, but Company revenue demands contributed to famines such as the Bengal famine of 1770, which killed about a third of the province’s people. Construction and architecture # Fort William in Calcutta, Fort St George in Madras and neo-classical government buildings. Technology and knowledge # Surveys such as the Great Trigonometrical Survey (from 1802), which later measured Everest; steamships and the first telegraph lines. How it rose # Victory at Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) turned the Company into a territorial power; wars against Mysore, the Marathas and Sikhs extended its rule. How it declined or fell # The 1857 uprising led Parliament to abolish Company rule in 1858. Legacy # Colonial administration, the drain of wealth, and the deindustrialisation of Indian textiles.

d: Ended with Independence and Partition in 1947.
x: Overview # Ended with Independence and Partition in 1947. Government and society # India was ruled by a Viceroy responsible to the Secretary of State in London; about 1,000 Indian Civil Service officers governed 300 million people. About 560 princely states remained under indirect rule. Limited reforms (1909, 1919, 1935) gave Indians some elected seats. How people lived # Most Indians remained farmers facing famines; cities grew with mills, railways and an English-educated middle class. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Bengal Renaissance, new Indian newspapers, and the rise of nationalism. Food # Most Indians ate rice or wheat, pulses and vegetables; famines in 1876–78, 1896–1902 and 1943 killed tens of millions while grain was exported. Construction and architecture # New Delhi by Lutyens and Baker, Indo-Saracenic buildings such as Victoria Terminus (Mumbai) and the Victoria Memorial (Kolkata), hill stations and cantonments. Technology and knowledge # About 67,000 km of railways, telegraph, canals in Punjab, and the census; but designed largely to serve British commercial and military needs. How it rose # After 1857 the British Crown took direct control (1858); Victoria became Empress of India in 1877. How it declined or fell # The mass freedom movement led by Gandhi, Nehru, Bose, Patel and many others, the 1946 naval mutiny, Britain’s exhaustion after WWII, and the end of Indian soldiers’ loyalty led to independence and Partition on 15 August 1947. Legacy # Parliamentary institutions, English as a link language and railways, but also famines, poverty, communal division and Partition.

d: The earliest Chinese writing on oracle bones.
x: Overview # The earliest Chinese writing on oracle bones. Government and society # Shang kings ruled with the help of ancestors, consulted through divination; they led armies, performed sacrifices (including human sacrifice) and controlled bronze production. How people lived # Millet farmers, bronze casters and diviners lived around royal centres. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ancestor worship and oracle-bone divination. Food # Millet in the north and rice in the south, plus pigs, dogs and fermented alcoholic drinks made in bronze vessels. Construction and architecture # The capital Yin (Anyang) had rammed-earth palace foundations and royal tombs; Erlitou (possibly Xia) had the earliest palaces in China. Technology and knowledge # Sophisticated bronze casting with piece-moulds, horse-drawn chariots, silk and the oracle-bone script, ancestor of Chinese characters. How it rose # The Shang overthrew the semi-legendary Xia around 1600 BCE according to tradition. How it declined or fell # The last Shang king, remembered as a tyrant, was defeated by the Zhou around 1046 BCE. Legacy # Writing, bronze art and ancestor veneration that shaped Chinese civilisation.

d: China's longest dynasty.
x: Overview # China’s longest dynasty. Government and society # The Western Zhou kings granted land to relatives and allies in a feudal system, justified by the Mandate of Heaven: heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from tyrants. After 771 BCE royal power faded and states competed in the Spring and Autumn (770–476) and Warring States (475–221) periods. How people lived # Peasants worked land for lords under a feudal order. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Confucian rites, the Book of Songs and Taoist ideas. Food # Millet, wheat, soybeans, vegetables and meat for nobles; elaborate ritual banquets were described in the Book of Rites. Construction and architecture # Walled cities, ancestral temples and elaborate ritual bronze vessels with long inscriptions. Technology and knowledge # Iron tools and casting, the crossbow, cavalry, and large irrigation works such as Dujiangyan (256 BCE), still in use. How it rose # King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king at Muye around 1046 BCE. How it declined or fell # Nomad attacks and rebellion forced the move east in 771 BCE; afterwards the Zhou kings were figureheads until Qin extinguished them in 256 BCE. Legacy # Confucius, Laozi, Mencius and Sunzi lived in the Zhou era, the classical age of Chinese philosophy.

d: Gave China its name.
x: Overview # Gave China its name. Government and society # Qin Shi Huang ruled by Legalist principles: strict laws, harsh punishments, collective responsibility, and abolition of feudal fiefs in favour of 36 commanderies run by appointed officials. How people lived # Peasants were conscripted for armies and huge building projects. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Standardised writing and legalist philosophy. Food # Millet and wheat, with state granaries feeding armies. Construction and architecture # The emperor’s tomb near Xi’an, guarded by about 8,000 life-size terracotta soldiers, horses and chariots; the first connected Great Wall; and the vast Epang Palace. Technology and knowledge # The Qin standardised script, coins, weights, measures and axle widths, built about 6,800 km of roads and the Lingqu canal linking the Yangtze and Pearl river systems, and mass-produced crossbows with interchangeable parts. How it rose # Qin, a western state, became powerful after Shang Yang’s Legalist reforms (4th century BCE). King Ying Zheng conquered the other six Warring States by 221 BCE and named himself First Emperor. How it declined or fell # Massive forced labour, harsh laws and book burning provoked hatred. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, the Chen Sheng–Wu Guang uprising and other rebellions brought down the dynasty by 206 BCE. Legacy # The name ‘China’ probably comes from Qin; the unified written language and centralised state lasted two millennia.

d: Han is still the name of China's majority people.
x: Overview # Han is still the name of China’s majority people. Government and society # The Han combined Qin centralisation with Confucian ideals. Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BCE) made Confucianism the state ideology and founded an Imperial Academy; officials were recommended for virtue and tested on the classics. Commanderies and counties were run by appointed officials, with state monopolies on salt and iron to raise revenue. How people lived # Peasant families farmed with iron ploughs; officials studied Confucian classics. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Silk, lacquer, paper and the historian Sima Qian. Food # Millet, wheat (as noodles), rice, soybeans and tofu (traditionally Han), plus pork and tea. Construction and architecture # Han cities such as Chang’an and Luoyang had walled palaces and markets; tombs held clay models of houses, watchtowers and farms showing everyday buildings. The Han extended the Great Wall west into the Gansu corridor to protect Silk Road trade. Technology and knowledge # Cai Lun refined papermaking around 105 CE; Zhang Heng built a seismoscope (132 CE) and a water-powered armillary sphere; the Han also developed the wheelbarrow, blast furnaces producing cast iron, the rudder, the horse collar and acupuncture texts. How it rose # Liu Bang, a peasant-born official, rebelled after the Qin collapse and defeated the aristocrat Xiang Yu in 202 BCE, founding the Han. He softened Qin’s harsh laws while keeping its centralised structure. How it declined or fell # Land concentration, court intrigue between eunuchs and consort families, and natural disasters led to the Yellow Turban rebellion (184 CE). Warlords who suppressed it carved up China; in 220 the last Han emperor abdicated, beginning the Three Kingdoms. Legacy # The Han defined Chinese identity; the majority ethnic group still calls itself Han. Paper, the Silk Road and the Confucian civil service were its lasting gifts.

d: A golden age of Chinese culture.
x: Overview # A golden age of Chinese culture. Government and society # The Tang emperor ruled through the Three Departments and Six Ministries: a Secretariat drafted edicts, a Chancellery reviewed them, and the Department of State Affairs carried them out through ministries of personnel, revenue, rites, war, justice and works. Officials were increasingly chosen by competitive imperial examinations on the Confucian classics and poetry. The ‘equal-field’ system allotted land to peasant households in return for taxes in grain and cloth and labour service, and the Tang Code (624) became the model for law across East Asia. Wu Zetian (r. 690–705) became China’s only woman emperor in her own name. How people lived # Chang’an was a cosmopolitan city of about a million. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Poetry of Li Bai and Du Fu, tea culture and Buddhist art. Food # Rice, wheat cakes, mutton and tea, which became a national drink; foreign foods such as grapes and sesame cakes were popular in Chang’an. Construction and architecture # Chang’an, the capital, was the largest city in the world (~1 million people), laid out on a strict grid of 108 walled wards around a central avenue 150 m wide, with two great markets where Persians, Sogdians, Arabs and Indians traded. The Tang built the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda to house sutras brought from India by Xuanzang, the vast Daming Palace, Buddhist cave temples at Longmen and Dunhuang, and wooden halls that influenced Japanese temples like those of Nara. Technology and knowledge # The Tang produced the world’s oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra (868), by woodblock printing; early porcelain and sancai three-colour glazed ceramics; mechanical clocks with water-driven escapements; advances in medicine (Sun Simiao’s encyclopaedias), cartography and astronomy (Yi Xing measured the meridian). Alchemists experimenting with saltpetre and sulphur took the first steps toward gunpowder. How it rose # After the short Sui dynasty reunified China (581) but exhausted it with huge canal projects and failed wars in Korea, rebellions broke out. Li Yuan, a Sui general, and his son Li Shimin captured Chang’an and founded the Tang in 618. Li Shimin, as Emperor Taizong (r. 626–649), defeated the Eastern Turks, extended control along the Silk Road into Central Asia, and governed so effectively his reign became a byword for good rule. How it declined or fell # In 751 the Tang lost to the Abbasids at the Battle of Talas, ending expansion westward. In 755 the general An Lushan rebelled; the eight-year An Lushan rebellion devastated the north and may have cost millions of lives. Afterwards provincial military governors (jiedushi) became semi-independent, eunuchs dominated the court, and the equal-field system collapsed. The Huang Chao rebellion (874–884) sacked Chang’an, and in 907 the warlord Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor, opening the Five Dynasties period. Legacy # The

d: The world's most advanced economy of its time.
x: Overview # The world’s most advanced economy of its time. Government and society # The Song placed civilian scholar-officials above generals, recruiting them through greatly expanded examinations. Reformers like Wang Anshi tried state loans to farmers and new taxes; Neo-Confucian thinkers like Zhu Xi reshaped education. How people lived # Commercial towns, rice farmers and scholar-officials. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Landscape painting, printed books and the tea house. Food # Champa rice, tea, restaurants and teahouses in cities; the first known restaurant menus. Construction and architecture # Song builders wrote the Yingzao Fashi construction manual (1103), built tall pagodas and covered bridges, and laid out bustling commercial cities like Kaifeng, shown in the scroll ‘Along the River During the Qingming Festival’. Technology and knowledge # The Song had the world’s most advanced economy: gunpowder weapons and fire lances, the magnetic compass for navigation, movable type (Bi Sheng, ~1040), the first government paper money (jiaozi), large ocean-going junks with watertight bulkheads, and new rice varieties from Champa that doubled harvests. How it rose # General Zhao Kuangyin was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 960 and reunified most of China, ending the Five Dynasties chaos. How it declined or fell # The Song lost the north to the Jurchen Jin in 1127 and moved its capital to Hangzhou. The Mongols conquered the Jin, then besieged Song cities for decades; the last Song emperor died at the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279. Legacy # Printing, the compass and gunpowder spread from Song China to the world; Song landscape painting and porcelain set lasting standards.

d: Founded by Genghis Khan's grandson.
x: Overview # Founded by Genghis Khan’s grandson. Government and society # Kublai Khan ruled China as Great Khan and Emperor, dividing society into four ranks: Mongols, Semu (Central Asians and others), northern Chinese and southern Chinese. The examination system was suspended until 1315 and many officials were foreigners, among them Persians, Uyghurs and, by his own account, Marco Polo. How people lived # Mongol, Chinese and foreign populations under a layered order. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Yuan drama and blue-and-white porcelain. Food # Mongol mutton, dairy and soups combined with Chinese rice dishes. Construction and architecture # The new capital Dadu (Khanbaliq, today’s Beijing) was laid out on a classical grid with palaces, lakes and the White Pagoda, built by the Nepali architect Araniko. Technology and knowledge # Paper money circulated empire-wide. The Grand Canal was extended to Beijing. Guo Shoujing built observatories and calculated the year to within 26 seconds. Postal relay stations (yam) linked China to Persia. How it rose # Genghis Khan’s Mongols attacked the Jin from 1211. His grandson Kublai declared the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and destroyed the Southern Song in 1279, the first time a non-Chinese people ruled all of China. How it declined or fell # Failed invasions of Japan (1274, 1281) and Java drained the treasury, and paper-money inflation and Yellow River floods followed. Plague and ethnic discrimination fuelled the Red Turban revolts. Zhu Yuanzhang took Dadu in 1368 and the Mongols withdrew to the steppe. Legacy # It reunified China after centuries of division and opened the age of Silk Road contact with Europe described by Marco Polo. It also produced zaju drama.

d: Rebuilt the Great Wall in stone.
x: Overview # Rebuilt the Great Wall in stone. Government and society # The founding emperor Hongwu abolished the post of chancellor and ruled personally through ministries, with a secret police (the Embroidered Uniform Guard). Later emperors relied heavily on eunuchs. The examination system and the eight-legged essay dominated elite life. How people lived # A large farming population and busy market towns. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Porcelain, Ming novels and the Forbidden City. Food # Rice and new American crops: maize, sweet potatoes and chillies. Construction and architecture # The Ming built the Forbidden City in Beijing (1406–1420), the Temple of Heaven, the Ming tombs and rebuilt the Great Wall in brick and stone into the form seen today. Technology and knowledge # Zheng He’s treasure fleets (1405–1433) sailed ships far larger than European vessels to India, Arabia and East Africa. The Ming produced famous blue-and-white porcelain, encyclopaedias like the Yongle Encyclopedia, and adopted New World crops such as maize and sweet potatoes. How it rose # Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant orphan and former monk, led the Red Turban rebellion against the Mongol Yuan and founded the Ming in 1368. How it declined or fell # Bureaucratic paralysis, eunuch corruption, costly wars in Korea against Japan, silver shortages, Little Ice Age famines and epidemics led to peasant revolts. Rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing in 1644; the last emperor hanged himself, and the Manchus swept in as the Qing. Legacy # The Forbidden City, the Great Wall in its famous form, porcelain trade with the world and classic novels like Journey to the West.

d: China's last imperial dynasty.
x: Overview # China’s last imperial dynasty. Government and society # The Manchu Qing ruled with a dual Manchu–Han bureaucracy and the Eight Banners military system. Emperors Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong (1661–1796) presided over a long era of prosperity and territorial expansion into Tibet, Xinjiang and Mongolia. How people lived # A population boom to about 400 million farmers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Peking opera and Qing literature. Food # Rice, maize and the Manchu–Han imperial feast. Construction and architecture # The Qing expanded the Summer Palace and Old Summer Palace (destroyed by British and French troops in 1860), and the Potala-style temples at Chengde. Technology and knowledge # Qing China adopted Jesuit astronomy and cartography, but by the 19th century fell behind Europe’s industrial technology. How it rose # The Manchus, unified by Nurhaci, took Beijing in 1644 after the Ming collapse. How it declined or fell # Population pressure, corruption, the Opium Wars (1839–42, 1856–60), the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) and other revolts, unequal treaties, defeat by Japan (1895), and the Boxer Rebellion (1900) undermined the dynasty. The 1911 Xinhai Revolution ended over 2,000 years of imperial rule. Legacy # Modern China’s borders largely reflect Qing conquests.

d: Silla's capital Gyeongju had an observatory (Cheomseongdae).
x: Overview # Silla’s capital Gyeongju had an observatory (Cheomseongdae). Government and society # In the Three Kingdoms period, Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla were monarchies ruled with powerful aristocracies. Silla used the ‘bone-rank’ system: birth into ‘sacred bone’ or ‘true bone’ lineages decided who could hold office. How people lived # Farmers and aristocratic elites. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Buddhist temples such as Bulguksa. Food # Rice, barley and fermented vegetables. Construction and architecture # Goguryeo left painted tombs and mountain fortresses. Baekje’s Mireuksa temple pagoda and Silla’s capital Gyeongju (Cheomseongdae observatory, Bulguksa temple, Seokguram grotto) survive. Technology and knowledge # Silla’s Cheomseongdae (7th century) is among the oldest surviving observatories in East Asia. Baekje transmitted writing, Buddhism and craftsmen to Japan. All three produced superb gold crowns and metalwork. How it rose # The kingdoms took shape from the 1st century BCE to the 4th century CE. Goguryeo grew to rule much of Manchuria under Gwanggaeto the Great (r. 391–413). How it declined or fell # Silla allied with Tang China to conquer Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668), then expelled the Tang by 676 to unify most of the peninsula. Unified Silla later split amid noble revolts and gave way to Goryeo in 935. Legacy # The first unification of Korea, Korean Buddhist art and the transmission of continental culture to Japan.

d: King Sejong created Hangul.
x: Overview # King Sejong created Hangul. Government and society # Joseon was a Neo-Confucian monarchy run by scholar-officials (yangban) chosen by civil service examinations. Royal records (the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty) were kept with such independence that even kings could not read them. How people lived # Confucian society of yangban, farmers and artisans. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Hangul, pansori and kimchi culture. Food # Rice, kimchi (chilli was added in the 18th century) and many banchan side dishes. Construction and architecture # Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces in Seoul, Jongmyo royal shrine and the Hwaseong fortress at Suwon. Technology and knowledge # King Sejong (r. 1418–1450) commissioned Hangul (1443), a phonetic alphabet designed so ordinary people could read. His scholars also built rain gauges, water clocks and sundials. Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s ironclad ‘turtle ships’ defeated Japanese fleets in the 1590s. How it rose # General Yi Seong-gye overthrew the Goryeo dynasty in 1392 and moved the capital to Hanyang (Seoul). How it declined or fell # Japanese (1592–98) and Manchu (1627, 1636) invasions devastated the country. Factional strife and isolation as the ‘Hermit Kingdom’ followed. Japan forced open its ports (1876), made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910. Legacy # Hangul, Confucian family culture and one of the world’s longest-ruling dynasties (518 years).

d: The world's first novel by Murasaki Shikibu.
x: Overview # The world’s first novel by Murasaki Shikibu. Government and society # The emperor reigned in Heian-kyō (Kyoto), but real power passed to the Fujiwara clan, who ruled as regents by marrying daughters into the imperial family. Later, retired emperors ruled ‘from the cloister’ (insei). How people lived # Aristocrats in Kyoto; peasants farmed rice. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Tale of Genji and waka poetry. Food # Rice, fish and vegetables; Buddhism discouraged meat. Construction and architecture # Kyoto was laid out on a grid modelled on Chang’an. Byōdō-in’s Phoenix Hall and shinden-style aristocratic mansions with gardens and ponds also survive. Technology and knowledge # The kana syllabaries developed, letting writers, many of them court women, write Japanese phonetically. How it rose # Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō in 794 to escape the power of Nara’s Buddhist monasteries. How it declined or fell # Provincial warrior clans grew strong. The Genpei War (1180–85) between the Taira and Minamoto ended with Minamoto no Yoritomo founding the Kamakura shogunate in 1185. Legacy # Murasaki Shikibu’s The Tale of Genji (~1010), often called the world’s first novel, and Sei Shōnagon’s Pillow Book.

d: Edo became one of the largest cities.
x: Overview # Edo became one of the largest cities. Government and society # The shogun ruled from Edo, while about 260 daimyo governed their domains. The ‘alternate attendance’ system (sankin-kōtai) made daimyo spend every other year in Edo and leave families there as hostages. Society was ranked as samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. How people lived # Samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Kabuki, haiku (Bashō) and ukiyo-e prints. Food # Rice, miso, tofu; sushi and tempura stalls in Edo. Construction and architecture # Edo Castle, Himeji Castle (completed 1609), Nikkō’s Tōshō-gū shrine and merchant townhouses. Technology and knowledge # Japan was largely closed to foreigners (sakoku) except the Dutch at Dejima, through whom ‘Dutch learning’ (rangaku) brought European medicine and science. Literacy was high and woodblock printing (ukiyo-e) became a mass art. How it rose # Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara (1600) and became shogun in 1603, ending a century of civil war. How it declined or fell # Commodore Perry’s US ships (1853) forced Japan open. Unequal treaties and domestic unrest followed, and samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū overthrew the shogunate in the Meiji Restoration (1868). Legacy # Two and a half centuries of peace, haiku (Bashō), kabuki, Hokusai’s woodblock prints and the foundations of modern Japan.

d: An early Southeast Asian state.
x: Overview # An early Southeast Asian state. Government and society # Funan, known from Chinese records, was ruled by kings, said to descend from the marriage of an Indian Brahmin named Kaundinya and a local queen named Soma. How people lived # Farmers and port traders. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Hindu and Buddhist worship. Food # Rice from the Mekong delta and fish. Construction and architecture # Óc Eo, its port in the Mekong delta, had canals linking it to inland cities, brick buildings and workshops. Technology and knowledge # Canals for drainage and transport. Roman, Indian and Chinese goods have been found at Óc Eo. How it rose # It grew from about the 1st century CE as a stop on the sea route between India and China. How it declined or fell # Shifts in shipping routes through the Strait of Malacca weakened it, and by the 7th century Chenla had absorbed it. Legacy # The earliest Indianised state of mainland Southeast Asia.

d: Studied by Chinese pilgrim Yijing.
x: Overview # Studied by Chinese pilgrim Yijing. Government and society # A thalassocracy: maharajas at Palembang controlled the Strait of Malacca and Sunda Strait through allied ports and the loyalty of sea peoples (orang laut). How people lived # Sailors and traders around Palembang. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Buddhist learning centres. Food # Rice, sago, fish and spices. Construction and architecture # Little survives at Palembang. Related monuments include Muara Takus and, in Java, the Sailendra dynasty’s Borobudur. Technology and knowledge # Navigation with monsoon winds and control of shipping and taxes on the China–India sea trade. How it rose # Srivijaya emerged around 650 CE in Sumatra. The Chinese monk Yijing (671) found over a thousand monks studying there. How it declined or fell # The Chola king Rajendra I raided its ports in 1025. Later, Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit took over its role. Legacy # A major centre of Buddhist learning; Old Malay inscriptions are the ancestors of Malay and Indonesian.

d: Angkor may have been the largest pre-industrial city.
x: Overview # Angkor may have been the largest pre-industrial city. Government and society # The god-king (devaraja) cult linked the Khmer king to Shiva or Vishnu. The king ruled a vast network of provinces through officials and temple foundations. How people lived # Rice farmers supporting temple cities. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Apsara dance and Angkor’s reliefs. Food # Rice, fish (prahok paste) and fruit. Construction and architecture # Angkor Wat (early 12th century, built by Suryavarman II) is the largest religious monument in the world. Angkor Thom, the faces of the Bayon, and Ta Prohm (built by Jayavarman VII) also survive. Technology and knowledge # A huge hydraulic system of barays (reservoirs), canals and moats. Lidar shows Angkor was a sprawling low-density city of perhaps 750,000–900,000 people. How it rose # Jayavarman II declared independence from Java and himself universal monarch in 802 at Phnom Kulen. How it declined or fell # Overstretched water infrastructure, alternating mega-droughts and floods in the 14th–15th centuries, a shift to Theravada Buddhism and maritime trade, and attacks by Ayutthaya (1431) led the capital to move south. Legacy # Angkor Wat is on Cambodia’s flag. Khmer architecture influenced all of mainland Southeast Asia.

d: Inspired Indonesian nationalism.
x: Overview # Inspired Indonesian nationalism. Government and society # Kings ruled from Trowulan in East Java with powerful ministers, most famously Gajah Mada, who swore the Palapa oath not to rest until the archipelago was united. How people lived # Farmers and traders across Java. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Wayang shadow puppetry and Old Javanese poetry. Food # Rice, spices and coconut. Construction and architecture # Red-brick temples (candi) and gates such as Bajang Ratu, with the canals of Trowulan. Technology and knowledge # Rice irrigation, a large fleet and the spice trade. How it rose # Raden Wijaya used a Mongol invasion force to defeat his rival in 1293, then drove the Mongols out. How it declined or fell # Succession wars, the rise of Muslim port states such as Demak and Malacca, and Demak’s conquest around 1527. Legacy # A symbol of Indonesian unity; the Nagarakretagama poem. Bali preserves its Hindu culture.

d: Spread across the largest area of any pre-modern culture.
x: Overview # Spread across the largest area of any pre-modern culture. Government and society # Chiefs (ariki) of ranked lineages, tracing descent from gods and founding canoe voyagers, led island societies. Hawai’i and Tonga developed paramount kingships. How people lived # Settled Hawaii, New Zealand, Easter Island Culture, beliefs and heritage # Tattooing, navigation lore and oral genealogies. Food # Voyagers carried ‘canoe plants’ — taro, breadfruit, yam, banana, sugarcane, coconut and later sweet potato — plus pigs, dogs and chickens. Fish and shellfish provided protein. Construction and architecture # Marae temples, Tonga’s Ha’amonga trilithon, Rapa Nui’s moai statues and Hawai’i’s heiau and fishponds. Technology and knowledge # Double-hulled voyaging canoes navigated without instruments, using star paths, ocean swells, birds and clouds. The Hōkūleʻa voyages since 1976 proved such journeys possible. How it rose # Lapita ancestors reached Tonga and Samoa by about 800 BCE. Their descendants settled East Polynesia, Hawai’i, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa (~1250 CE). How it declined or fell # European contact from the 18th century brought diseases that killed many, missionaries, plantations and colonial annexation. Legacy # The most widespread human migration before modern times, across a third of the globe’s surface.

d: Weakened by the Thera eruption.
x: Overview # Weakened by the Thera eruption. Government and society # Minoan Crete was organised around large ‘palaces’ at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, which acted as administrative, religious and storage centres, collecting and redistributing oil, wine and grain recorded in Linear A. Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, Minoan art shows no images of a mighty warrior-king, and towns lacked strong walls, suggesting a relatively peaceful society under priestly or elite rule, perhaps with prominent priestesses. How people lived # People farmed olives, grapes and grain, raised sheep for wool, fished, and worked as potters and metalworkers. Women appear prominently in religious scenes. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Religion centred on goddesses, sacred horns, the double axe (labrys) and peak sanctuaries; bull-leaping was a ritual sport. Food # Olives, wine, honey, barley, legumes and fish; storage jars (pithoi) filled palace magazines. Construction and architecture # Knossos covered about 20,000 m² with multi-storey wings around a central court, columns tapering downward, light wells, grand staircases, and painted frescoes of dolphins, bull-leaping and processions. It had clay pipes for water and drainage, and some of the earliest flushing toilets. Its maze-like plan may have inspired the labyrinth myth. Technology and knowledge # Minoans were skilled sailors who traded across the Aegean, Egypt and the Levant. They made fine pottery like Kamares ware, gold jewellery and seal stones, and wrote Linear A (undeciphered) and Cretan hieroglyphs. The Phaistos Disc is the earliest stamped text. How it rose # Neolithic farmers settled Crete around 7000 BCE. By about 2000 BCE wealth from olive oil, wine and sea trade allowed palaces to rise. After an earthquake destroyed them around 1700 BCE, even grander ‘new palaces’ were built. How it declined or fell # The eruption of Thera around 1600 BCE devastated Minoan towns and trade. Around 1450 BCE most palaces were burned, and Mycenaean Greeks took over Knossos, writing in Linear B. Minoan culture faded by about 1100 BCE. Legacy # Arthur Evans named the civilisation after the mythical King Minos when he excavated Knossos (from 1900). Minoan art and myths of the Minotaur, Daedalus and Icarus shaped European imagination.

d: Fell in the Bronze Age collapse.
x: Overview # Fell in the Bronze Age collapse. Government and society # Mycenaean Greece was a set of palace kingdoms — Mycenae, Pylos, Tiryns, Thebes — each ruled by a wanax (king) with officials like the lawagetas (military leader). Linear B tablets from Pylos record taxes, rations, land holdings, bronze smiths and slaves, showing a centralised palace economy. How people lived # Most people farmed, raised livestock and worked for palaces as craftsmen or labourers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # They worshipped gods like Zeus, Poseidon and Dionysus, recorded in Linear B. Food # Barley, wheat, olive oil, figs and wine; Linear B tablets record rations. Construction and architecture # Massive ‘Cyclopean’ walls made of huge stones (Greeks later thought giants built them), the Lion Gate of Mycenae (about 1250 BCE), megaron throne halls and beehive tholos tombs like the Treasury of Atreus. Technology and knowledge # Bronze weapons and armour, chariots, and Linear B — the earliest form of Greek, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952. Their ships traded across the Mediterranean. How it rose # Mainland Greek chiefdoms grew rich from about 1650 BCE, as shown by the gold death masks of Mycenae’s Shaft Graves (including the ‘Mask of Agamemnon’). They absorbed Minoan culture and took over Crete around 1450 BCE. How it declined or fell # Around 1200 BCE palaces were burned and abandoned in the Bronze Age collapse. Causes included drought, earthquakes, internal revolts and attacks; Greece entered a ‘Dark Age’ without writing. Legacy # Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey preserve memories of the Mycenaean world; heroes like Agamemnon, Achilles and Odysseus are set in it.

d: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Parthenon.
x: Overview # Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Parthenon. Government and society # Hundreds of city-states (poleis) had different constitutions. Athens built a direct democracy in which citizen men voted in the Assembly and juries were chosen by lot after Cleisthenes’ reforms (508 BCE). Sparta was a militarised oligarchy with two kings. How people lived # Citizens farmed, traded and served as soldiers; women managed households with limited rights in Athens but more in Sparta; slaves did much labour. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Greeks worshipped the Olympian gods and held festivals like the Panathenaia and Dionysia, with theatre. Food # Bread or barley porridge, olives, cheese, figs and wine mixed with water; meat came mainly from sacrifices. Spartans ate a notorious black broth. Construction and architecture # Greek architects developed the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders. The Parthenon (447–432 BCE) used subtle curves to look perfectly straight; theatres like Epidaurus had remarkable acoustics; and cities had an agora, stoas, temples and gymnasia. Technology and knowledge # Greeks developed the trireme warship, advances in geometry (Pythagoras, Euclid), astronomy (Aristarchus proposed a Sun-centred model), medicine (Hippocrates) and engineering, including the Antikythera mechanism, an analogue astronomical computer from the Hellenistic period. How it rose # After the Greek Dark Ages, city-states revived from the 8th century BCE with the alphabet, colonies and the Olympic Games (776 BCE). They defeated Persia at Marathon (490), Salamis (480) and Plataea (479). How it declined or fell # The Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) exhausted Athens and Sparta. Thebes briefly dominated, then Philip II of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea (338 BCE). Rome conquered Greece in 146 BCE. Legacy # Democracy, philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle), drama (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Aristophanes), history (Herodotus, Thucydides), the Olympic Games, mathematics and science all shaped Western and world civilisation.

d: Reached the Beas River in Punjab (326 BCE).
x: Overview # Reached the Beas River in Punjab (326 BCE). Government and society # Philip II reformed Macedon into a powerful monarchy and dominated Greece through the League of Corinth. Alexander ruled as king of Macedon, hegemon of Greece, pharaoh of Egypt and Great King of Persia, keeping Persian satrapies and officials, and encouraging intermarriage between Macedonians and Persians (the Susa weddings, 324 BCE). How people lived # Soldiers settled in new cities; Greek became the common language of trade. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Greek gods and culture mixed with Egyptian, Persian and Indian traditions. Food # Greek foods spread across the east; Alexander’s troops encountered sugarcane (‘honey without bees’) in India. Construction and architecture # Alexander founded around 20 cities named Alexandria, including Alexandria in Egypt with its Lighthouse (Pharos) and Library. The royal tombs at Vergina, including Philip II’s, contain painted frescoes and gold. Technology and knowledge # The Macedonian phalanx with 6-metre sarissa pikes, combined with Companion cavalry, plus siege engineers who built towers and torsion catapults, made Alexander’s army formidable. How it rose # Philip II (r. 359–336 BCE) built a professional army and defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea (338). Alexander, after Philip’s assassination, conquered Persia, Egypt and lands to the Indus in 334–325 BCE. How it declined or fell # Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32, without a clear heir. His generals (the Diadochi) fought the Wars of the Successors, splitting the empire into the Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid kingdoms; Rome conquered Macedon in 168 BCE. Legacy # The Hellenistic age spread Greek language, art and science from Egypt to Afghanistan and influenced Indian art in Gandhara.

d: Conquered the Mediterranean; ended with Julius Caesar and Augustus.
x: Overview # Conquered the Mediterranean; ended with Julius Caesar and Augustus. Government and society # The Roman Republic (509–27 BCE) balanced power among two consuls elected annually, a Senate of former magistrates that controlled finances and foreign policy, and popular assemblies that elected officials and passed laws. Tribunes of the plebs could veto actions harmful to commoners. In emergencies, a dictator could be appointed for six months. The Twelve Tables (451–450 BCE) were Rome’s first written laws. How people lived # Most Romans were farmers or urban workers; patron-client relationships tied rich and poor. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Romans honoured ancestors and gods like Jupiter, and valued virtue (virtus) and duty (pietas). Food # Puls (wheat porridge), bread, olives, cheese and vegetables; garum fish sauce. Construction and architecture # The Republic built the Via Appia (312 BCE), aqueducts like the Aqua Appia, basilicas and temples in the Forum, and invented Roman concrete with volcanic ash (pozzolana), allowing arches and vaults. Technology and knowledge # Roman engineers built roads, bridges and aqueducts; the legion’s organisation, training and equipment (the gladius and pilum) made it highly effective. How it rose # After expelling King Tarquin the Proud in 509 BCE, Rome conquered its Latin, Etruscan and Samnite neighbours, defeated Pyrrhus and Carthage (Punic Wars), and took Greece, Spain and the eastern Mediterranean. How it declined or fell # Conquest brought wealth to the elite while small farmers lost land. The Gracchi brothers’ reforms ended in their murders; Marius’s army reforms created soldiers loyal to generals; civil wars between Marius and Sulla, then Caesar and Pompey, followed. After Caesar’s assassination, Octavian became Augustus in 27 BCE. Legacy # The Republic inspired the US Constitution and later democracies: the Senate, checks and balances, vetoes and the idea of citizenship.

d: The Western Empire fell in 476 CE; the Eastern lasted to 1453.
x: Overview # The Western Empire fell in 476 CE; the Eastern lasted to 1453. Government and society # Augustus kept the outward forms of the Republic (Senate, consuls) but held real power as princeps, ‘first citizen’, commanding the army and controlling key provinces. The empire was divided into provinces governed by senators or imperial appointees. Roman law developed into a sophisticated system, and citizenship expanded until in 212 CE the emperor Caracalla granted it to nearly all free inhabitants. Society divided into senators, equestrians, citizens, freedmen and enslaved people. How people lived # City dwellers in insulae, peasants and enslaved workers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Baths, games, Latin literature. Food # Bread was so central that the state distributed free grain (the annona) to about 200,000 Roman citizens; Egyptian grain fleets fed the capital. Wealthy Romans dined reclining on dormice, oysters and peacock, recorded in Apicius’ cookbook. Construction and architecture # Romans perfected the arch, vault and dome using concrete: the Pantheon (~125 CE) still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome. They built the Colosseum (seating ~50,000), aqueducts like the Pont du Gard, baths, basilicas, triumphal arches, theatres, apartment blocks (insulae) and planned colonial towns with grid streets, forums and sewers like the Cloaca Maxima. Technology and knowledge # Roman engineers built over 80,000 km of paved roads, aqueducts carrying water by gravity over long distances, hydraulic mining, water mills, cranes powered by treadwheels, underfloor heating (hypocausts), glass-blowing, and concrete using volcanic ash that self-heals in seawater. Medicine advanced under Galen, and the Julian calendar (46 BCE) was a lasting reform. How it rose # Rome grew from a city-state to master of Italy and then the Mediterranean through disciplined citizen legions, alliances, colonies and road-building. After a century of civil wars ended with Octavian’s victory at Actium (31 BCE), the Senate granted him the title Augustus (27 BCE), beginning the Empire. Expansion continued until Trajan’s reign (117 CE). How it declined or fell # The Western Empire weakened over centuries: the Crisis of the Third Century (235–284) brought civil wars, plague, invasions and inflation; Diocletian divided the empire; and it was formally split in 395. Pressure from Germanic peoples displaced by the Huns, the Visigoths’ sack of Rome (410), the Vandals’ seizure of North Africa’s grain (439) and their sack of Rome (455) left the West unable to pay its armies. In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus. The Eastern Empire continued until 1453. Legacy # Roman law underlies many legal systems; Latin gave rise to the Romance languages and much scientific vocabulary; Christianity spread through the empire; and Roman architecture, engineering, the calendar and ideas of citizenship shaped Europe and beyond.

d: Fell to the Ottomans in 1453.
x: Overview # Fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Government and society # The Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire was ruled by an emperor seen as God’s representative, crowned by the Patriarch of Constantinople. A large salaried bureaucracy, the theme system of military provinces and a professional army supported him. Justinian’s Corpus Juris Civilis codified Roman law. Palace intrigue, blinding of rivals and coups were common. How people lived # Constantinople had perhaps 500,000 people; chariot races in the Hippodrome drew fans of Blue and Green factions. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Orthodox Christianity, icons and theological debates, including the Iconoclasm controversy. Food # Bread, fish, olive oil, cheese, wine and fasting foods for Orthodox fasts. Construction and architecture # Hagia Sophia (537), whose dome seemed to float, was the world’s largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years. The Theodosian Walls protected Constantinople for a millennium. Byzantine mosaics decorate Ravenna and Kyiv. Technology and knowledge # Greek fire, a liquid weapon that burned on water, destroyed Arab fleets. The gold solidus coin was stable for 700 years, and Constantinople’s silk industry used smuggled silkworms. How it rose # Constantine founded Constantinople (330) on the site of Byzantium. When the Western Empire fell in 476, the East continued. Justinian (r. 527–565) reconquered Italy and North Africa. How it declined or fell # Arab conquests took Egypt and Syria in the 7th century; Seljuks won at Manzikert (1071); the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople (1204). The Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453. Legacy # Byzantium preserved Greek classics, spread Orthodox Christianity and the Cyrillic alphabet to the Slavs, and its scholars helped spark the Renaissance.

d: Conquered by Rome except in Ireland and northern Britain.
x: Overview # Conquered by Rome except in Ireland and northern Britain. Government and society # Celtic peoples were organised into tribes led by kings or chiefs and warrior aristocracies. Druids served as priests, judges, teachers and keepers of oral law and lore; they trained for up to 20 years. Women sometimes led, like Boudica of the Iceni. How people lived # People farmed, raised cattle and lived in roundhouses; feasting and raiding were central. Culture, beliefs and heritage # They worshipped many gods, held sacred groves, and celebrated Samhain (ancestor of Halloween). Food # Wheat, barley, pork, beer and mead. Construction and architecture # Celts built hillforts such as Maiden Castle, fortified towns (oppida) like Bibracte and Manching, crannogs (lake dwellings), and roundhouses. Technology and knowledge # Celts were expert ironworkers, inventing chain mail and making fine swords, shields and torcs in the curvilinear La Tène style. How it rose # The Hallstatt culture (about 800–450 BCE) in Austria grew rich from salt mining; La Tène culture (from about 450 BCE) spread across Europe. Celts sacked Rome around 390 BCE and Delphi (279 BCE), and settled Anatolia as the Galatians. How it declined or fell # Rome conquered northern Italy, Spain, Gaul (Caesar) and Britain. Germanic migrations later pushed Celtic speakers to the fringes. Legacy # Celtic languages survive in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Brittany; Celtic art inspired the Book of Kells.

d: Reached North America ~1000 CE.
x: Overview # Reached North America ~1000 CE. Government and society # Viking Age Scandinavia had kings, jarls (earls) and free men (karls), with thralls (slaves) at the bottom. Free men met at the thing assembly to settle disputes and make laws; Iceland’s Althing (930) is one of the oldest parliaments. How people lived # Most Vikings were farmers, fishers and traders; raiding was seasonal. Culture, beliefs and heritage # They worshipped Odin, Thor and Freyja; skaldic poetry praised heroes. Food # Porridge, bread, dried fish, meat and dairy; ale and mead. Construction and architecture # Longhouses, ring fortresses like Trelleborg, and later stave churches. Technology and knowledge # Clinker-built longships with shallow drafts could cross oceans and sail up rivers; sun compasses may have aided navigation. They wrote in runes. How it rose # Population pressure, wealth from trade and fast ships led Scandinavians to raid Lindisfarne (793). They settled England’s Danelaw, Ireland (Dublin), Normandy, Iceland and Greenland, reached North America (about 1000), and as the Rus founded states in Russia. How it declined or fell # Christianisation, stronger kingdoms and the defeat at Stamford Bridge (1066) ended the Viking Age. Legacy # Normandy, Kievan Rus, Iceland’s sagas, and words like ‘sky’, ‘egg’ and ‘window’ in English.

d: 'Neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire' — Voltaire.
x: Overview # ‘Neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire’ — Voltaire. Government and society # The Holy Roman Empire was a loose union of hundreds of kingdoms, duchies, bishoprics and free cities in central Europe. The emperor was elected by prince-electors (seven under the Golden Bull of 1356) and crowned by the pope until 1530. The Imperial Diet (Reichstag) and courts brought rulers together, but real power lay with the princes. From 1438 the emperors were almost always Habsburgs. How people lived # Peasants worked lords’ land; towns like Nuremberg and the Hanseatic League’s Lübeck flourished through trade. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Catholic and, after Luther, Protestant Christianity defined the empire’s cultural map. Food # Bread, beer, cabbage and pork. Construction and architecture # Romanesque cathedrals at Speyer, Worms and Mainz, Charlemagne’s Palatine Chapel at Aachen where kings were crowned, and Gothic masterpieces like Cologne Cathedral. Technology and knowledge # Gutenberg’s printing press at Mainz (around 1450) spread knowledge; mining in Saxony and Bohemia (silver of Joachimsthal gave us the word ‘dollar’) and clockmaking flourished. How it rose # Otto I of Saxony defeated the Magyars at Lechfeld (955) and was crowned emperor by the pope in 962, reviving Charlemagne’s title. How it declined or fell # The Investiture Controversy, the Reformation and the devastating Thirty Years’ War (1618–48) weakened imperial authority; the Peace of Westphalia gave princes near-sovereignty. Napoleon defeated Austria and forced Francis II to dissolve the empire in 1806. Legacy # German federalism, as Voltaire mocked: ‘neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire’.

d: Destroyed by the Mongols.
x: Overview # Destroyed by the Mongols. Government and society # Kievan Rus was a federation of East Slavic principalities ruled by the Rurikid dynasty, with the Grand Prince of Kiev at the top. Princes ruled cities with their retinues (druzhina) and councils of boyars; town assemblies (veche) were powerful, especially in Novgorod. Yaroslav the Wise issued the Russkaya Pravda law code. How people lived # Most people farmed rye and wheat in forests; cities hosted merchants and craftsmen. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Orthodox Christianity, icons and Old Church Slavonic in Cyrillic script. Food # Rye bread, kasha and kvass. Construction and architecture # St Sophia’s Cathedral in Kyiv (1037), with Byzantine mosaics, the Golden Gate, and wooden churches and fortresses. Technology and knowledge # Rus traders sailed the Dnieper ‘route from the Varangians to the Greeks’, trading furs, honey, wax and slaves for Byzantine silks and silver. How it rose # Varangian (Viking) chiefs led by Rurik and Oleg took control of Novgorod and Kiev in the late 9th century. Vladimir the Great’s baptism (988) brought Orthodox Christianity. How it declined or fell # Succession disputes split the realm, and the Mongols destroyed Kiev in 1240, ending its unity. Legacy # Christianisation by Vladimir (988); shared heritage of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.

d: 'The empire on which the sun never sets' (first).
x: Overview # ‘The empire on which the sun never sets’ (first). Government and society # The Spanish monarchy governed its American empire through the Council of the Indies in Spain and viceroys in Mexico City (New Spain) and Lima (Peru), later also Bogotá and Buenos Aires. Audiencias served as courts, and the encomienda system gave conquistadors the labour of Indigenous people in return for ‘protection’ and Christian instruction. A rigid caste system ranked people by birth and ancestry. How people lived # Indigenous people worked in mines and haciendas under forced labour (mita); enslaved Africans worked on plantations; Spanish-born elites held power. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Catholic missions converted millions, often blending with Indigenous beliefs, as with the Virgin of Guadalupe. Food # The Columbian Exchange brought maize, potatoes, tomatoes and chocolate to Europe and wheat and cattle to the Americas. Construction and architecture # Spanish colonial cities were laid out on grids around a central plaza with a cathedral and government palace, following the Laws of the Indies (1573). Baroque churches, such as Mexico City’s Metropolitan Cathedral built over the Aztec Templo Mayor, and missions across California and South America remain. Technology and knowledge # Spanish ships, cannon, steel and horses gave conquistadors advantages, while galleons carried silver across the Atlantic and Pacific (Manila galleons from 1565). Silver from Potosí and Zacatecas, refined with mercury amalgamation, flooded the world economy, much of it ending up in China. How it rose # After completing the Reconquista (1492), Spain sponsored Columbus, then conquered the Aztecs (1521) and Incas (1532) with Indigenous allies and the devastation of smallpox. Under Charles V and Philip II, Spain combined American silver with Habsburg possessions in Europe, becoming the dominant world power in the 16th century. How it declined or fell # Costly wars, inflation from silver, the expulsion of Jews and Moriscos, and the defeat of the Armada weakened Spain. Napoleon’s invasion of Spain (1808) triggered independence wars led by Bolívar, San Martín and Hidalgo, and most of Latin America was free by 1825. Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines to the US in 1898. Legacy # Spanish is the world’s second-most spoken native language; Catholicism, legal systems and mixed (mestizo) societies shaped Latin America. The conquest also caused the deaths of millions of Indigenous people and the African slave trade to the Americas.

d: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498.
x: Overview # Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. Government and society # Portugal’s empire was a network of fortified trading posts (feitorias) and colonies, governed through viceroys in Goa (the Estado da Índia) and captaincies in Brazil. The crown controlled the spice trade through the Casa da Índia. The cartaz pass system forced Asian ships to buy Portuguese permits. How people lived # Settlers, sailors, missionaries and enslaved Africans moved across the empire; Brazil’s sugar economy relied on slavery. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Catholic missions spread across Asia; Goan culture blends Portuguese and Konkani traditions. Food # Spice trade; chillies brought from America to India. Construction and architecture # Portuguese forts at Elmina (Ghana), Mombasa (Fort Jesus), Diu, Malacca and Macau, and Goa’s Basilica of Bom Jesus with St Francis Xavier’s tomb, remain. The Manueline style decorated Lisbon’s Jerónimos Monastery with maritime motifs. Technology and knowledge # Portuguese navigators developed the caravel, which could sail against the wind, and used the astrolabe and quadrant to calculate latitude, building on Prince Henry’s patronage. Mapmakers charted Africa’s coast. How it rose # Under Prince Henry the Navigator, Portugal explored Africa’s coast; Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape (1488) and Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (1498). Afonso de Albuquerque seized Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515), and Cabral claimed Brazil (1500). How it declined or fell # The Dutch and English took most Asian posts in the 17th century; Brazil became independent in 1822. Portugal clung to Africa until the Carnation Revolution of 1974 led to independence for Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau. India took Goa in 1961, and Macau returned to China in 1999. Legacy # Portuguese is spoken by about 260 million people. Portugal brought chillies, cashews, potatoes and papaya to India, and words like ‘pão’ (pav) and ‘janela’.

d: India was its most valuable colony.
x: Overview # India was its most valuable colony. Government and society # The British Empire was a patchwork: self-governing dominions (Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa) had their own parliaments; crown colonies were ruled by governors; India was ruled first by the East India Company and from 1858 by a Viceroy; and protectorates and princely states were governed indirectly through local rulers. Policy was set in London by Parliament and the Colonial and India Offices. Colonised peoples had little or no representation. How people lived # In Britain, imperial trade brought tea, sugar, cotton and wealth, especially to the middle and upper classes. In colonies, life ranged from settler farms to plantations worked by indentured labourers and Indian villages paying heavy revenue. Culture, beliefs and heritage # British imperial culture promoted a sense of racial and civilisational superiority, while colonised societies blended and resisted it, producing new literatures in English and movements of cultural revival. Food # Tea, sugar and spices were traded; slave plantations produced sugar. Construction and architecture # Britain built government houses, railway stations and churches in neoclassical, Gothic Revival and Indo-Saracenic styles, such as Mumbai’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, Kolkata’s Victoria Memorial and Lutyens’s New Delhi.
