Cantonments and hill stations like Shimla separated Europeans from local populations. Technology and knowledge # Britain’s Industrial Revolution gave it steamships, railways, the telegraph (an undersea cable reached India in 1870) and the Maxim gun. These let it move troops and goods across the world. Surveys mapped colonies, and botanical gardens like Kew transferred crops — tea to India, rubber to Malaya. How it rose # England founded colonies in North America and the Caribbean in the 17th century, built on sugar and the Atlantic slave trade. After the Seven Years’ War (1756–63) and Plassey (1757) it dominated North America and India. Despite losing the 13 colonies in 1783, it expanded across India, Australia, Africa and Asia. At its height in 1920 it ruled about a quarter of the world’s land and people — ‘the empire on which the sun never set’. How it declined or fell # Two world wars bankrupted Britain, and nationalist movements, above all in India, made empire impossible to sustain. India and Pakistan became independent in 1947; Burma and Ceylon in 1948; the Suez Crisis (1956) showed Britain could no longer act alone; and most African and Caribbean colonies became independent in the 1950s–60s. The handover of Hong Kong to China in 1997 is often seen as its end. Legacy # English became a global language, and parliamentary government, common law, railways and cricket spread through former colonies, many now in the Commonwealth. The empire’s legacies also include famines, partitions (India, Ireland, Palestine), arbitrary borders, the slave trade and the

d: Ended in the 1917 revolution.
x: Overview # Ended in the 1917 revolution. Government and society # The Russian Empire was an autocracy: the tsar held unlimited power, supported by the nobility and the Orthodox Church, with a large bureaucracy and secret police. Peter the Great created a Senate and Table of Ranks. Serfdom bound most peasants to the land until Alexander II freed 23 million serfs in 1861. After the 1905 revolution an elected Duma was created but had limited power. How people lived # Most people were peasants living in village communes (mir), paying taxes and serving long military terms. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Orthodox Christianity, icons and church music shaped Russian culture. Food # Rye bread, cabbage soup (shchi) and kasha. Construction and architecture # Peter the Great built St Petersburg from 1703 on the Neva marshes as a European-style capital, with the Winter Palace and Peterhof designed by architects like Rastrelli. Onion-domed Orthodox churches such as St Basil’s Cathedral in Moscow (from Ivan IV’s era) are iconic. Technology and knowledge # Russia built the Trans-Siberian Railway (1891–1916), the longest in the world. Dmitri Mendeleev created the periodic table (1869), and Alexander Popov experimented with radio. How it rose # Muscovy threw off Mongol rule under Ivan III and was proclaimed a tsardom by Ivan IV (1547). After the Time of Troubles, the Romanovs (from 1613) expanded across Siberia to the Pacific. Peter the Great defeated Sweden and declared the Russian Empire in 1721; Catherine the Great took Crimea and parts of Poland. It became the largest country on Earth. How it declined or fell # Defeat by Japan (1905), revolution, the strain of World War I and food shortages led to the February Revolution of 1917, when Nicholas II abdicated. The Bolsheviks seized power in October, and the royal family was executed in 1918. Legacy # The empire left a vast multi-ethnic territory, and a cultural golden age: Pushkin, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Chekhov and Tchaikovsky.

d: Dissolved into 15 states in 1991.
x: Overview # Dissolved into 15 states in 1991. Government and society # The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) was a one-party state ruled by the Communist Party, nominally a federation of 15 republics. Real power lay with the Party’s Politburo and General Secretary. Under Stalin, the secret police (NKVD, later KGB) arrested millions, and the Gulag labour camp system held about 18 million people over its history. The economy was centrally planned through five-year plans. How people lived # Soviet citizens had guaranteed jobs, free education and health care, and subsidised housing, but faced shortages, queues and limited freedom. Women entered the workforce in large numbers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Socialist realism dictated art; writers such as Pasternak and Solzhenitsyn faced persecution. The state promoted atheism. Food # Bread, potatoes and cabbage; famines in 1932–33 killed millions. Construction and architecture # Early Soviet architects explored Constructivism; Stalin preferred monumental ‘Stalinist Empire’ style, such as Moscow’s ‘Seven Sisters’ skyscrapers and ornate metro stations. From the 1950s, millions of prefabricated apartment blocks (khrushchyovkas) were built to address housing shortages. Technology and knowledge # Rapid industrialisation built steel, dams and tractors. The USSR tested an atomic bomb in 1949, launched Sputnik (1957), the first satellite, and sent Yuri Gagarin into orbit (1961) and Valentina Tereshkova (1963), the first woman. It was a world leader in rocketry, mathematics and chess. How it rose # The Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power in the October Revolution of 1917 and won the Russian Civil War (1918–21). The USSR was formed in 1922. Stalin’s forced collectivisation and industrialisation transformed the economy at the cost of famines, including the Holodomor in Ukraine. Victory over Nazi Germany in 1945, at the cost of about 27 million lives, made it a superpower controlling Eastern Europe. How it declined or fell # Economic stagnation under Brezhnev, the costly war in Afghanistan (1979–89), and the Chernobyl disaster weakened the system. Mikhail Gorbachev’s reforms — glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring) — let nationalism and criticism surface. Eastern European communist regimes fell in 1989, a hard-line coup failed in August 1991, and on 26 December 1991 the USSR dissolved into 15 states. Legacy # The USSR defeated Nazism, achieved mass literacy and launched the space age, but its terror, famines and the Gulag killed millions. The Cold War rivalry shaped the second half of the 20th century, and the USSR was a close partner of India from the 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty.

d: Contemporaneous with Egypt's pyramids.
x: Overview # Contemporaneous with Egypt’s pyramids. Government and society # Norte Chico (or Caral-Supe) society on Peru’s central coast had no evidence of warfare, defensive walls or weapons. Elites probably organised the labour to build monumental platforms through religious authority and control of trade between fishing villages on the coast and cotton-growing inland towns. About 30 urban centres existed. How people lived # Fishing villages traded dried fish for cotton nets and vegetables; people lived in small houses around ceremonial centres. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ceremonies with music and fire rituals were held in sunken plazas. Food # Anchovies and sardines from the coast traded for squash, beans and cotton. Construction and architecture # Caral, the largest site, has six stepped platform pyramids up to 18 m high, sunken circular plazas and residential areas, built around 2600 BCE — contemporary with Egypt’s pyramids. Builders used shicra, mesh bags filled with stones, which made structures resistant to earthquakes. Technology and knowledge # People grew cotton for fishing nets, squash, beans and chillies with irrigation canals. A knotted string found at Caral may be an early quipu. Flutes made of condor and pelican bones show music. How it rose # Around 3000 BCE, rich anchovy and sardine fisheries combined with irrigated cotton farming in the Supe, Pativilca and Fortaleza valleys supported the rise of towns. How it declined or fell # Around 1800 BCE the region was abandoned, perhaps due to climate shifts, El Niño floods or sand dunes covering fields, as other Andean centres rose. Legacy # The oldest known civilisation in the Americas, laying foundations for Andean traditions such as platform mounds and quipus.

d: The 'mother culture' of Mesoamerica.
x: Overview # The ‘mother culture’ of Mesoamerica. Government and society # Olmec centres were ruled by powerful chiefs or kings, depicted on colossal stone heads up to 3 m tall and on ‘altars’ (actually thrones), which show rulers emerging from caves, linking them to the supernatural. How people lived # Farmers grew maize, beans and squash and fished in rivers; artisans carved jade. Culture, beliefs and heritage # They worshipped jaguar-like deities and practised ritual bloodletting. Food # Maize processed with lime (nixtamalisation), beans and squash. Construction and architecture # San Lorenzo (about 1200–900 BCE) was built on an artificial plateau; La Venta (about 900–400 BCE) had a 30-m earthen pyramid, plazas and buried mosaic pavements of serpentine blocks. Technology and knowledge # The Olmecs made rubber balls for the Mesoamerican ballgame, possibly developed the earliest Mesoamerican writing (the Cascajal Block) and the Long Count calendar, and carved jade and basalt brought from far away. How it rose # Around 1500 BCE, farming villages in the fertile river lowlands of Veracruz and Tabasco grew into the first complex society in Mesoamerica. How it declined or fell # By 400 BCE Olmec centres were abandoned, possibly due to rivers changing course, volcanic activity, or overuse of land. Legacy # Often called Mesoamerica’s ‘mother culture’, the Olmec influenced the Maya and later peoples in religion, ballgames, calendars and art, such as the feathered serpent and were-jaguar.

d: Classic cities declined amid drought and war around 800–900 CE.
x: Overview # Classic cities declined amid drought and war around 800–900 CE. Government and society # Maya cities were independent city-states ruled by divine kings (k’uhul ajaw) who performed bloodletting rituals and led wars. Great powers such as Tikal and Calakmul built alliance networks and fought ‘star wars’ timed by Venus. Kings recorded their deeds on stone stelae. How people lived # Most people were farmers in thatched houses growing maize in milpas; nobles, scribes and artisans lived near city centres. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Maize gods, the underworld Xibalba, the Hero Twins and the ballgame were central to religion. Food # Maize was sacred; people ate tortillas, tamales and atole, with beans, squash, chilli and turkey. Elites drank frothy cacao. Construction and architecture # Maya cities had stepped pyramids such as Tikal’s Temple I, palaces, ball courts, causeways (sacbeob) and observatories like Chichén Itzá’s El Caracol. Lidar surveys since 2018 have revealed millions of buildings and huge farming systems around cities. Technology and knowledge # The Maya developed a full writing system of about 800 glyphs, deciphered mostly since the 1970s; the concept of zero; the Long Count calendar; and accurate astronomical tables in the Dresden Codex. They built reservoirs and raised fields. How it rose # Maya villages appeared by 2000 BCE; large Preclassic cities like El Mirador and Nakbé rose by 600 BCE. The Classic period (250–900 CE) saw dozens of great cities. How it declined or fell # Classic southern cities were abandoned around 800–950 CE after droughts, warfare and overpopulation. Northern cities and highland kingdoms lasted until Spanish conquest (the last, Nojpetén, fell in 1697). Legacy # About six million Maya live in Mexico, Guatemala and Belize today, speaking about 30 Maya languages and preserving the Popol Vuh and traditions.

d: Its name means 'place where the gods were created'.
x: Overview # Its name means ‘place where the gods were created’. Government and society # Teotihuacan’s rulers are mysterious: there are few images of individual kings, leading some scholars to suggest collective or council rule. Its influence reached the Maya; a Teotihuacan warrior, Siyaj K’ak’, installed a new king at Tikal in 378 CE. How people lived # Residents lived in apartment compounds organised by family or trade; neighbourhoods housed migrants from Oaxaca and the Gulf coast. Culture, beliefs and heritage # They worshipped the Feathered Serpent, the Storm God and the Great Goddess. Food # Maize, beans, squash, amaranth and pulque. Construction and architecture # The city covered 20 km² on a grid aligned 15.5° east of north, along the ‘Avenue of the Dead’, with the Pyramid of the Sun (about 65 m), Pyramid of the Moon, and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. About 2,000 multi-family apartment compounds housed residents. Technology and knowledge # Teotihuacan controlled obsidian mines and workshops making blades, and had standardised architecture with talud-tablero style. How it rose # It grew from about 100 BCE, possibly boosted by refugees from the eruption of Popocatépetl and Xitle, reaching 100,000–200,000 people by 450 CE — one of the largest cities in the world. How it declined or fell # Around 550 CE the centre was burned, perhaps in an internal revolt amid drought and inequality; the city declined. Legacy # The Aztecs, who found its ruins, named it Teotihuacan, ‘the place where gods were born’, and believed the current sun was born there.

d: Tenochtitlan (~200,000) fell to Cortés and smallpox.
x: Overview # Tenochtitlan (~200,000) fell to Cortés and smallpox. Government and society # The Aztec Empire was the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, formed in 1428. The huey tlatoani (‘great speaker’) was elected by a council of nobles. Conquered city-states kept their own rulers but paid tribute in maize, cotton, cacao, feathers and gold, recorded in the Codex Mendoza. How people lived # Commoners (macehualtin) farmed and served in the army; children attended schools. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Religion required human sacrifice to sustain the sun; poets like Nezahualcoyotl wrote verse. Food # Maize tortillas, beans, squash, chilli, amaranth and chinampa vegetables; nobles drank chocolate. Construction and architecture # Tenochtitlan, on an island in Lake Texcoco, had about 200,000 people, causeways, aqueducts from Chapultepec and the Templo Mayor, a twin pyramid to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc. Technology and knowledge # Chinampas — floating gardens — produced several harvests a year; dikes separated fresh and salt water. How it rose # The Mexica arrived in the Valley of Mexico as poor migrants, founding Tenochtitlan in 1325; under Itzcoatl they overthrew Azcapotzalco, and Moctezuma I and Ahuitzotl expanded the empire. How it declined or fell # Spanish conquistadors under Cortés, allied with tens of thousands of Tlaxcalans and others, and aided by smallpox, besieged Tenochtitlan, which fell in 1521. Legacy # Mexico City stands on Tenochtitlan; Nahuatl words like chocolate, tomato and avocado spread worldwide.

d: The largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas.
x: Overview # The largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas. Government and society # The Sapa Inca, believed to descend from the sun god Inti, ruled Tawantinsuyu through four provinces with governors and a decimal administration. Instead of taxes in money, subjects owed mit’a labour on roads, farms and armies. Conquered peoples were sometimes relocated (mitmaq) to prevent revolt. How people lived # Communities (ayllu) farmed potatoes and maize collectively and herded llamas. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Inti, the earth mother Pachamama and mummified ancestors were worshipped. Food # Potatoes (freeze-dried as chuño), maize, quinoa and llama meat; storehouses (qollqa) held food for years. Construction and architecture # Inca masons fitted huge stones without mortar, as at Sacsayhuamán and Cusco; Machu Picchu (about 1450) was a royal estate. Terraces made mountainsides farmable. Technology and knowledge # About 40,000 km of roads (Qhapaq Ñan) with rope suspension bridges; relay runners (chasquis); quipus recorded numbers; storehouses (qollqa) held food for years. How it rose # Pachacuti (r. 1438–1471) defeated the Chanka and expanded the Cusco kingdom; his son Topa Inca expanded it from Ecuador to Chile. How it declined or fell # Smallpox killed Huayna Capac, causing civil war between his sons. Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532; Vilcabamba resisted until 1572. Legacy # About 8 million speak Quechua; the potato spread worldwide.

d: Abandoned many sites during the great drought of 1276–99.
x: Overview # Abandoned many sites during the great drought of 1276–99. Government and society # The Ancestral Puebloans (Anasazi) of the Four Corners region lived in villages led by clan and religious leaders; Chaco Canyon may have been a ceremonial and political centre. How people lived # People farmed maize, beans and squash and made pottery. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Kivas, underground ceremonial rooms, were central to religion. Food # Maize, beans and squash, plus wild game. Construction and architecture # Great houses like Pueblo Bonito (about 800 rooms) at Chaco Canyon, and cliff dwellings like Mesa Verde’s Cliff Palace, built in alcoves. Technology and knowledge # Water management, roads up to 60 km straight, and astronomical alignments like Fajada Butte’s ‘sun dagger’. How it rose # From about 750 CE farming communities grew maize in the arid southwest; Chaco flourished from 850 to 1150. How it declined or fell # Drought (including the Great Drought, 1276–1299) and conflict led people to migrate south and east. Legacy # Descendants include the Hopi, Zuni and Rio Grande Pueblos.

d: Monks Mound is the largest pre-Columbian earthwork north of Mexico.
x: Overview # Monks Mound is the largest pre-Columbian earthwork north of Mexico. Government and society # Mississippian chiefdoms were ruled by paramount chiefs and elites, with Cahokia the largest. How people lived # Farmers lived in thatched houses around plazas. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Southeastern Ceremonial Complex shows birdman imagery. Food # Maize, beans and squash. Construction and architecture # Cahokia’s Monks Mound covers 6 hectares — the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas; ‘Woodhenge’ circles of posts tracked the sun. Technology and knowledge # Intensive maize farming and copper and shell crafts. How it rose # Cahokia grew rapidly around 1050 CE to perhaps 10,000–20,000 people. How it declined or fell # Floods, drought, political instability and deforestation led to Cahokia’s abandonment by 1350. Legacy # It was the largest city north of Mexico before the 18th century.

d: Influenced debates about American federalism.
x: Overview # Influenced debates about American federalism. Government and society # The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy united the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca (and later Tuscarora) under the Great Law of Peace. A Grand Council of 50 chiefs (hoyaneh) made decisions by consensus; clan mothers chose and could remove them. How people lived # Women farmed and owned houses; men hunted and fought. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ceremonies like the Green Corn festival marked the year. Food # The Three Sisters: maize, beans and squash planted together. Construction and architecture # Longhouses up to 100 m long housed several families of a matrilineal clan; villages were palisaded. Technology and knowledge # The Three Sisters farming (maize, beans, squash) and wampum belts recording treaties. How it rose # Tradition says the Peacemaker (Deganawida) and Hiawatha united warring nations; dates range from 1142 to around 1450. How it declined or fell # Wars, disease and siding with Britain in the American Revolution led to land loss. Legacy # Some historians argue it influenced the US Constitution; it still exists.

d: Became the leading world power after 1945.
x: Overview # Became the leading world power after 1945. Government and society # The United States is a federal constitutional republic created by the Constitution of 1787, the oldest written national constitution still in use. Power is divided between the federal government and the states, and federal power is split among Congress (Senate and House), the President, and the courts, led by the Supreme Court, which can strike down laws. The Bill of Rights (1791) protects free speech, religion and fair trials. Voting was first limited to white male property owners; the 15th (1870), 19th (1920) amendments and the Voting Rights Act (1965) extended it to Black citizens and women. How people lived # Americans’ lives changed from farming (90% rural in 1790) to industrial cities and then suburbs. Millions of immigrants arrived through Ellis Island; millions of enslaved Africans worked on plantations until 1865. The 20th century brought cars, television and mass consumer culture. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Christianity, especially Protestant denominations, has shaped American culture, alongside religious freedom. Jazz, blues and rock ‘n’ roll grew from African American music; Hollywood dominated world cinema. Food # Corn, wheat and beef; fast food spread worldwide in the 20th century. Construction and architecture # Early public buildings such as the Capitol and the White House followed neoclassical models, symbolising links to the Roman Republic. Chicago pioneered the steel-framed skyscraper after the 1871 fire, leading to the Empire State Building (1931). Frank Lloyd Wright developed ‘organic’ architecture, and the interstate highway system (from 1956) reshaped cities into suburbs. Technology and knowledge # Americans invented or commercialised the cotton gin (1793), telegraph (Morse, 1844), telephone (Bell, 1876), electric light and power grid (Edison), aeroplane (Wright brothers, 1903) and assembly-line car (Ford, 1913). The Manhattan Project built the atomic bomb, NASA landed humans on the Moon (1969), and Silicon Valley developed the microchip, personal computer and internet, built on the Pentagon’s ARPANET. How it rose # Thirteen British colonies on the Atlantic coast declared independence in 1776 and won it in 1783. The country expanded west through the Louisiana Purchase (1803), war with Mexico (1846–48) and the forced removal of Native Americans (Trail of Tears, 1830s). After the Civil War ended slavery, industrialisation and immigration made the US the world’s largest economy by about 1890; victory in the two world wars made it a superpower. How it declined or fell # The United States has not fallen. It faced existential crises: the Civil War (1861–65), the Great Depression and the civil rights struggle. Since the Cold War’s end it has been the sole superpower, though China’s rise, political polarisation and debt are debated as signs of relative decline. Legacy # The US Constitution and D

How it rose to power # Bimbisara (r. c. 544–492 BCE) built Magadha’s power by marriage alliances with Kosala, the Licchavis and Madra, and by annexing Anga, which gave him the port of Champa and Ganga trade. He organised officials to collect land revenue directly. His son Ajatashatru fought a long war against the Vajji confederacy, reportedly using new weapons such as a catapult and a scythed chariot, and fortified the village of Pataligrama, later Pataliputra. How it lost power # Haryanka kings are remembered in Buddhist texts as patricides: Ajatashatru is said to have killed Bimbisara, and his successors killed their fathers in turn. Disgusted, the people and ministers deposed the last Haryanka king, Nagadasaka, and raised the minister Shishunaga to the throne around 413 BCE.

How it rose to power # Mahapadma Nanda, said by Puranas to be the son of a Shudra woman, overthrew the Shishunagas and defeated many older kshatriya dynasties, earning the title ‘destroyer of all kshatriyas’. The Nandas built the first huge standing army in India — Greek sources speak of 200,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, 2,000 chariots and 3,000–6,000 elephants — which deterred Alexander’s tired troops from crossing the Beas in 326 BCE. How it lost power # Heavy taxation and the low-born status ascribed to them made the Nandas unpopular. Tradition says the Brahmin Chanakya, insulted at Dhana Nanda’s court, trained the young Chandragupta Maurya, who raised an army in the northwest and overthrew Dhana Nanda around 322 BCE.

How it rose to power # Chandragupta Maurya, advised by the Brahmin strategist Chanakya, overthrew the unpopular Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 322 BCE, after Alexander’s withdrawal from Punjab left a power vacuum in the northwest. In about 303 BCE he defeated or made peace with Seleucus I, gaining Afghanistan and Baluchistan in exchange for 500 war elephants. His son Bindusara expanded into the Deccan, and Ashoka conquered Kalinga (261 BCE), bringing almost the whole subcontinent except the far south under one rule. How it lost power # After Ashoka’s death in 232 BCE the empire split between successors, provinces broke away, and revenue fell. Some historians blame the costs of a vast bureaucracy and army; others cite Ashoka’s pacifism weakening the military, though this is disputed. In 185 BCE the general Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, during an army review and founded the Shunga dynasty, while Indo-Greeks invaded from the northwest.

How it rose to power # In about 185 BCE the commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated the last Maurya emperor, Brihadratha, during a military parade and took the throne. He performed Vedic horse sacrifices (ashvamedha) to proclaim sovereignty and fought off Indo-Greek raids; his grandson Vasumitra defeated Greeks on the Sindhu river. How it lost power # The Shunga realm shrank to Magadha and central India (Vidisha). Its last king Devabhuti was killed in a palace plot by his minister Vasudeva Kanva around 73 BCE, who founded the short-lived Kanva dynasty. Shunga-era art survives on the Bharhut stupa and the Sanchi gateways’ early phases.

d: 200 BCE–10 CE
x: How it rose to power # Greek kingdoms of Bactria, left over from Alexander’s conquest and the Seleucid empire, crossed the Hindu Kush around 200 BCE under Demetrius I as Mauryan power faded. Menander I (Milinda, r. c. 165–130 BCE) ruled from Sagala (Sialkot) and is remembered in the Buddhist Milindapanha dialogue with the monk Nagasena. How it lost power # The Indo-Greeks fragmented into some 30 rival kings and were squeezed by Scythians (Sakas), Parthians and finally the Kushans; the last ruler, Strato II, disappears around 10 CE. They left bilingual Greek–Kharosthi coins with realistic portraits and contributed to Gandhara art.

d: c. 100 BCE–220 CE
x: How it rose to power # After the Mauryas declined, Simuka founded the dynasty around the 1st century BCE in the western Deccan. How it lost power # Wars with the Western Kshatrapas and internal division split the realm into smaller kingdoms by the early 3rd century.

How it rose to power # Saka (Scythian) governors who had served the Kushans established themselves in Gujarat, Malwa and Saurashtra in the 1st century CE. Rudradaman I (r. c. 130–150) defeated the Satavahanas twice and left the Junagadh rock inscription (150 CE) — the earliest long inscription in Sanskrit — recording repairs to the Mauryan Sudarshana lake. How it lost power # Gupta emperor Chandragupta II conquered them around 395–415 CE, gaining the rich ports of western India; legend links this victory to the hero Vikramaditya. Their dated coins are a key source for Indian chronology.

How it rose to power # The Guptas began as a minor family in Magadha. Chandragupta I (r. ~320–335) married Kumaradevi, a princess of the powerful Licchavi clan, which raised his status. His son Samudragupta (r. ~335–375), celebrated in the Allahabad pillar inscription, conquered or subdued kings across northern India and received tribute from the south. Chandragupta II (r. ~375–415) defeated the Western Kshatrapas, gaining Gujarat’s sea trade. How it lost power # From around 460 CE the Alchon Huns (Hunas) invaded from Central Asia. Skandagupta repelled them at first, but later attacks under Toramana and Mihirakula devastated the northwest and drained the treasury. At the same time feudatories such as the Maukharis and Maitrakas became independent, trade with the Roman world declined, and the dynasty faded by around 550.

How it rose to power # Founded by Vindhyashakti around 250 CE in the Deccan after the Satavahanas collapsed, the Vakatakas performed Vedic sacrifices and ruled central India. Chandragupta II married his daughter Prabhavatigupta to the Vakataka king; as regent she ruled for years, binding the two dynasties. How it lost power # The kingdom split into two branches, which declined in the late 5th century under pressure from neighbours such as the Vishnukundins and Kalachuris. Their great legacy is the later Ajanta caves, sponsored under King Harishena (r. c. 460–478).

How it rose to power # The Pushyabhutis ruled Thanesar (Haryana) and rose by fighting the Hunas. Harshavardhana (r. 606–647) took over Kannauj after his sister’s husband was killed, uniting most of north India. Xuanzang described his huge assemblies at Prayag, where Harsha gave away all his wealth every five years. How it lost power # Harsha was defeated by Pulakeshin II on the Narmada (c. 618) and left no heir; after his death in 647 a minister usurped the throne and the empire disintegrated. Kannauj became the prize fought over by Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas.

How it rose to power # Nagabhata I (c. 730–760) won fame by repelling Arab armies from Sindh, protecting western India. His successors took Kannauj (c. 816) and under Mihira Bhoja (r. 836–885) ruled from Gujarat to Bengal; the Arab traveller Sulaiman called them hostile to Islam but praised their security. How it lost power # A century of tripartite struggle with Palas and Rashtrakutas exhausted them; Rashtrakuta Indra III sacked Kannauj in 916. Mahmud of Ghazni’s raid in 1018 broke them, and smaller Rajput clans (Chandela, Paramara, Chauhan) succeeded.

How it rose to power # Gopala’s election around 750; Dharmapala and Devapala expanded the realm across north India. How it lost power # Weakened by Pratihara and Rashtrakuta wars, they were overthrown by the Senas in the 12th century.

How it rose to power # Dantidurga, a Chalukya feudatory, overthrew Kirtivarman II around 753 and founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty in the Deccan. His successor Krishna I commissioned the monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora. Dhruva and Govinda III raided as far as Kannauj, and Amoghavarsha I (r. 814–878), who reigned 64 years, founded the capital Manyakheta and wrote the Kannada poetics work Kavirajamarga. How it lost power # Their wars with Pratiharas, Palas, Cholas and Eastern Chalukyas were endless. Krishna III won a great victory over the Cholas at Takkolam (949), but soon after Paramara king Siyaka sacked Manyakheta (972). A feudatory, Tailapa II, overthrew the last Rashtrakuta king in 973, founding the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.

How it rose to power # The early Cholas appear in Sangam literature, but the Imperial Cholas began when Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars around 848. Rajaraja I (985–1014) conquered the Cheras, Pandyas, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives; his son Rajendra I (1014–1044) marched to the Ganga, founding Gangaikonda Cholapuram (‘city of the Chola who conquered the Ganga’), and sent a naval expedition against the Srivijaya empire in 1025. How it lost power # Long wars with the Western Chalukyas drained resources. In the 12th–13th centuries, provincial chiefs grew powerful, the Pandyas revived in the south and the Hoysalas in the west. The last Chola king, Rajendra III, was defeated by the Pandya Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan around 1279.

How it rose to power # Tailapa II, a Rashtrakuta feudatory claiming Chalukya descent, overthrew his overlords in 973 and ruled from Kalyani. His dynasty fought long wars with the Cholas over the Raichur doab. Vikramaditya VI (r. 1076–1126) started his own era and patronised the poet Bilhana and jurist Vijnaneshwara, author of the Mitakshara law commentary. How it lost power # Feudatories grew powerful — the Kalachuris seized Kalyani in 1157, and Hoysalas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas divided the realm by 1189. Their ornate temples in Lakkundi and Itagi developed the Kalyani Chalukya style.

How it rose to power # Hill chiefs from the Malnad region of Karnataka, the Hoysalas served as Chalukya feudatories and became independent under Vishnuvardhana (r. 1108–1152), who reportedly converted from Jainism to Vaishnavism under Ramanuja. How it lost power # They were caught between Pandyas and Yadavas, and the Delhi Sultanate’s general Malik Kafur sacked their capital Dwarasamudra in 1311. Veera Ballala III died fighting the Madurai Sultanate in 1343; his officers Harihara and Bukka helped found Vijayanagara. Their star-shaped temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are UNESCO-listed.

How it rose to power # Kakatiyas were Chalukya feudatories in Telangana who became independent under Prola II and Rudra I (c. 1163). Ganapati (r. 1199–1262) and his daughter Rudramadevi, one of India’s few reigning queens, built Warangal fort and the Thousand Pillar and Ramappa temples, and an irrigation system of tanks. How it lost power # The Delhi Sultanate attacked repeatedly; Muhammad bin Tughlaq (then Ulugh Khan) captured Warangal in 1323 and took Prataparudra prisoner. The Kakatiya tanks and Ramappa temple (UNESCO 2021) remain.

How it rose to power # Anantavarman Chodaganga (r. 1078–1147) ruled from the Godavari to the Ganga and began the Jagannath temple at Puri. Narasimhadeva I (r. 1238–1264) defeated Bengal’s Muslim rulers and built the Sun Temple at Konark, conceived as a giant stone chariot with 24 wheels. How it lost power # Weakened by Delhi and Bengal sultanates and internal revolts, the last Ganga king was overthrown in 1434 by his minister Kapilendra Deva, founder of the Gajapati dynasty.

How it rose to power # Qutb ud-Din Aibak, a Turkic slave who rose as Muhammad of Ghor’s general, ruled from Delhi from 1206. Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236) consolidated the Sultanate, received caliphal recognition and introduced silver tanka and copper jital coins; his daughter Razia (r. 1236–40) was the only woman to rule Delhi. Balban (r. 1266–87) held off the Mongols with harsh rule. How it lost power # After Balban’s death his weak grandson Kaiqubad was killed, and the Khalji nobles took power in 1290.

How it rose to power # Jalaluddin Khalji seized power in 1290, ending the Turkish nobles’ monopoly. His nephew Alauddin murdered him in 1296 and, with the loot of Devagiri, made himself sultan. Alauddin defeated several Mongol invasions, introduced market price controls, and sent Malik Kafur on raids to Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai. How it lost power # After Alauddin’s death in 1316, Malik Kafur’s brief regency and the murders of rival princes led to the rise of Khusrau Khan, killed by Ghazi Malik (Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq) in 1320.

How it rose to power # Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded the dynasty in 1320 and built Tughlaqabad. Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325–51) was brilliant but erratic: token currency, a move of capital to Daulatabad and a planned conquest of Khurasan all failed. Firuz Shah (r. 1351–88) built canals, towns and hospitals. How it lost power # Revolts produced the Bahmani Sultanate and Vijayanagara (1336–47). Timur sacked Delhi in 1398, killing tens of thousands; the dynasty limped on until 1414.

How it rose to power # Bahlul Lodi, an Afghan governor, took the throne in 1451. Sikandar Lodi (r. 1489–1517) founded Agra and made it his capital. How it lost power # Ibrahim Lodi alienated Afghan nobles, who invited Babur from Kabul. Babur’s field guns and tactics defeated him at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

How it rose to power # Founded in 1347 by Alauddin Bahman Shah, who rebelled against Muhammad bin Tughlaq, with capitals at Gulbarga and Bidar. Minister Mahmud Gawan reformed administration and built a madrasa in Bidar. How it lost power # Factional conflict between Deccani and foreign nobles, and Gawan’s execution in 1481, led to five successor sultanates: Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Berar and Bidar.

How it rose to power # Brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family founded the empire in 1336 to resist the Delhi Sultanate’s raids into the south. How it lost power # An alliance of the Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565; Hampi was sacked for months. The dynasty continued weakly until 1646.

How it rose to power # Babur, a Timurid prince from Fergana descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded India and defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527). His son Humayun lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri (1540) and regained it in 1555. Akbar (r. 1556–1605) won the Second Battle of Panipat and built a stable empire through conquest, alliances and reforms. How it lost power # Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707) expanded the empire to its largest extent but spent 25 years at war in the Deccan against the Marathas, emptying the treasury, while reimposing the jizya alienated many subjects. After his death, wars of succession, rebellious governors (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad), Maratha expansion, Sikh and Jat revolts, Nadir Shah’s devastating sack of Delhi (1739) and Afghan invasions shattered central power. The East India Company reduced the emperors to pensioners, and the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was exiled after 1857.

How it rose to power # Sher Shah Suri, an Afghan commander, defeated the Mughal Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540) and ruled north India. He introduced the silver rupiya, land measurement, and rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road with caravanserais. How it lost power # Sher Shah died in a gunpowder explosion in 1545. Succession quarrels let Humayun return; Akbar’s general defeated Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat (1556).

How it rose to power # Hammir Singh recaptured Chittor around 1326 after Alauddin Khalji’s siege of 1303. Rana Kumbha (r. 1433–68) built the Vijay Stambh and Kumbhalgarh fort; Rana Sanga united Rajputs against Babur. How it lost power # Mewar never fully submitted: Maharana Pratap fought Akbar at Haldighati (1576). It accepted Mughal suzerainty in 1615 and British protection in 1818, and merged into India in 1948.

How it rose to power # The Tai prince Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills in 1228 and united local peoples. How it lost power # Civil war, Burmese invasions (1817–1826) and British annexation after the Treaty of Yandabo (1826).

How it rose to power # Shivaji (1630–1680) built a state in the Western Ghats by seizing Bijapur forts, defeated Afzal Khan (1659), escaped from Aurangzeb’s custody at Agra (1666) and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. After Aurangzeb’s death the Marathas expanded across India under Peshwa Bajirao I. How it lost power # Defeat by Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) cost a generation of leaders. Internal rivalries let the British win three Anglo-Maratha Wars; the confederacy ended in 1818.

How it rose to power # Ranjit Singh unified the Sikh misls and captured Lahore in 1799, then Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar. How it lost power # After his death in 1839, court intrigue and assassinations weakened the state; the British won the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–46, 1848–49) and annexed Punjab.

How it rose to power # Hyder Ali seized power from the Wodeyars and expanded Mysore across the south. How it lost power # Four Anglo-Mysore Wars; Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, and the British restored the Wodeyars as subordinate rulers.

How it rose to power # Asaf Jah I, the Mughal viceroy of the Deccan, became independent in 1724. Later Nizams allied with the British as a ‘subsidiary’ state. How it lost power # The last Nizam, Osman Ali Khan, one of the world’s richest men, refused to join India; Operation Polo (1948) integrated Hyderabad.

How it rose to power # Cyrus the Great overthrew the Medes (550 BCE), conquered Lydia and Babylon (539 BCE), and his successors took Egypt and northwest India. How it lost power # Costly wars with Greece, palace intrigue and revolts weakened it; Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela (331 BCE).

How it rose to power # Seleucus I, Alexander’s general, took Babylon in 312 BCE and built an empire from Anatolia to Bactria; he traded India’s eastern provinces to Chandragupta for 500 elephants. Antioch became a great city. How it lost power # Parthians and Bactrians broke away; Rome defeated Antiochus III at Magnesia (190 BCE). Pompey annexed Syria in 63 BCE.

d: 247 BCE–224 CE
x: How it rose to power # Arsaces I led the Parni nomads to seize Parthia around 247 BCE; Mithridates I conquered Mesopotamia. Parthian horse archers destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae (53 BCE). How it lost power # Repeated Roman invasions and civil wars weakened them; their vassal Ardashir I of Persis killed the last king in 224 CE.

How it rose to power # Ardashir I founded the empire in 224, promoting Zoroastrianism as state religion. Shapur I captured the Roman emperor Valerian (260). Khosrow I (r. 531–579) reformed taxes and welcomed scholars. How it lost power # An exhausting war with Byzantium (602–628) and civil war left them weak against the Arab armies, which won at Qadisiyya (636) and Nahavand (642).

How it rose to power # After Muhammad’s death in 632, Abu Bakr was chosen caliph and reunited Arabia. Umar’s armies conquered Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia. How it lost power # Uthman was killed in 656; the first civil war between Ali and Muawiya followed, and Ali was murdered in 661.

How it rose to power # Muawiya founded the Umayyad dynasty in Damascus. Its armies reached Spain (711) and Sindh (712). Abd al-Malik built the Dome of the Rock and made Arabic the administrative language. How it lost power # Non-Arab Muslims resented their status; the Abbasid revolution defeated them on the Zab in 750. An Umayyad prince founded the Emirate of Córdoba.

How it rose to power # Founded on the Abbasid revolution in 750; al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762. Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Mamun the House of Wisdom translated Greek and Indian works. How it lost power # Provincial dynasties split away, Turkish soldiers took control, and the Mongols under Hulagu sacked Baghdad in 1258.

How it rose to power # Ismaili Shia leader al-Mahdi founded the caliphate in Tunisia (909); they conquered Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo and al-Azhar. How it lost power # Crusades, famine and military feuds; Saladin abolished it in 1171.

How it rose to power # Tughril Beg led Oghuz Turks to take Baghdad in 1055. Alp Arslan defeated Byzantium at Manzikert (1071), opening Anatolia to Turks; vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded madrasas. How it lost power # It fragmented after Malik Shah’s death (1092); the Khwarazmians defeated the last Great Seljuk in 1194.

How it rose to power # Saladin, a Kurdish general, ended the Fatimids, united Egypt and Syria, and recaptured Jerusalem in 1187. How it lost power # Family rivalries; Mamluk soldiers killed the last sultan in 1250.

How it rose to power # Turkic and Circassian slave soldiers (mamluks) killed the last Ayyubid sultan in 1250. They defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260) under Baybars and expelled the last crusaders (Acre, 1291); Cairo became the Islamic world’s greatest city. How it lost power # Plague, Portuguese disruption of the spice trade and outdated tactics weakened them; Selim I’s Ottoman artillery won at Marj Dabiq (1516) and Ridaniya (1517).

How it rose to power # Hulagu Khan, Genghis Khan’s grandson, destroyed the Assassins’ fortresses and sacked Baghdad (1258), killing the last Abbasid caliph, and founded the Ilkhanate in Persia and Iraq. Ghazan Khan converted to Islam (1295), and his vizier Rashid al-Din wrote the Jami al-Tawarikh, the first world history. How it lost power # The Mamluks stopped Ilkhanid expansion at Ain Jalut (1260). Abu Said died in 1335 without an heir, and the realm split into regional dynasties such as the Jalayirids and Muzaffarids, later swept up by Timur.

How it rose to power # Timur conquered from Delhi to Anatolia and made Samarkand dazzling. His grandson Ulugh Beg built an observatory. How it lost power # Divided among heirs; Uzbeks took Samarkand in 1500–07. Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

How it rose to power # Osman I’s frontier principality in Anatolia expanded into the Balkans; Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453; Selim I took Egypt and Arabia; Suleiman reached Vienna (1529). How it lost power # Military defeats from 1683, nationalism in the Balkans, economic dependence on Europe and defeat in World War I led to its dissolution and the Turkish Republic (1923).

How it rose to power # Ismail I, head of a Sufi order, took Tabriz (1501) and imposed Shia Islam. Shah Abbas I (r. 1588–1629) moved the capital to Isfahan. How it lost power # Weak shahs and the Afghan siege of Isfahan (1722); Nader Shah ended the dynasty in 1736.

How it rose to power # Agha Mohammad Khan, a Turkmen chief, reunited Iran by 1794 and made Tehran his capital. How it lost power # Losses to Russia, concessions to foreigners, the 1906 Constitutional Revolution, and Reza Khan’s coup (1921) led to their deposition in 1925.

How it rose to power # The Yuezhi nomads, pushed from China’s frontier, conquered Bactria; Kujula Kadphises united them in the 1st century CE. How it lost power # Defeats by the Sasanians in the 3rd century and the rise of the Guptas in India reduced them to minor rulers.

How it rose to power # Central Asian nomads who defeated the Sasanians in 484 and, under Toramana and Mihirakula, raided Gupta India. How it lost power # Yashodharman defeated Mihirakula around 528; the Sasanians and Turks crushed them around 560.

How it rose to power # Bumin Qaghan revolted against the Rouran (552). The Orkhon inscriptions are the earliest written Turkic. How it lost power # Divided into east and west, then destroyed by the Uyghurs in 744.

How it rose to power # The Shang overthrew the semi-legendary Xia around 1600 BCE according to tradition. How it lost power # The last Shang king, remembered as a tyrant, was defeated by the Zhou around 1046 BCE.

How it rose to power # The Shang overthrew the semi-legendary Xia around 1600 BCE according to tradition. How it lost power # The last Shang king, remembered as a tyrant, was defeated by the Zhou around 1046 BCE.

How it rose to power # King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king at Muye around 1046 BCE. How it lost power # Nomad attacks and rebellion forced the move east in 771 BCE; afterwards the Zhou kings were figureheads until Qin extinguished them in 256 BCE.

How it rose to power # Qin, a western state, became powerful after Shang Yang’s Legalist reforms (4th century BCE). King Ying Zheng conquered the other six Warring States by 221 BCE and named himself First Emperor. How it lost power # Massive forced labour, harsh laws and book burning provoked hatred. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, the Chen Sheng–Wu Guang uprising and other rebellions brought down the dynasty by 206 BCE.

d: 206 BCE–220 CE
x: How it rose to power # Liu Bang, a peasant-born official, rebelled after the Qin collapse and defeated the aristocrat Xiang Yu in 202 BCE, founding the Han. He softened Qin’s harsh laws while keeping its centralised structure. How it lost power # Land concentration, court intrigue between eunuchs and consort families, and natural disasters led to the Yellow Turban rebellion (184 CE). Warlords who suppressed it carved up China; in 220 the last Han emperor abdicated, beginning the Three Kingdoms.

How it rose to power # Yang Jian (Emperor Wen) reunified China in 589 and restored examinations. How it lost power # Emperor Yang’s Grand Canal and failed Korean wars caused revolts; Tang took over in 618.

How it rose to power # After the short Sui dynasty reunified China (581) but exhausted it with huge canal projects and failed wars in Korea, rebellions broke out. Li Yuan, a Sui general, and his son Li Shimin captured Chang’an and founded the Tang in 618. Li Shimin, as Emperor Taizong (r. 626–649), defeated the Eastern Turks, extended control along the Silk Road into Central Asia, and governed so effectively his reign became a byword for good rule. How it lost power # In 751 the Tang lost to the Abbasids at the Battle of Talas, ending expansion westward. In 755 the general An Lushan rebelled; the eight-year An Lushan rebellion devastated the north and may have cost millions of lives. Afterwards provincial military governors (jiedushi) became semi-independent, eunuchs dominated the court, and the equal-field system collapsed. The Huang Chao rebellion (874–884) sacked Chang’an, and in 907 the warlord Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor, opening the Five Dynasties period.

How it rose to power # General Zhao Kuangyin was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 960 and reunified most of China, ending the Five Dynasties chaos. How it lost power # The Song lost the north to the Jurchen Jin in 1127 and moved its capital to Hangzhou. The Mongols conquered the Jin, then besieged Song cities for decades; the last Song emperor died at the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279.

How it rose to power # Genghis Khan’s Mongols attacked the Jin from 1211. His grandson Kublai declared the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and destroyed the Southern Song in 1279, the first time a non-Chinese people ruled all of China. How it lost power # Failed invasions of Japan (1274, 1281) and Java drained the treasury, and paper-money inflation and Yellow River floods followed. Plague and ethnic discrimination fuelled the Red Turban revolts. Zhu Yuanzhang took Dadu in 1368 and the Mongols withdrew to the steppe.

How it rose to power # Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant orphan and former monk, led the Red Turban rebellion against the Mongol Yuan and founded the Ming in 1368. How it lost power # Bureaucratic paralysis, eunuch corruption, costly wars in Korea against Japan, silver shortages, Little Ice Age famines and epidemics led to peasant revolts. Rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing in 1644; the last emperor hanged himself, and the Manchus swept in as the Qing.

How it rose to power # The Manchus, unified by Nurhaci, took Beijing in 1644 after the Ming collapse. How it lost power # Population pressure, corruption, the Opium Wars (1839–42, 1856–60), the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) and other revolts, unequal treaties, defeat by Japan (1895), and the Boxer Rebellion (1900) undermined the dynasty. The 1911 Xinhai Revolution ended over 2,000 years of imperial rule.

d: c. 250 CE–today
x: How it rose to power # The Yamato kingdom unified Japan in the 3rd–6th centuries; the emperor line is the world’s oldest hereditary monarchy. How it lost power # Not fallen; the 1947 constitution made the emperor a symbol of the state.

How it rose to power # Minamoto no Yoritomo won the Genpei War and in 1192 was named shogun, creating rule by warriors from Kamakura; the Hōjō family later ruled as regents. How it lost power # Repelling the Mongol invasions (1274, 1281) left warriors unrewarded; Emperor Go-Daigo’s revolt with Ashikaga Takauji ended it in 1333.

How it rose to power # Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara (1600) and became shogun in 1603, ending a century of civil war. How it lost power # Commodore Perry’s US ships (1853) forced Japan open. Unequal treaties and domestic unrest followed, and samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū overthrew the shogunate in the Meiji Restoration (1868).

How it rose to power # Wang Geon reunified Korea in 918; Goryeo printed the Tripitaka Koreana and the first metal movable type (Jikji, 1377). How it lost power # Mongol domination and Yi Seong-gye’s coup (1392).

How it rose to power # General Yi Seong-gye overthrew the Goryeo dynasty in 1392 and moved the capital to Hanyang (Seoul). How it lost power # Japanese (1592–98) and Manchu (1627, 1636) invasions devastated the country. Factional strife and isolation as the ‘Hermit Kingdom’ followed. Japan forced open its ports (1876), made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910.

How it rose to power # Jayavarman II declared independence from Java and himself universal monarch in 802 at Phnom Kulen. How it lost power # Overstretched water infrastructure, alternating mega-droughts and floods in the 14th–15th centuries, a shift to Theravada Buddhism and maritime trade, and attacks by Ayutthaya (1431) led the capital to move south.

How it rose to power # Srivijaya emerged around 650 CE in Sumatra. The Chinese monk Yijing (671) found over a thousand monks studying there. How it lost power # The Chola king Rajendra I raided its ports in 1025. Later, Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit took over its role.

How it rose to power # Anawrahta united the Irrawaddy valley in 1044 and adopted Theravada Buddhism; over 10,000 temples, stupas and monasteries were built at Bagan. How it lost power # Overspending on temples, tax-exempt land and Mongol invasions in 1287 broke the kingdom.

How it rose to power # U Thong (Ramathibodi I) founded Ayutthaya in 1351 on an island where three rivers meet, ideally placed for rice farming and for ships coming up the Chao Phraya. It absorbed Sukhothai, conquered Angkor in 1431, and developed the sakdina system that ranked every person by notional land rights. By the 17th century it was one of Asia’s great ports, trading with China, Japan, Persia, the Dutch, French and English; the Greek adventurer Constantine Phaulkon became a royal minister under King Narai. How it lost power # Ayutthaya fought Burma for two centuries; it fell once in 1569 and was restored by King Naresuan, who won a famous elephant duel in 1593. In 1767 a Burmese army of the Konbaung dynasty besieged and burned the city after a 14-month siege, destroying temples, archives and the royal family. General Taksin rallied resistance from Thonburi within months, and in 1782 Rama I founded the Chakri dynasty at Bangkok, which still reigns.

How it rose to power # Lý Thái Tổ moved the capital to Thăng Long (Hanoi) in 1010 and founded the Temple of Literature (1070). The Trần (1225–1400), with General Trần Hưng Đạo, defeated three Mongol invasions, including at Bạch Đằng (1288). How it lost power # Hồ Quý Ly usurped the throne in 1400; Ming China invaded in 1407.

How it rose to power # Raden Wijaya used a Mongol invasion force to defeat his rival in 1293, then drove the Mongols out. How it lost power # Succession wars, the rise of Muslim port states such as Demak and Malacca, and Demak’s conquest around 1527.

How it rose to power # Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, founded Malacca around 1400 and gained Ming Chinese protection; Zheng He’s fleets visited. Conversion to Islam drew Muslim merchants, and Malacca controlled the strait trade in spices and textiles. How it lost power # Afonso de Albuquerque captured Malacca for Portugal in 1511; the sultan’s heirs founded Johor and Perak.

d: 27 BCE–68 CE
x: How it rose to power # Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BCE) and in 27 BCE took the title Augustus. He kept the forms of the Republic while controlling the army and provinces, ushering in the Pax Romana. His successors Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius (who invaded Britain in 43 CE) and Nero came from his family by adoption and marriage. How it lost power # Nero’s extravagance, the Great Fire of Rome (64), the persecution of Christians and revolts in Judaea and Gaul led the Senate to declare him a public enemy; he took his own life in 68. The ‘Year of the Four Emperors’ (69) ended with Vespasian founding the Flavian dynasty.

How it rose to power # Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge (312), credited a Christian vision, issued the Edict of Milan (313), called the Council of Nicaea (325) and founded Constantinople (330). How it lost power # His sons fought each other; Julian ‘the Apostate’ tried to revive paganism and died campaigning in Persia in 363.

How it rose to power # Pepin the Short deposed the last Merovingian with papal approval (751). His son Charlemagne conquered Lombards and Saxons and was crowned emperor in Rome (800), fostering the Carolingian Renaissance of learning. How it lost power # Charlemagne’s grandsons split the empire (Verdun, 843); Viking raids weakened them; Hugh Capet became king of France in 987.

t: House of Wessex and Anglo-Saxon England
x: How it rose to power # Alfred the Great (r. 871–899) of Wessex defeated the Danish Great Heathen Army at Edington (878) and built fortified towns (burhs) and a navy. His son Edward and daughter Æthelflæd, ‘Lady of the Mercians’, reconquered the Danelaw, and grandson Æthelstan became the first king of all England (927). How it lost power # Renewed Viking attacks under Æthelred the Unready led to Danish rule under Cnut (1016–35). Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066; Harold Godwinson defeated a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge but died at Hastings against William of Normandy.

How it rose to power # William of Normandy won at Hastings in 1066, compiled the Domesday Book and built castles. Henry II founded the Plantagenet line (1154), ruling an ‘Angevin empire’ from Scotland to the Pyrenees. King John signed Magna Carta (1215). How it lost power # After the Hundred Years’ War, the Wars of the Roses (1455–85) between Lancaster and York ended with Richard III’s death at Bosworth.

How it rose to power # Henry VII won at Bosworth (1485) and married Elizabeth of York to unite the rival houses. Henry VIII broke with Rome to annul his marriage (1534), dissolving monasteries; Elizabeth I’s reign saw the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588) and Shakespeare. How it lost power # Elizabeth I died unmarried in 1603, and the crown passed to James VI of Scotland, beginning the Stuart line.

How it rose to power # Rudolf I was elected King of the Romans in 1273; marriage alliances brought Burgundy, Spain, Bohemia and Hungary. Charles V (r. 1519–56) ruled an empire ‘on which the sun never set’. How it lost power # Austria lost to Prussia (1866) and became Austria-Hungary (1867); the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand (1914) triggered World War I, and defeat dissolved the empire in 1918.

How it rose to power # Henry IV, a Protestant who converted (‘Paris is worth a mass’), became king in 1589 and ended the Wars of Religion with the Edict of Nantes (1598). Louis XIII and Cardinal Richelieu centralised power; Louis XIV (r. 1643–1715) built Versailles and made France Europe’s dominant power. How it lost power # Costly wars, including support for the American Revolution, bankrupted the state. Louis XVI called the Estates-General in 1789; the Revolution abolished the monarchy in 1792 and executed him in 1793. Bourbons briefly returned (1814–30).

How it rose to power # After the ‘Time of Troubles’, a Zemsky Sobor elected 16-year-old Michael Romanov tsar in 1613. Peter the Great (r. 1682–1725) modernised Russia, and Catherine the Great expanded to the Black Sea. How it lost power # Defeat in the Russo-Japanese War, the 1905 revolution, World War I disasters and food shortages led to the February Revolution of 1917; Nicholas II abdicated, and the Bolsheviks shot the family at Yekaterinburg in July 1918.

How it rose to power # The Hohenzollerns, electors of Brandenburg, became kings in Prussia in 1701. Frederick William I built a disciplined army, and Frederick the Great (r. 1740–86) seized Silesia and survived the Seven Years’ War, making Prussia a great power. After defeat by Napoleon, reforms rebuilt it; Bismarck’s wars with Denmark, Austria and France united Germany, and William I became German Emperor at Versailles in 1871. How it lost power # Kaiser William II dismissed Bismarck, pursued a naval race with Britain and backed Austria in July 1914. Germany’s defeat in World War I and the November Revolution of 1918 forced William to abdicate and flee to the Netherlands; the Weimar Republic replaced the monarchy.

How it rose to power # Basil I, a peasant-born groom who rose as a favourite of Michael III, had his patron murdered and took the throne in 867. His dynasty presided over the ‘Macedonian Renaissance’ in learning and art, the conversion of the Rus (988) and the reconquest of Crete, Cyprus and Antioch. Basil II ‘the Bulgar-Slayer’ (r. 976–1025) annexed Bulgaria. How it lost power # After Basil II’s death the throne passed through the daughters Zoe and Theodora and their husbands; aristocratic factions and court intrigue weakened the army. When Theodora died in 1056 the dynasty ended, and within 15 years Byzantium lost Anatolia at Manzikert and southern Italy to the Normans.

How it rose to power # Michael VIII Palaiologos, regent for a boy emperor of the Nicaean exile state, recaptured Constantinople from the Latin crusaders in 1261 and blinded the rightful heir to take sole power. He outmanoeuvred Charles of Anjou partly by financing the Sicilian Vespers revolt (1282). The dynasty ruled for nearly two centuries, presiding over a cultural ‘Palaiologan Renaissance’ of scholarship and mosaics such as those of the Chora church. How it lost power # The restored empire was poor and small; civil wars in the 14th century invited Ottoman mercenaries into Europe, and the Black Death struck in 1347. By 1400 Byzantium was little more than Constantinople. Constantine XI died defending the walls when Mehmed II’s cannons breached them on 29 May 1453; the last Palaiologan outposts in the Morea fell by 1460.

How it rose to power # Rurik, a Varangian, reportedly came to rule Novgorod in 862; his successors ruled Kiev. After the Mongol conquest, the Muscovite branch rose; Ivan III ended Mongol tribute (1480) and Ivan IV crowned himself tsar (1547). How it lost power # Ivan IV killed his heir in a rage (1581); his son Fyodor I died in 1598 without children, beginning the Time of Troubles.

How it rose to power # Mieszko I accepted Christianity in 966, founding the Polish state; Bolesław I was crowned king in 1025. Casimir III the Great (r. 1333–70) codified laws and founded Kraków University. Queen Jadwiga married Lithuania’s Grand Duke Jogaila (Władysław II Jagiełło) in 1386, creating a union that defeated the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald (1410). How it lost power # Sigismund II Augustus, last of the Jagiellonians, created the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (Union of Lublin, 1569) but died childless in 1572, after which kings were elected by the nobility.

How it rose to power # Building on the unification of Egypt around 3100 BCE, the Third Dynasty king Djoser and his architect Imhotep raised the Step Pyramid at Saqqara (c. 2670 BCE), the first monumental stone building. The Fourth Dynasty (Sneferu, Khufu, Khafre, Menkaure) built the Bent, Red and Giza pyramids, organising tens of thousands of paid labourers fed by state granaries. A powerful king ruled as a living god, supported by a vizier, scribes and provincial nomarchs. How it lost power # From the Fifth and Sixth Dynasties, royal power waned as nomarchs became hereditary and wealthy, and temples won tax exemptions. Pepi II’s reign of perhaps 90 years ended in succession problems. Around 2200 BCE the ‘4.2-kiloyear event’, a global drought, brought low Nile floods and famine; Egypt split into rival centres in the First Intermediate Period (c. 2181–2055 BCE).

How it rose to power # Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos around 1550 BCE. Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten (who tried to impose worship of the Aten) and Ramesses II built an empire into Syria and Nubia, with temples at Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel. How it lost power # After Ramesses III fought the Sea Peoples (~1175 BCE), the Bronze Age collapse, tomb robbing, and the rise of Amun priests at Thebes split Egypt by 1070 BCE.

How it rose to power # Ptolemy I, Alexander’s general, took Egypt in 305 BCE; Alexandria’s Library and Lighthouse were built. How it lost power # Cleopatra VII allied with Caesar and Antony, but defeat at Actium (31 BCE) and her suicide made Egypt a Roman province in 30 BCE.

How it rose to power # Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso at Kirina (1235). Mansa Musa (r. 1312–1337) made his famous hajj in 1324, so lavish with gold that he depressed its price in Cairo, and built mosques in Timbuktu. How it lost power # Succession disputes, Mossi and Tuareg raids and the rise of Songhai shrank Mali by the 1400s; the Keita lingered as local rulers until about 1670.

How it rose to power # In 1270 Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty, claiming descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba as recorded in the Kebra Nagast. Emperors such as Zara Yaqob reformed the church; in the 16th century Portuguese help saved Ethiopia from Ahmad Gragn’s invasion. Menelik II defeated Italy at Adwa (1896), keeping Ethiopia independent. How it lost power # Haile Selassie modernised the state but faced famine, inequality and protests; the Marxist Derg military junta deposed him in 1974 and abolished the monarchy in 1975.

How it rose to power # Shaka (r. 1816–1828), a son of a minor chief, reorganised Zulu warriors into regiments (amabutho) armed with the short stabbing spear (iklwa) and large shields, using the ‘bull’s horns’ encircling formation. In the turmoil of the mfecane he forged a kingdom of perhaps 250,000 people in what is now KwaZulu-Natal. How it lost power # Shaka was assassinated by his half-brothers in 1828. Under Cetshwayo, the Zulu defeated a British army at Isandlwana (January 1879) but lost at Ulundi in July. Britain split the kingdom into 13 chiefdoms, civil war followed, and Zululand was annexed in 1887 and joined to Natal in 1897.

How it rose to power # Around 1701 Osei Tutu, with the priest Okomfo Anokye, united Akan states; tradition says the Golden Stool descended from the sky, embodying the soul of the nation. Kumasi controlled the gold and kola nut trade and the Atlantic slave trade. How it lost power # Seven Anglo-Ashanti wars (1823–1900) followed; Yaa Asantewaa led the 1900 War of the Golden Stool. Britain annexed Ashanti in 1901; the Asantehene remains a traditional ruler in Ghana.

d: c. 100 BCE–900 CE
x: How it rose to power # Villages from about 2000 BCE became cities such as El Mirador in the Preclassic period. How it lost power # Classic southern cities were abandoned around 800–950 CE after droughts, warfare and overpopulation. Northern cities and highland kingdoms lasted until Spanish conquest (the last, Nojpetén, fell in 1697).

How it rose to power # The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 and the Triple Alliance formed in 1428. How it lost power # Hernán Cortés, with tens of thousands of indigenous allies and a smallpox epidemic, besieged Tenochtitlan until it fell in 1521.

How it rose to power # Pachacuti (r. 1438–1471) turned the Cusco kingdom into an empire. How it lost power # Smallpox, a civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa, and Pizarro’s capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca (1532).

d: The supercontinent split into Laurasia and Gondwana; India drifted north and hit Asia ~50 million years ago.
x: What happened # The supercontinent split into Laurasia and Gondwana; India drifted north and hit Asia ~50 million years ago. Causes, course and consequences # Pangaea, the supercontinent assembled around 335 million years ago, began to rift about 200 million years ago as magma welled up along cracks; the eruption of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province coincided with the end-Triassic mass extinction. First the Atlantic opened between North America and Africa, then Gondwana split into South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia and India. India drifted north at up to 15 cm a year and collided with Asia about 50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya. The separation of continents explains why marsupials dominate Australia and why fossils of the same reptiles appear in India, Africa and Antarctica.

d: A ~10 km asteroid hit Yucatán; mammals later inherited the Earth.
x: What happened # A ~10 km asteroid hit Yucatán; mammals later inherited the Earth. Causes, course and consequences # About 66 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 km wide struck the Yucatán Peninsula, gouging a crater 180 km across and releasing energy equal to billions of atomic bombs. Tsunamis, global wildfires and a ‘impact winter’ of soot and sulphate aerosols blocked sunlight for years, collapsing food chains. About three-quarters of all species died, including all non-bird dinosaurs; the iridium-rich clay layer found worldwide (identified by Luis and Walter Alvarez in 1980) is its fingerprint. India’s Deccan Traps eruptions at the same time added climate stress. Small mammals survived and later diversified, eventually leading to primates and humans.

t: Onset of the Quaternary ice ages
d: Ice sheets advanced and retreated about every 41,000, then 100,000 years.
x: What happened # Ice sheets advanced and retreated about every 41,000, then 100,000 years. Causes, course and consequences # Around 2.6 million years ago, Earth’s climate cooled enough for great ice sheets to grow and shrink over the northern continents in cycles paced by variations in Earth’s orbit (Milankovitch cycles), at first every 41,000 years and, after about 1 million years ago, every 100,000 years. Africa became drier and more variable, with savannas expanding — a backdrop to the emergence of the genus Homo and stone tool making. Falling sea levels repeatedly exposed land bridges such as Beringia and Sundaland, which humans later crossed.

d: One of the largest eruptions in 2 million years; Indian sites like Jwalapuram suggest people survived it.
x: What happened # One of the largest eruptions in 2 million years; Indian sites like Jwalapuram suggest people survived it. Causes, course and consequences # The Youngest Toba eruption in Sumatra about 74,000 years ago ejected roughly 2,800 cubic km of material, leaving Lake Toba’s caldera and spreading ash over India, where a layer up to several metres thick still lies. Scientists once argued it caused a ‘volcanic winter’ and a human population bottleneck. Excavations at Jwalapuram in Andhra Pradesh found stone tools above and below the ash, and studies in South Africa suggest people coped, so its human impact is now debated rather than assumed catastrophic.

d: Humans crossed Beringia into the Americas around this time or after.
x: What happened # Humans crossed Beringia into the Americas around this time or after. Causes, course and consequences # Between about 26,000 and 19,000 years ago ice sheets reached their greatest recent extent, covering Canada, Scandinavia and the British Isles under up to 3 km of ice. Sea level was about 120 m lower, joining Britain to Europe, Sri Lanka to India and Siberia to Alaska. People retreated to refugia such as southern France, Iberia and Ukraine, hunting mammoth and reindeer and building mammoth-bone huts. As the ice melted, they recolonised northern lands and the Americas were settled.

d: A sudden 1,200-year chill, possibly from meltwater shutting the Atlantic circulation.
x: What happened # A sudden 1,200-year chill, possibly from meltwater shutting the Atlantic circulation. Causes, course and consequences # About 12,900 years ago, while the world was warming, the Northern Hemisphere abruptly snapped back to near-glacial cold for about 1,200 years, probably because meltwater weakened the Atlantic’s ocean currents. In the Levant the cold and drought may have pushed Natufian foragers to cultivate wild cereals, a step toward farming. It ended suddenly around 11,700 years ago, marking the start of the Holocene, the warm, stable climate in which agriculture and civilisation developed.

d: Caused by human hunting combined with climate change.
x: What happened # Caused by human hunting combined with climate change. Causes, course and consequences # Between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, most large animals over 45 kg disappeared from Australia, the Americas and northern Eurasia: mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, Diprotodon, Smilodon and many others. The timing often follows human arrival — Australia around 45,000 years ago, the Americas around 13,000 years ago — suggesting hunting played a big part, combined with climate change at the end of the Ice Age. Africa and South Asia, where animals evolved alongside humans, lost far fewer species.

d: Drying pushed people into the Nile valley as Egypt's state formed.
x: What happened # Drying pushed people into the Nile valley as Egypt’s state formed. Causes, course and consequences # During the African Humid Period (about 14,500–5,500 years ago), stronger monsoon rains turned the Sahara into grassland with lakes, hippos and crocodiles; rock art shows cattle herders and swimmers. As Earth’s orbit shifted, rains weakened and the Sahara dried, sometimes abruptly, around 5,500 years ago. Herders moved toward the Nile and the Sahel, a migration that some historians link to the concentration of people that led to Egyptian civilisation.

d: Defines the start of the Meghalayan Age, named from a Meghalaya cave stalagmite.
x: What happened # Defines the start of the Meghalayan Age, named from a Meghalaya cave stalagmite. Causes, course and consequences # Around 2200 BCE a severe, centuries-long drought affected regions from the Mediterranean to India and China. It coincides with the collapse of the Akkadian Empire, the end of Egypt’s Old Kingdom, and changes in the Indus Valley, where cities later declined as monsoons weakened. It is used to define the boundary between the Middle and Late Holocene (the Meghalayan Age, named after a cave in Meghalaya, India).

d: One of the largest eruptions of human history.
x: What happened # One of the largest eruptions of human history. Causes, course and consequences # Around 1600 BCE the volcanic island of Thera exploded in one of the largest eruptions of the past 10,000 years. It buried the Minoan town of Akrotiri under ash (its inhabitants had already fled), triggered tsunamis on Crete, and probably weakened Minoan civilisation. Some scholars think it inspired the legend of Atlantis.

d: Preserved a Roman town frozen in time.
x: What happened # Preserved a Roman town frozen in time. Causes, course and consequences # On 24–25 August 79 CE (some evidence suggests October), Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pyroclastic flows, killing perhaps 2,000 people. Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters; his uncle Pliny the Elder died trying to rescue people. Preserved houses, bread and graffiti make Pompeii a snapshot of everyday Roman life.

d: Followed by the Late Antique Little Ice Age and Justinian's plague.
x: What happened # Followed by the Late Antique Little Ice Age and Justinian’s plague. Causes, course and consequences # In 536 CE an eruption, probably in Iceland, filled the Northern Hemisphere sky with dust; Procopius wrote that the sun shone without brightness for a year. Summer temperatures fell sharply, crops failed from Ireland to China, and further eruptions in 539–540 deepened the cold of the Late Antique Little Ice Age. It was followed by the Plague of Justinian.

d: Caused famine in Europe; possibly linked to a new cholera strain in Bengal (1817).
x: What happened # Caused famine in Europe; possibly linked to a new cholera strain in Bengal (1817). Causes, course and consequences # Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia, erupted in April 1815, the largest eruption in recorded history, killing over 70,000 people locally. Its aerosols caused 1816’s ‘Year Without a Summer’, with crop failures in Europe and North America, and contributed to a cholera outbreak in Bengal. That cold summer, Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein.

d: Its sound was heard 4,800 km away.
x: What happened # Its sound was heard 4,800 km away. Causes, course and consequences # After months of activity, Krakatoa, a volcanic island between Java and Sumatra, exploded on 27 August 1883 with a blast heard 4,800 km away on Rodrigues Island — the loudest sound in recorded history. Tsunamis up to 40 m high killed about 36,000 people on nearby coasts. Ash cooled global temperatures by about 1.2 °C and caused blood-red sunsets for months; telegraph cables spread the news worldwide within hours. A new island, Anak Krakatau (‘child of Krakatoa’), emerged in 1927.

d: Struck during the Peloponnesian War.
x: What happened # Struck during the Peloponnesian War. Causes, course and consequences # In 430 BCE, in the second year of the Peloponnesian War, an epidemic struck Athens, crowded with refugees inside the Long Walls. It killed perhaps a quarter of the population, including the leader Pericles. Thucydides, who survived it, described its symptoms; its cause is still debated (typhoid is one candidate).

d: Brought back by soldiers from Mesopotamia.
x: What happened # Brought back by soldiers from Mesopotamia. Causes, course and consequences # Roman troops returning from the siege of Seleucia in Mesopotamia brought an epidemic around 165 CE, probably smallpox, which spread across the empire. The physician Galen described fever, diarrhoea and a black rash. It may have killed 10% of the population — 5 to 10 million people — including perhaps co-emperor Lucius Verus, and it recurred in 189 CE. Labour and army shortages weakened Marcus Aurelius’s defence of the Danube frontier.

d: The first plague pandemic.
x: What happened # The first plague pandemic. Causes, course and consequences # From 541 CE the bubonic plague (Yersinia pestis, confirmed by ancient DNA) spread from Egypt across the Byzantine Empire; Constantinople may have lost thousands a day at its peak. Recurrences for two centuries weakened Byzantium and Persia just before the Arab conquests.

d: Spread along Mongol trade routes; transformed labour and religion.
x: What happened # Spread along Mongol trade routes; transformed labour and religion. Causes, course and consequences # Yersinia pestis, carried by fleas on rats and spread along trade routes from Central Asia, reached the Crimea in 1346 and Europe in 1347. Within five years it killed perhaps a third to half of Europe’s population and many in the Middle East. Labour shortages raised wages, weakened serfdom and fuelled revolts, while persecutions of Jews followed. Repeated outbreaks continued until the 18th century.

d: Smallpox, measles and flu brought by Europeans.
x: What happened # Smallpox, measles and flu brought by Europeans. Causes, course and consequences # Europeans brought smallpox, measles and influenza, to which Native Americans had no immunity. Smallpox reached Mexico in 1520 and devastated Tenochtitlan during Cortés’s siege, and swept through the Inca Empire, killing the emperor Huayna Capac and triggering civil war. Epidemics may have killed up to 90% of the indigenous population over a century.

d: The first pandemic began in the Ganges delta; John Snow traced cholera to water in 1854.
x: What happened # The first pandemic began in the Ganges delta; John Snow traced cholera to water in 1854. Causes, course and consequences # Cholera, a waterborne bacterial disease, had long been endemic in the Ganges delta. In 1817 it spread along British military and trade routes to Asia, the Middle East and Russia, then to Europe and the Americas in later waves; seven pandemics have occurred, the latest beginning in 1961. In 1854 John Snow traced a London outbreak to a contaminated water pump, and Robert Koch identified the bacterium in Calcutta in 1884. These discoveries led cities to build sewers and clean water supplies.

d: Bombay's 1896 plague led to harsh British measures; Yersin found the bacterium.
x: What happened # Bombay’s 1896 plague led to harsh British measures; Yersin found the bacterium. Causes, course and consequences # Beginning in Yunnan, China in the 1850s, bubonic plague reached Hong Kong in 1894 and Bombay in 1896 via shipping.
