India suffered about 12 million deaths of the global 15 million. Alexandre Yersin and Kitasato Shibasaburō identified the plague bacterium in Hong Kong. Harsh British measures in Pune — house searches and forced segregation — led the Chapekar brothers to assassinate plague commissioner W. C. Rand in 1897.

d: India suffered the most deaths of any country.
x: What happened # India suffered the most deaths of any country. Causes, course and consequences # A deadly H1N1 influenza strain spread in three waves from 1918 to 1920, carried by troopships at the end of World War I. It infected about a third of the world’s population and killed perhaps 50 million, unusually striking healthy young adults. India lost an estimated 12–17 million, more than any other country, as the virus arrived via Bombay with returning soldiers during a drought. It was called ‘Spanish’ only because neutral Spain’s newspapers reported it freely.

d: Antiretroviral drugs turned it into a manageable condition.
x: What happened # Antiretroviral drugs turned it into a manageable condition. Causes, course and consequences # HIV-1 crossed from chimpanzees to humans in southeastern Cameroon, probably through bushmeat hunting, and spread via colonial-era Kinshasa in the early 20th century. AIDS was recognised in 1981 and HIV identified in 1983. About 40 million people have died, and sub-Saharan Africa was hit hardest. Antiretroviral therapy since 1996, and later cheaper Indian generic drugs, turned it into a manageable chronic condition.

d: Led to lockdowns and record-speed vaccines.
x: What happened # Led to lockdowns and record-speed vaccines. Causes, course and consequences # A new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, was identified in Wuhan, China, in December 2019 and declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Lockdowns closed schools and borders worldwide; India’s 2021 Delta wave overwhelmed hospitals and oxygen supplies. mRNA and other vaccines were developed within a year, and India produced Covishield and Covaxin. WHO estimates over 7 million recorded deaths, with excess deaths perhaps closer to 15–20 million.

d: Cuneiform and hieroglyphs started as accounting marks.
x: What happened # Cuneiform and hieroglyphs started as accounting marks. Causes, course and consequences # Writing was invented independently at least four times: in Mesopotamia (cuneiform, about 3200 BCE), Egypt (hieroglyphs, about 3200 BCE), China (oracle bones, about 1250 BCE) and Mesoamerica (about 900–600 BCE). In Sumer it grew from clay tokens used for accounting to record goods, then laws, letters and literature. Writing let states keep records, collect taxes and preserve knowledge across generations — the dividing line between prehistory and history.

d: Narmer united Upper and Lower Egypt.
x: What happened # Narmer united Upper and Lower Egypt. Causes, course and consequences # Around 3100 BCE Upper (southern) and Lower (northern) Egypt were united under one king, traditionally Menes, usually identified with Narmer. The Narmer Palette shows him wearing both crowns and smiting enemies. Unification created the first territorial state, with Memphis as capital.

d: Ramesses II vs the Hittites, the largest chariot battle.
x: What happened # Ramesses II vs the Hittites, the largest chariot battle. Causes, course and consequences # Around 1274 BCE Ramesses II fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II at Kadesh in Syria, in perhaps the largest chariot battle ever (about 5,000 chariots). Ramesses was nearly trapped but rallied; both sides claimed victory. About 15 years later they signed the earliest known peace treaty.

d: Romulus and Remus legend.
x: What happened # Romulus and Remus legend. Causes, course and consequences # According to legend, Romulus founded Rome on 21 April 753 BCE after killing his twin Remus. Archaeology shows villages on the Palatine hill from about 1000 BCE that merged into a city by the 7th century BCE, ruled by kings, some Etruscan, until about 509 BCE.

d: Siddhartha Gautama became the Buddha under the Bodhi tree.
x: What happened # Siddhartha Gautama became the Buddha under the Bodhi tree. Causes, course and consequences # Prince Siddhartha Gautama of the Shakya clan, born at Lumbini, renounced his comfortable life after seeing old age, sickness and death. After six years of extreme austerity, he chose a ‘middle way’ and meditated under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya until he attained enlightenment, becoming the Buddha (‘awakened one’), probably in the 5th century BCE. He gave his first sermon at Sarnath on the Four Noble Truths, and taught for 45 years across the Ganga plain.

d: Greek city-states repelled Persia.
x: What happened # Greek city-states repelled Persia. Causes, course and consequences # The Ionian Greek cities revolted against Persia (499 BCE) with Athenian help. Darius’s army lost at Marathon (490 BCE); Xerxes’ huge invasion was delayed at Thermopylae by Leonidas’s Spartans and defeated at sea at Salamis (480) and on land at Plataea (479). Victory gave Athens confidence and an empire, leading to its golden age.

d: His army mutinied at the Beas.
x: What happened # His army mutinied at the Beas. Causes, course and consequences # In 327–325 BCE Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush, took Taxila’s surrender and defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes (Jhelum) in 326 BCE despite war elephants. His troops mutinied at the Beas river, and he returned via the Indus and the Gedrosian desert. The invasion weakened northwestern kingdoms, helping Chandragupta Maurya build his empire.

d: Led Ashoka to spread Buddhism and dhamma.
x: What happened # Led Ashoka to spread Buddhism and dhamma. Causes, course and consequences # Kalinga, on India’s east coast, controlled sea trade to Southeast Asia and had resisted Mauryan rule. About 261 BCE Ashoka conquered it. His own Rock Edict XIII records that 150,000 people were deported, 100,000 killed and many more died of famine and disease. Ashoka’s remorse turned him toward Buddhism and dhamma; he gave up wars of conquest in favour of ‘conquest by righteousness’.

d: Standardised writing, coins and weights.
x: What happened # Standardised writing, coins and weights. Causes, course and consequences # Between 230 and 221 BCE, King Ying Zheng of Qin, using Legalist reforms that made Qin’s farmers and soldiers efficient and disciplined, conquered the six other Warring States one by one: Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi. He proclaimed himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He standardised writing, coins, laws and axle widths and created commanderies run by appointed officials, which shaped Chinese government for two millennia.

d: Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants.
x: What happened # Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants. Causes, course and consequences # Rome and Carthage fought three wars over the western Mediterranean. In the First (264–241 BCE) Rome built a navy and won Sicily; in the Second (218–201 BCE) Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and destroyed Roman armies at Lake Trasimene and Cannae, but Scipio invaded Africa and defeated him at Zama. In the Third (149–146 BCE) Rome besieged and destroyed Carthage, selling its survivors into slavery.

d: Julius Caesar defeated Vercingetorix at Alesia.
x: What happened # Julius Caesar defeated Vercingetorix at Alesia. Causes, course and consequences # Julius Caesar, governor of Gaul from 58 BCE, used conflicts among Gallic tribes to intervene, defeating the Helvetii, Belgae and Veneti and crossing to Britain and the Rhine. In 52 BCE the Arverni chief Vercingetorix united the Gauls; Caesar besieged him at Alesia and defeated a relief army. Plutarch claims a million Gauls died and a million were enslaved. Gaul became Romanised, and French developed from Latin.

d: Boudica's revolt (60 CE) was crushed.
x: What happened # Boudica’s revolt (60 CE) was crushed. Causes, course and consequences # Emperor Claudius invaded in 43 CE with four legions, seeking glory. Boudica of the Iceni revolted in 60–61 CE after Roman abuses, burning Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before being defeated. Hadrian’s Wall (from 122 CE) marked the northern frontier. Rome built roads, towns and villas, but withdrew around 410 as the empire weakened.

d: Led to Augustus becoming emperor.
x: What happened # Led to Augustus becoming emperor. Causes, course and consequences # After winning the civil war, Caesar was named dictator for life in 44 BCE, alarming senators who feared monarchy. On the Ides of March, about 60 conspirators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed him 23 times at a Senate meeting in the Theatre of Pompey. Instead of restoring the Republic, his death led to civil wars between the conspirators and Antony and Octavian, ending in Augustus’s empire.

d: Christianity became Rome's state religion by 380.
x: What happened # Christianity became Rome’s state religion by 380. Causes, course and consequences # Jesus, a Jewish preacher from Galilee, came to Jerusalem at Passover around 30–33 CE. Temple authorities saw him as a threat, and the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate had him crucified, a punishment for rebels. His followers proclaimed that he rose from the dead; the apostle Paul and others spread the faith across the Roman world, and Christianity became the empire’s religion by the late 4th century.

t: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
d: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus.
x: What happened # Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus. Causes, course and consequences # Pressure from Goths, Vandals and Huns, civil wars, economic decline and dependence on barbarian soldiers weakened the West. Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 and Vandals in 455. In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer deposed Emperor Romulus Augustulus. The eastern empire continued as Byzantium.

d: Prophet Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina.
x: What happened # Prophet Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina. Causes, course and consequences # Muhammad began preaching in Mecca around 610, facing persecution from the Quraysh elite. In 622 he and his followers migrated to Yathrib (Medina), where he led a community governed by the Constitution of Medina — the year 1 of the Islamic calendar. After battles at Badr, Uhud and the Trench, Mecca surrendered in 630, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted Islam.

d: Led by Muhammad bin Qasim.
x: What happened # Led by Muhammad bin Qasim. Causes, course and consequences # After pirates seized ships carrying gifts to the Umayyad governor al-Hajjaj, he sent his 17-year-old nephew Muhammad bin Qasim to Sindh. In 712 Qasim took the port of Debal with catapults and defeated King Dahir at Aror. Sindh became an Umayyad province, Hindus and Buddhists were treated as protected people paying jizya, and Arab scholars learned Indian mathematics and astronomy.

d: Charles Martel's victory.
x: What happened # Charles Martel’s victory. Causes, course and consequences # After conquering Spain from 711, Umayyad armies raided into Gaul. In October 732 Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi’s army met Charles Martel’s Franks between Tours and Poitiers; the Frankish infantry formed a solid square and Abd al-Rahman was killed. The Arabs withdrew, and Charles’s family, the Carolingians, rose to power.

d: Abbasids defeated the Tang.
x: What happened # Abbasids defeated the Tang. Causes, course and consequences # In 751 a Tang army under the Korean-born general Gao Xianzhi fought an Abbasid army near the Talas river in Kyrgyzstan. The Karluk Turks switched sides, and the Tang lost. It ended Chinese expansion into Central Asia, and tradition says captured Chinese papermakers taught the craft in Samarkand.

d: Rajendra Chola's navy raided Srivijaya's ports.
x: What happened # Rajendra Chola’s navy raided Srivijaya’s ports. Causes, course and consequences # Srivijaya controlled the straits through which Chola merchants traded with Song China. In 1025 Rajendra I sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal that captured Srivijaya’s king and raided ports including Kadaram (Kedah) and Palembang, as recorded in the Tanjore inscription. It secured Chola commerce, making it a rare example of Indian overseas military power.

d: William the Conqueror defeated Harold II.
x: What happened # William the Conqueror defeated Harold II. Causes, course and consequences # Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, and three men claimed England’s throne. Harold Godwinson was crowned, defeated the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge, then marched south to meet William of Normandy, who had landed at Pevensey. On 14 October 1066, after a day-long fight, Harold was killed (perhaps by an arrow in the eye, as the Bayeux Tapestry suggests). William was crowned on Christmas Day, built castles, replaced the English nobility with Normans and ordered the Domesday Book; French words flooded into English.

d: The start of two centuries of crusades.
x: What happened # The start of two centuries of crusades. Causes, course and consequences # In 1095, after the Byzantine emperor asked for help against the Seljuk Turks, Pope Urban II called on Western Christians to free Jerusalem, promising remission of sins. A popular ‘People’s Crusade’ massacred Jews in the Rhineland before being destroyed in Anatolia. The knights’ armies took Antioch (1098) and Jerusalem (July 1099), slaughtering many Muslim and Jewish inhabitants, and founded four crusader states. Muslim memory of this violence shaped later relations, and Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187.

d: Opened North India to the Delhi Sultanate.
x: What happened # Opened North India to the Delhi Sultanate. Causes, course and consequences # In 1191 the Chauhan king Prithviraj III defeated Muhammad of Ghor at Tarain near Thanesar. Ghori returned in 1192 with mounted archers who used feigned retreats to break the Rajput army; Prithviraj was captured and killed. Ghori’s slave-general Qutb ud-Din Aibak took Delhi, and after Ghori’s death founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206, beginning six centuries of Turkic, Afghan and Mughal rule in north India.

d: The largest contiguous land empire.
x: What happened # The largest contiguous land empire. Causes, course and consequences # After Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, Mongol armies of mounted archers, organised in decimal units with strict discipline and fast messengers, conquered northern China, destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire (1219–21), and, under his successors, Russia (1237–40), Baghdad (1258) and all of China (1279). Cities that resisted were often massacred; tens of millions may have died. Yet the Pax Mongolica also reopened the Silk Road, allowing Marco Polo’s travels and the spread of gunpowder, paper and, tragically, the Black Death. They were stopped by the Mamluks at Ain Jalut (1260), the Delhi Sultanate, and storms off Japan.

d: Attributed to Bakhtiyar Khilji's forces.
x: What happened # Attributed to Bakhtiyar Khilji’s forces. Causes, course and consequences # Nalanda, a great monastic university founded in the 5th century, had trained scholars from China, Tibet and Korea for 700 years. Around 1193 forces of Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked Nalanda and Vikramashila, killing monks; the Persian historian Minhaj-i-Siraj records the attacks, and later tradition says the library burned for months. Combined with the decline of royal patronage, it ended institutional Buddhism in India, though it survived in Tibet, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. A new Nalanda University opened nearby in 2014.

d: An early step toward constitutional rule.
x: What happened # An early step toward constitutional rule. Causes, course and consequences # King John of England lost Normandy to France, raised heavy taxes and quarrelled with the Pope. In June 1215 rebel barons forced him to seal the ‘Great Charter’ at Runnymede, which said that no free man could be imprisoned or punished except by lawful judgement of his peers or the law of the land, and that the king must consult barons on taxes. The Pope annulled it within weeks and civil war followed, but reissued versions became part of English law. Later, Parliament, American colonists and Indian freedom fighters cited it as a symbol of rights against arbitrary power.

d: By Hulagu Khan.
x: What happened # By Hulagu Khan. Causes, course and consequences # Hulagu Khan’s Mongol army, with Christian Georgian and Armenian allies and Chinese siege engineers, besieged Baghdad in January–February 1258. After the caliph al-Musta’sim surrendered, the city was sacked for a week; estimates of the dead range from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands, and the caliph was reportedly rolled in a carpet and trampled. The House of Wisdom’s books were said to have turned the Tigris black with ink. The fall ended the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad and shifted Islamic cultural centres to Cairo, Delhi and later Istanbul.

d: Ottoman cannons broke the walls.
x: What happened # Ottoman cannons broke the walls. Causes, course and consequences # By 1453 the Byzantine Empire was little more than its capital, defended by about 7,000 men. Sultan Mehmed II, 21 years old, besieged it with perhaps 80,000 troops and giant bronze cannon cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban, and dragged ships overland into the Golden Horn. On 29 May the walls were breached; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died fighting. Mehmed made the city his capital, turned Hagia Sophia into a mosque, and Greek scholars who fled to Italy helped fuel the Renaissance; Europeans sought sea routes to Asia, leading to the Age of Exploration.

d: Movable type printing in Europe.
x: What happened # Movable type printing in Europe. Causes, course and consequences # Around 1440–1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type cast in a hand mould, oil-based ink and a screw press adapted from wine presses. His Bible (about 1455) was printed in some 180 copies. By 1500 presses in over 250 European cities had printed perhaps 20 million volumes. Printing spread Renaissance learning, made Luther’s Reformation possible and standardised languages. Earlier, China had invented woodblock printing (Diamond Sutra, 868) and Korea metal type (Jikji, 1377).

d: Connected the Old and New Worlds.
x: What happened # Connected the Old and New Worlds. Causes, course and consequences # Christopher Columbus, a Genoese navigator sponsored by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, sailed west seeking Asia and landed in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492, then reached Cuba and Hispaniola. He believed he had reached the Indies, hence the name ‘Indians’. His voyages began European colonisation, the Columbian Exchange of crops and animals, the enslavement and catastrophic population collapse of the Taíno and other peoples, and later the Atlantic slave trade.

d: Began European colonial trade in Asia.
x: What happened # Began European colonial trade in Asia. Causes, course and consequences # Sailing around the Cape of Good Hope with an East African pilot’s help, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (Kozhikode) on 20 May 1498. The Zamorin was unimpressed by his gifts, but he returned to Lisbon with spices worth many times the voyage’s cost. Portugal soon used warships and forts (Goa, 1510) to control Indian Ocean trade, beginning European colonial involvement in India.

d: Babur's cannons defeated Ibrahim Lodi.
x: What happened # Babur’s cannons defeated Ibrahim Lodi. Causes, course and consequences # On 21 April 1526 Babur, ruler of Kabul, with about 12,000–25,000 men, met Sultan Ibrahim Lodi’s much larger army and about 100 elephants. Babur used the tulughma flanking tactic and field guns and matchlocks behind carts; the guns panicked the elephants. Ibrahim Lodi died in battle, the first Indian ruler killed on the battlefield in this era, and Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

d: Cortés with Indigenous allies and smallpox.
x: What happened # Cortés with Indigenous allies and smallpox. Causes, course and consequences # Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519 with about 500 men and allied with the Tlaxcalans and others who resented Aztec tribute. Moctezuma II received him, was taken hostage and died in 1520; the Spanish were driven out on the ‘Noche Triste’. A smallpox epidemic then killed many, including Emperor Cuitláhuac. After a 75-day siege with brigantines on the lake, Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521; Mexico City was built on its ruins.

d: Pizarro captured Atahualpa.
x: What happened # Pizarro captured Atahualpa. Causes, course and consequences # Francisco Pizarro arrived in 1532 as the Inca Empire was weakened by smallpox and a civil war between Atahualpa and Huáscar. At Cajamarca, Pizarro’s 168 men ambushed Atahualpa’s unarmed retinue, captured him, collected a room full of gold as ransom, and executed him in 1533. Resistance continued until the last Inca, Túpac Amaru, was executed in 1572.

d: Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara.
x: What happened # Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara. Causes, course and consequences # On 23 January 1565 an alliance of the Deccan sultanates of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeated Vijayanagara’s army under the regent Aliya Rama Raya, who was captured and beheaded. Two Muslim commanders in Vijayanagara service reportedly switched sides. The capital Hampi was looted for six months and never recovered; its ruins are now a UNESCO site.

t: Founding of the East India Company
d: Granted a royal charter by Elizabeth I.
x: What happened # Granted a royal charter by Elizabeth I. Causes, course and consequences # On 31 December 1600 Elizabeth I chartered the ‘Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading into the East Indies’. It set up factories at Surat (1613), Madras (1639), Bombay (1668) and Calcutta (1690), trading in cotton, silk, indigo, saltpetre and tea. After Plassey (1757) it became a ruler with a private army of 260,000, until the Crown took over in 1858.

d: One of history's greatest crimes.
x: What happened # One of history’s greatest crimes. Causes, course and consequences # From the 16th to 19th centuries about 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic, and nearly 2 million died on the Middle Passage. Enslaved people worked on sugar, tobacco and cotton plantations in Brazil, the Caribbean and North America. African resistance, revolts like Haiti’s, and abolitionist movements led Britain to ban the trade in 1807 and slavery in 1833; Brazil was last in 1888.

d: Created the modern idea of state sovereignty.
x: What happened # Created the modern idea of state sovereignty. Causes, course and consequences # Beginning in 1618 when Protestant nobles threw imperial officials out of a window in Prague, the war pitted Catholic Habsburgs against Protestant princes, Sweden and Catholic France. Armies, famine and plague killed perhaps 8 million, a third of some German regions. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) recognised state sovereignty.

d: Robert Clive defeated Siraj ud-Daulah through Mir Jafar's betrayal.
x: What happened # Robert Clive defeated Siraj ud-Daulah through Mir Jafar’s betrayal. Causes, course and consequences # On 23 June 1757 Robert Clive’s 3,000 troops faced Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah’s 50,000. Clive had bribed the Nawab’s commander Mir Jafar, who held back his troops. The Nawab fled and was killed; Mir Jafar became a puppet Nawab, and the Company gained control of Bengal’s revenues.

d: One of the bloodiest battles of the 18th century.
x: What happened # One of the bloodiest battles of the 18th century. Causes, course and consequences # The Marathas, controlling much of India, clashed with Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani, allied with Najib-ud-Daula and Shuja-ud-Daula. After months of standoff, the hungry Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau attacked on 14 January 1761 and was annihilated; Vishwasrao and Bhau died. Perhaps 100,000 died including civilians. It halted Maratha expansion and left a power vacuum the British exploited.

d: Treaty of Allahabad (1765).
x: What happened # Treaty of Allahabad (1765). Causes, course and consequences # After Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Bengal, tried to curb Company privileges, he allied with Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. On 22 October 1764 Hector Munro’s Company army of about 7,000 defeated them. The resulting Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha.

d: Worsened by Company revenue collection.
x: What happened # Worsened by Company revenue collection. Causes, course and consequences # In 1769–70 a failed monsoon struck Bengal and Bihar. The Company, newly in charge of revenue, kept collecting taxes and its officials hoarded rice. About 10 million people — a third of Bengal’s population — died, and farmland went back to jungle. It is a classic example of colonial famine policy.

d: Inspired later anti-colonial movements.
x: What happened # Inspired later anti-colonial movements. Causes, course and consequences # After the Seven Years’ War, Britain taxed its American colonies (Stamp Act, Tea Act), provoking protests like the Boston Tea Party (1773). Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in 1775; the Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776), written by Thomas Jefferson, declared that ‘all men are created equal’. With French help, George Washington won at Yorktown (1781), and the US Constitution (1787) created a federal republic.

d: Followed by Napoleon.
x: What happened # Followed by Napoleon. Causes, course and consequences # France was bankrupt from wars, and bread prices were high. In 1789 the Third Estate formed a National Assembly, crowds stormed the Bastille, and feudal privileges were abolished. The monarchy fell in 1792; Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette were guillotined, and Robespierre’s Terror executed about 17,000. Napoleon seized power in 1799, but the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity spread worldwide.

d: Led by Toussaint Louverture.
x: What happened # Led by Toussaint Louverture. Causes, course and consequences # Saint-Domingue was the world’s richest colony, producing sugar with about 500,000 enslaved Africans. In August 1791 a revolt began after the Bois Caïman ceremony; Toussaint Louverture became its leader, defeating Spanish and British forces. Napoleon tried to restore slavery and captured Toussaint, but Jean-Jacques Dessalines defeated the French, and Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804.

d: Spread the Napoleonic Code.
x: What happened # Spread the Napoleonic Code. Causes, course and consequences # Napoleon, crowned emperor in 1804, won brilliant victories at Austerlitz (1805), Jena (1806) and Wagram (1809), dominating Europe and spreading the Napoleonic Code. The British navy won at Trafalgar (1805), and the Peninsular War drained France. His invasion of Russia in 1812 lost most of his 600,000-man army. Defeated at Leipzig (1813), he returned from Elba and lost at Waterloo (1815).

d: Mangal Pandey, Rani Lakshmibai, Tantia Tope, Bahadur Shah Zafar.
x: What happened # Mangal Pandey, Rani Lakshmibai, Tantia Tope, Bahadur Shah Zafar. Causes, course and consequences # Sepoys at Meerut rose on 10 May 1857 over greased cartridges, annexations and grievances. Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow and Jhansi became centres, with Bahadur Shah Zafar, Rani Lakshmibai and Tatya Tope. It was crushed with great brutality; the Company was abolished in 1858.

d: Britain forced China to accept opium grown in India.
x: What happened # Britain forced China to accept opium grown in India. Causes, course and consequences # British merchants smuggled opium grown in Bengal into China to pay for tea, creating millions of addicts. When Commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed 1,400 tonnes of opium at Canton in 1839, Britain sent gunboats; the Treaty of Nanking (1842) ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports and imposed an indemnity. A Second Opium War (1856–60) with France ended with the looting and burning of the Old Summer Palace and legalised opium. China calls the era that followed the ‘century of humiliation’.

t: Abolition of slavery in the British Empire
d: Indentured Indian labourers then went to Mauritius, Fiji, the Caribbean.
x: What happened # Indentured Indian labourers then went to Mauritius, Fiji, the Caribbean. Causes, course and consequences # Campaigners such as Olaudah Equiano, Thomas Clarkson and William Wilberforce, along with major slave revolts in Jamaica (Baptist War, 1831–32), pushed Parliament to end the slave trade (1807) and then slavery itself. The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 freed about 800,000 people from 1834, though most had to serve ‘apprenticeships’ until 1838. Slave owners received £20 million in compensation — the enslaved received nothing. Plantation owners then turned to indentured labourers from India, sending over a million to the Caribbean, Mauritius, Fiji and Africa.

d: Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.
x: What happened # Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation. Causes, course and consequences # When Abraham Lincoln was elected in 1860 on a platform opposing slavery’s expansion, eleven southern states seceded as the Confederacy. War began at Fort Sumter in 1861; key battles included Antietam, Gettysburg (1863) and Sherman’s march through Georgia. About 620,000–750,000 soldiers died. Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation (1863) and the 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery; Lincoln was assassinated days after the Confederacy surrendered at Appomattox.

d: The Berlin Conference divided the continent.
x: What happened # The Berlin Conference divided the continent. Causes, course and consequences # In 1870 Europeans controlled about 10% of Africa; by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent. Quinine, steamships and the Maxim gun gave Europeans an edge. Borders drawn at the Berlin Conference (1884–85) ignored ethnic and linguistic realities. Colonial rule brought forced labour, the Congo atrocities, the Herero and Nama genocide in German South-West Africa, and economies built around exporting raw materials.

d: El Niño drought plus colonial grain policy.
x: What happened # El Niño drought plus colonial grain policy. Causes, course and consequences # A failed monsoon linked to a strong El Niño hit Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay presidencies. Viceroy Lytton, following free-market principles, refused to control prices while grain was exported to Britain, and relief camps gave rations (the ‘Temple wage’) below those in Buchenwald, as historian Mike Davis notes. Some 5.5–10 million people died. Outrage over this famine helped give birth to Indian economic nationalism and the Congress.

t: Founding of the Indian National Congress
d: Early leaders included Dadabhai Naoroji.
x: What happened # Early leaders included Dadabhai Naoroji. Causes, course and consequences # Educated Indians frustrated by limited representation met in Bombay in December 1885, with 72 delegates under W. C. Bonnerjee, helped by retired civil servant A. O. Hume. The Moderates (Naoroji, Gokhale) petitioned for reforms; Extremists (Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal) demanded swaraj. Under Gandhi from 1920 it became a mass movement and later India’s ruling party.

d: Reversed in 1911.
x: What happened # Reversed in 1911. Causes, course and consequences # In 1905 Viceroy Curzon divided Bengal into a Muslim-majority east and Hindu-majority west, officially for administration but widely seen as divide and rule. Bengalis protested with the Swadeshi movement — boycotting British cloth, burning foreign goods, singing Tagore’s songs — and revolutionary groups formed. The partition was annulled in 1911, and the capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi.

d: About 1.3 million Indian soldiers served.
x: What happened # About 1.3 million Indian soldiers served. Causes, course and consequences # Rivalries, an arms race and alliances turned the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo (28 June 1914) into a world war. Trench warfare on the Western Front, poison gas, tanks, machine guns and aircraft killed about 9–10 million soldiers and millions of civilians. About 1.3 million Indian soldiers served in France, Mesopotamia, Gallipoli and East Africa, and some 74,000 died. The war destroyed the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires and set the stage for World War II.

d: Lenin and the Bolsheviks seized power.
x: What happened # Lenin and the Bolsheviks seized power. Causes, course and consequences # Food shortages and military defeats led to strikes in Petrograd in February 1917; Tsar Nicholas II abdicated. A Provisional Government continued the war, and in October the Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power with the slogan ‘Peace, land, bread’. A civil war (1918–21) killed millions and created the Soviet Union in 1922.

d: Turned millions against British rule.
x: What happened # Turned millions against British rule. Causes, course and consequences # After protests against the Rowlatt Act, which allowed imprisonment without trial, crowds gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar on Baisakhi, 13 April 1919. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer blocked the narrow exit and ordered troops to fire for about ten minutes; official figures said 379 died, Indian estimates over 1,000. Tagore renounced his knighthood, and Udham Singh later shot Michael O’Dwyer, Punjab’s former governor, in London (1940).

d: Gandhi's first nationwide campaign.
x: What happened # Gandhi’s first nationwide campaign. Causes, course and consequences # Launched by Gandhi in 1920 with the Khilafat movement, it asked Indians to give up titles, boycott government schools, courts, legislatures and foreign cloth, and spin khadi. Millions joined, uniting Hindus and Muslims. After a mob killed 22 policemen at Chauri Chaura in February 1922, Gandhi called it off, insisting on non-violence.

d: Helped bring fascism to power.
x: What happened # Helped bring fascism to power. Causes, course and consequences # After the Wall Street crash of October 1929, banks failed, trade collapsed and world unemployment soared — in the US to 25%. Farm prices fell, hurting India’s peasants. Desperation helped Hitler win power in 1933, while Roosevelt’s New Deal expanded government’s role.

d: Gandhi walked 390 km to Dandi to make salt.
x: What happened # Gandhi walked 390 km to Dandi to make salt. Causes, course and consequences # On 12 March 1930 Gandhi and 78 volunteers left Sabarmati Ashram and walked 385 km to Dandi, where on 6 April he picked up salt, breaking the British salt monopoly. Civil disobedience spread; about 60,000 were arrested. The march drew world attention.

d: 2.5 million Indians served, the largest volunteer army.
x: What happened # 2.5 million Indians served, the largest volunteer army. Causes, course and consequences # Germany’s invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 started the war in Europe; Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor (1941) widened it. The Axis was defeated at Stalingrad, El Alamein, Midway, and on D-Day (1944). About 70–85 million people died, including the 6 million Jews of the Holocaust and about 27 million Soviet citizens. India sent 2.5 million volunteers; the war hastened decolonisation and created the UN and Cold War.

d: Plus millions of Roma, disabled people and others.
x: What happened # Plus millions of Roma, disabled people and others. Causes, course and consequences # The Nazis’ antisemitic laws from 1933 escalated into ghettos, mass shootings by Einsatzgruppen, and death camps such as Auschwitz, Treblinka and Sobibor. About 6 million Jews were murdered, along with Roma, disabled people, Soviet POWs and others. The Nuremberg Trials and the Genocide Convention (1948) followed.

d: Mass arrests followed.
x: What happened # Mass arrests followed. Causes, course and consequences # On 8 August 1942 Congress demanded an immediate British withdrawal, Gandhi calling ‘Do or die’. Leaders were arrested next morning, and spontaneous protests, strikes and sabotage spread; about 100,000 were arrested and hundreds killed. Parallel governments formed in Satara, Tamluk and Ballia.

d: Caused largely by wartime policy.
x: What happened # Caused largely by wartime policy. Causes, course and consequences # The loss of Burmese rice after Japan’s conquest, a cyclone, wartime inflation, hoarding, and British ‘denial’ policy, plus Churchill’s war cabinet refusing food imports, caused a famine that killed about 3 million. Amartya Sen’s work showed it was a failure of entitlement, not of food supply.

t: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
d: The only nuclear weapons used in war.
x: What happened # The only nuclear weapons used in war. Causes, course and consequences # The Manhattan Project built atomic bombs in the US. On 6 August 1945 ‘Little Boy’ destroyed Hiroshima, and on 9 August ‘Fat Man’ struck Nagasaki; about 110,000–210,000 people died by the end of 1945. With the Soviet Union also declaring war on Japan, Emperor Hirohito announced surrender on 15 August. The bombings began the nuclear age.

d: One of the largest migrations in history.
x: What happened # One of the largest migrations in history. Causes, course and consequences # Weakened by World War II and facing the naval mutiny of 1946, Britain decided to leave India. Mountbatten advanced the date to August 1947, and the Radcliffe Line split Punjab and Bengal. India and Pakistan became independent on 14–15 August. About 15 million people crossed the new borders and up to 1–2 million died in communal violence. The princely states had to choose sides, leading to conflict in Kashmir.

d: Drafted under B. R. Ambedkar.
x: What happened # Drafted under B. R. Ambedkar. Causes, course and consequences # The Constituent Assembly debated for nearly three years; the drafting committee was chaired by Ambedkar. Adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force on 26 January 1950, it guaranteed fundamental rights, universal adult franchise and abolished untouchability.

d: Mao Zedong.
x: What happened # Mao Zedong. Causes, course and consequences # After eight years fighting Japan and four years of civil war, Mao Zedong’s Communists defeated Chiang Kai-shek’s Nationalists, who fled to Taiwan. On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People’s Republic of China from Tiananmen. Land reform redistributed land but killed perhaps 1–2 million landlords, and the new state allied with the Soviet Union.

d: India's independence inspired others.
x: What happened # India’s independence inspired others. Causes, course and consequences # World War II exhausted Britain, France and the Netherlands while nationalist movements grew. India and Pakistan (1947), Burma and Sri Lanka (1948), Indonesia (1949), Ghana (1957) and 17 African countries in 1960 alone won independence. Some struggles were bloody — Algeria (1954–62), Kenya’s Mau Mau, Vietnam — and colonial borders often left lasting conflicts.

d: India intervened after a genocide and refugee crisis.
x: What happened # India intervened after a genocide and refugee crisis. Causes, course and consequences # In 1970 the Awami League under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman won a majority in Pakistan’s elections, but West Pakistan’s leaders refused to transfer power. On 25 March 1971 the army launched Operation Searchlight; hundreds of thousands to millions were killed and about 10 million fled to India. India intervened in December alongside the Mukti Bahini, and 93,000 Pakistani soldiers surrendered in Dhaka on 16 December.

d: Apollo 11.
x: What happened # Apollo 11. Causes, course and consequences # The Soviet Union launched Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961); President Kennedy then pledged to land Americans on the Moon. On 20 July 1969 Apollo 11’s lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility, and Neil Armstrong stepped out saying ‘That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.’ Six missions landed 12 astronauts by 1972.

d: Germany reunified in 1990.
x: What happened # Germany reunified in 1990. Causes, course and consequences # Built in 1961 to stop East Germans fleeing west, the Wall became the symbol of the Cold War. As reform swept Eastern Europe in 1989, an official mistakenly announced on 9 November that borders were open; crowds poured through and began chipping the Wall. Germany reunified on 3 October 1990.

d: Ended the Cold War.
x: What happened # Ended the Cold War. Causes, course and consequences # Gorbachev’s glasnost and perestroika loosened control, and the Baltic states, Ukraine and others pushed for independence. A failed hard-line coup in August 1991 discredited the Communist Party; Boris Yeltsin rose. On 26 December 1991 the Soviet Union dissolved into 15 states.

d: Manmohan Singh's reforms.
x: What happened # Manmohan Singh’s reforms. Causes, course and consequences # In 1991 India’s foreign reserves could cover only weeks of imports, and it pledged gold to borrow. Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh devalued the rupee, cut tariffs, ended most industrial licensing and opened sectors to foreign investment. Growth accelerated, creating India’s IT boom and a large middle class.

d: Reshaped global security.
x: What happened # Reshaped global security. Causes, course and consequences # On 11 September 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers seized four airliners, crashing two into New York’s World Trade Center and one into the Pentagon; the fourth crashed in Pennsylvania. Nearly 3,000 people died. The US invaded Afghanistan (2001) and Iraq (2003), launching the ‘war on terror’.

d: Hit Tamil Nadu and the Andamans.
x: What happened # Hit Tamil Nadu and the Andamans. Causes, course and consequences # On 26 December 2004 a magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off Sumatra caused waves up to 30 m high. About 230,000 people died in 14 countries, including Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India (Tamil Nadu and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands) and Thailand. It led to an Indian Ocean tsunami warning system.

d: India became the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon.
x: What happened # India became the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon. Causes, course and consequences # After Chandrayaan-2’s lander crashed in 2019, ISRO launched Chandrayaan-3 on 14 July 2023. Its Vikram lander touched down near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon and the first near the south pole. The Pragyan rover confirmed sulphur in the lunar soil.

d: Our ancestors diverged from those of chimpanzees, probably in a mosaic of forest and woodland.
x: What happened # Our ancestors diverged from those of chimpanzees, probably in a mosaic of forest and woodland. Causes, course and consequences # Genetic comparisons show humans and chimpanzees share about 98.8% of their DNA and a common ancestor that lived roughly 6–8 million years ago in Africa. The split was messy: populations may have interbred for some time after separating. Fossils near this time — Sahelanthropus in Chad, Orrorin in Kenya — show early signs of upright walking, as forests broke into woodland mosaics.

d: Ardipithecus walked upright on the ground but still climbed trees; leaving the forest canopy was gradual.
x: What happened # Ardipithecus walked upright on the ground but still climbed trees; leaving the forest canopy was gradual. Causes, course and consequences # Bipedalism appeared before big brains or stone tools. Sahelanthropus (about 7 million years ago) had a skull opening suggesting upright posture, and Orrorin’s thigh bones (6 million years ago) show walking. Theories for why include freeing hands to carry food, seeing over grass, keeping cool in the sun and moving efficiently between patches of forest. Lucy’s species (3.2 million years ago) walked well but still climbed.

d: Three hominins walked through wet volcanic ash, leaving the oldest human-like footprints.
x: What happened # Three hominins walked through wet volcanic ash, leaving the oldest human-like footprints. Causes, course and consequences # About 3.66 million years ago, at Laetoli in Tanzania, three individuals of Australopithecus afarensis walked across wet volcanic ash, which then hardened. Mary Leakey’s team found the 27-metre trail in 1978. The footprints show a human-like arched foot and big toe in line with the others, proving fully upright walking long before stone tools.

d: Large stone cores and flakes made before the genus Homo appeared.
x: What happened # Large stone cores and flakes made before the genus Homo appeared. Causes, course and consequences # In 2015 archaeologists announced stone flakes and cores from Lomekwi 3 near Lake Turkana, Kenya, dated to 3.3 million years ago — 700,000 years older than the Oldowan and before the genus Homo. The makers (perhaps Kenyanthropus or Australopithecus) struck big rocks against anvils. Cut-marked bones from Dikika, Ethiopia (3.4 million years ago) suggest early meat-eating.

d: Sharp flakes let early humans cut meat and break bones for marrow.
x: What happened # Sharp flakes let early humans cut meat and break bones for marrow. Causes, course and consequences # From about 2.6 million years ago at Gona, Ethiopia, hominins knapped simple sharp flakes from river cobbles to cut meat and crack bones for marrow. Named after Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, the Oldowan is associated with Homo habilis and later early Homo erectus. Meat and marrow may have supplied energy for bigger brains.

d: Small-brained humans reached the Caucasus and soon East Asia.
x: What happened # Small-brained humans reached the Caucasus and soon East Asia. Causes, course and consequences # By about 1.8 million years ago Homo erectus, taller and with longer legs, reached Dmanisi in Georgia, and soon Java and China. Stone tools in Shanghuang (China) and Attirampakkam (India, 1.5 million years ago) show how quickly hominins spread. Erectus survived in Java until about 110,000 years ago — the longest-lived human species.

d: The longest-lasting tool tradition, used for over 1.5 million years.
x: What happened # The longest-lasting tool tradition, used for over 1.5 million years. Causes, course and consequences # About 1.76 million years ago in Kenya, Homo erectus began shaping symmetrical teardrop hand-axes — the first tools made to a mental template. The Acheulean tradition lasted over a million years from Africa to India (Attirampakkam, Bhimbetka) and Europe. Making them may have required planning and teaching, perhaps related to language origins.

d: Burned bones and plant ash show fire inside a cave a million years ago.
x: What happened # Burned bones and plant ash show fire inside a cave a million years ago. Causes, course and consequences # Burnt bone and plant ash deep inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, about 1 million years ago, are the earliest secure evidence of hominins using fire. Fire allowed cooking, which makes food easier to digest; Richard Wrangham argues cooking drove brain growth and smaller guts. Fire also gave warmth, protection and social gatherings.

d: Repeated hearth use shows fire had become part of daily life.
x: What happened # Repeated hearth use shows fire had become part of daily life. Causes, course and consequences # At Qesem Cave in Israel, a hearth used repeatedly from about 300,000 years ago shows habitual fire use, with burnt bones from butchered fallow deer. Similar evidence appears at Gesher Benot Ya’aqov (780,000 years ago). Regular hearths show fire had become part of daily life.

d: Wooden throwing spears found with butchered horses.
x: What happened # Wooden throwing spears found with butchered horses. Causes, course and consequences # Wooden spears about 2 m long, found preserved in a German coal mine, date to about 300,000 years ago. Balanced like javelins, they were found with butchered horses, proving early humans (probably Homo heidelbergensis) hunted large animals rather than only scavenging.

d: The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils.
x: What happened # The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils. Causes, course and consequences # Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, a cave in Morocco, were long thought to be about 40,000 years old. In 2017 new dating of burnt flints put them at about 315,000 years, making them the oldest known Homo sapiens. They had modern faces but elongated braincases, suggesting our species evolved across Africa over a long time.

d: Engraved ochre and shell beads show abstract symbols.
x: What happened # Engraved ochre and shell beads show abstract symbols. Causes, course and consequences # Blombos Cave on South Africa’s southern coast contains ochre pieces engraved with cross-hatched patterns about 75,000–100,000 years old, shell beads and a 100,000-year-old paint workshop with abalone shells. A 73,000-year-old drawing in red ochre on a stone flake is the oldest known drawing. They show early symbolic and planning abilities.

d: People crossed open water to reach Sahul.
x: What happened # People crossed open water to reach Sahul. Causes, course and consequences # Modern humans crossed at least 90 km of open sea from Southeast Asia to reach Sahul (Australia and New Guinea joined by low sea levels), probably by raft or boat. The Madjedbebe rock shelter suggests arrival about 65,000 years ago, though some argue about 50,000. Aboriginal Australians have continuous cultures, with art, songlines and fire management of landscapes.

d: Our ancestors mixed with Neanderthals, leaving ~1–2% of their DNA in most people today.
x: What happened # Our ancestors mixed with Neanderthals, leaving ~1–2% of their DNA in most people today. Causes, course and consequences # Ancient DNA (Svante Pääbo, Nobel 2022) shows modern humans outside Africa carry 1–2% Neanderthal DNA from interbreeding about 50,000–60,000 years ago; Melanesians also carry Denisovan DNA. Some genes affect immunity and altitude adaptation (Tibetans).

d: A painted scene of humans and a pig in Leang Karampuang.
x: What happened # A painted scene of humans and a pig in Leang Karampuang. Causes, course and consequences # In Leang Karampuang cave on Sulawesi, Indonesia, a painting of three human-like figures interacting with a wild pig was dated in 2024 to at least 51,200 years ago, using uranium-series dating. It is the oldest known figurative and narrative art, showing that storytelling art emerged in Asia, not only Europe.

d: Small populations, competition and climate shifts ended the Neanderthals.
x: What happened # Small populations, competition and climate shifts ended the Neanderthals. Causes, course and consequences # Neanderthals had lived in Europe and western Asia for over 300,000 years, burying their dead, making jewellery from eagle talons and possibly painting caves. They vanished around 40,000 years ago, a few thousand years after Homo sapiens spread into Europe. Likely causes combine small, inbred populations, abrupt climate swings, competition with modern humans for game, and absorption through interbreeding — so part of them lives on in our DNA.

d: Lions, rhinos and horses painted with shading and perspective.
x: What happened # Lions, rhinos and horses painted with shading and perspective. Causes, course and consequences # Discovered in 1994 in the Ardèche gorge of France, Chauvet holds over 400 animal images made around 36,000–30,000 years ago: lions, rhinos, cave bears, mammoths and horses, drawn with shading and overlapping figures to suggest movement. A cave bear skull placed on a rock and footprints of a child show human activity. Its age proved that sophisticated art appeared early, not gradually.

d: Wolves became dogs alongside Ice Age hunters.
x: What happened # Wolves became dogs alongside Ice Age hunters. Causes, course and consequences # Dogs descend from a now-extinct population of grey wolves and were domesticated by Ice Age hunter-gatherers, at least 15,000 and possibly over 20,000 years ago. A dog was buried with humans at Bonn-Oberkassel about 14,000 years ago. Dogs helped hunting, guarding and hauling, and ancient DNA shows they travelled with human migrations, including into the Americas.

d: Human footprints in ancient lake mud.
x: What happened # Human footprints in ancient lake mud. Causes, course and consequences # Footprints of adults and children preserved in ancient lake beds at White Sands, New Mexico, were dated by seeds and pollen to 21,000–23,000 years ago. They show people living in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum, earlier than the old ‘Clovis first’ model. The prints also record mammoths and giant sloths walking alongside.

d: Fluted spear points spread across North America.
x: What happened # Fluted spear points spread across North America. Causes, course and consequences # From about 13,000 years ago, people across North America made distinctive fluted ‘Clovis’ points, found with mammoth and mastodon kills. The Anzick child burial in Montana (12,600 years ago) is genetically ancestral to many Native Americans. Clovis lasted only a few centuries as megafauna disappeared.

d: Hunter-gatherers harvested wild grains and built stone houses.
x: What happened # Hunter-gatherers harvested wild grains and built stone houses. Causes, course and consequences # Between about 15,000 and 11,500 years ago, the Natufians of the Levant lived in villages of round stone houses year-round, harvesting wild wheat and barley with flint sickles and grinding stones. They buried their dead with ornaments and kept dogs. Their settled life and cereal use paved the way for farming.

d: Carved stone pillars raised by hunter-gatherers.
x: What happened # Carved stone pillars raised by hunter-gatherers. Causes, course and consequences # Around 9600 BCE hunter-gatherers in southeast Turkey carved and raised T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.5 m tall, decorated with foxes, snakes, vultures and scorpions, in circular enclosures. It is about 6,000 years older than Stonehenge and suggests monumental religion may have come before farming.

d: A stone tower and wall around an early farming town.
x: What happened # A stone tower and wall around an early farming town. Causes, course and consequences # Around 8000 BCE the Neolithic town of Jericho in the Jordan valley, supported by a spring, had perhaps 1,000–2,000 people. They built a stone wall and an 8.5-metre tower with an internal staircase — among the oldest monumental buildings. Later residents plastered and painted the skulls of ancestors, a form of ancestor veneration.

d: Shangshan and Hemudu villages grew rice.
x: What happened # Shangshan and Hemudu villages grew rice. Causes, course and consequences # Wild rice was gathered in the Yangtze valley from about 10,000 years ago; by 7,000 years ago, at Hemudu and Tianluoshan, people grew domesticated rice in paddies, kept pigs and built wooden stilt houses. Rice farming spread south into Southeast Asia and, mixing with locally cultivated rice, into India. Rice supports more people per hectare than most crops, enabling dense populations in Asia.

d: Teosinte was bred into maize in the Balsas valley.
x: What happened # Teosinte was bred into maize in the Balsas valley. Causes, course and consequences # About 9,000 years ago farmers in the Balsas river valley of southern Mexico began selecting teosinte, a grass with tiny hard kernels. Over thousands of years, maize became a large-cobbed crop that could not seed itself without humans. Combined with beans and squash (the ‘Three Sisters’), it fed the Olmec, Maya, Aztec and Puebloan worlds, and after 1492 it spread across Africa, India and China.

d: The earliest known smelted copper.
x: What happened # The earliest known smelted copper. Causes, course and consequences # At Belovode in Serbia, people smelted copper around 5000 BCE; Iran and Anatolia show early metallurgy too. Smelting required furnaces reaching 1,100 °C. Copper tools and ornaments marked the Chalcolithic, and mixing copper with tin or arsenic made bronze, harder and better for weapons, around 3300 BCE.

d: Ancient DNA shows today's horses descend from steppe horses domesticated around 4,200 years ago.
x: What happened # Ancient DNA shows today’s horses descend from steppe horses domesticated around 4,200 years ago. Causes, course and consequences # People at Botai in Kazakhstan used horses around 3500 BCE, but ancient DNA (2021) shows the horses we ride today came from the lower Volga–Don steppe about 2200 BCE. They spread across Eurasia within centuries along with spoke-wheeled chariots, transforming warfare, trade and migration.

d: Solid wooden wheels appeared almost simultaneously across Eurasia.
x: What happened # Solid wooden wheels appeared almost simultaneously across Eurasia. Causes, course and consequences # The earliest wheels, for pottery, appear in Mesopotamia around 3500 BCE; soon after, solid wooden wheels on axles carried wagons, depicted on the Bronocice pot in Poland (about 3400 BCE). Ox-drawn wagons let steppe peoples move herds and homes. Spoked wheels (about 2000 BCE) made fast chariots possible.

d: The Narmer Palette shows a king wearing both crowns.
x: What happened # The Narmer Palette shows a king wearing both crowns. Causes, course and consequences # Around 3100 BCE Narmer, a king from Upper Egypt, brought the Nile valley and delta under one rule. The Narmer Palette, found at Hierakonpolis, shows him wearing the white crown of the south on one side and the red crown of the north on the other. He founded the First Dynasty, beginning 3,000 years of pharaonic history.

d: Uruk grew to over 40,000 people.
x: What happened # Uruk grew to over 40,000 people. Causes, course and consequences # By 3200 BCE Uruk covered 2.5 square km with perhaps 40,000 people, monumental temples such as the White Temple of Anu, and specialised craftsmen. Its administrators invented proto-cuneiform writing to track grain, beer and labour. Its expansion spread Mesopotamian culture across the Near East; later Gilgamesh was remembered as its king.

d: Built for Khufu by organised paid crews.
x: What happened # Built for Khufu by organised paid crews. Causes, course and consequences # The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the Fourth Dynasty king Khufu around 2560 BCE, about 146 m tall from around 2.3 million blocks. Workers were paid labourers housed in a nearby village, and the Wadi al-Jarf papyri, the oldest inscribed papyri, record a team transporting limestone. It was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.

d: Sargon united Sumerian city-states.
x: What happened # Sargon united Sumerian city-states. Causes, course and consequences # About 2334 BCE Sargon, a cupbearer to the king of Kish, seized power, built a new capital at Akkad, and conquered the Sumerian cities, creating the first multi-ethnic empire. He kept a standing army and appointed Akkadians as governors. His grandson Naram-Sin called himself ‘king of the four quarters’.

d: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira flourish.
x: What happened # Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira flourish. Causes, course and consequences # From about 2600 to 1900 BCE, the Indus or Harappan civilisation had over 1,000 settlements across 1 million square km. Cities like Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi had planned streets, covered drains, standard bricks and weights, and the Great Bath. They traded with Mesopotamia (‘Meluhha’). Weakening monsoons and shifting rivers led to de-urbanisation.

d: 282 laws carved on a stele.
x: What happened # 282 laws carved on a stele. Causes, course and consequences # Around 1754 BCE King Hammurabi of Babylon placed 282 laws on a basalt stele, topped with an image of him receiving authority from Shamash. Laws covered trade, wages, divorce and medicine, with punishments that depended on class. The stele was taken to Susa and found there in 1901.

d: A massive eruption buried Akrotiri.
x: What happened # A massive eruption buried Akrotiri. Causes, course and consequences # The Minoan eruption of Thera (Santorini) around 1600 BCE was one of the largest in the past 10,000 years, burying Akrotiri under metres of ash. It produced tsunamis that struck Crete. Its exact date is debated, with radiocarbon and archaeology pointing to slightly different times.

d: Ahmose I drove out Asian rulers.
x: What happened # Ahmose I drove out Asian rulers. Causes, course and consequences # The Hyksos, West Asian rulers who introduced horses, chariots and composite bows, controlled northern Egypt from about 1650 BCE. Kings of Thebes fought back; Ahmose I captured their capital Avaris around 1550 BCE. Egypt then built an empire in the Levant and Nubia, the New Kingdom.

d: A pharaoh promoted a single sun-disc god.
x: What happened # A pharaoh promoted a single sun-disc god. Causes, course and consequences # Amenhotep IV renamed himself Akhenaten, promoting the Aten, the sun disc, as Egypt’s supreme god, closing other temples and building a new capital, Amarna. Art became naturalistic. After his death, the old gods returned under Tutankhamun, and Akhenaten’s name was erased.

d: Excavations at Hisarlik show a destroyed city around this time.
x: What happened # Excavations at Hisarlik show a destroyed city around this time. Causes, course and consequences # Homer’s Iliad tells of Greeks besieging Troy to recover Helen. Excavations at Hisarlik in Turkey by Schliemann and later teams found a city destroyed around 1180 BCE. Hittite records mention ‘Wilusa’, likely Troy. Whether the war happened as told is debated.

d: Cheap iron tools made farming and armies larger.
x: What happened # Cheap iron tools made farming and armies larger. Causes, course and consequences # Iron requires hotter furnaces and forging but iron ore is more common than tin. After the Bronze Age collapse disrupted tin trade around 1200 BCE, iron spread across the Near East and Mediterranean. In India, iron appears at sites in the Ganga valley and south India by 1800–1500 BCE; in Africa, Nok and Meroë became iron centres.

d: Hymns preserved orally for millennia.
x: What happened # Hymns preserved orally for millennia. Causes, course and consequences # Between about 1500 and 1200 BCE, poet-priests in the Punjab composed over 1,000 hymns to Agni, Indra, Soma and others. They were memorised exactly using techniques such as pada and ghana recitation, and written down only around 1000 CE. UNESCO lists Vedic chanting as intangible heritage.

d: Held every four years for over 1,000 years.
x: What happened # Held every four years for over 1,000 years. Causes, course and consequences # In 776 BCE, according to tradition, the first Olympic Games were held at Olympia in honour of Zeus, with a single footrace. Held every four years, they grew to include wrestling, chariot races and the pankration; a sacred truce allowed athletes to travel. Theodosius I may have ended them around 393 CE; Pierre de Coubertin revived them in 1896.

d: Romulus and Remus legend.
x: What happened # Romulus and Remus legend. Causes, course and consequences # Roman tradition held that Romulus and Remus, twin sons of the god Mars and the princess Rhea Silvia, were abandoned on the Tiber, suckled by a she-wolf and raised by a shepherd. Romulus founded the city on the Palatine on 21 April 753 BCE, killing Remus in a quarrel, and populated it by welcoming outlaws and seizing Sabine women. Archaeology shows Iron Age villages from around 1000 BCE merging into a city by the 7th century BCE, ruled by kings until about 509 BCE.

d: Babylonians and Medes destroyed the Assyrian capital.
x: What happened # Babylonians and Medes destroyed the Assyrian capital. Causes, course and consequences # After the death of Ashurbanipal (c. 631 BCE), the Assyrian Empire fell into civil war. The Babylonian Nabopolassar and the Median king Cyaxares allied and besieged Nineveh, which fell in 612 BCE after a three-month siege; flooding of the Khosr river may have breached walls. Assyria’s last king held out at Harran until 609 BCE. Ashurbanipal’s buried library preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh.

d: Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the First Temple.
x: What happened # Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the First Temple. Causes, course and consequences # After Judah rebelled, Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem, deporting King Jehoiachin and elites in 597 BCE, then destroyed the city and Solomon’s Temple in 587/586 BCE. In Babylon, exiled Jews kept their identity through the Sabbath, scripture and synagogue-like gatherings; much of the Hebrew Bible was edited then. When Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE he allowed them to return and rebuild the Temple.

d: Cyrus freed the exiled Jews.
x: What happened # Cyrus freed the exiled Jews. Causes, course and consequences # The Babylonian king Nabonidus had alienated Marduk’s priests by favouring the moon god Sin and spending years in Arabia. In October 539 BCE, after defeating the Babylonian army at Opis, Cyrus’s forces entered Babylon with little resistance. The Cyrus Cylinder presents him as chosen by Marduk, restoring temples and returning deported peoples, which the Bible echoes for the Jews.

d: Cleisthenes' reforms.
x: What happened # Cleisthenes’ reforms. Causes, course and consequences # After the tyrant Hippias was expelled, Cleisthenes in 508 BCE reorganised Athenian citizens into ten tribes mixing different regions, and created a Council of 500 chosen by lot. Under Ephialtes and Pericles, the Assembly of all adult male citizens voted on laws and war, juries of hundreds judged cases, and officials were paid so poor citizens could serve. Women, slaves and resident foreigners — most of the population — were excluded.

d: The legend of the runner.
x: What happened # The legend of the runner. Causes, course and consequences # In 490 BCE Darius I sent a fleet to punish Athens for supporting the Ionian revolt. At Marathon, about 10,000 Athenian and 1,000 Plataean hoplites under Miltiades charged the Persians, strengthening their wings to envelop the enemy. Herodotus counts 6,400 Persian and 192 Athenian dead. The legend of a runner carrying news to Athens inspired the modern marathon.

d: Recorded by Thucydides.
x: What happened # Recorded by Thucydides. Causes, course and consequences # Fear of Athens’ growing empire led Sparta and its allies to war in 431 BCE. Pericles kept Athenians behind their walls, but plague killed a quarter of them, including him. Athens’ disastrous Sicilian Expedition (415–413 BCE) lost its fleet; Sparta, funded by Persia, destroyed Athens’ navy at Aegospotami (405) and starved it into surrender in 404 BCE. Thucydides wrote its history.

d: Condemned for impiety.
x: What happened # Condemned for impiety. Causes, course and consequences # Socrates questioned Athenians about justice and virtue, angering powerful men. In 399 BCE, after the defeat in the Peloponnesian War and the rule of the Thirty Tyrants (some his former pupils), he was tried for impiety and corrupting the young. Found guilty, he refused to flee and drank hemlock; Plato’s Apology and Phaedo record his defence and last hours.

d: Alexander defeated Darius III.
x: What happened # Alexander defeated Darius III. Causes, course and consequences # Crossing the Hellespont in 334 BCE with about 40,000 men, Alexander won at the Granicus, then at Issus (333 BCE) where Darius III fled. He took Tyre after a seven-month siege and Egypt without a fight, then crushed Darius at Gaugamela (331 BCE). He took Babylon, Susa and Persepolis, which burned; Darius was murdered by his own nobles in 330 BCE.

d: Seleucus traded lands for 500 war elephants.
x: What happened # Seleucus traded lands for 500 war elephants. Causes, course and consequences # Seleucus I tried to reclaim Alexander’s Indian provinces around 305 BCE but came to terms with Chandragupta Maurya. Seleucus ceded Arachosia, Gedrosia and Paropamisadae (parts of Afghanistan and Baluchistan) in exchange for 500 war elephants, which helped him win at Ipsus (301 BCE). A marriage alliance and the embassy of Megasthenes to Pataliputra followed.

d: Rock edicts in Brahmi and Kharosthi.
x: What happened # Rock edicts in Brahmi and Kharosthi. Causes, course and consequences # From about 260 BCE Ashoka had his messages carved on rocks and polished pillars across his empire, mostly in Prakrit in Brahmi script, but in Greek and Aramaic in Afghanistan. They speak of his remorse after Kalinga, tolerance for all sects, medical care for people and animals, and officials (dhamma-mahamattas) to spread welfare. James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837, recovering Ashoka for history.

d: Earlier walls joined under Qin Shi Huang.
x: What happened # Earlier walls joined under Qin Shi Huang. Causes, course and consequences # After 221 BCE, Qin Shi Huang sent General Meng Tian with 300,000 men to drive back the Xiongnu and link older state walls of rammed earth into a frontier wall. Many forced labourers died. The famous brick-and-stone Great Wall seen today was mostly built by the Ming dynasty.

d: Han envoy Zhang Qian reached Bactria.
x: What happened # Han envoy Zhang Qian reached Bactria. Causes, course and consequences # Han Emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian west in 138 BCE to find allies against the Xiongnu; captured for ten years, he escaped and reached Bactria. His reports opened official contact with Central Asia. Silk, horses, paper, Buddhism, spices and ideas soon flowed along routes linking China, India, Persia and Rome.

d: Crushed by Crassus.
x: What happened # Crushed by Crassus. Causes, course and consequences # In 73 BCE Spartacus, a Thracian gladiator, escaped from a school in Capua with about 70 others and hid on Vesuvius. Slaves joined him, building an army of perhaps 70,000–120,000 that defeated several Roman armies. Marcus Crassus finally defeated him in 71 BCE, and 6,000 captured slaves were crucified along the Appian Way.

d: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra.
x: What happened # Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra. Causes, course and consequences # Mark Antony and Cleopatra controlled the eastern Roman provinces; Octavian declared war on Cleopatra. On 2 September 31 BCE, off Actium in western Greece, Agrippa’s fleet defeated them; Cleopatra’s ships fled and Antony followed. Both took their own lives in Alexandria in 30 BCE. Octavian became sole ruler and, in 27 BCE, Augustus.

d: Three legions destroyed by Arminius.
x: What happened # Three legions destroyed by Arminius. Causes, course and consequences # In 9 CE Arminius, a Cheruscan chief who had served as a Roman officer, led the governor Varus’s three legions into an ambush in the Teutoburg Forest. Over three days in rain, about 15,000–20,000 Romans were killed. Augustus reportedly cried ‘Varus, give me back my legions!’ Rome gave up conquering Germany, keeping the Rhine as the frontier.

d: Kushan patronage.
x: What happened # Kushan patronage. Causes, course and consequences # Kanishka the Kushan emperor convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir, around the 1st–2nd century CE, under Vasumitra and Ashvaghosha. Scholars compiled the Mahavibhasha commentaries of the Sarvastivada school. The council marked the rise of Mahayana Buddhism and the use of Sanskrit for Buddhist texts, which spread to Central Asia and China.

d: Peasant revolt led to warlordism and the Three Kingdoms.
x: What happened # Peasant revolt led to warlordism and the Three Kingdoms. Causes, course and consequences # In 184 CE, after famine, land concentration and court corruption, the Daoist healer Zhang Jue led hundreds of thousands of peasants, wearing yellow headbands, against the Han, proclaiming a new ‘Yellow Heaven’. The rebellion was crushed within a year, but the generals who suppressed it — Dong Zhuo, Cao Cao, Liu Bei, Sun Jian — became warlords, ending the Han and creating the Three Kingdoms.

d: Over 20 emperors in 50 years.
x: What happened # Over 20 emperors in 50 years. Causes, course and consequences # Between 235 and 284 CE Rome had around 26 emperors, most murdered or killed in battle. Persian and Gothic invasions, plague, and silver-debased coinage caused inflation. The Persian king Shapur I captured Emperor Valerian (260), and the empire split into the Gallic Empire, Palmyrene Empire under Queen Zenobia, and Rome. Aurelian reunited it, and Diocletian reformed it into a tetrarchy.

d: Edict of Milan.
x: What happened # Edict of Milan. Causes, course and consequences # Christians faced persecution, especially under Diocletian (303). Constantine, after attributing his victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) to the Christian God, issued with Licinius the Edict of Milan (313), granting religious tolerance. He funded churches, called the Council of Nicaea (325) and was baptised on his deathbed. Theodosius I made Christianity the state religion in 380.

d: Alaric's army sacked Rome.
x: What happened # Alaric’s army sacked Rome. Causes, course and consequences # Alaric, king of the Visigoths, besieged Rome three times after the emperor refused his demands for land and titles. On 24 August 410 his troops entered and looted the city for three days, though they spared churches. It was the first sack in 800 years, shocking the Roman world; Augustine wrote City of God to defend Christianity against blame.

d: Toramana and Mihirakula attacked northern India.
x: What happened # Toramana and Mihirakula attacked northern India. Causes, course and consequences # The Alchon Huns, a branch of the ‘White Huns’, invaded north-west India from about 460 CE; Skandagupta repelled them, but under Toramana and Mihirakula they took Punjab, Gandhara and Malwa. Xuanzang later reported Mihirakula destroyed Buddhist monasteries. The Aulikara king Yashodharman defeated Mihirakula around 528, but the invasions weakened Gupta power and trade.

d: Muslims defeated the Meccans.
x: What happened # Muslims defeated the Meccans. Causes, course and consequences # In March 624 about 313 Muslims from Medina intercepted a Meccan caravan and fought a Quraysh army roughly three times larger at the wells of Badr. The Muslim victory, seen as divine support (the Quran refers to angels), killed several Meccan leaders including Abu Jahl. It established Muhammad as a political and military leader and strengthened the community in Medina.

d: Arab armies defeated the Persians.
x: What happened # Arab armies defeated the Persians. Causes, course and consequences # In 636 an Arab army under Sa’d ibn Abi Waqqas met the Sasanian Persian army led by Rustam near Kufa in Iraq. After three or four days of fighting, including against Persian war elephants, Rustam was killed. The victory opened Mesopotamia, and the capital Ctesiphon fell in 637; Persia gradually converted to Islam while keeping its language and culture.

d: Studied at Nalanda and brought texts to China.
x: What happened # Studied at Nalanda and brought texts to China. Causes, course and consequences # Defying a travel ban, the monk Xuanzang left Chang’an in 629 and crossed the Taklamakan desert and the Pamirs to reach India. He studied for years at Nalanda under Shilabhadra, debated at Harsha’s court, and returned in 645 with 657 texts, which he spent his life translating. His ‘Great Tang Records on the Western Regions’ describes Indian cities, customs and rulers and guided archaeologists to sites like Nalanda.

d: Songtsen Gampo's successors rivalled the Tang.
x: What happened # Songtsen Gampo’s successors rivalled the Tang. Causes, course and consequences # Under Songtsen Gampo, Tibet became an empire in the 7th century; he married a Chinese princess (Wencheng) and a Nepali princess, bringing Buddhism. Tibet and Tang China fought for the Tarim basin’s Silk Road oasis cities for two centuries. In 763, when the Tang was weakened by the An Lushan rebellion, Tibetan armies briefly occupied Chang’an; a treaty pillar of 821–822 in Lhasa records peace.

d: One of the deadliest conflicts of pre-modern times.
x: What happened # One of the deadliest conflicts of pre-modern times. Causes, course and consequences # An Lushan, a general of Sogdian–Turkic descent who commanded border armies, rebelled in 755, capturing Luoyang and Chang’an. Emperor Xuanzong fled, and his beloved consort Yang Guifei was executed by his own troops. The war lasted until 763 with help from Uyghur mercenaries; census numbers dropped sharply, and the Tang never fully recovered central control.

d: Crowned by Pope Leo III.
x: What happened # Crowned by Pope Leo III. Causes, course and consequences # Charlemagne, king of the Franks, had conquered the Lombards and Saxons and protected Pope Leo III from Roman enemies. On Christmas Day 800, Leo crowned him ‘Emperor of the Romans’ in St Peter’s. The title, rejected by Byzantium, laid the basis for the Holy Roman Empire and long rivalry between popes and emperors.

d: Monks massacred at a famous monastery.
x: What happened # Monks massacred at a famous monastery. Causes, course and consequences # On 8 June 793 Norse raiders attacked the island monastery of Lindisfarne off Northumberland, killing monks and seizing treasures. The scholar Alcuin wrote that such terror had never appeared in Britain. It marks the start of the Viking Age, when Scandinavians raided, traded and settled from Ireland to Russia.

d: Seljuks defeated Byzantium.
x: What happened # Seljuks defeated Byzantium. Causes, course and consequences # On 26 August 1071 the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine army in eastern Anatolia and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes, after some Byzantine units deserted. Civil war at Constantinople followed, and Turkish groups poured into Anatolia, which became ‘Turkey’. The Byzantine plea for help led to the First Crusade.

d: One of 17 raids into India.
x: What happened # One of 17 raids into India. Causes, course and consequences # Mahmud, ruler of Ghazni in Afghanistan, raided north India about 17 times between 1000 and 1027, looting temple wealth from Mathura, Kannauj and Thanesar. In 1025–26 he plundered the Somnath temple in Gujarat. Al-Biruni accompanied his court and wrote a study of India; the temple was rebuilt many times, most recently in 1951.

d: Built by Suryavarman II.
x: What happened # Built by Suryavarman II. Causes, course and consequences # Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat between about 1113 and 1150 as a temple to Vishnu and probably his own mausoleum, facing west. Its five towers represent Mount Meru, and 800 metres of bas-reliefs show the churning of the ocean of milk and battles from the Mahabharata and Ramayana. It later became a Buddhist site and is now on Cambodia’s flag.

d: After the Battle of Hattin.
x: What happened # After the Battle of Hattin. Causes, course and consequences # Saladin united Egypt and Syria and, on 4 July 1187, destroyed the crusader army at the Horns of Hattin. He took Jerusalem in October after negotiations, allowing many Christians to ransom themselves, in contrast to the 1099 massacre. The Third Crusade under Richard the Lionheart failed to retake it.

d: Crusaders attacked a Christian city.
x: What happened # Crusaders attacked a Christian city. Causes, course and consequences # Crusaders, indebted to Venice for ships, were diverted to Constantinople to back a Byzantine claimant. In April 1204 they stormed and sacked the city, looting churches and taking the bronze horses now in Venice. A Latin Empire ruled until 1261, permanently weakening Byzantium and the relationship between Catholic and Orthodox churches.

d: Mamluks defeated the Mongols.
x: What happened # Mamluks defeated the Mongols. Causes, course and consequences # On 3 September 1260 the Mamluks of Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol army in Galilee, the first major check on Mongol expansion. Hulagu had withdrawn much of his army after the Great Khan’s death. Baybars soon killed Qutuz and became sultan.

d: His book inspired Columbus.
x: What happened # His book inspired Columbus. Causes, course and consequences # The Venetian Marco Polo travelled with his father and uncle along the Silk Road, reaching Kublai Khan around 1275 and serving him for 17 years. Imprisoned in Genoa after returning, he dictated his travels to Rustichello. His book described paper money, coal and great cities, and inspired Columbus.

d: Typhoons wrecked Kublai's fleets.
