x: What happened # Typhoons wrecked Kublai’s fleets. Causes, course and consequences # Kublai Khan demanded Japan’s submission; when refused, he sent a fleet in 1274 and a much larger one, possibly 140,000 men, in 1281. Samurai fought fiercely and built a stone wall at Hakata Bay, and typhoons — the kamikaze or ‘divine winds’ — destroyed the fleets. The failure strained the Kamakura shogunate.

d: Rain-ruined harvests at the start of the Little Ice Age.
x: What happened # Rain-ruined harvests at the start of the Little Ice Age. Causes, course and consequences # Torrential rains from 1315 to 1317 rotted crops across northern Europe, followed by livestock disease. Perhaps 5–12% of the population died, and there were reports of cannibalism. It marked the end of medieval population growth, just before the Black Death.

d: Joan of Arc; the longbow at Agincourt.
x: What happened # Joan of Arc; the longbow at Agincourt. Causes, course and consequences # English kings claimed the French throne; the war (1337–1453) saw English longbow victories at Crécy, Poitiers and Agincourt. Joan of Arc helped lift the siege of Orléans (1429), and France eventually drove the English out except from Calais. The war strengthened national identities and the use of cannon.

d: Tens of thousands killed.
x: What happened # Tens of thousands killed. Causes, course and consequences # Timur invaded India in 1398, defeated Sultan Nasir-ud-din Mahmud Tughlaq, and sacked Delhi in December. He massacred about 100,000 prisoners before the battle and took artisans to build Samarkand. The Tughlaq state collapsed; his descendant Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

d: Treasure fleets reached Calicut and East Africa.
x: What happened # Treasure fleets reached Calicut and East Africa. Causes, course and consequences # Between 1405 and 1433, the Muslim eunuch admiral Zheng He led seven Ming fleets of up to 300 ships and 27,000 men to Southeast Asia, Calicut, Hormuz, Arabia and East Africa. They brought back tributes, including a giraffe from Malindi. After 1433 the Ming stopped the voyages and turned inward.

d: One of medieval Europe's largest battles.
x: What happened # One of medieval Europe’s largest battles. Causes, course and consequences # The Teutonic Knights, a crusading order, ruled Prussia and fought Christian Lithuania and Poland. On 15 July 1410 King Władysław II Jagiełło and Grand Duke Vytautas led about 30,000 Poles, Lithuanians, Ruthenians and Tatars against the Order; the Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen was killed. It broke the Order’s power and remains a symbol of Polish and Lithuanian pride.

d: Expulsion of Jews followed.
x: What happened # Expulsion of Jews followed. Causes, course and consequences # The Christian reconquest of Iberia from Muslim rulers took over 700 years. Ferdinand and Isabella besieged Granada, the last Nasrid kingdom, which surrendered on 2 January 1492. That year Jews were expelled, Muslims were later forced to convert, and Columbus sailed under the same monarchs.

d: Afonso de Albuquerque captured it.
x: What happened # Afonso de Albuquerque captured it. Causes, course and consequences # Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate in 1510, with help from local ally Timmayya. Goa became the capital of Portugal’s Asian empire and a centre of Catholic missions, including the Inquisition (1560). It remained Portuguese until India took it in 1961.

d: Luther's 95 theses.
x: What happened # Luther’s 95 theses. Causes, course and consequences # Martin Luther, a German monk, attacked the sale of indulgences in his Ninety-five Theses (1517), arguing salvation came through faith alone. Printing spread his ideas; Zwingli, Calvin and Henry VIII’s break with Rome followed. Wars of religion and the Catholic Counter-Reformation reshaped Europe.

d: Babur defeated Rana Sanga.
x: What happened # Babur defeated Rana Sanga. Causes, course and consequences # After Panipat, the Rajput leader Rana Sanga of Mewar, allied with Afghan chiefs, gathered an army of perhaps 100,000 to drive Babur out. On 17 March 1527, near Fatehpur Sikri, Babur rallied his troops by renouncing wine and declaring the war a jihad, then used artillery and cavalry flanking. The Rajputs were defeated and Sanga died soon after, securing Mughal power.

d: Hemu defeated.
x: What happened # Hemu defeated. Causes, course and consequences # After Humayun’s death, Hemu, a Hindu general of the Suri dynasty, took Delhi and proclaimed himself Raja Vikramaditya. On 5 November 1556 Akbar’s army under Bairam Khan fought him; an arrow struck Hemu’s eye, his army broke, and he was executed. Akbar’s long reign began.

d: Maharana Pratap fought Akbar's army.
x: What happened # Maharana Pratap fought Akbar’s army. Causes, course and consequences # Maharana Pratap of Mewar refused to accept Mughal overlordship. On 18 June 1576, at a narrow pass near Gogunda, his army of about 3,000 cavalry and Bhil archers fought a larger Mughal army led by Raja Man Singh of Amber. Pratap escaped on his horse Chetak, which died after carrying him to safety. He waged guerrilla war for 20 years and recovered most of Mewar except Chittor.

d: Storms and fireships scattered the fleet.
x: What happened # Storms and fireships scattered the fleet. Causes, course and consequences # Philip II of Spain, angered by English raids and the execution of Mary Queen of Scots, sent an Armada of about 130 ships in 1588 to escort an invasion army from the Netherlands. English ships harassed it in the Channel, and fireships broke its formation off Calais, followed by battle at Gravelines. Storms wrecked many ships as they sailed around Scotland and Ireland.

d: Admiral Yi's turtle ships.
x: What happened # Admiral Yi’s turtle ships. Causes, course and consequences # Toyotomi Hideyoshi, having unified Japan, invaded Korea in 1592 with about 158,000 troops armed with muskets, capturing Seoul in weeks. Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s turtle ships destroyed Japanese supply fleets at Hansan and Myeongnyang, and Ming China sent armies. After Hideyoshi’s death in 1598, Japan withdrew; Korea lost perhaps a million people.

d: Decided Japan's unification.
x: What happened # Decided Japan’s unification. Causes, course and consequences # After Hideyoshi’s death, regents competed for power. On 21 October 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu’s Eastern Army of about 75,000 fought Ishida Mitsunari’s Western Army at Sekigahara; Kobayakawa Hideaki’s defection decided the battle. Ieyasu became shogun in 1603, founding the Tokugawa shogunate that ruled until 1868.

d: Monopoly on Asian spice trade.
x: What happened # Monopoly on Asian spice trade. Causes, course and consequences # Founded in 1602, the VOC was the first company to issue public shares on a stock exchange (Amsterdam). With power to wage war and make treaties, it seized the Spice Islands, based itself in Batavia (Jakarta), and controlled the nutmeg and clove trade through violence, including the massacre of Banda islanders (1621).

d: First permanent English colony.
x: What happened # First permanent English colony. Causes, course and consequences # In 1607 the Virginia Company founded Jamestown, the first permanent English colony in America. Many settlers starved; tobacco became the cash crop, and in 1619 the first enslaved Africans arrived in Virginia. Relations with the Powhatan Confederacy included Pocahontas’s marriage to John Rolfe.

d: Charles I beheaded (1649).
x: What happened # Charles I beheaded (1649). Causes, course and consequences # Charles I ruled without Parliament for 11 years and imposed religious reforms. War began in 1642 between Royalists and Parliamentarians; Oliver Cromwell’s New Model Army won at Naseby (1645). Charles was tried and beheaded in 1649, England became a republic, and Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector. The monarchy returned in 1660 under Charles II.

d: Ming collapsed after Li Zicheng's revolt.
x: What happened # Ming collapsed after Li Zicheng’s revolt. Causes, course and consequences # Rebels under Li Zicheng took Beijing in April 1644, and the last Ming emperor hanged himself. General Wu Sangui opened the Shanhai Pass to the Manchus, who defeated Li and took Beijing, proclaiming the Qing dynasty. Ming loyalists resisted in the south for decades, and Taiwan fell only in 1683; Han men were forced to adopt the Manchu queue.

d: Crowned Chhatrapati.
x: What happened # Crowned Chhatrapati. Causes, course and consequences # Shivaji had built a state from Bijapur and Mughal lands, but needed formal kingship to treat with other rulers as an equal. On 6 June 1674 at Raigad fort, the scholar Gaga Bhatt crowned him Chhatrapati with Vedic rites; he took the title Haindava Dharmoddharak and began a new era (Rajyabhishek Shaka). He issued coins and established the Ashta Pradhan council.

d: Bill of Rights (1689).
x: What happened # Bill of Rights (1689). Causes, course and consequences # James II, a Catholic, angered Parliament, especially when his son was born in 1688, raising the prospect of a Catholic dynasty. Leading nobles invited the Dutch William of Orange, married to James’s Protestant daughter Mary; William landed in November and James fled. The Bill of Rights (1689) limited royal power, establishing parliamentary sovereignty.

d: Succession wars followed.
x: What happened # Succession wars followed. Causes, course and consequences # Aurangzeb ruled the Mughal Empire at its largest extent but spent his last 25 years fighting Marathas in the Deccan. He reimposed jizya and alienated Rajputs and Sikhs. He died at Ahmednagar in 1707, aged 88. Wars of succession followed, governors in Bengal, Hyderabad and Awadh became independent, and Maratha power expanded.

d: A massacre in Delhi.
x: What happened # A massacre in Delhi. Causes, course and consequences # Nadir Shah, ruler of Persia, invaded India in 1738–39, defeating Emperor Muhammad Shah’s army at Karnal. In Delhi, after a rumour of his death sparked attacks on his troops, he ordered a massacre on 22 March 1739 that killed about 20,000–30,000 people. He carried off the Peacock Throne, the Koh-i-Noor and vast treasure, exposing Mughal weakness.

d: Called the first world war.
x: What happened # Called the first world war. Causes, course and consequences # From 1756 to 1763 Britain and Prussia fought France, Austria and Russia in Europe, North America, the Caribbean and India — often called the first world war. In India, Clive’s victory at Plassey and Eyre Coote’s at Wandiwash (1760) ended French ambitions. Britain gained Canada and dominance in India, but its war debts led to taxes on American colonies.

d: A disputed incident used in British propaganda.
x: What happened # A disputed incident used in British propaganda. Causes, course and consequences # After Siraj ud-Daulah captured Fort William in June 1756, British prisoners were held overnight in a small guardroom. John Holwell claimed 123 of 146 died of suffocation; historians think the numbers were exaggerated. The story was used to justify the British counter-attack leading to Plassey.

d: The Company became Bengal's tax collector.
x: What happened # The Company became Bengal’s tax collector. Causes, course and consequences # Signed in August 1765 after Buxar, it gave the East India Company the diwani — the right to collect revenue — of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha from Mughal emperor Shah Alam II, in return for an annual tribute. This ‘dual government’ made the Company a territorial power.

d: Efficient steam power for factories.
x: What happened # Efficient steam power for factories. Causes, course and consequences # Newcomen’s 1712 steam engine pumped water from mines but wasted fuel. James Watt, an instrument maker at Glasgow University, added a separate condenser in 1769 and later a rotary motion mechanism. With Matthew Boulton, he sold engines that powered cotton mills, foundries and later locomotives — the heart of the Industrial Revolution.

d: Fixed land revenue.
x: What happened # Fixed land revenue. Causes, course and consequences # In 1793 Governor-General Cornwallis fixed land revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha permanently, making zamindars owners of land if they paid on time. The revenue fixed was high, and estates of defaulters were auctioned, creating new landlords from merchants. Peasants lost customary rights and faced rack-renting, while the Company gained a stable income.

d: British control of the south.
x: What happened # British control of the south. Causes, course and consequences # After Tipu Sultan sought French alliance, Governor-General Wellesley launched the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War. In May 1799 British and Hyderabadi forces stormed Srirangapatna’s walls; Tipu died fighting near a gate. Mysore was given back to the Wodeyar dynasty as a subsidiary ally, and much of Tipu’s territory was annexed.

d: Wellington and Blücher won.
x: What happened # Wellington and Blücher won. Causes, course and consequences # Escaping exile on Elba, Napoleon returned to power in 1815 for the ‘Hundred Days’. On 18 June near Waterloo in Belgium, he attacked the Duke of Wellington’s Anglo-allied army; the arrival of Blücher’s Prussians in the afternoon decided the battle. Napoleon abdicated and was exiled to St Helena, ending 23 years of war.

d: Bolívar and San Martín led wars of independence.
x: What happened # Bolívar and San Martín led wars of independence. Causes, course and consequences # Napoleon’s invasion of Spain (1808) set off independence movements. Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led armies that liberated most of Spanish South America by 1825; Mexico won independence in 1821 and Brazil in 1822. New republics faced inequality and military rule.

d: Campaign led by Ram Mohan Roy.
x: What happened # Campaign led by Ram Mohan Roy. Causes, course and consequences # Sati, the burning of widows on their husband’s pyre, was practised among some communities, with hundreds of cases a year recorded in Bengal. Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against it, quoting scriptures. In 1829 Governor-General Bentinck’s Regulation XVII made sati illegal, and the Privy Council rejected an appeal by orthodox groups in 1832.

d: Created an English-educated class.
x: What happened # Created an English-educated class. Causes, course and consequences # In February 1835 Thomas Babington Macaulay argued that government money should fund English education rather than Sanskrit and Arabic, claiming ‘a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India’. Bentinck adopted it in the English Education Act. It created an English-educated middle class that later led the freedom movement.

d: Potato blight and British policy.
x: What happened # Potato blight and British policy. Causes, course and consequences # Potato blight (Phytophthora infestans) struck in 1845, destroying the staple food of Ireland’s poor. British relief was limited and food exports continued. About 1 million people died and another million emigrated, many to America. Ireland’s population fell from 8.5 million to about 6.5 million.

d: A wave across Europe.
x: What happened # A wave across Europe. Causes, course and consequences # Economic crisis and demands for constitutions and national unity sparked revolts in France, the German and Italian states, Austria and Hungary in 1848. The French monarchy fell and a republic was declared; Metternich fled Vienna. Most revolts were crushed by 1849, but serfdom was abolished in Austria, and that year Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto.

d: 34 km run.
x: What happened # 34 km run. Causes, course and consequences # On 16 April 1853 a train with 14 carriages and three locomotives ran 34 km from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane. Lord Dalhousie promoted railways for trade and military use; by 1900 India had about 40,000 km. Railways also helped unify Indians and moved famine grain — but freight rates favoured British exports.

d: Led by a man claiming to be Jesus's brother.
x: What happened # Led by a man claiming to be Jesus’s brother. Causes, course and consequences # Hong Xiuquan, a failed examination candidate, believed after a vision that he was Jesus’s younger brother. His Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, promising land equality and banning opium and foot-binding, captured Nanjing in 1853. Qing armies, led by Zeng Guofan and aided by Western-led forces, crushed it by 1864. About 20–30 million died.

d: End of the shogunate.
x: What happened # End of the shogunate. Causes, course and consequences # After Commodore Perry forced Japan open (1853–54), samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū rebelled against the Tokugawa shogunate and restored power to the young Emperor Meiji in 1868. The new government abolished feudal domains and the samurai class, adopted Western technology, built railways and a modern army and navy, and drafted a constitution (1889). Japan defeated China (1895) and Russia (1905).

d: Cut sailing distance by ~7,000 km.
x: What happened # Cut sailing distance by ~7,000 km. Causes, course and consequences # The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps obtained a concession from Egypt’s ruler and built the 164 km canal between 1859 and 1869, using forced labour; thousands died. It opened on 17 November 1869, cutting the London–Bombay sea voyage by about 7,000 km. Britain bought Egypt’s shares in 1875 and occupied Egypt in 1882.

d: Bismarck's wars.
x: What happened # Bismarck’s wars. Causes, course and consequences # Otto von Bismarck, Prussia’s minister-president, used ‘blood and iron’. Prussia defeated Denmark (1864) over Schleswig-Holstein, Austria (1866) to exclude it from Germany, and France (1870–71). On 18 January 1871, William I was proclaimed German Emperor in Versailles’ Hall of Mirrors, and France lost Alsace-Lorraine.

d: No Africans were invited.
x: What happened # No Africans were invited. Causes, course and consequences # From November 1884 to February 1885, convened by Bismarck, 14 powers met to regulate colonisation in Africa. They agreed that claims required ‘effective occupation’ and recognised King Leopold II’s Congo Free State. No African was invited. Within 30 years, Europeans controlled 90% of Africa.

d: Menelik II defeated Italy.
x: What happened # Menelik II defeated Italy. Causes, course and consequences # Italy claimed a protectorate over Ethiopia based on a disputed treaty. On 1 March 1896 Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu’s army of about 100,000, armed with modern rifles, defeated about 17,000 Italian troops at Adwa. Italy recognised Ethiopian independence, making Ethiopia a symbol of African freedom.

d: 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk.
x: What happened # 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk. Causes, course and consequences # Bicycle makers Orville and Wilbur Wright studied gliders and built a wind tunnel to test wings. On 17 December 1903 at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville flew the Wright Flyer for 12 seconds and 37 m; Wilbur later flew 260 m. Within 15 years aircraft were used in World War I.

d: Inspired anti-colonial movements.
x: What happened # Inspired anti-colonial movements. Causes, course and consequences # Russia and Japan clashed over Manchuria and Korea. Japan attacked Port Arthur in February 1904, won at Mukden, and destroyed Russia’s Baltic Fleet at Tsushima (May 1905). The Treaty of Portsmouth gave Japan Korea and southern Manchuria. Asia’s first modern victory over a European power inspired nationalists from India to Egypt.

d: Sun Yat-sen's republic.
x: What happened # Sun Yat-sen’s republic. Causes, course and consequences # The Qing dynasty faced foreign humiliation and reform demands. On 10 October 1911 an army uprising at Wuchang spread across provinces; Sun Yat-sen was elected provisional president. The child emperor Puyi abdicated in February 1912, ending over 2,000 years of imperial rule, but China soon fell into warlord division.

d: Against forced indigo farming.
x: What happened # Against forced indigo farming. Causes, course and consequences # Under the tinkathia system, farmers in Champaran, Bihar, had to grow indigo on 3/20 of their land for European planters. In 1917, at the request of farmer Raj Kumar Shukla, Gandhi went there, defied an order to leave, and recorded farmers’ testimonies. The government formed an inquiry and abolished the system — Gandhi’s first successful satyagraha in India.

d: Atatürk's reforms.
x: What happened # Atatürk’s reforms. Causes, course and consequences # After the Ottoman defeat in World War I, the Allies planned to partition Anatolia. Mustafa Kemal led the Turkish War of Independence (1919–22) against Greek, Armenian and Allied forces. The Treaty of Lausanne (1923) recognised Turkey, and the Republic was proclaimed on 29 October 1923; Atatürk abolished the caliphate, adopted the Latin alphabet and secularised the state.

d: Long March (1934–35).
x: What happened # Long March (1934–35). Causes, course and consequences # The Nationalists (Kuomintang) under Chiang Kai-shek turned on their Communist allies in 1927. Mao Zedong’s Red Army survived the Long March (1934–35) and grew during the war against Japan. Civil war resumed in 1946; the Communists won and Chiang retreated to Taiwan in 1949.

d: Rehearsal for WWII.
x: What happened # Rehearsal for WWII. Causes, course and consequences # In July 1936 army generals led by Francisco Franco rebelled against Spain’s elected Popular Front government. Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy aided Franco, while the Soviet Union and International Brigades backed the Republic. The bombing of Guernica (1937), painted by Picasso, became a symbol of horror. Franco won in 1939 and ruled until 1975.

d: Nearly 2 million casualties.
x: What happened # Nearly 2 million casualties. Causes, course and consequences # In the summer of 1942 Germany’s Sixth Army attacked Stalingrad on the Volga. Brutal street fighting followed; in November the Soviets launched Operation Uranus, encircling the Germans. Field Marshal Paulus surrendered on 2 February 1943; total casualties reached about 2 million. It marked the turning point on the Eastern Front.

d: Called Britain's greatest battle.
x: What happened # Called Britain’s greatest battle. Causes, course and consequences # In March 1944 Japan, with Bose’s Indian National Army, invaded Manipur and Nagaland aiming to reach India. British and Indian troops, supplied by air, held Imphal and fought at close quarters at Kohima’s tennis court. Japan lost about 55,000 men, its largest defeat on land; in 2013 the battles were voted Britain’s greatest battle.

d: India was a founding member.
x: What happened # India was a founding member. Causes, course and consequences # The League of Nations failed to prevent World War II. In April–June 1945, 50 nations met in San Francisco and signed the UN Charter on 26 June; it came into force on 24 October 1945. The Security Council has five permanent members with vetoes. India was a founding member, and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights followed in 1948.

d: Sukarno declared independence.
x: What happened # Sukarno declared independence. Causes, course and consequences # After Japan’s surrender, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta declared independence on 17 August 1945. The Dutch returned and fought a four-year war with ‘police actions’. Under UN and US pressure, the Netherlands recognised Indonesia’s sovereignty in December 1949.

t: Creation of Israel and the Nakba
d: Arab–Israeli war followed.
x: What happened # Arab–Israeli war followed. Causes, course and consequences # After the Holocaust, the UN voted in November 1947 to partition Palestine. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, and neighbouring Arab states attacked. Israel won; about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled — the Nakba (‘catastrophe’), creating a refugee problem that persists.

d: Killed by Nathuram Godse.
x: What happened # Killed by Nathuram Godse. Causes, course and consequences # On 30 January 1948, at Birla House in Delhi, Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who blamed Gandhi for Partition and concessions to Pakistan, shot him three times. Gandhi died aged 78. Godse and Narayan Apte were hanged in 1949. The government briefly banned the RSS.

d: An armistice, never a peace treaty.
x: What happened # An armistice, never a peace treaty. Causes, course and consequences # Korea was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945. On 25 June 1950 North Korea invaded the South; UN forces led by the US drove north to the Chinese border, then Chinese troops pushed them back. After about 3 million deaths, an armistice in July 1953 restored a border near the 38th parallel. India chaired the commission for prisoner repatriation.

d: Kwame Nkrumah.
x: What happened # Kwame Nkrumah. Causes, course and consequences # The Gold Coast’s Convention People’s Party, led by Kwame Nkrumah, campaigned for self-government with strikes and boycotts. On 6 March 1957 Ghana became independent, the first sub-Saharan colony to do so. Nkrumah championed Pan-Africanism, inspiring independence movements across the continent.

d: China won a short war.
x: What happened # China won a short war. Causes, course and consequences # Disputes over the McMahon Line and Aksai Chin, India’s ‘forward policy’ and China’s anger over the Dalai Lama’s asylum led China to attack on 20 October 1962. Chinese forces advanced in Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh and then declared a ceasefire, withdrawing in the east. India’s defeat led to military modernisation.

d: Thirteen days.
x: What happened # Thirteen days. Causes, course and consequences # In October 1962 US spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. Kennedy imposed a naval ‘quarantine’, and the world came closer to nuclear war than ever before. Khrushchev withdrew the missiles in exchange for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and the secret removal of US missiles from Turkey.

d: High-yield wheat and rice.
x: What happened # High-yield wheat and rice. Causes, course and consequences # After droughts in 1965–66 forced India to import food, scientists M. S. Swaminathan and Norman Borlaug introduced high-yield dwarf wheat and rice. With irrigation, fertilisers and support prices, Punjab and Haryana’s output soared and India became self-sufficient. It also caused groundwater depletion and soil problems.

d: Indira Gandhi's rule by decree.
x: What happened # Indira Gandhi’s rule by decree. Causes, course and consequences # After a court voided her election and opposition protests grew, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency on 25 June 1975. Opposition leaders were jailed, the press censored, and forced sterilisation campaigns were run. She lost the 1977 election to the Janata Party.

d: Shah overthrown.
x: What happened # Shah overthrown. Causes, course and consequences # Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi’s autocratic modernisation and secret police (SAVAK) provoked protests by clerics, students and workers. The Shah fled in January 1979, and Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile to found an Islamic Republic. US embassy staff were held hostage for 444 days.

d: The worst industrial disaster.
x: What happened # The worst industrial disaster. Causes, course and consequences # On the night of 2–3 December 1984 about 40 tonnes of methyl isocyanate leaked from Union Carbide’s pesticide plant in Bhopal. Thousands died within days and estimates of total deaths reach 15,000–20,000, with hundreds of thousands injured. It is the world’s worst industrial disaster.

d: A reactor exploded.
x: What happened # A reactor exploded. Causes, course and consequences # On 26 April 1986 a safety test went wrong at Reactor 4 of the Chernobyl plant in Soviet Ukraine, causing an explosion and fire. Radioactive fallout spread over Europe, 350,000 people were relocated, and an exclusion zone remains. Soviet secrecy damaged trust and helped glasnost.

d: Mandela elected.
x: What happened # Mandela elected. Causes, course and consequences # Apartheid, enforced from 1948, segregated South Africa by race. Under internal resistance and international sanctions, President F. W. de Klerk released Nelson Mandela in 1990. Negotiations led to the first democratic elections in April 1994, and Mandela became president.

d: In about 100 days.
x: What happened # In about 100 days. Causes, course and consequences # After the president’s plane was shot down on 6 April 1994, Hutu extremist militias and soldiers killed about 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in about 100 days, often with machetes, encouraged by radio broadcasts. The UN failed to intervene. The Tutsi-led RPF ended the genocide in July.

d: Mortgage collapse.
x: What happened # Mortgage collapse. Causes, course and consequences # Low interest rates and lax regulation fuelled risky subprime mortgages bundled into complex securities. When US house prices fell in 2007, losses spread; Lehman Brothers collapsed on 15 September 2008. Governments bailed out banks and central banks slashed rates. The Great Recession followed, with millions losing jobs and homes.

d: Started in Tunisia.
x: What happened # Started in Tunisia. Causes, course and consequences # In December 2010 the self-immolation of Tunisian street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi sparked protests that toppled Tunisia’s Ben Ali. Uprisings spread to Egypt, Libya, Yemen, Bahrain and Syria. Tunisia briefly democratised, Egypt returned to military rule, and Syria, Libya and Yemen fell into civil wars.

d: Overtook China.
x: What happened # Overtook China. Causes, course and consequences # In April 2023, according to UN estimates, India overtook China with about 1.43 billion people, while China’s population had begun to decline. India’s population is young, with a median age under 30. The shift has implications for jobs, resources and global influence.

d: A small population of Homo sapiens left Africa, probably across the Bab-el-Mandeb strait or through Sinai, and spread along the southern coasts of Arabia and India to Southeast Asia and Australia within about 15,000 years. They met and interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans, which is why most people outside Africa carry about 2% Neanderthal DNA. Ancient DNA and stone tools from sites such as Jwalapuram in India help map the route.

d: When sea levels were low in the Ice Age, Beringia linked Siberia and Alaska. People crossed and moved south along the Pacific coast or through an ice-free corridor; footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, suggest presence by about 21,000 years ago, and Monte Verde in Chile was occupied by 14,500 years ago. Within a few thousand years humans reached Tierra del Fuego.

d: Farmers speaking Bantu languages spread from the Cameroon–Nigeria borderlands across central, eastern and southern Africa over 2,000 years, carrying yams, sorghum, cattle and, later, ironworking. Today about 350 million people speak some 500 Bantu languages, including Swahili, Zulu and Kikongo, and genetic studies trace the movement.

d: Austronesian-speaking farmers sailed out of Taiwan to the Philippines and Indonesia, then east into the Pacific as the Lapita culture and west to Madagascar, using outrigger canoes. d: Ancient DNA shows that pastoralists of the Yamnaya culture, using wagons and horses, moved into Europe around 3000 BCE, and related steppe groups reached Central Asia and later South Asia around 2000–1500 BCE, mixing with local populations. The spread explains why Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, Persian and English share many words.

d: Grandson of Chandragupta, Ashoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) conquered Kalinga in a war that his own edict says killed 100,000 and deported 150,000. Filled with remorse, he embraced Buddhism and dhamma — non-violence, tolerance and welfare — building hospitals, wells and rest houses and sending missions abroad. His lion capital at Sarnath is India's national emblem and his wheel is on its flag.

d: King Ying Zheng of Qin conquered the six rival Warring States and in 221 BCE proclaimed himself First Emperor. He standardised script, coins, weights and roads, joined border walls into an early Great Wall, and ordered the burning of books and the persecution of scholars. Obsessed with immortality, he died in 210 BCE and was buried with the Terracotta Army.

d: A Roman general and politician (100–44 BCE), Caesar conquered Gaul, crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE to start a civil war, and became dictator. He reformed the calendar (the Julian calendar) and expanded the Senate. Senators who feared he would become king stabbed him on the Ides of March, 44 BCE; his heir Octavian became Rome's first emperor.

d: Born Octavian, Caesar's adopted heir defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BCE) and in 27 BCE became Augustus, the first Roman emperor. d: Rajaraja I (r. 985–1014) transformed the Chola kingdom into an empire, conquering the Cheras and Pandyas, Vengi, Gangavadi, northern Sri Lanka (destroying Anuradhapura) and the Maldives with a powerful navy. He organised a detailed land survey and revenue system, and built the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur (1010), whose vimana rises about 66 m and whose walls record gifts and temple staff. His son Rajendra I extended his conquests to the Ganga and Southeast Asia.

d: Razia (r. 1236–1240), daughter of Iltutmish, was named heir by her father ahead of her brothers. The only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate, she discarded the veil, wore a tunic and turban, held open court and led armies. Her promotion of the Abyssinian noble Jamal-ud-Din Yaqut angered the Turkish nobles (the 'Forty'). Governor Altunia of Bathinda rebelled and captured her; she married him and tried to regain Delhi, but both were killed in 1240.

d: Mansa Musa (r. about 1312–1337) ruled the Mali Empire at its height, controlling gold fields that supplied much of the Old World's gold. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, with thousands of attendants and camels carrying gold, made him famous; his spending in Cairo depressed gold prices for years. He returned with scholars and the architect Es-Saheli, building the Djinguereber mosque and making Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning. The 1375 Catalan Atlas shows him holding a gold nugget.

d: Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529) of the Tuluva dynasty was Vijayanagara's greatest emperor. He defeated the Bijapur Sultanate at Raichur (1520), took territories from the Gajapatis of Odisha and kept Portuguese friendship for horses. He built gopurams at Hampi and Tirupati, and his court hosted the 'Ashtadiggajas', eight great Telugu poets, as well as Tenali Rama of folk tales. He wrote Amuktamalyada, a Telugu poem on statecraft and devotion.

d: Shah Jahan (r. 1628–1658), the fifth Mughal emperor, presided over the empire's architectural golden age. He built the Taj Mahal (1632–1653) in Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their 14th child; the new capital Shahjahanabad with the Red Fort and Jama Masjid in Delhi; and the jewelled Peacock Throne. Costly wars and building strained finances. His son Aurangzeb defeated his brothers and imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort, where he died in 1666 looking at the Taj.

d: Shivaji Bhonsle (1630–1680) grew up in Pune under his mother Jijabai and began seizing forts from the Bijapur Sultanate as a teenager. He killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khan at Pratapgad (1659), surprised Mughal governor Shaista Khan in Pune (1663), raided Surat, and escaped from Aurangzeb's house arrest in Agra (1666) reportedly hidden in fruit baskets. He was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674, set up the Ashta Pradhan council, a navy and a revenue system, and promoted Marathi and Sanskrit in administration.

d: Peter I (1672–1725) became tsar as a boy and travelled incognito to the Netherlands and England (1697–98), working in shipyards. Determined to modernise Russia, he built a navy, reorganised the army, forced nobles to shave beards and wear European clothes, and created the Table of Ranks based on service. He defeated Sweden in the Great Northern War (Poltava, 1709), founded St Petersburg as a 'window on Europe', and declared Russia an empire in 1721. He was brutal: thousands of serfs died building his capital, and he had his own son tortured to death.

d: Ranjit Singh (1780–1839), who lost an eye to smallpox as a child, became chief of the Sukerchakia misl and captured Lahore in 1799, uniting the Sikh misls into an empire covering Punjab, Kashmir, Multan and Peshawar. He modernised his Khalsa army with European officers, ruled with ministers of all faiths, and gilded the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple). He owned the Koh-i-Noor diamond. After his death, intrigues weakened the state and the British annexed Punjab in 1849.

d: Tipu Sultan (1750–1799), son of Hyder Ali, ruled Mysore from 1782. Called the 'Tiger of Mysore', he fought four wars against the East India Company, using iron-cased rockets that later inspired Britain's Congreve rockets. He introduced a new calendar, coins and silk farming, and sought alliances with Napoleon and the Ottomans. He is admired as an anti-colonial fighter but criticised for violence against Kodavas, Malabar Hindus and Christians. He died defending Srirangapatna in 1799.

d: Napoleon Bonaparte (1769–1821), a Corsican artillery officer, rose through the French Revolution's wars, seized power in a coup in 1799 and crowned himself Emperor in 1804. His victories at Austerlitz, Jena and Wagram made him master of Europe; his Napoleonic Code established legal equality and property rights still influential worldwide. His invasion of Egypt (1798) aimed to threaten British India and led to the discovery of the Rosetta Stone. The invasion of Russia (1812) destroyed his army, and after defeat at Waterloo (1815) he died in exile on St Helena.

d: Victoria (1819–1901) became Queen of the United Kingdom at 18 in 1837 and reigned for 63 years. After the 1857 rebellion, the Crown took over India, and in 1877 she became Empress of India; she learned Hindustani from her Indian attendant Abdul Karim. Her era saw industrial growth, railways, the expansion of the British Empire to a quarter of the world, but also famines in India and Ireland. Her nine children married into Europe's royal families, earning her the title 'grandmother of Europe'.

d: Lakshmibai (about 1828–1858), born Manikarnika in Varanasi, married the Raja of Jhansi. When he died in 1853, Governor-General Dalhousie used the Doctrine of Lapse to annex Jhansi, refusing to recognise their adopted son. In 1857 she joined the rebellion, defending Jhansi against Sir Hugh Rose's siege in 1858, then escaped with her son tied to her back and joined Tatya Tope to capture Gwalior. She died fighting near Gwalior's Phool Bagh in June 1858. Rose called her 'the most dangerous of all Indian leaders'.

He was hanged on 8 April. His act preceded the Meerut uprising of 10 May, and he became a symbol of the 1857 rebellion; 'Pandy' became British slang for rebels.

d: Jawaharlal Nehru (1889–1964), educated at Harrow and Cambridge, became Gandhi's close ally and a Congress leader, spending about nine years in prison. As India's first Prime Minister (1947–64), he built democratic institutions, a secular constitution, five-year plans, IITs, AIIMS and the atomic energy and space programmes. His 'Tryst with Destiny' speech marked independence. He led the Non-Aligned Movement, but the 1962 war with China damaged his reputation. He wrote The Discovery of India in jail.

d: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891–1956), born into the Mahar caste, considered 'untouchable', overcame discrimination to earn doctorates from Columbia and the London School of Economics. He led the Mahad satyagraha (1927) for Dalits' right to use public water, and debated Gandhi over separate electorates (Poona Pact, 1932). As chairman of the Constituent Assembly's drafting committee, he shaped India's Constitution, abolishing untouchability. As law minister he pushed the Hindu Code Bill for women's rights. In 1956 he converted to Buddhism with about 500,000 followers, founding Navayana.

d: Subhas Chandra Bose (1897–1945), called Netaji, resigned from the Indian Civil Service to join the freedom movement and was elected Congress president in 1938 and 1939, but clashed with Gandhi over non-violence. Escaping house arrest in 1941, he sought help from Germany and then Japan, leading the Azad Hind government and Indian National Army in Southeast Asia with the slogan 'Give me blood, and I will give you freedom'. The INA fought at Imphal and Kohima. He reportedly died in a plane crash in Taiwan in 1945; the INA trials of 1945–46 inspired mass protests.

d: Bhagat Singh (1907–1931), from a Punjabi family of revolutionaries, was shaken by the Jallianwala Bagh massacre at 12. He joined the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association; to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai's death after a police beating, he and Rajguru shot police officer John Saunders in 1928. He and Batukeshwar Dutt threw non-lethal bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly in 1929 to 'make the deaf hear'. He wrote 'Why I Am an Atheist' in jail and was hanged with Rajguru and Sukhdev on 23 March 1931, aged 23.

As independent India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, he persuaded or pressured over 560 princely states to join India, using military action in Hyderabad (1948). He created the modern IAS. The 182-metre Statue of Unity in Gujarat honours him.

d: Sarojini Naidu (1879–1949), the 'Nightingale of India', was a poet who published The Golden Threshold and joined the freedom struggle. She became the first Indian woman president of the Congress (1925), marched in the Salt March and was jailed during Quit India. After independence she became Governor of the United Provinces, India's first woman governor. National Women's Day is celebrated on her birthday.

d: Birsa Munda (1875–1900), from the Munda tribe of Chota Nagpur, led the Ulgulan ('great tumult') of 1899–1900 against British rule, landlords, moneylenders and missionaries who took tribal land. He founded a religious movement, the Birsait faith, and was called 'Dharti Aba' (father of the earth). He died in Ranchi jail aged 25. His uprising led to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908); 15 November, his birthday, is Janjatiya Gaurav Divas and Jharkhand's foundation day.

d: Nelson Mandela (1918–2013), a Xhosa lawyer, co-founded the ANC Youth League and fought apartheid, South Africa's system of racial segregation. After the Sharpeville massacre (1960), he helped found the ANC's armed wing and was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964, spending 27 years in jail, 18 of them on Robben Island. Released in 1990, he negotiated the end of apartheid with F. W. de Klerk, shared the Nobel Peace Prize (1993) and became South Africa's first Black president in 1994, promoting reconciliation. India awarded him the Bharat Ratna in 1990.

d: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968), a Baptist minister from Atlanta, led the US civil rights movement. Inspired by Gandhi's satyagraha (he visited India in 1959), he led the Montgomery bus boycott (1955–56) after Rosa Parks' arrest, the Birmingham campaign and the 1963 March on Washington, where he gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech. His work helped pass the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965), and he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

d: Winston Churchill (1874–1965), a British aristocrat, soldier and journalist, served in India, Sudan and the Boer War before entering Parliament. As First Lord of the Admiralty he backed the disastrous Gallipoli campaign (1915). In the 1930s he warned against Hitler, and as Prime Minister from May 1940 he refused to negotiate with Nazi Germany, rallying Britain with speeches like 'We shall fight on the beaches'. He worked closely with Roosevelt and Stalin, won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature, and returned as PM in 1951–55. In India he is remembered for opposing independence, calling Gandhi a 'half-naked fakir', and for his war cabinet's role in the Bengal famine of 1943.

d: Franklin Delano Roosevelt (1882–1945), the only US president elected four times, took office in 1933 at the depth of the Great Depression. His New Deal created jobs programmes, Social Security, banking reforms and huge public works like the Tennessee Valley Authority, greatly expanding government's role. Paralysed from the waist down by polio at 39, he hid his disability from the public. He led the US into World War II after Pearl Harbor (1941), shaped the Atlantic Charter with Churchill, and planned the United Nations, but died in April 1945, weeks before victory in Europe. He also ordered the internment of Japanese Americans.

d: Adolf Hitler (1889–1945), born in Austria, was a failed artist and World War I corporal who led the Nazi Party. Exploiting resentment over the Treaty of Versailles and the Great Depression, he became German Chancellor in 1933 and quickly made himself dictator. His regime persecuted Jews, Roma, disabled people and political opponents, rearmed Germany, and started World War II by invading Poland in 1939. Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust. Facing defeat, Hitler killed himself in his Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945. He is history's most notorious example of how democracy can be destroyed from within.

d: Joseph Stalin (1878–1953), born Ioseb Jughashvili in Georgia, was a Bolshevik revolutionary who rose to rule the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until his death. His five-year plans forced rapid industrialisation, and collectivisation of agriculture caused famines, including the Holodomor in Ukraine. The Great Purge (1936–38) executed about 750,000 people, and millions passed through the Gulag. He signed a pact with Hitler in 1939 but, after Germany invaded in 1941, led the USSR to victory at enormous cost, then imposed communist rule on Eastern Europe, beginning the Cold War.

d: Mao Zedong (1893–1976), son of a farmer in Hunan, co-founded the Chinese Communist Party and built a peasant-based revolution. He led the Long March (1934–35), fought Japan and won the civil war, proclaiming the People's Republic of China in 1949. Land reform and campaigns against 'enemies' followed. The Great Leap Forward (1958–62) caused a famine that killed perhaps 15–45 million people, and the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) unleashed Red Guards against intellectuals and officials. He unified China and raised literacy, but at a massive human cost.

d: Kong Qiu (551–479 BCE), known as Kongzi or Confucius, was a minor official in the state of Lu during the Spring and Autumn period. He taught that society is harmonious when people follow ritual (li), practise humaneness (ren), honour their parents (filial piety) and rulers govern by virtue rather than force. He travelled among states seeking a ruler to apply his ideas, without success, and taught many students who compiled his sayings in the Analects. Under the Han dynasty Confucianism became the state ideology, shaping East Asia for 2,000 years.

d: Laozi ('Old Master') is the traditional author of the Daodejing, a short book of 81 poetic chapters on the Dao ('the Way'), the natural order of the universe. Legend says he was a Zhou archivist who, leaving China on a water buffalo, wrote the book for a border guard. It teaches simplicity, humility and wu wei (effortless action). Historians debate whether he was a real person. He is honoured as the founder of Taoism.

d: Siddhartha Gautama was born in Lumbini (Nepal), a prince of the Shakya republic, probably in the 5th century BCE. Moved by seeing old age, sickness and death, he left home at 29, tried severe asceticism, then found the 'Middle Way' and attained enlightenment under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya. He preached his first sermon at Sarnath on the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, founded the sangha including nuns, and taught for 45 years under the patronage of kings like Bimbisara. He died at Kushinagar aged 80.

d: Vardhamana Mahavira (traditionally 599–527 BCE; many scholars place him in the 5th century BCE) was born near Vaishali into a kshatriya family. At 30 he renounced his home, practised austerities for 12 years and attained kevala jnana (omniscience). He taught the five vows — non-violence (ahimsa), truth, non-stealing, chastity and non-attachment — and organised monks, nuns and laity. He is the 24th tirthankara of Jainism and attained nirvana at Pawapuri.

d: Socrates (about 470–399 BCE) was an Athenian stonemason's son who served as a hoplite in the Peloponnesian War. He wrote nothing; we know him through Plato and Xenophon. He questioned people about justice, courage and virtue (the Socratic method), claiming wisdom lay in knowing that he knew nothing. Accused of impiety and corrupting youth, he was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock in 399 BCE, refusing to escape.

d: Plato (about 428–348 BCE), Socrates's student, founded the Academy in Athens, which lasted centuries. His dialogues, such as the Republic, Symposium and Phaedo, discuss justice, love, the soul and his theory of Forms — that the physical world is a shadow of eternal ideas (the Allegory of the Cave). The Republic imagined a state ruled by philosopher-kings. Alfred North Whitehead said Western philosophy is 'a series of footnotes to Plato'.

d: Aristotle (384–322 BCE), from Stagira, studied at Plato's Academy for 20 years, tutored the young Alexander the Great, and founded the Lyceum in Athens. He wrote on logic, biology, physics, ethics, politics, poetry and rhetoric, classifying animals and developing syllogistic logic. His works were preserved by Islamic scholars and dominated European thought in the Middle Ages.

d: Chanakya, also called Kautilya or Vishnugupta, was a Brahmin scholar, traditionally from Taxila, who helped Chandragupta Maurya overthrow the Nanda dynasty around 322 BCE and served as his chief minister. He is credited with the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft, economics, law, espionage and war, rediscovered in 1905. His realism has led to comparisons with Machiavelli. Legends also attribute aphorisms (Chanakya Niti) to him.

d: Panini, a grammarian from Shalatula near Gandhara (around the 5th–4th century BCE), wrote the Ashtadhyayi, about 4,000 concise rules (sutras) describing Sanskrit's sounds, word formation and syntax. His system uses meta-rules, recursion and abbreviations similar to modern formal languages; the Backus–Naur form used in computer science is sometimes called Panini–Backus form. His grammar standardised Classical Sanskrit.

d: Archimedes (about 287–212 BCE) of Syracuse in Sicily was the greatest mathematician of antiquity. He approximated π, calculated areas and volumes using methods close to integral calculus, discovered the principle of buoyancy (reportedly shouting 'Eureka!' in his bath), and explained levers ('Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth'). He designed war machines to defend Syracuse against Rome and was killed by a Roman soldier during the city's fall.

d: Sushruta, a physician traditionally said to have taught at Kashi (Varanasi) around the 6th century BCE (the text took shape over centuries), is credited with the Sushruta Samhita. It describes over 300 surgical procedures and 120 instruments, including rhinoplasty using a cheek or forehead flap, cataract surgery and treatment of fractures, and recommends practising on gourds and dead animals. He is called the 'father of surgery'.

It explains health as a balance of three doshas (vata, pitta, kapha), describes diagnosis, diet, herbal medicines and preventive care, and contains an oath for physicians. It was translated into Persian and Arabic.

Its universal ethics, free of sectarian references, made it one of the most translated Indian works. A 133-foot statue of him stands at Kanyakumari.

d: Aryabhata (476–550 CE) wrote the Aryabhatiya at age 23 in Kusumapura (Pataliputra) during the Gupta era. He explained solar and lunar eclipses through shadows rather than the demon Rahu. India's first satellite (1975) was named after him.

His poems Meghaduta (a cloud carries a message to a lover) and Raghuvamsha are masterpieces of nature imagery.

d: Brahmagupta (598–668), from Bhinmal in Rajasthan, wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628), the first text to treat zero as a number with rules for arithmetic: a number minus itself is zero; negative times negative is positive. He solved quadratic equations and gave Brahmagupta's formula for cyclic quadrilaterals. His work, translated into Arabic in Baghdad around 771, shaped Islamic and later European mathematics.

d: Adi Shankara (traditionally 788–820, though some date him earlier) was born at Kaladi in Kerala and became a renunciant as a boy. He wrote commentaries on the Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita and Brahma Sutras, teaching Advaita Vedanta: the self (atman) is identical with Brahman, and the world is maya. He travelled across India debating rival schools and founded four mathas at Sringeri, Dwarka, Puri and Jyotirmath.

d: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (about 780–850), a Persian scholar at Baghdad's House of Wisdom, wrote al-Kitab al-Mukhtasar fi Hisab al-Jabr wal-Muqabala, from which 'algebra' comes. His book on Indian numerals introduced decimal place-value arithmetic to the Islamic world and, when translated into Latin, to Europe; the word 'algorithm' comes from the Latin form of his name. He also worked on astronomy and geography.

d: Ibn Sina (980–1037), born near Bukhara, memorised the Quran by 10 and was treating patients by 18. He served Samanid and Buyid rulers as physician and vizier. His Canon of Medicine, a five-volume encyclopaedia, described contagion, clinical trials of drugs and hundreds of medicines, and was a standard textbook in Europe until the 17th century. His Book of Healing covered philosophy, logic and science, integrating Aristotle with Islamic thought.

He calculated the Earth's radius with impressive accuracy using a mountain and the horizon, and wrote on mineralogy and pharmacology.

He solved Pell's equation with the cyclic chakravala method, described ideas resembling the derivative and Rolle's theorem, and calculated the time Earth takes to orbit the Sun.

d: Ibn Battuta (1304–1369), a Moroccan legal scholar, left Tangier in 1325 for Mecca and kept travelling for 29 years, covering about 120,000 km — Africa, Arabia, Anatolia, Central Asia, India, the Maldives, Southeast Asia and China. In Delhi he served as a judge under Muhammad bin Tughlaq for eight years. His Rihla describes the Mali Empire, the Delhi Sultanate and the Black Death.

d: Kabir (about 1440–1518), a weaver of Varanasi raised in a Muslim family, became a key Bhakti poet-saint. His dohas (couplets), in simple Hindi, mocked caste, idol worship, ritual and religious hypocrisy of both Hindus and Muslims, teaching devotion to a formless God within. His verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Kabir Panth follows him.

He settled at Kartarpur and was the first of the ten Sikh Gurus.

He painted The Last Supper and the Mona Lisa, and filled about 7,000 surviving notebook pages, in mirror writing, with studies of anatomy (dissecting about 30 corpses), flying machines, water, geology and engineering. He embodies the 'Renaissance man'.

The book was published as he lay dying. His heliocentric model began the Scientific Revolution.

d: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), an Italian mathematician, improved the telescope and in 1610 discovered Jupiter's moons, Venus's phases and mountains on the Moon, supporting Copernicus. He studied falling bodies and pendulums, founding modern physics through experiment. The Roman Inquisition tried him in 1633 and forced him to recant; he spent his last years under house arrest. The Church acknowledged its error in 1992.

d: Isaac Newton (1643–1727) of England developed calculus (independently of Leibniz), discovered that white light is a spectrum, and built the reflecting telescope. In Principia Mathematica (1687) he described three laws of motion and universal gravitation, explaining both falling apples and planetary orbits. He later ran the Royal Mint and was President of the Royal Society. He also spent years on alchemy and biblical prophecy.

He later ran the Royal Mint and was President of the Royal Society. He also spent years on alchemy and biblical prophecy.

d: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) sailed on HMS Beagle (1831–36), studying fossils and wildlife, including Galápagos finches and tortoises. After 20 years of research, prompted by Alfred Russel Wallace's similar ideas, he published On the Origin of Species (1859), arguing species evolve by natural selection. The Descent of Man (1871) applied this to humans, sparking debates with religious thinkers.

d: Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772–1833), a Bengali scholar fluent in Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English, campaigned against sati, polygamy and child marriage and for women's property rights and modern education. He founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828), a monotheistic reform movement, and newspapers. His campaign led to the abolition of sati (1829). He died in Bristol, England, while representing the Mughal emperor.

d: Savitribai Phule (1831–1897), married at nine to Jyotirao Phule, who taught her to read, became India's first woman teacher. In 1848 they opened a school for girls in Pune, facing people throwing dung at her on the way. They opened schools for Dalit children, a home for widows and their children, and founded the Satyashodhak Samaj. She died nursing plague patients in 1897.

d: Narendranath Datta (1863–1902), a disciple of the mystic Ramakrishna, became Swami Vivekananda. His speech at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago in 1893, opening 'Sisters and brothers of America', introduced Vedanta and yoga to the West. He founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) for social service and inspired Indian nationalism. National Youth Day is on his birthday.

d: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941), Bengali poet, novelist, composer and painter, became the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature (1913) for Gitanjali. He wrote the national anthems of India (Jana Gana Mana) and Bangladesh (Amar Shonar Bangla), founded Visva-Bharati University at Santiniketan, and returned his knighthood after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. He called Gandhi 'Mahatma'.

d: Marie Skłodowska Curie (1867–1934), born in Warsaw, studied in Paris, where women could attend university. With Pierre Curie she discovered polonium (named after Poland) and radium, and coined 'radioactivity'. She won the Nobel Prize in Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911), the first person to win two. In World War I she developed mobile X-ray units. She died of radiation-induced illness.

d: Albert Einstein (1879–1955), working in a Swiss patent office, published four groundbreaking papers in 1905, including special relativity and E=mc². His general relativity (1915) described gravity as the curvature of spacetime. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. A Jew, he fled Nazi Germany in 1933 to the US, and his 1939 letter to Roosevelt led to the Manhattan Project, which he later regretted. He corresponded with Tagore and admired Gandhi.

He founded the Raman Research Institute in Bangalore. India celebrates National Science Day on 28 February, the day of his discovery.

d: Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920), a largely self-taught mathematician from Kumbakonam, sent a letter of theorems to G. H. Hardy at Cambridge in 1913. Hardy brought him to England, where he produced remarkable results on partitions, infinite series, mock theta functions and the number 1729. He became a Fellow of the Royal Society but fell ill and died in India at 32. His notebooks still inspire research.

d: Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam (1931–2015), from Rameswaram, sold newspapers as a boy and became an aerospace scientist. He led the development of India's first satellite launch vehicle (SLV-3, 1980) and the Agni and Prithvi missiles, earning the title 'Missile Man', and played a key role in the 1998 Pokhran nuclear tests. As President (2002–07) he was called the 'People's President' and inspired students.

d: Enheduanna (about 2285–2250 BCE), daughter of Sargon of Akkad, was appointed high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur, uniting Akkadian and Sumerian religion. She composed hymns, including 'The Exaltation of Inanna' and 42 temple hymns, and is the earliest known author identified by name. She was briefly exiled during a revolt but restored.

d: Imhotep (about 2650–2600 BCE) served Pharaoh Djoser as chancellor, high priest of Ra and architect. He designed the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first monumental stone building, stacking six mastabas. Later Egyptians credited him with medicine and wisdom, and he was deified; the Greeks identified him with Asclepius.

d: Amenhotep IV (r. about 1353–1336 BCE) renamed himself Akhenaten, promoting the sun disc Aten as the supreme or only god. He closed temples of Amun, built a new capital at Amarna, and encouraged naturalistic art showing his family. His wife was Nefertiti. After his death, his son Tutankhamun restored the old gods and Akhenaten was condemned as a heretic.

d: Zoroaster (Zarathustra), a priest-prophet of ancient Iran, probably lived between 1500 and 1000 BCE. He taught that Ahura Mazda, the wise lord, is the supreme god, opposed by the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu, and that humans must choose good thoughts, words and deeds. His hymns, the Gathas, are in the Avesta. His ideas of heaven, hell, judgement and a saviour may have influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Parsis in India follow his faith.

d: Bimbisara (r. about 558–491 BCE) of the Haryanka dynasty made Magadha the strongest state in north India. He annexed Anga, married princesses of Kosala, Vaishali and Madra, and built Rajagriha as capital. He was a patron of the Buddha and is also honoured by Jains. His son Ajatashatru imprisoned him and he died in captivity.

d: Pericles (about 495–429 BCE), an aristocrat and orator, led Athens during its golden age. He led Athens into the Peloponnesian War and died in the Plague of Athens.

d: Hippocrates of Kos (about 460–370 BCE) is called the father of Western medicine. He and his school argued diseases have natural causes rather than divine punishment, and stressed careful observation, diet and the 'four humours'. The Hippocratic Corpus contains about 60 works, and the Hippocratic Oath, with principles like 'do no harm', still inspires medical ethics.

d: Sun Tzu, traditionally a general of the state of Wu in the 6th century BCE, is credited with The Art of War, a 13-chapter treatise. It teaches that the best victory is won without fighting, through deception, intelligence and knowing yourself and the enemy. It influenced Mao, Japanese strategists and modern business.

d: Hannibal Barca (247–183 BCE) of Carthage marched an army with elephants across the Pyrenees and Alps in 218 BCE. He destroyed Roman armies at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae (216 BCE), where about 50,000 Romans died. He was recalled to defend Carthage and lost to Scipio at Zama (202 BCE). He later took poison to avoid capture.

d: Euclid of Alexandria (about 300 BCE), working in the Ptolemaic capital's Museum, wrote the Elements, 13 books building geometry and number theory from definitions and five postulates. It proved that there are infinitely many primes and constructed the five Platonic solids. It was the main geometry textbook for over 2,000 years, translated into Arabic and Latin.

d: Muhammad (about 570–632), born in Mecca, an orphan raised by his uncle, became a trader. From about 610 he received revelations that became the Quran. d: Wu Zetian (624–705) was a concubine of Emperor Taizong who became Emperor Gaozong's empress, ruling behind him and then for her sons. d: Xuanzang (602–664), a Chinese Buddhist monk, left Chang'an in 629 without permission to seek authentic texts. He crossed the Gobi and Central Asia, studied for years at Nalanda, debated at the court of Harsha, and returned in 645 with 657 texts, which he spent his life translating. His Great Tang Records on the Western Regions guided archaeologists to Indian sites, and he inspired the novel Journey to the West.

d: Ramanuja (traditionally 1017–1137) was a Tamil Vaishnava philosopher who taught Vishishtadvaita ('qualified non-dualism'): the soul and world are real, distinct parts of Brahman (Vishnu), and liberation comes through devotion (bhakti) and surrender. He reorganised worship at Srirangam and, according to tradition, shared the sacred mantra publicly from a temple tower so all castes could be saved. He is said to have fled Chola persecution to the Hoysala court, where he converted King Vishnuvardhana.

d: Basava (Basavanna, 1105–1167), a minister of the Kalachuri king Bijjala at Kalyana in Karnataka, founded the Lingayat (Veerashaiva) movement. He rejected caste, temple ritual and gender discrimination, teaching devotion to Shiva symbolised by a personal linga, and that 'work is worship' (kayaka). His Anubhava Mantapa gathered saints of all castes, including women like Akka Mahadevi, who composed vachanas, free-verse poems in Kannada. A marriage between a Brahmin girl and a Dalit boy sparked violence that ended the community at Kalyana.

d: Rudramadevi (ruled about 1262–1289) was one of the few women to rule an Indian kingdom in her own right. Her father, the Kakatiya king Ganapati, named her heir and she was raised as a prince. She defeated rebellious nobles and invasions by the Yadavas of Devagiri and the Eastern Gangas, completed Warangal fort, and built tanks for irrigation. Marco Polo praised her rule. Her grandson Prataparudra succeeded her.

d: Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), a poet, musician and Sufi disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi, served seven Delhi sultans. He wrote in Persian and Hindavi, composing ghazals, riddles and histories of Alauddin Khalji's campaigns. He is credited with developing qawwali and the tarana, and legends credit him with inventing the sitar and tabla, though historians doubt this. He called himself the 'Parrot of India'.

d: Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406), born in Tunis, was a scholar, judge and diplomat in North Africa, Spain and Egypt. His Muqaddimah (1377) analysed why dynasties rise and fall: tribal groups with strong solidarity (asabiyyah) conquer settled societies, then grow soft and lose power within about four generations. He is seen as a founder of sociology and economics. In 1401 he met Timur outside Damascus.

d: Zheng He (1371–1433), born to a Muslim family in Yunnan, was captured as a boy by Ming armies, castrated and became a eunuch servant of Prince Zhu Di (later the Yongle Emperor). He commanded seven 'treasure fleet' voyages (1405–1433) with up to 300 ships and 27,000 men, visiting Java, Sri Lanka, Calicut, Hormuz, Mecca and East Africa, and bringing back envoys and a giraffe. After his death, the Ming abandoned the voyages.

d: Joan of Arc (about 1412–1431), a peasant girl from Domrémy, said saints' voices told her to help Charles VII drive the English out of France during the Hundred Years' War. At 17 she led troops to lift the siege of Orléans (1429) and saw Charles crowned at Reims. Captured by Burgundians and handed to the English, she was tried for heresy and burned at Rouen at 19. She was declared innocent in 1456 and made a saint in 1920.

d: Maharana Pratap Singh (1540–1597) of Mewar refused to accept Mughal overlordship, unlike many Rajput rulers. At Haldighati in 1576 he fought Akbar's army led by Man Singh; his horse Chetak carried him to safety before dying. Living in the Aravalli hills with Bhil allies and supported by the merchant Bhamashah's wealth, he waged guerrilla war and regained much of Mewar except Chittor. He remains a symbol of Rajput pride.

d: Chand Bibi (1550–1599), a princess of Ahmadnagar married into Bijapur's royal family, served as regent of Bijapur and later of Ahmadnagar. In 1595 she defended Ahmadnagar fort against Akbar's son Murad, rallying troops and repairing a breached wall overnight, forcing a treaty. She was killed in 1599, reportedly by her own soldiers, before the Mughals took the fort.

d: Abbakka Chowta, the 16th-century Tuluva queen of Ullal near Mangalore, resisted Portuguese attempts to control the coast's trade and demand tribute. A Jain who ruled a mixed Hindu–Muslim–Jain population, she allied with the Zamorin of Calicut and Bijapur. She fought the Portuguese for decades, reportedly using fire arrows at night, before being captured. She is celebrated as one of India's first freedom fighters.

d: Lachit Borphukan (1622–1672) was commander of the Ahom army. In 1671, though seriously ill, he led the Ahoms to defeat a much larger Mughal fleet under Raja Ram Singh at the Battle of Saraighat on the Brahmaputra near Guwahati, using river warfare and fortifications. Legends say he beheaded his own uncle for failing to complete a defensive wall overnight. Lachit Divas is celebrated on 24 November.

d: Ahilyabai Holkar (1725–1795) was widowed at 29 and lost her father-in-law Malhar Rao and son, then took over as ruler of the Holkar state of Malwa from Maheshwar. She ruled for 28 years with justice and prosperity, defended her lands and built or restored hundreds of temples, ghats and rest houses across India, including the Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi (1780) and Somnath. d: The Bishnoi community of Rajasthan follows 29 principles taught by Guru Jambheshwar in 1485, including protecting trees and animals. In 1730 Amrita Devi and 362 Bishnois died hugging khejri trees to stop the Jodhpur king's men cutting them, inspiring the Chipko movement.

d: The Siddis, about 50,000 people of African descent in Karnataka, Gujarat and Maharashtra, descend from Bantu people brought as soldiers, sailors and slaves. Malik Ambar, a Siddi general, ruled Ahmadnagar; the Siddis of Janjira ruled a sea fort.

d: The Rabaris (Rebari) are semi-nomadic pastoralists of Kutch, Saurashtra and western Rajasthan who herd camels, sheep and goats along seasonal migration routes. Their origin legends link them to Shiva and Parvati, who created the first Rabari to tend camels. Women wear black woollen garments and are famed for mirror-work and chain-stitch embroidery, each sub-group with its own motifs. Shrinking grazing land and development have pushed many to settle.

d: The San of the Kalahari are among the oldest continuous cultures, with genetic lineages diverging over 100,000 years ago. Their click languages, persistence hunting and rock art are famous. Many have lost land.

d: The Maasai, about 1.5 million people of southern Kenya and northern Tanzania, speak Maa, a Nilotic language, and traditionally live by herding cattle, which provide milk, blood and meat and measure wealth. Men pass through age-sets from warriors (moran) to elders, and the adumu jumping dance is part of ceremonies. Colonial treaties (1904, 1911) took much of their best land, and today they face pressure from national parks and farming.

d: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for at least 50,000–65,000 years, forming the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. Over 250 languages were spoken before 1788. The Dreaming connects law, land, ancestors and stories, and songlines mapped routes across the continent; 'fire-stick farming' shaped landscapes. British colonisation from 1788 brought frontier massacres, disease, dispossession and, until the 1970s, the forced removal of children (the Stolen Generations). The 1992 Mabo decision recognised native title.

d: The Inuit of Greenland, Canada and Alaska descend from the Thule people, who spread east from Alaska about 1,000 years ago, replacing the earlier Dorset culture. They hunted seals, walrus, caribou and bowhead whales from kayaks and umiaks, built snow houses (igloos) and sod houses, and travelled by dog sled. Their clothing of caribou skin and their tools were masterpieces of Arctic adaptation. Today Nunavut (1999) and Greenland have Inuit self-government.

d: The Sámi are the Indigenous people of Sápmi, spanning northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia's Kola Peninsula. Traditionally they fished, hunted and, from the 16th century, herded reindeer on seasonal migrations. Joik is their distinctive form of singing. Assimilation policies suppressed their languages and religion, but Sámi parliaments now exist in Norway, Sweden and Finland.

d: The Ainu are the Indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, descended in part from Jōmon people. They hunted, fished for salmon and held the Iomante bear ceremony, believing kamuy (spirits) dwell in nature. From the Meiji era, Japan banned their language and customs and took their land. In 2019 Japan legally recognised them as an Indigenous people, and the Upopoy museum opened in 2020.

d: The Yanomami, about 38,000 people, live in the Amazon rainforest on the Brazil–Venezuela border in large circular communal houses (shabono). They farm plantains and manioc in forest gardens and hunt and fish. Illegal gold miners have repeatedly invaded their land, bringing violence, mercury pollution and diseases; the 1993 Haximu massacre and a 2023 health emergency drew global attention. Davi Kopenawa is a leading spokesman.

d: The Lakota, part of the Sioux (Očhéthi Šakówiŋ) nation, became mounted buffalo hunters on the Great Plains after horses arrived in the 18th century. When gold was found in the sacred Black Hills, the US broke the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty; Lakota and Cheyenne under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated Custer at the Little Bighorn (1876). The near-extermination of the buffalo and the 1890 Wounded Knee massacre ended their independence. In 1980 the US Supreme Court ruled the Black Hills had been taken illegally.

d: Polynesian voyagers settled Aotearoa (New Zealand) around 1250–1300 CE in waka canoes, forming iwi (tribes) with chiefs, marae meeting grounds and carved wharenui houses. They adapted Polynesian crops to the colder climate and hunted moa to extinction. The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) with Britain was followed by land wars and confiscation. Today te reo Māori is an official language, and the Waitangi Tribunal addresses treaty breaches.

d: The Bedouin are Arabic-speaking nomadic pastoralists of the deserts of Arabia, the Levant, Sinai and North Africa, herding camels, goats and sheep. Organised in tribes and clans, they value hospitality, honour and poetry; Arab culture idealised Bedouin virtues. Camels, domesticated around 3,000 years ago, made long-distance desert trade and raiding possible. Modern states have encouraged them to settle.

d: The Mongols are herders of the Central Asian steppe who live in portable felt gers and move seasonally with horses, sheep, goats, yaks and camels. In 1206 Temüjin united the tribes as Genghis Khan, and his successors built the largest contiguous land empire. Mongols adopted Tibetan Buddhism in the 16th century. Today about 10 million Mongols live in Mongolia, China's Inner Mongolia and Russia.

d: The Scythians were Iranian-speaking nomadic horse archers who dominated the Pontic steppe from about the 9th to the 3rd century BCE. Herodotus described their kurgan burials with sacrificed horses and their use of cannabis in steam tents. They produced superb gold animal-style art, found in tombs such as Arzhan and Tolstaya Mogila. Related Saka groups invaded India as the Indo-Scythians.

d: The Etruscans flourished in Etruria (Tuscany) from about 900 to 100 BCE, in a league of city-states such as Tarquinia, Veii and Caere. They spoke a non-Indo-European language, built painted tombs, practised divination from livers, and traded with Greeks and Phoenicians. Three of Rome's kings were Etruscan, and Romans adopted their gladiatorial games, arch and togas before absorbing them.

d: Neanderthals were Ice Age humans who lived in Europe and western and Central Asia from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. They hunted large animals, cared for the injured, buried their dead, used fire and made jewellery. Their DNA lives on in most people outside Africa. See also the Human Species entry.

d: Denisovans were an Asian human group known mostly from DNA in Siberia's Denisova Cave, a Tibetan jaw and, since 2025, the Harbin 'Dragon Man' skull. They interbred with modern humans, passing genes to Melanesians, Aboriginal Australians and Tibetans. See also the Human Species entry.

d: Homo floresiensis, the 'Hobbit', was about 1.1 m tall, lived on Flores in Indonesia until about 50,000 years ago, and made stone tools and hunted dwarf elephants. Its small body may result from island dwarfism. See also the Human Species entry.

d: Diwali, the festival of lights, falls on the new moon of Kartika (October–November) and lasts five days, from Dhanteras to Bhai Dooj. Hindus celebrate Rama's return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana and the worship of Lakshmi, goddess of wealth; in Bengal it is Kali Puja. Jains mark Mahavira's nirvana, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, Guru Hargobind's release from Mughal prison. Homes are cleaned and lit with diyas and rangoli, sweets are exchanged, and firecrackers are lit. The 7th-century Sanskrit play Nagananda already mentions a lamp festival.

d: Holi marks the end of winter on the full moon of Phalguna (March). The night before, bonfires (Holika Dahan) recall the burning of the demoness Holika and the survival of the devotee Prahlada; next day people throw coloured powder (gulal) and water, remembering Krishna's play with Radha and the gopis in Braj. Social hierarchies are briefly set aside. Mathura, Vrindavan and Barsana's Lathmar Holi are famous. It is mentioned in early texts like Ratnavali (7th century).

d: Durga Puja, Bengal's greatest festival in Ashvin (September–October), celebrates the goddess Durga's victory over the buffalo demon Mahishasura. Clay idols are made by artisans of Kumartuli in Kolkata and installed in elaborate pandals; Durga is welcomed as a daughter returning home with her children. Large public 'baroari' pujas began in the 18th century, sponsored by zamindars like Raja Nabakrishna Deb. On Vijaya Dashami, idols are immersed in rivers. UNESCO listed Kolkata's Durga Puja as intangible heritage in 2021.

d: Navratri ('nine nights') in Ashvin honours the goddess in her nine forms, with fasting and devotion. In Gujarat, people dance garba and dandiya; in the south, golu doll displays are set up. The tenth day, Dussehra or Vijayadashami, celebrates Rama's victory over Ravana, with Ramlila plays and burning of Ravana effigies in north India; Mysore Dasara features a royal elephant procession begun by Vijayanagara and continued by the Wodeyars.

d: Ganesh Chaturthi in Bhadrapada (August–September) celebrates the birth of the elephant-headed god Ganesha, remover of obstacles. Household worship was long practised; in 1893 Bal Gangadhar Tilak turned it into a public festival in Pune to unite people against colonial rule. Clay idols are worshipped for up to ten days and then immersed in water amid processions. Mumbai's Lalbaugcha Raja draws millions.

d: Pongal, the Tamil harvest festival in mid-January (month of Thai), lasts four days. Bhogi burns old things; on Thai Pongal, new rice is boiled with milk and jaggery until it overflows ('pongal' means boiling over), symbolising abundance; Mattu Pongal honours cattle; and Kaanum Pongal is for family visits. Jallikattu bull-taming is held in some districts. Sangam-era poems mention a Thai festival.

d: Makar Sankranti, around 14 January, marks the Sun's entry into Capricorn and lengthening days. It is one of few Hindu festivals following the solar calendar. People bathe in rivers (Ganga Sagar Mela), eat sesame and jaggery sweets, and fly kites in Gujarat (Uttarayan). It is called Lohri in Punjab, Magh Bihu in Assam and Pongal in Tamil Nadu.

d: Onam, Kerala's harvest festival in Chingam (August–September), welcomes the legendary king Mahabali, under whose rule all were equal, who returns from the underworld once a year. Celebrations include pookalam flower carpets, the sadya feast of over 20 dishes on banana leaves, snake-boat races (vallam kali) and the Pulikali tiger dance. An inscription from 861 CE mentions it.

d: Rongali (Bohag) Bihu marks the Assamese New Year and spring in mid-April. Young people perform the energetic Bihu dance with dhol, pepa (buffalo horn) and gogona. Cattle are bathed on Goru Bihu, and people exchange gamosa cloths. Its roots lie in agricultural fertility festivals of the Brahmaputra valley.

d: Baisakhi (Vaisakhi), on 13–14 April, celebrates the wheat harvest in Punjab. For Sikhs it marks the founding of the Khalsa by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699 at Anandpur Sahib, when he initiated the Panj Pyare. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre happened on Baisakhi in 1919. People dance bhangra and gidda, and gurdwaras hold processions.

d: Eid al-Fitr ('festival of breaking the fast') ends the month of Ramadan when the new moon is sighted. Muslims attend special prayers, give zakat al-fitr charity so the poor can celebrate, wear new clothes and share sweets like sheer khurma and seviyan. It dates from Muhammad's time in Medina (624).

d: Eid al-Adha, during the Hajj in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, commemorates Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son, replaced by a ram. Muslims sacrifice a goat, sheep or other animal, dividing the meat among family, friends and the poor. It is called Bakrid in India.

d: Christmas on 25 December celebrates Jesus's birth; the date was set in Rome by the 4th century, possibly to coincide with winter festivals like Saturnalia. Customs like Christmas trees (from Germany), carols and Santa Claus (from St Nicholas) spread in the 19th century. In India, Goa, Kerala and the northeast celebrate with midnight mass and plum cake.

d: Celebrated on the full moon of Kartika, it marks the birth of Guru Nanak (1469) at Talwandi (Nankana Sahib, Pakistan). Sikhs hold an Akhand Path (48-hour continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib), dawn processions (prabhat pheri), and langar for all.

d: On the full moon of Vaishakha (April–May), Buddhists commemorate the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death (parinirvana). Pilgrims gather at Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Lumbini; homes are lit, and people offer flowers and practise generosity. Sri Lanka calls it Vesak, recognised by the UN since 1999.
